16475-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
This December 16, 1897 number of The Great Round World, a children's current-events paper, tells young readers they are living through history. Cuba, Turkey, Haiti, and Hawaii are making stirring chapters, and Austria has joined the procession with an episode that will fill an exciting page of its history. The voice of the people, the paper says, must now be heard.

The issue explains the news in plain, lively language for school readers, with pictures to match. It shows how American children learned world affairs in the 1890s: as an unfolding story they were part of. Collectors of children's periodicals will find it a bright survivor.
22719-old-fort-snelling-1819-1858:
Marcus L. Hansen wrote Old Fort Snelling, 1819–1858, a history of the famous frontier post at the meeting of the Mississippi and Minnesota rivers. The catalog record gives no year. Fort Snelling guarded the upper Mississippi, hosted fur traders and soldiers, and stood at the center of early Minnesota history.

The preface tells the book's own story: the work began as research at the State University of Iowa and was accepted as a graduate thesis in June 1917. At the urging of Dr. Shambaugh of the State Historical Society of Iowa, Hansen enlarged its scope, consulted many new sources, and rewrote the whole manuscript. The result is a documented history of the fort's first four decades. Hansen later became a leading historian of immigration, and his care with sources shows here.
27366-a-journey-in-russia-in-1858:
Robert Heywood of Bolton, England, wrote this privately printed account of his 1858 journey to Russia, first read as a lecture at the Bolton Mechanics' Institute. Members of the institute asked him to publish it so their families and fellow workmen could share what he had learned, since Bolton traded heavily with St. Petersburg and Moscow.

Heywood describes the two Russian capitals as a visiting English manufacturer saw them in 1858, with an eye to commerce as well as to sights and customs. The short volume gives a plain, firsthand picture of Russia just before the great reforms of the next decade. It suits readers who like travel writing grounded in trade and daily life.
aelian-works-hercher-1858:
Claudius Aelianus, a Roman-era Greek with a storyteller's ear, left two great stores of lore. Aelian's works, in Rudolf Hercher's 1858 edition, gather all that survives of him in one set. Seventeen books On the Nature of Animals stand first in the file.

Beside them sit the Historical Miscellany, a heap of short tales and facts, plus his letters and fragments. Bees, elephants, kings, and fools pass through his pages in bright, brief scenes. Naturalists mined him for animal lore; tale tellers mined him for plots. Hercher's edition is the full Aelian in one scholarly home.
allibone-critical-dictionary-english-lit:
Samuel Allibone, a Philadelphia bookseller and bibliographer, published Volume One of his Critical Dictionary of English Literature in 1858. It covers authors from A to J. The full work notices some 30,000 British and American writers.

Each entry gives the author's life, a list of works, and judgments gathered from reviews and histories. Forty subject indexes help readers find writers by theme, from poetry to voyages. Allibone labored for years among his own vast book collection. The dictionary became the great Victorian bio-bibliography, the first place to learn what an author wrote and what critics said of it.
arxiv-2412-01558:
Dhiman Paul, Md Rizwan Parvez, Nabeel Mohammed, and Shafin Rahman built a model that finds video highlights and moments. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, tackles two linked tasks at once. One task flags the best parts of a video. The other finds the span that matches a text query. Past joint models were weak at cross task links and at matching video with text.

Their model, VideoLights, adds parts to refine features and align the two tasks. A fusion network joins video and text both ways. A feedback path lets each task help the other. They also used a large vision-language model to enrich the features. Tests on three known sets put the model ahead of prior work.
arxiv-2412-01758:
Hvozd, Patsahan, Patsahan, Kalyuzhnyi, and Holovko study how ionic liquids behave when trapped in porous matter in two thousand twenty-four. Ionic liquids are salts that flow at room temperature, and their gas-liquid balance shifts inside pores. The team treats the question with theory rather than lab work.

Two models differ in the shape of the charged molecule: a bendy chain in one, a stiff rod in the other. Each model mixes paired and free ions inside a disordered bed of hard spheres. Rod-shaped ions gave lower turning points for both heat and density, and a narrower band where liquid and vapor coexist. The work is the first theory pass at rod-shaped molecular ions in such pores.
arxiv-2412-01958:
Said Togru, Youssef Sameh Mostafa, and Karim Lotfy test whether rule-based retraining can make image models harder to fool, in a report from two thousand twenty-four. The method uses fixed rules about how a changed input should change the output, called metamorphic relations. Retraining runs in cycles with methods that learn from both labeled and unlabeled images.

Tests used three standard image sets and a mix of ready-made and fresh models. On average the score for toughness rose by about seventeen points for each model. Four named retraining methods were built into one shared frame so runs could repeat with ease. Readers get a hands-on route to tougher vision models for real use.
arxiv-2412-04358:
Oscar Key and four co-authors evaluated faster ways to find the largest values in a data array in twenty twenty-four. Picking the exact top k values forces a whole array to be funneled through one merge step, which wastes the parallel power of AI chips. Bucketed methods split the array into groups and take the top values of each group, giving an answer that is close but not exact.

The team studied the design choices of this method family with both theory and tests on real tasks. Their test cases come from sparsity methods for language models, which use top-k picks to keep only the most important weights or signals. They also released a fast bucketed top-k tool for PyTorch. The trade is small accuracy loss for large speed gains on parallel hardware.
arxiv-2412-05258:
Schulik and Owen use a helium line trio to read big world outflows in this twenty twenty-four paper. Close big worlds leak gas that cools as it spreads in space. That cool fall can pack the trio state past plain counts.

Inside, flow sims show the trio glut springs from cool gas acts. The glut may solve one world's wide line tale in past reads. Those reads then prove the leak runs as true flow, not still gas. The pair also maps which falls feed or drain the trio state. Far worlds past a set gap lose trio depth to drift splits.
arxiv-2412-05458: Pereira and Vachaspati test in twenty twenty-four whether a special electric field pattern in a gauge theory can hold steady under small disturbances. The theory pairs a force field with a scalar field that sources electric patterns unlike standard ones. They probe the pattern for growing wobbles that would tear it apart. They find a region of settings where the pattern is stable. Where the scalar field has a negative mass term, the pattern splits into two branches, and one branch proves unstable.
arxiv-2412-06258:
Li Yin and co-authors wrote this sports analytics paper, published in two thousand twenty-four, on tracking players in three-on-three basketball. Players collide, cross, and look alike, so trackers swap identities and coaches lose clean movement data.

The team paints each player with a virtual marker, a pose-based tag learned from body shape rather than jersey color. Active learning keeps the hand-labeling bill low while the marker model improves. The markers are stamped onto video, poses are pulled out with steady identities, and boxes are derived for scoring against standard trackers. On their new three-on-three data set, the method scored well above rival trackers, with zero identity switches. Manual fixes during training also dropped. The authors see the approach serving any multi-agent analysis where bodies tangle, from sports to animal groups.
arxiv-2412-07558:
Riccardo Scotti and five co-authors set out a hybrid quantum-classic method to merge many clusterings of a data set into one strong one. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Clustering splits data into groups, but each method has weak spots. Merging the results can patch those spots, and the merged form is of wide use. The team casts the merge task in two known hard forms. One suits atom-based quantum machines, and one suits quantum annealers. They test the method first on a fake of the atom machine, then on a next fake built on tensors. The aim is to let quantum gear take on a core data task.
arxiv-2412-11758:
Gabriel de Jesus and Sérgio Nunes build search tools for the Tetun language in a 2024 arXiv paper. Tetun, spoken in Timor-Leste, lacks the basic resources that web search needs. The team set out to create that foundation and test how well retrieval can work.

They built a stopword list of 160 words, a stemmer with three variants, and a test collection with 59 topics and many documents. Tests compared many strategies on titles and full text. One simple title-based strategy beat the baseline clearly, with faster runs and better scores. The resources are public to support future Tetun search research.
arxiv-2412-19658:
Buzzi, Luo, and Yang study how the count of top-chaos states shifts when a smooth surface map is nudged in this twenty twenty-four paper. Such maps twist a surface in a smooth, two-way way, and some reach high chaos. Each map has states that reach that top chaos level, and their count can jump as the map shifts.

Inside, the team works with maps whose chaos beats a bound set by their smooth grade. They prove the count of top states can only fall, not rise, when such a map is nudged a bit. The count stays fixed near a map just when each top state can be tracked through small nudges. Then the limit points of those states stay in the top class as well. The facts are new even for the smoothest maps.
arxiv-2501-00558:
Xavier Emery, Moreno Bevilacqua, and Emilio Porcu introduce new families of correlation functions in a 2025 statistics study. Correlation functions describe how values at nearby places in space relate, including how smooth a random process is and how far its influence reaches. Most standard families only allow positive correlation.

Their two new families also allow negative dependence, known as a hole effect, while keeping control of smoothness and range. Both generalize famous older models, which appear as special cases. The authors also link the two families to each other. Tests on estimation and prediction show how the added flexibility performs on real tasks.
arxiv-2501-01558:
Dylan Sam, Marc Finzi, and Zico Kolter predict a black-box language model's correctness by asking it follow-up questions. Their paper from twenty twenty-five treats the answers' probabilities as a fingerprint of the model's state. A linear probe trained on those fingerprints calls right and wrong answers with care. The trick needs no access to the model's guts, only its API.

The follow-up probe even beats white-box probes that read internal activations. It also flags models that were secretly bent by a hostile system prompt. Code bugs planted the same way surface too. Swapped models behind an API can be told apart by their follow-up style. The authors pitch the method as a monitor for models that serve inside bigger autonomous systems.
arxiv-2501-01958:
Hyunwook Kim and co-authors survey computer methods that swap recipe ingredients, in work published in 2024. Swaps help cooks meet diet rules, allergies, and bare shelves. A good swap must weigh taste, kitchen role, and health fit at once, which makes the search hard. AI tools now take the task on in many forms.

The survey sorts the field by data sets, methods, and the context each tool weighs, from nutrition to flavor pairing. It also sorts the uses served and grades how safe and clear the tools are. The authors point to hybrid logic-plus-learning designs and knowledge graphs as the next steps.
arxiv-2501-05358:
Magagnin and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a better test for antiferroelectric films. Such films flip their internal charge pattern under voltage, unlike standard ferroelectrics. A classic pulse test mixes switching currents with background currents. Their revised protocol separates the two, allowing clean reads of key values. They apply it to zirconium oxide films of varied thickness. Thicker films hold more leftover polarization, a sign of stabler domains. Their switching thresholds fall as thickness grows.

Repeated cycling shows a wake-up gain that later fades from fatigue. Thicker films degrade faster in those cycles. The authors link the trends to defects, grain size, and wall pinning in the films. They call the protocol a key tool for this material class.
arxiv-2501-05658:
Hidetoshi Nishimori, writing alone, shows that a magnetic phase thought stable can collapse when disorder is correlated. His 2025 paper studies an Ising spin glass, a magnet with random competing links between spins. For the classic versions with uncorrelated disorder, the ferromagnetic phase, where spins align, survives random fields in three or more dimensions.

Nishimori adds spatial correlation to the disorder and proves the opposite: the aligned phase becomes unstable under random fields in any dimension, given a chaos property in the standard model. The same instability can be traced to bond chaos. He also argues the phase can persist under symmetry-breaking fields when the standard model keeps its spin glass phase. The results show how strongly correlation in disorder reshapes magnetic order.
arxiv-2501-06558:
Alessandro Santoni, Enrique Muñoz, Hartmut Abele, and Benjamin Koch wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about testing a variant of relativity with ultracold neutrons. The variant, called Very Special Relativity, allows a preferred direction in space. Ultracold neutrons bouncing in gravity form a sensitive probe, used by a known experiment.

The authors compute how the neutron energy levels shift in an accelerated frame under this theory. At the leading order they find no real change beyond a trivial mass shift, so mass equivalence stays intact. At the next order, time-dependent effects tied to the preferred direction appear. Using the experiment's sensitivity as a yardstick, they set a first rough bound on the neutron parameter and suggest spin-flip setups.
arxiv-2501-06658:
Sanjit Kakarla, Conrad Borchers, and colleagues compare two AI graders for open-ended answers in tutor training in a 2025 education study. Trainee tutors answer equity scenarios in free text, and judging those answers needs sensitivity to context. A large commercial model brings broad knowledge but cannot be fine-tuned freely, while an older encoder model learns the local rubric yet knows less about the world.

Few-shot prompting of the large model is tested head to head against fine-tuned smaller classifiers. The comparison tells training programs which grader to trust for nuanced, values-laden responses where a careless score can teach the wrong lesson.
arxiv-2501-07058:
ZeKe Xiao, Qin Wang, Hammond Pearce, and Shiping Chen wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It tests how well large language models can find flaws in smart contracts, the code that runs deals on blockchains.

Such flaws have cost users dearly, and hand checks are slow. The team ran five top models on contracts in Solidity version nought point eight, newer than the code most past work used. A well-made prompt cut false alarms by over half. But the catch rate for some flaw kinds had fallen hard next to older code. The drop traces to the models keying on shifts in new libraries, the authors find.
arxiv-2501-09558:
Latour and five co-authors measure metal content in stars of globular clusters in a 2025 astronomy paper. Globular clusters hold several generations of stars, and whether even the first generation varies in iron content has become a hot question. The team used spectra of more than eight thousand giant stars in twenty one Milky Way clusters.

Each star was assigned to the first or later population using space telescope photo catalogs. In nearly all clusters, metal content within the first population rose with a color based marker. The spread ranged widely and grew with cluster mass. Later population stars showed equal or tighter spreads than first population stars. The results inform how clusters formed their stars.
arxiv-2501-11558:
Bruno Casella, in a solo paper from twenty twenty-five, graded the speed cost of safe enclaves for federated learning. Such learning trains across many sites with data kept home. It still faces poison and spy attacks on models and data. Hardware enclaves can shield both, but the old kind caps memory and fights the coder. A new kind wraps a whole virtual machine, which eases port of old code.

Casella ran fed learn loads in such VM enclaves and read the tax: time, memory, and throughput next to bare runs. Readers who must keep training private get a count based read on what the shield costs in speed.
arxiv-2501-12258:
Patel, Quarles, and Cuntz test in twenty twenty-five which moon and submoon orbits can survive around known giant planets. Claims of moons beyond our solar system are growing, and a claimed moon may even host its own submoon. The team ran body-by-body simulations for a star-planet-moon system based on one claimed case, then added a fourth body as a submoon.

Most of the tested space for the moon case proved stable. The submoon case split into stable and unstable zones with clear resonance patterns, which they traced to slow secular effects. Two further systems were checked in three-body form, and one in four-body form. The authors offer the work as a template for future cases.
arxiv-2501-13058:
David Lehavi and Brian Osserman solve a camera geometry problem in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The perspective n-points problem asks where a camera is, given points in space and their images. Their fast, accurate solution tackles the four-point case with a new split of the problem.

First, they place new points along the camera rays so that distances between them match the original points as closely as possible. That step turns the problem into an absolute orientation task, which has an explicit formula solution. Their coordinates use squared distances and dot products to stay orientation-free. Tests showed an order of magnitude speed gain over top methods, at similar accuracy under noise. The split also speeds seed rejection in RANSAC.
arxiv-2501-14558:
A. D. Helgeland and colleagues measure the speed and size of plasma blobs drifting across the edge of a tokamak. They compare ordinary and high-performance operating modes. The blobs are filamentary bursts in the scrape-off layer, the thin region outside the confined plasma. They carry heat toward the walls. Using gas puff imaging on the Alcator C-Mod device and an improved timing method, the team tracks outward radial motion in three plasmas. One is ohmic; two run in high-confinement regimes. A stochastic model interprets the fluctuations as overlapping uncorrelated blobs.

In every regime, large-amplitude filaments dominated. They moved outward at several hundred meters per second, up to about a thousand. Blob speeds and sizes barely changed between ohmic and high-confinement operation. Burst shapes and spectra were nearly identical too. The stubbornness of edge turbulence across regimes is the practical message for reactor wall design.
arxiv-2501-15258:
Yiling Pan, Zhixin Xu, Bin Wang, and Bailin Deng present a geometry processing method in this two thousand twenty-five paper. A ruled surface is swept out by a moving straight line. Such surfaces are prized in architecture and engineering for how plain they are to build. Past work has matched odd shapes with developable surfaces, but general ruled surfaces have had less study, and past methods set bounds on the shape. This work takes on freeform meshes.

First, a group-sparsity step reshapes the mesh close to a form made of ruled parts, piece by piece, with a tangent field that shows the ruling lines. Next, seams that split smooth sets of rulings are pulled out and used to build the first rulings. A last step shifts ruling spots and angles to hug the shape sought. Tests on shapes of many kinds and topologies showed it matching freeform shapes.
arxiv-2501-16858:
Benedikt Jahnel, Lukas Luchtrath, and Christian Monch study when an infection-like process can die out on a one-dimensional random network, in work from 2025. The network starts from the integer line and adds long-range links at random. Contact processes on such networks can either survive for good or fade away, with a sharp threshold between the two.

The authors give conditions that guarantee a fading zone exists, so the threshold is real and not trivial. Their results cover scale-free geometric random graphs with any well-behaved degree pattern, a wider class than past methods could handle. For one classic graph type, their condition is exact. For long-range percolation on the integers, they confirm a standing conjecture about when the threshold is nontrivial. The work widens the map of survival thresholds on random networks.
arxiv-2501-17458:
Cristiano Cantore and Edoardo Leonardi ask how the mix of central bank and state policy shapes how households save, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Their model has three kinds of households that hold assets with mixed ease of sale. The key gap is the extra return people need to hold a hard-to-sell asset instead of state debt.

The authors find two forces that push that gap in rival ways. One force comes from state supply of debt, and the other comes from households saving to guard themselves. Which force wins turns on the policy mix and on the kind of shock that hits the economy. Readers get a fresh way to think about how joint policy steadies growth.
arxiv-2501-18558:
David Bolin, Damilya Saduakhas, and Alexandre Simas wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds log-Gaussian Cox processes on metric graphs, a way to model event counts on networks such as roads.

The fields at the core solve fractional stochastic equations right on the graph. A new likelihood shortcut skips the need to approximate the field itself. With exact finite laws for smooth cases, the method stays both fast and sound, with proven rates for the posterior. It ships in an open R package tied to a Bayesian engine. A case on road crashes in Saudi Arabia, over a huge road net, flags the risky stretches by exceedance odds.
arxiv-2501-19058:
Haoying Zhou and five co-authors improve control of a surgical robot arm in a 2025 paper. The arm belongs to a newer research version of the da Vinci surgical system, whose redesigned structure makes gravity impossible to ignore, unlike the older model. Heavy gravity offsets hurt accuracy and slow responses.

The team first builds a full movement model of the new arm. Then they identify its dynamic parameters from data and use the fitted model to cancel gravity's pull in the controller. The work extends earlier model based control research from the older robot to the upgraded hardware. Better gravity handling matters for the growing community using this open surgical platform for research.
arxiv-2502-01058:
Zhang, Guo, and Wang set out a magnetometer, a gauge for magnetic fields, built on a single giant emitter tied in at many points, in work from twenty twenty-five. A giant atom sheds light at a rate that hangs sharply on its frequency. In the model, a bias magnetic field tunes that frequency in step. The emitter crosses its own light paths at the tie points, and that self-interference steepens the slope of its loss curve.

The slope grows in a straight line with the count of tie points, by design. The gauge can feel fields as faint as ten to the minus eight or nine tesla per root hertz. That reach dwarfs gauges built on small emitters much like it. Self-interference is the key edge in the plan. If built, the gauge would widen the uses of giant emitters in fine gauging work.
arxiv-2502-02258:
Qi Chen, Di Wu, and Zhifei Zhang settle a long-open question about when flow over a flat plate turns unstable, in a 2025 paper. Boundary layer flow can sprout Tollmien-Schlichting waves, the first stirrings of turbulence. Theory long posited a neutral curve: for wave numbers between its two branches, unstable waves exist. A landmark 2016 work built those waves rigorously but left the curve itself unconfirmed.

The authors confirm the neutral curve exists. Their route solves the governing Orr-Sommerfeld equation with finer tools, borrowing ideas from triple-deck theory. That lets them construct the waves in a neighborhood hugging the curve itself. The result tightens the mathematical foundations of how smooth flow begins to break down.
arxiv-2502-02358:
Guo, Hu, Soh, and Zhao introduced MotionLab in twenty twenty-five, a unified system for generating and editing human motion. Motion work in computer vision usually splits into separate tools per task, which wastes effort. Earlier unifying attempts used outside signals to guide generation but could not edit motion.

Their Motion-Condition-Motion paradigm frames every task with three parts: a source motion, a condition, and a target motion. MotionLab learns the mapping between source and target using rectified flows, guided by the condition. Parts include a transformer tuned for conditional editing, a rotation encoding that keeps source and target in sync, instruction modulation per task, and a curriculum for learning many tasks together. Tests across benchmarks showed strong generalization and speed.
arxiv-2502-02558:
Sam Young, Yeon-jae Jwa, and Kazuhiro Terao teach a model to read particle tracks in a neutrino detector by hiding and guessing parts of the data, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Liquid argon chambers image particle paths in fine three-dimensional detail, but labeled training data come from simulations that can bias results.

Their autoencoder learns from unlabeled real images, masking chunks of the point cloud and predicting missing energies. Fine-tuned on only a hundred labeled events, it matched a supervised champion trained on over a hundred thousand. Its attention maps even separated individual particle tracks on their own. The team released a million-event dataset to push foundation models for this physics.
arxiv-2502-02758:
Hugo Carrillo, Alberto Mercado, and Roberto Morales solve a double puzzle in wave physics: recovering two unknown fields at once. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. The setting is a Schrödinger equation, the core equation of quantum mechanics, in a form that does not conserve energy.

The system has mixed edge rules, one of them changing over time in what is called Wentzell form. From a single measure of flow at the edge, the authors show both unknown fields can be pinned down with a firm stability bound. Their proof uses a classic method for inverse problems and a weighted estimate built from a distance-like function. The result says one good measurement carries enough information for both unknowns.
arxiv-2502-02958:
Youssef and four co-authors wrote a position paper in twenty twenty-five warning that editing the facts stored inside large language models is a safety risk the field has largely missed. Editing tools can change one stored fact, such as a capital city, while leaving the rest of the model mostly untouched.

The authors note that these tools are cheap, easy to find, and hard to spot after the fact, which makes them inviting for bad actors. They sketch ways edits could plant false claims or weaken a model's guardrails. They also point out that edited models can be uploaded and shared with no checks at all. Low public and institutional awareness makes the danger worse, they argue. The paper calls for research on tamper-resistant models and for stronger safeguards across the places where models are shared.
arxiv-2502-03558:
Rodrigo Becerra Silva and five co-authors study how light excited carriers move in thin ribbons of a special material, in a 2025 paper. The material is a topological insulator, which conducts on its surface but not inside. Understanding fast carrier motion in it matters for spin control with light and for new light based devices.

Using a microscope method with very short light pulses, the team watched carriers spread far faster than normal. At low temperature and low carrier density, they traveled up to ten micrometers in a few hundred trillionths of a second range, at speeds far above those of ordinary carriers. Motion was fastest in the purest samples and slowed as temperature rose. The authors discuss hot carriers and paired states as possible causes.
arxiv-2502-04558:
Lu and four colleagues probe a robot control model for hidden symbol like states in twenty twenty-five. The model turns camera views and words into arm actions, but works as a black box. The team read its inner layers while it did pick and place tasks. Simple probes decoded object traits, spatial relations, and action states from those layers.

Decoding topped ninety percent accuracy for most states and layers. Object states did not sit earlier than action states, against the team's guess. They wired the readouts into a reasoning shell for live state checks. The blend lays ground for robot control that can be watched and trusted more, they argue.
arxiv-2502-05858:
Sergey Komech and Jonathan Mosheiff introduce a new family of error-correcting codes built from alphabet permutations, in work from 2025. Error-correcting codes protect data by adding structure that survives noise. A key measure is list recoverability, which asks how well a code can be decoded when each position offers a small set of candidate symbols.

Their codes start from one fixed word and apply random permutations symbol by symbol, again and again. With a well-mixing choice of permutations, the code is almost surely list-recoverable with list sizes near the best possible. Older linear codes need far larger lists at the same rate. Fully random codes match the performance but need vast randomness and offer no structure. The new codes need only modest randomness, a structured route to near-optimal recovery.
arxiv-2502-09258:
Upadhyay, Saini, and Sethi wrote a methods paper in twenty twenty-five on cleaning up a known bias in supernova cosmology. The galaxies that host these exploding stars drift with their own motion, called peculiar velocity, and that drift skews the distance estimates used to measure how the universe expands.

The usual fixes rebuild the drift from maps of galaxies, which assumes a cosmology in advance, or pad the error bars using rough shortcuts. The authors instead built a Bayesian method that fits the expansion model and the drift correction at the same time. It treats the problem as fitting a curved relation with errors on both axes, dropping the straight-line shortcut. They checked the method on simulated data at the sharpness of current and future surveys, then on a real supernova sample. The approach offers a cross-check on standard corrections.
arxiv-2502-10058:
Qingliang Meng and four co-authors rethink how language models are trained for speech to text work. Stock speech language models train left to right to match code that builds word by word. That bars them from use of right side words while they learn. Their MTLM plan joins train in one way and in both ways through three aims.

The joint train lets the model take in rich word trends from both sides. It stays fit with plain code steps. It also backs more than one code plan. They are light join and re score of pick lists in each way or both. Tests on the LibriSpeech test set show the way beats one way train in a firm way. That holds through code plans. The team sets MTLM out as a bendy lift for the language model stage of speech paths.
arxiv-2502-10558:
Younghoon Kim, Sumanta Basu, and Samprit Banerjee detect emotional stress in therapy patients from phone-sensor streams. They cut the streams into segments where the stress signal actually lives. Their data mix passive sensing, such as movement and phone use, with self-reported stress. The patients are middle-aged and older adults in mood-disorder therapy. Some also live with chronic pain. Global machine learning smears the link, because sensors and stress connect only in short windows. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their algorithm first finds change points in the passive streams. It then keeps segments where sensor behavior and self-reports move together distinctively. Predictors are trained on those co-segments.

Applied to a real clinical study's data, the approach identified stress periods more accurately than standard models. The unit of analysis shifts from single moments to episodes, matching how stress actually unfolds.
arxiv-2502-11358:
Ziyou Jiang and six co-authors proposed AutoCMD in twenty twenty-five, a dynamic attack on language model systems that call external tools. An attacker who compromises a tool can inject commands that trick the model into leaking sensitive information to it. Earlier attacks used fixed commands, which adapt poorly as conversations and tool chains evolve, and so get caught.

AutoCMD mimics the familiar: it learns, from open-source systems and a few target examples, what information upstream tools legitimately handle, then crafts theft commands that blend in. In evaluations it beat baselines on theft success rate by over thirteen points and transferred to new systems. The authors also propose four defenses that effectively blunt the attack, mapping both sides of this vulnerability.
arxiv-2502-12258:
Xuesong Liu and Emmett Ientilucci wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents SmokeNet, a lean model that traces smoke plumes in images for safety and environmental watch.

Finding plume edges fast guides blast checks, fire response, and rule enforcement. Past models are heavy and stiff when smoke changes shape. SmokeNet mixes convolutions at many scales with a light attention plan that looks from many angles. A loss tuned per layer steadies the learning. Four data sets test it, one a fresh quarry blast set the team shares. Scores stay high while the cost stays low. That balance suits field gear with small budgets of power and chips.
arxiv-2502-13658:
Faheem Ullah and colleagues mine the job market to answer a practical question: what skills does a cybersecurity career actually require? Attacks keep rising, demand for defenders follows, and would-be entrants lack a clear map. The team analyzed over twelve thousand job advertisements. Nearly forty-nine thousand developer forum posts added a practitioner's view.

Communication and project management topped the soft skills. Technical skill demand varied far more between roles, from analyst to architect, than soft skill demand did. Java emerged as the most commonly used programming language in the field's postings. The authors aim the findings at two audiences. Career changers get a target list for their preparation. Universities get evidence for which skills their degrees should teach. Role-specific breakdowns keep the advice from going generic.
arxiv-2502-14258:
Yein Park and colleagues located the attention heads that handle time in language models in a 2025 paper. Facts change: a champion or office holder this year differs from last year, and models must answer for the year asked. Circuit analysis revealed specific heads, dubbed temporal heads, that specialize in time-specific recall across several models, though their addresses differ from model to model.

Switching those heads off damaged recall of dated facts while leaving timeless knowledge and general question answering intact. The heads react to written-out year phrases as well as numerals, so they encode time itself, not digit patterns. Editing the heads' values even changed the model's dated answers, opening a surgical route to updating stale facts.
arxiv-2502-14758:
Cagliari and co-authors bound the size of first-era lumps from quasar maps. The mark fNL sizes how far first mass spread strays from smooth. Their maps come from the eBOSS DR16 quasar set in full. Two counts join: a paired count and a triple count of spread. Best weight picks squeeze the most fNL facts from the pair count. Stock weights drive the triple count in their runs.

Fix terms for whole and ray-based count warps join the frame. The ray fix shifts marks the most of the two in tests. Bounds land from minus 6 to 20 at the 68 mark. That span beats the past pair-count span by near 16 percent. A low-quasar-pull case gives minus 23 to 14 in its place. Both spans track the counts the team first sketched.
arxiv-2503-00258:
Guangsheng Bao and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on how to detect text that an artificial intelligence model helped to write. Existing detection studies are scattered, with no shared framework. The team first sets out a hierarchy of risk levels for AI involvement, from a light touch to a fully fabricated text. Each level forms its own detection task.

Their method splits a text into two parts: its content, meaning what it says, and its expression, meaning how it says it. They find that content stays stable when the expression is altered, which makes content a strong signal for detection. On the highest-level tests, their two-part method beat the best earlier detectors by a wide margin on a standard curve score. It also won on a well-known difficult test set. The team released their data and code for free reuse.
arxiv-2503-02358:
Xinyu Wang, Bohan Zhuang, and Qi Wu test vision-language models as game players in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Standard benchmarks, like image question answering, miss many skills these models need. Games instead demand perception, rule following, and multi-step reasoning in a structured setting.

Their framework sorts play into four tasks: perceiving the scene, answering questions, following rules, and playing end to end. Extensive experiments expose current limits. Models stumble on long, structured outputs and on dense visual detail. The authors release code and data in public. They argue game play gives a fuller picture of model cognition than static benchmarks.
arxiv-2503-03558:
Yuna Kato and five co-authors automate the camera alignment behind a clever surgical video system. Several cameras ride on the surgical light so that at least one sees past the surgeons' hands and heads. But every time the light moves, the cameras' geometry changes, and someone must realign the feeds by hand.

Their algorithm detects the frames where the light is moving, recalibrates the cameras geometrically, and picks the least occluded view moment by moment. The output is a stable virtual single-viewpoint video of the operative field. Quantitative comparisons beat conventional approaches, and a user study with medical doctors confirmed the improvement. The goal is occlusion-free surgical video without a technician in the loop.
arxiv-2503-09358:
Jiushen Cai and co-authors present language models that standardise clinical reports of fundus eye images, in work from 2025. Eye doctors' reports vary in format, terms, and style, which blocks data integration and confuses automated systems. The team built a bilingual standard terminology for eye findings and common clinical descriptions.

Their first model was fine-tuned on an augmented dataset that simulates clinic scenarios and learned strong standardising behaviour, but covered a narrow disease range. A second model was then trained on standardised data generated by the first, plus matched English data, covering far more cases. It achieved report-level standardisation for the first time in this setting. In tests, it beat rival language models on the bilingual task. Model checkpoints are public.
arxiv-2503-09858:
Nataliya Balabanova and co-authors model how media coverage shapes whether AI gets governed well, in a 2025 paper. Four actors interact: developers, regulators, users, and the press. Using game theory about how strategies spread, plus runs acted out by language models, the team tested what happens under different rule regimes. Two levers stood out: reporting that rewards good oversight, and user trust that follows commentators' advice.

Sharp reporting, they find, can act as soft oversight, probing developers or watchdogs where formal rules are absent. Both the math and the model runs show trustworthy AI emerging only under the right mix of rewards and costs. Good commentary is not free, and its price matters. The authors conclude that governing AI well means managing commentators' rewards too.
arxiv-2503-09958:
Liu and six colleagues propose Progressive In-Context Alignment for language models in twenty twenty-five. In-context learning teaches a model a task from examples in the prompt. How those examples shape token representations was unclear for alignment tasks. The team finds the learned task function is stored in the separator token.

Once the first response tokens are set, the examples become redundant, they show. Their method first runs a few shot stage and extracts that stored vector. A zero shot stage then uses the vector alone to guide generation. No further examples are needed in that stage. Tests beat standard in-context learning and matched tuning based alignment methods. The training free method also cut time cost in their experiments.
arxiv-2503-12358:
In-Chang Baek and four co-authors presented IPCGRL in twenty twenty-five, a method for generating game levels from written instructions using reinforcement learning. Designers increasingly want generative tools they can steer with plain language. Their system pairs a learning agent with a sentence embedding model that turns instructions into compact task codes.

Fine-tuning the embeddings for the task sharpens how level conditions are packed into those codes. On a two-dimensional level generation task, IPCGRL improved controllability by up to about twenty-one percent over a general-purpose embedding method. It also handled unseen instructions better, gaining about seventeen percent in generalization. The approach widens the kinds of input a procedural generation system can take, promising a more flexible dialogue between designer and generator.
arxiv-2503-12758:
Zhifeng Wang, Renjiao Yi, Xin Wen, Chenyang Zhu, and Kai Xu present a model that creates angiography images without contrast dye. Their 2025 paper tackles a trade-off: dye makes blood vessels visible for diagnosis, but it brings extra radiation and health risks for some patients.

Earlier methods worked slice by slice and broke the continuity of vessels in three dimensions. Their model builds a state space that follows the tree shape of vessels, then joins it with a diffusion generator. A pre-trained vision tool helps keep vessel structure consistent across scan types. Tests on varied angiographic data sets checked the approach. Clean synthetic angiography could spare patients dye exposure while keeping the vessel maps doctors rely on.
arxiv-2503-12858:
Duke Nguyen, Aditya Joshi, and Flora Salim adapt language understanding models to dialects at test time in a 2025 study. Models are usually trained on standard American English, then judged on Indian, Singaporean, or Nigerian English, whose grammar and vocabulary shift noticeably. Labeled dialect data are scarce, so retraining for each variety is impractical.

Test-time adaptation adjusts the model using only the unlabeled inputs it is currently reading. That makes it attractive for dialect settings, where new text arrives with its variety baked in. The authors test how far such adaptation closes the dialect gap on understanding tasks, a fairness question for global English tools.
arxiv-2503-14858:
Kevin Wang and co-authors scale self-taught robot learning by stacking networks a thousand layers deep, in work from 2025. In this setup, no rewards or demos are given. The agent must explore on its own and learn to reach goals it is told. Most past work used shallow nets of two to five layers.

Depth up to over a thousand layers lifted scores on a contrast-based method by two to fifty times. Gains beat other goal-based rivals on fake walking and handling tasks. Depth did more than raise scores: the moves the agents learned changed in kind. The team shares code and a project page for the work.
arxiv-2503-16158:
Shenbin Qian and three co-authors craft tricky Chinese test words to probe whether translation quality checkers really protect emotional tone. User-generated content often carries feelings that a translation should preserve. Emotion-focused evaluation models exist, but their robustness had not been stress-tested.

The method generates emotion-related homophones, words that sound alike but differ in writing and meaning, guided by self-information from information theory. These homophones were observed to trigger emotion-losing translation errors. Human judges rated the generated words, and the new method matched their judgments better than an existing generator. The team then used the words, with manual translations, to perturb texts and expose weaknesses in evaluation models.
arxiv-2503-16358:
Nicholas Fleming-Vázquez measures how fast a chaos theorem kicks in in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The weak invariance principle says wild deterministic motion, watched long enough, mimics random wandering. Knowing the limit is not enough; users need the error at finite times. Fleming-Vázquez proves error rates for maps that stretch unevenly, losing grip in places. The observables can point in several dimensions at once.

Models include the famous Sinai billiard and certain smooth chaotic systems. The rate follows a clean power law in the time span. Even some slow-mixing invertible maps, long left out, are covered. The work grows out of the author's doctoral thesis. Dynamicists and probabilists share the audience.
arxiv-2503-16958:
Kim, Kwon, and Baek wrote in twenty twenty-five about simulation methods for active particles that respect thermodynamics. Active particles power their own motion and form dissipative structures. Finite-size effects in such systems are strong, so efficient simulation matters. The challenge is discretizing space and time without breaking the physics. They propose two kinetic Monte Carlo methods for active lattice gases. Both reproduce the correct continuous dynamics in the limit.

One method follows conventional Kawasaki-style updates. The other adds a state-dependent factor to the jump rates. That factor captures self-propulsion speed more accurately in their tests. Error shrank linearly as the time step shrank. At high activity the improved method gained accuracy by a squared factor. Proofs and extensive simulations support the claims. The tools should help study energy costs of active matter.
arxiv-2503-17358:
Jerred Chen and Ronald Clark turn motion blur, the smear in fast-moving shots, into a clue for how the camera moved. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Robots and headsets often lose track of position when the camera swings fast. Standard pose tools fail on blurred frames.

From one blurred image, their model predicts a full flow field and a depth map. A least-squares step then turns those outputs into the camera's speed and spin. The result acts like a reading from a motion sensor chip. To train the model, they built a large set of shots with fake blur drawn from real indoor scans. Fine-tuning on real footage sharpened it further. On real tests it beat leading rivals at gauging both swing and drift.
arxiv-2503-18458:
Luchao Wang, Qian Ren, and colleagues address stray artifacts in three-dimensional scene reconstruction in a 2025 computer vision study. A popular method builds scenes from many small soft blobs fitted to photos. Loose blobs, called floaters, often hang in empty space and spoil both shape and appearance.

The authors trace floaters to vanishing opacity gradients once blended colors reach a false balance against the background. Their framework splits rendering into two paths, one enforcing depth based geometry and one refining appearance on that stable base. A dual opacity design keeps the two jobs apart. The goal is clean reconstructions without floating debris.
arxiv-2503-18758:
Yunus Can Gültekin and four co-authors settle a question about neural decoders in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Neural networks have been proposed to decode error-correcting codes, with single-label and multi-label designs each claiming near-optimal results on short codes. Whether they can truly match the best possible decoding was open.

The authors prove that certain versions of both designs can always realize optimal decoding, for any code. Their architectures are fixed by the codebook itself, with binary weights and no training needed. Tests on three classic short codes confirm optimal performance with simpler designs than earlier proposals. A catch remains: the approach explodes in size for longer codes. Optimality, they show, is achievable but not yet practical at scale.
arxiv-2503-20358:
Radek Zavorka and co-authors compare ways to cluster radio echoes inside a car cabin at millimeter waves, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Cabin links face safety stakes and car-to-car talks. A known echo model with fading clusters fits the cabin too.

Measured echo profiles from inside a car fed the race. A sparse reweighted method ran against the classic k-means split. The work sets up which tool reads cabin echoes best. Trusty links start with knowing where echoes bunch. Readers in car radio get a methods check for a tight, metal room on wheels.
arxiv-2503-20858:
Silvio Fortuné and four co-authors trace how galaxies switch star birth off and on across cosmic time. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-five, uses the Magneticum Pathfinder simulations. The standard story says galaxies form stars steadily, then quench for good. Recent observations hint the truth is messier. The team follows central galaxies in the highest-resolution run of the suite.

They sort each galaxy's path by its place on the star formation main sequence. A major share of galaxies cycle through long quiet and active phases, each lasting billions of years. Only a small share of field galaxies stay active the whole way. Gas inflow and the wider setting both shape these cycles. The work widens the standard story from one slow fade to many phases.
arxiv-2503-21958:
Kibon Ku and co-authors wrote this paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on making 3D models of plants without moving the camera. In fast plant labs, plants ride conveyors or turntables past fixed sensors, so the usual trick of walking a camera around the subject does not work.

Their method flips the setup: the plant rotates on a pedestal while one camera stays still. Software first estimates poses as if the camera had moved, then trains a neural radiance field, a model that learns the scene from photos. A cropped region of interest keeps stray background out. The result is a dense point cloud of about ten million points with near-perfect scores on their checks. The authors say fixed-camera setups can serve costly, delicate sensors like hyperspectral cameras. Speeding up the pose step is their next goal.
arxiv-2503-22458:
Shengyue Guan and five co-authors survey how researchers judge chat agents over long, multi-turn talks. Their survey appeared in twenty twenty-five. Language model agents now hold conversations, use tools, and recall context, so scoring a single reply no longer tells the whole story.

The authors reviewed nearly two hundred fifty sources in a structured way. They build two linked maps. The first lists what to judge: task success, reply quality, user experience, memory, planning, and tool use. The second lists how to judge: human scoring, automatic metrics, mixed methods, and models judging themselves. Older scores like BLEU and ROUGE sit beside newer methods built for live dialogue. The maps give builders a shared frame for fair tests.
arxiv-2503-22558:
Lorenzo Clemente decides deep traits of polynomial control systems with exact, terminating algorithms. The paper from twenty twenty-five studies systems whose input enters in affine form and whose state flows by polynomial rules. Four traits are in view: being zero, being equivalent, ignoring input, being linear, and being analytic. Chen-Fliess series give each system a unique generating series.

Classic work by Fliess mirrors each trait in the series' combinatorics. Those series match a class called shuffle-finite, a nonlinear kin of rational series. Recent results on such series decide their core traits by algorithm. Clemente extends those results and ports them back to systems. A closure result on support restrictions is proved on the way. The work serves formal checks of control systems in full rigor.
arxiv-2503-23958:
Nima Torbati and five co-authors automate the reading of melanoma tissue images in a 2025 paper. Melanoma is the deadliest skin cancer, and diagnosis rests on spotting tissue regions and classifying cell nuclei in stained slides. Most computer methods handle tissue and nuclei as separate jobs, which can waste information.

Their multi stage framework feeds each stage the other's context, unifying both tasks. On a public challenge dataset it took second place in one track and first in the other, with strong overlap and classification scores. Tests on an outside dataset showed the method travels well to new data. Step by step ablation confirmed each part of the framework earns its place. Code is public.
arxiv-2503-24058:
Bogomila Nikolova, Moritz Göb, Kilian Singer, and Peter Ivanov propose a new quantum device built from a single trapped ion in a tapered trap. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The taper makes the ion's sideways and lengthwise motions talk to each other. That talk bends the sideways motion into a Kerr-type behavior.

The strength of the bend is set by the trap's tone settings. Such bent motion enables a class of gates that round out the full set for continuous quantum computing. A wobbling electric field can also squeeze the sideways motion, thanks to the same bend. The team further maps the tone spread of ion chains in such traps. Stronger bends widen the gaps between tones, which should allow faster gates. The design offers a fresh route to non-Gaussian quantum tools.
arxiv-2504-00558:
Marek Vaško, Adam Herout, and Michal Hradiš build a data set for finding faces in digitized historical newspapers in a two thousand twenty-five computer vision paper. Archivists need faces linked to the text around them, but modern detectors fail badly on old scans.

Off-the-shelf tools reach only about twenty-four percent mean average precision on old documents. The authors annotated by hand twenty-two hundred images from nineteenth- and twentieth-century newspapers, adding eleven thousand bounding boxes with facial landmarks in the style of the Wider Face data set. Retrained detectors from several families improve greatly in their tests. Ablation studies across detector sizes chart the detection and landmark accuracy now within reach on archival material.
arxiv-2504-04058:
Anirban Mukherjee and Hannah Hanwen Chang argue that agentic AI blurs who made what, past the reach of law. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Such systems chase goals on their own, shift plans as they learn, and vary run to run. Deep research tools are their case in point.

They name the trait a fluid, chance-led autonomy. Human and machine shares in a joint work melt into one stream that cannot be split back. Authorship, patent, and liability rules all lean on that split, so they strain. The pair urge that law treat the shares as one, not from morals or money, but because split counts cannot be made in practice.
arxiv-2504-05358:
Chen, Mao, Li, and Shangguan built this legal prediction system in twenty twenty-five. AI tools that predict court judgments often lean on huge archives of past cases. They also underuse the reasoning power of modern language models. The authors borrow the debate stage of a real trial to structure the task.

Several model agents argue the case from opposing sides. A separate checker scores how reliable each round of debate is. Feedback from the checker steers later rounds. The setup needs far fewer past cases than older methods. In comparative tests it beat both general and legal-specific models. The authors present debate plus feedback as a light, dynamic route for legal AI.
arxiv-2504-06958:
Xinhao Li and co-authors presented VideoChat-R1 in 2025, a model that watches video and chats about it. Video is hard for such models: events stretch over time, and tracking things across frames strains them. Reward-based tuning had lifted text reasoning, so the team asked if time-aware rewards could lift video sense as well. They tuned the model on several space-and-time tasks at once.

The tuned model set new best marks on time-based tests. Its score for finding when an event happens jumped by about thirty-two points, and object tracking rose by a like amount. Plain question tests also improved, and chat skill stayed intact. At run time, the model now hunts for time clues before it answers. The authors offer the method as a data-light way to build video agents that hold up in the real world.
arxiv-2504-07958:
Hanxue Zhang and eight co-authors present DetAny3D, a foundation model that spots any object in 3D from a single camera view, even objects and cameras it never saw in training. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Labeled 3D data are scarce, which starves direct training. Two-dimensional models, by contrast, are rich with visual knowledge.

DetAny3D borrows that 2D wealth through two modules. One aligns features from several 2D foundation models into a shared form. The other maps those features into 3D while keeping early training steady. Users prompt the model for the objects they want found. Tests show top results on unseen classes and new camera setups. It even beats most rivals on familiar data. Uses range from rare-object spotting in driving to open-world robotics.
arxiv-2504-08658:
Giovanni Brigati, Jean Dolbeault, and Nikita Simonov reviewed stability results in twenty twenty-five for logarithmic Sobolev inequalities. These are key estimates in analysis and probability. They say entropy is held in check by energy. Stability asks a sharp next point. If a function is near equality, must it be near an optimizer? Does that hold in strong norms, or does it fail?

The review sets versions side by side on Euclidean space. It uses Lebesgue and Gaussian measures for that space. It weighs how moment assumptions shift the picture. The authors give new, direct proofs. They give counterexamples too. They take up stability of a logarithmic uncertainty principle as well. The piece maps where quantitative stability is proven. It maps where it breaks. It notes which forms should get the field's focus next.
arxiv-2504-10058:
Mendonça, Di Marzo, and Abdennadher reviewed in twenty twenty-five data co-ops as a fair way to hold and rule shared data. In a co-op, folks own and rule their data as a group by vote. That sets it apart from trusts, shared pools, and unions that hold data in other ways.

Uses span health, farms, and build work, they note. Blocks are hard group work, growth to scale, and low drive from parts. New rule forms, sound tech, and ways to line up group aims are needed. They back co-ops as a last-ing, fair frame for the data age.
arxiv-2504-10458:
The authors present GUI-R1, a vision-language model trained to operate software interfaces as an agent. Most interface agents learn by supervised fine-tuning, which demands huge training sets and still generalizes poorly to unseen screens. Inspired by reinforcement fine-tuning in reasoning models, the team trains with rewards instead. Their framework rests on a unified action space that describes interface actions by shared rules across platforms.

Training uses a small, carefully curated set of about three thousand examples spanning Windows, Linux, MacOS, Android, and the web. A policy optimization method updates the model from its own trial results. Across eight benchmarks on mobile, desktop, and web, the model beats prior leading systems while using only a tiny fraction of their data. The authors argue reinforcement learning with a unified action model holds large promise for real interface tasks.
arxiv-2504-11058:
Aamar Abbas, Touqeer Ahmad, and Ishfaq Ahmad model daily rainfall with a single distribution that handles dry days and deluges together, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Rain data are awkward: many days record exactly zero, while the wet tail stretches to dangerous extremes that hydrology cares about most.

Standard practice picks a threshold and models only what exceeds it, leaving the bulk and the tail in separate worlds. The proposed zero-inflated extended generalized Pareto model folds dry days, light rain, moderate rain, and extremes into one framework. Its tail index mirrors the classic extreme value distribution, so tail behavior comes built in rather than bolted on. Covariates can enter through generalized additive structure, though the current version treats days independently. Estimation runs by both maximum likelihood and Bayesian methods. Simulations and real data applications test the fit.
arxiv-2504-11358:
Liu and four co-authors built this detector in twenty twenty-five for prompt injection attacks on AI apps. Attackers hide instructions inside inputs to hijack a language model's output. Detectors must flag poisoned inputs, but attackers adapt to evade them. The authors frame the contest as a game between attacker and defender.

Their method, DataSentinel, fine-tunes a model to catch injections crafted to slip past it. Training alternates between strengthening the attack and strengthening the detector, a minimax loop. A gradient method solves that loop in practice. Tests across datasets and models showed strong catches of both known and adaptive attacks. The authors offer the game view as a sturdier base for defense.
arxiv-2504-11758:
The Anh Bui wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five on function spaces tied to Bessel operators. Bessel operators are math tools that show up in problems with round or radial shapes. Bui builds the theory of Hardy spaces and related BMO-type spaces for a version of the operator that works in many dimensions at once.

The paper then turns to higher order Riesz transforms, a family of operators linked to the Bessel operator. Bui shows that the transforms belong to a well understood class called Calderon-Zygmund operators. He also proves that they stay bounded, meaning controlled in size, on the new Hardy and BMO-type spaces he defines.
arxiv-2504-11858:
Joël Mathys, Andreas Plesner, Jorel Elmiger, and Roger Wattenhofer synthesize blood vessel data in two thousand twenty five. Brain vessel networks matter for stroke research and flow studies. Pulling their topology from microscopy images is hard. Labeled training data are scarce and accuracy demands are high.

Their pipeline builds synthetic sets that mimic real vessel networks. Stages run from abstract graphs to masks to full images. Two 3D U-Net stages then detect nodes and predict edges. Fine tuning on five hand labeled samples lifts edge scores a lot. Automated extraction looks close to practical use now.
arxiv-2504-12458:
Jansen Pereira, Giovani Valdrighi, and Marcos Medeiros Raimundo teach gradient boosting to mind subgroup fairness while it learns. Predictive models can quietly disadvantage marginalized groups defined by traits like gender and race. The team folds fairness directly into the boosting objective. Standard losses for classification and regression share the stage with a min-max fairness term that guards the worst-off subgroup.

Each boosting round solves a primal-dual pair for that combined objective. The theory shows the algorithm converges under mild conditions. The generic frame adapts to several fairness concepts, binary and subgroup alike. Experiments back the claim of a powerful, flexible approach. Rather than auditing a finished model for bias, the method bakes the fairness pressure into every tree it grows. Justice, here, is an optimization term, not a postscript.
arxiv-2504-15658:
Lachlan Dunn wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025. It tightens the known upper bound on Brun's constant, a famous number built from the twin primes, prime numbers that sit two apart, like five and seven.

Brun's constant adds up the reciprocals of every twin prime pair. Unlike the sum over all primes, this sum settles to a fixed value, but its exact size is unknown. Firm bounds that assume nothing extra were already known. Dunn proves the first firm bound that leans on the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, a major unproven claim about prime numbers. Under that assumption, the constant comes out below 2.1594. The result shows how a big conjecture, if true, sharpens what can be said about twin primes.
arxiv-2504-15958:
Yao and six co-authors present FreeGraftor, a method to place a subject from a photo into new AI images with no training, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Subject-driven generation must keep identity true while following text prompts. Tuning methods are slow and costly, while instant methods often lose the subject. FreeGraftor grafts features across images to bridge that gap.

Semantic matching finds matching parts between reference and draft images. A position-aware fusion step then blends those details in. A new noise start preserves the subject's shape for better matching. Tests show higher fidelity and better text fit than rival instant methods. The method extends to scenes with several subjects at once.
arxiv-2504-16058:
Hendrik Müller and Sanjay Bhatnagar speed up radio image cleaning in twenty twenty-five. Radio interferometers produce data that must be deconvolved to form images. The classic algorithm for this is CLEAN, the de facto standard. New telescopes bring far larger data, higher resolution, and wider dynamic range, straining existing pipelines.

Multiscale CLEAN variants beat the classic on quality but cost much more compute. The authors combine ideas into a new algorithm, Autocorr-CLEAN. It fits clusters of CLEAN components rather than single points. The autocorrelation function informs how those clusters are shaped. The goal is variant-level quality at closer to classic speed. Readers who reduce radio data get a deconvolution built for the coming data flood.
arxiv-2504-17758: The MicroBooNE team gives the first study of how well a neutrino's direction can be rebuilt from quasielastic-like events in its detector. The paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. MicroBooNE is a liquid argon time projection chamber that tracks hits in fine detail. The events they use leave one muon and one proton. They check how far the rebuilt muon-proton system sits from the known direction of the beam. It is tied to sub-GeV oscillation studies for DUNE.
arxiv-2504-18458:
Wenyi Xiao and Leilei Gan teach vision-language models to think fast or slow as the question demands. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, presents FAST-GRPO. Reward training often makes such models write long chains for every task. Length grows, but accuracy barely does, and tokens are wasted.

Tests first show that answer length and data mix shape results in a usable way. Two scores then rate how hard each question is. Rewards favor the right length for the difficulty, and a safety term scales with it too. Across seven reasoning tests, accuracy hit top marks. Token use fell by a third to two-thirds versus slow-only rivals.
arxiv-2504-19158:
Sijia Xiao and co-authors present a system that helps survivors of online harm make sense of what happened to them, in work from 2025. Harms such as cyberbullying and sexual harassment are widespread on social media. Standard moderation removes content but often ignores survivors' own needs and agency.

Drawing on restorative justice, their system guides survivors through reflective questions, offers tailored advice drawn from similar survivors' stories, and lets users map a plan on interactive sticky notes. A controlled experiment found the structured process improved sensemaking over an unstructured one. The authors argue the approach builds community awareness and a support network among survivors. They also discuss design lessons, such as giving guidance while keeping survivors in charge of their own story.
arxiv-2504-19358:
Fldzhyan, Saygin, and Straupe wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It proposes a new layout for programmable photonic circuits, chips that steer light to multiply matrices, a core task in both classical and quantum computing.

Large light-based circuits suffer from losses, hardware errors, and hard programming. The authors build on an overlooked fact: any matrix, even one that does not preserve length, can be written as a sum of two length-preserving ones. Circuits built from that sum stay shallow, at low depth, and can be programmed by formula rather than by search. Earlier designs could not offer both traits at once. The new circuits keep the perks of the standard approach based on splitting matrices into rotations and scalings. The authors present the design as a clear step up for light-based matrix multiplication.
arxiv-2504-20058:
Ambedkar Dukkipati and four co-authors build data sets and tests for stock forecasting that uses outside knowledge, not prices alone. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Prices move with company links, policy shifts, wars, and the wider economy, and all of those change over time.

No public data captured that web, so the team built time-stamped knowledge graphs for the stock market. Their method treats events on those graphs as sparks in a Hawkes process, a model where one event raises the odds of others. The learned patterns rank stocks by expected returns over several holding spans. In wide tests, the rankings beat rival baselines. The authors offer the data and benchmarks for others to build on.
arxiv-2505-00158:
Ribeiro, Lui, and Wolf add a restraining sensor to a stabilization scheme for simulating swirling compressible flows, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Large-eddy simulations resolve the big whirls and model the small ones. But sharp shock waves can spawn fake oscillations that ruin the run.

The standard fix adds artificial viscosity and heat conduction where the flow has sharp gradients. That added diffusion can also smear real vortices, especially the low-pressure cores that dominate many flows, and spoil turbulence statistics. The authors' sensor restrains the artificial shear diffusivity so it acts near shocks but holds back around vortical structures. Their solvers use high-order compact finite differences, prized for fidelity. The aim is stability without paying for it in blurred physics. The model targets vortex-dominated flows in aerospace and propulsion work.
arxiv-2505-00658:
Mohammed Saif and Shahrokh Valaee design resilient drone networks aided by reconfigurable intelligent surfaces in a two thousand twenty-five telecommunications paper. The surfaces can be virtually partitioned to create several relay links at once.

User equipment reaches blocked but reliable drones through these surface-aided links, with multiple users sharing one drone via non-orthogonal multiple access. The authors derive exact and approximate signal-to-interference-plus-noise formulas for aligned and non-aligned beams. Their two-step scheme clusters users by channel gain, associates drones by reliability, then partitions surfaces optimally. Simulations show connectivity gains of thirty to forty percent over traditional drone schemes.
arxiv-2505-03358:
Marios Michael, Eugene Demler, and Patrick Lee wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives a rival account of light tests on the cuprate YBCO, where terahertz pulses seem to wake a superconducting mark far above the true transition.

The mark had been read as proof that the pump built pair coherence up to the pseudogap heat. The authors posit that local pairs, with phase links of a few lattice steps, sit there all along at rest. The pump, by parametric boosting of the Josephson plasmon, aligns the currents between the layers. A Floquet frame then fits the data. No pump-made coherence is needed, but the pseudogap must hold local pairing at rest.
arxiv-2505-04558:
Wenzhao Liu and co-authors noted a structural find in 2025 about optimal answers to the travelling salesman problem. Neural solvers often fail to broaden to tours of new sizes or new point layouts, because they do not learn the underlying rules of good answers. The team looked for such a rule in the geometry of optimal tours themselves.

They identify what they call the Purity Law: in optimal tours. The prevalence of an edge grows exponentially as the points around it become sparser, a bias toward local thinness that held across many test instances. Building on it, their training method, Purity Policy Optimization, steers a neural solver's buildings toward that law during training. Tests showed it plugs into popular solvers and boosts their generalization without adding cost when solving.
arxiv-2505-05158:
Tiago de Souza Farias, Lucas Friedrich, and Jonas Maziero review machine learning with multi-level quantum systems in a 2025 survey. Qudits generalize qubits beyond two levels, offering larger state spaces in a single unit. That room allows richer data encodings, more compact circuits, and problems with many-valued structure that qubits handle awkwardly.

The review concentrates on variational algorithms and quantum neural networks built from qudits. Recent experiments show the hardware maturing toward practical use. The authors weigh where qudits beat qubits on expressivity and resource cost. For readers entering quantum learning, the survey maps a fast-moving alternative to the standard binary picture.
arxiv-2505-06058:
Beatrice Brienza, Anna Fino, Gueo Grantcharov, and Misha Verbitsky study the shape of a special class of geometric spaces in two thousand twenty-five. These spaces, called strong HKT manifolds, carry three complex structures at once plus a metric with a twist. The team asks what forms such spaces can take when they are closed and finite.

They prove that a wider class of such spaces, with full symmetry group, must in fact be of the simpler Kahler kind. A like result holds for strong HKT spaces as well. For spaces built from solvable groups, they prove a strict form and sort all cases where a key twist stays parallel. They also add a new leaf structure for these spaces and show that in eight dimensions the closed ones are always Hopf bundles.
arxiv-2505-06358:
Barber and co-authors announce a fourth, inner planet in the young TOI-2076 system. Young multi-planet systems let astronomers compare worlds born under the same conditions. TOI-2076 already held three planets of 2.5 to 4 Earth radii on 10 to 35 day orbits. The new planet is smaller, at 1.35 Earth radii. It circles in just 3.02 days, inside the others. All four are targets for space telescope air studies.

The team also re-dated the star system from spin, lithium, and star charts. TOI-2076 and its companion system are about 210 million years old. The find urges fresh searches of known systems with newer data.
arxiv-2505-06858:
Tianyu Chen and seven co-authors fix a weakness of Fourier neural operators, the workhorse neural solvers for partial differential equations. These models learn in the frequency domain, but high-frequency signals are sparse and usually truncated by a fixed pattern. The lost detail hurts high-resolution inputs and long-term forecasts exactly where accuracy matters.

FreqMoE first learns the low-frequency weights, exploiting the dependence of high frequencies on low ones. A sparse upward-cycling strategy then grows a mixture of experts that extends those weights into high-frequency regions. Across regular and irregular grids it gained up to about seventeen percent accuracy while using a fiftieth of the parameters of a dense model. Long-term prediction stayed stable, and the scheme ports to other operator variants.
arxiv-2505-07658:
Derks and five colleagues study error control codes for quantum computers with noisy readouts in twenty twenty-five. Quantum bits are fragile, so codes must check for errors again and again as they run. These codes are set by a schedule of checks. The team asked how to tune that schedule when the checks themselves add the most noise.

They found that repeating checks helps when readout noise dominates. When other noise rules, repeating checks gains little. They also built a broader score that counts both qubits and check rounds. How results were decoded mattered a lot: a smarter decoder turned the worst code into the best in one case.
arxiv-2505-09158:
Xiaohan Jiang, Yuanyuan Pan, Yang Zhang, and Ye Xiong study light waves in lattices that leak energy. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses microcavity lattices with strong loss, called non-Hermitian systems. Most states in such a lattice fade fast, yet one chosen excited state can keep moving in a coherent way.

In a one-dimensional lattice, that state shifts sideways from where it was injected. The shift is a hallmark of a point gap in the spectrum. In two dimensions, the packet spreads into a V shape whose arms can be steered by geometry alone. The team reads this as a way to steer light with no change to the device structure.
arxiv-2505-09358:
Bingxin Ke and seven co-authors set out Marigold, a plan to turn text to art spread models into tools for close art work. Models like Stable Diffusion learn rich sight facts from huge sets of shots with words. Marigold tunes such a model, with small change to its build, for tasks like depth gauge from one eye. It also fits tasks like face tilt calls and splits of a shot into its base parts.

Train uses small made up data sets on a lone art card through a few days. That keeps the shift cheap to run. In spite of the light purse, Marigold hits top zero shot scores on its goal tasks. The work says that train to make art is a base too scant used for class tasks of read. A page for the work comes with the set out.
arxiv-2505-12058:
Koc presents in twenty twenty-five a featherweight test kit for quick health checks of language model pipelines. Full benchmarks are slow and costly, which breaks the fast loop developers need while tuning prompts. The kit pairs a tiny hand-checked English question set with a generator that mints matching packs in any language, domain, or difficulty.

Ready packs already cover ten languages, and each ships with standard metadata and plug-in files for common test tools. A full run adds only seconds to a pipeline yet catches prompt template faults, tokeniser drift, and tuning side effects early. The author released the framework openly. It aims to give teams a unit-test style safety net for daily model work.
arxiv-2505-13458:
