Bandar Siddani and co-authors present a multiscale method for simulating dense flows of grains, in work from 2025. Coarse models of sand-like flows are fast but rely on closure rules that are often crude. A linked fine model can supply those rules, yet running it everywhere is far too costly.

Their method trains neural networks on fine simulations to stand in for the closure rules. A group of networks also estimates its own uncertainty at each point. Where the estimate looks unreliable, the system runs fresh fine simulations and updates the networks. The networks are shaped to keep the coarse model well behaved. Tests on sloped flows and a collapsing column of grains in three dimensions show the method stays accurate while cutting cost sharply.
arxiv-2505-13858:
Gonzalo Constante-Flores, Hao Chen, and Can Li enforce hard rules in deep learning in twenty twenty-five. Deployed models in safety-critical settings must satisfy strict constraints. Physical laws, fairness rules, and safety limits are examples. Standard networks have no built-in way to guarantee such limits.

Regularization and projection fixes are limited, costly, or lack guarantees. Their framework is model-agnostic and handles input-dependent linear constraints. A task network pursues prediction accuracy. A safe network, trained with decision rules from robust optimization, ensures feasibility. The final prediction mixes the two networks convexly. That mixture guarantees constraint satisfaction during training and deployment alike. Readers get predictions that cannot cross the lines their domain forbids.
arxiv-2505-14358:
Shobhana and colleagues presented a passive method in twenty twenty-five for measuring how long web services take to respond, without touching the client's device. Operators need that number to spot slowdowns and attacks, but return traffic often takes a different road back, hiding the timing.

Their system, PIRATE, watches only the outgoing requests at a middle point. Some requests trigger follow-ups, and the gap between such a causal pair stands in for the round-trip delay. The trick works even when packet headers are encrypted. In tests on a realistic web application, the estimates landed within one percent of the true client-side delay. Plugged into a load balancer, the measurements cut the slowest responses by thirty-seven percent. The authors say the method gives operators client-grade insight with no probing traffic and no client software.
arxiv-2505-14658:
Giovanni Rolandino and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a dry electrode grid that reads the fine movement signals of the hand from the skin, with no gel. The signals are the small electrical sparks of the arm, read in a dense grid. A known network then estimates the position of the hand from them. Gel electrodes are the norm, but they dry out, cost, and irritate.

The team built the dry grid with just two rows of electrodes. They ran it head to head with a gel setup, through the same position network. Skin-contact checks weighed two side effects: voltage division and power-line hum. The position estimates of the dry grid matched those of the gel setup, and at times beat them. A spread check showed the two rows lose little information. The team presents them as a cheap, friendly path for prosthetic and rehabilitation gear.
arxiv-2505-15658:
Šárka Nečasová, Tong Tang, Emil Wiedemann, and Lu Zhu prove energy conservation for weak solutions of the inviscid primitive equations. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works on a bounded domain, the setting of ocean and atmosphere models. Onsager-type smoothness terms are assumed. A prior result on domains with walls guides the path, but this system adds fresh snags.

The vertical velocity is barely known, which starves key estimates. Corner points in the domain add more trouble. The team brings new ideas to clear both. A side result gives a term that rules out stray energy loss as viscosity fades. The work ties a famous turbulence idea to a workhorse model of geophysics. Energy bookkeeping for rough flows gains a firmer base.
arxiv-2505-16758:
Qian-Xi Zhao, Jian-Jun Dong, and Zi-Xiang Hu measure the statistics of work done on strongly linked electrons. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Quantum work fluctuates when a system is driven out of equilibrium. Correlated electrons resist the usual analytic tools. Their testbed is the Ising-Kondo model of heavy fermion materials. A Monte Carlo framework does the heavy sampling.

The method builds the moment generating function of work step by step. Mean work, irreversible work, spread, and skew all follow from it. At low temperatures these quantities kink sharply at the metal-insulator transition. Heat smooths the kink into a crossover. Work statistics thus flag the phase change. Thermodynamics gains a fresh diagnostic for correlated matter.
arxiv-2505-23258:
Haojie Jia and four co-authors present SealOS Plus for securities trading systems in two thousand twenty-five. Trading systems now run as microservices, which strains resource plans. Delays grow and chips sit idle under old schedulers. Exchanges demand replies in tens of milliseconds.

Their stack adds three parts to a container platform. A deep reinforcement learner schedules resources on the fly. A three level cache speeds common trading steps. A memory based net predicts load ahead of time. In live use at an exchange, chip use rose high. Reply times fell and peak throughput hit a strong rate. Results met the strict demands of the floor.
arxiv-2505-23358:
Reem AlJunaid and Muzammil Behzad present a model that writes rich, knowledge-filled captions for images. Their paper appeared in 2025. Many caption systems produce bland lines that miss context. Their model replays stored knowledge while it writes, and uses beam search to draft several candidate captions before choosing. Attention modules inside the image encoder sharpen which features the writer sees.

Training schedules smooth the learning process. The authors report gains in both caption quality and recognition of the facts an image shows. The model also handled knowledge ideas it had not seen in training. They present the design as a step toward captions that inform, rather than merely label, useful for search, teaching, and access tools for blind users.
arxiv-2505-24458:
Tianlong Yu and ten co-authors release a data set for studying how augmented reality and chat models can be turned into tools of social manipulation. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The set records staged attacks in settings like meetings, classes, and mixers. Sixty people took part across many scripted talks.

Each record pairs headset video and audio with scene context and fake social profiles. It also holds trust ratings and measures of how open each target was to influence. The staged attacks worked at alarming rates: most targets clicked phishing links or took calls. Trust often rose after the talks rather than falling. Guards include scrubbed identities and ethics board approval. The authors offer the set to help build defenses against such attacks. It is shared in public for research use.
arxiv-2506-03258:
April Qiu Cheng and co-authors wrote this astronomy paper in 2025 on fast radio bursts, brief flashes from deep space. As a burst crosses space, loose electrons slow it by an amount called its dispersion measure. Match that delay to galaxy maps, and bursts can trace where matter sits. The catch is bias: some bursts and host galaxies are easier to spot than others.

The team ran fake skies through a large computer model of the cosmos and shot 3,000 test bursts through it. Most biases proved mild. Host traits, follow-up habits, and one survey's known quirks did not skew the signal much. But dropping the most delayed tenth of bursts bent the signal by over half at small scales. Surveys must count and correct that cut, the authors say.
arxiv-2506-03658:
Erika Hausenblas, Boris Jidjou Moghomye, and Paul Andre Razafimandimby wrote this mathematics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on simulating a coupled system from biology. The system joins a chemotaxis equation, which tracks cells moving toward chemical signals, with fluid flow equations shaken by random transport noise.

The model itself is already cut into pieces in space, and the authors add a matching cut in time. Their scheme is a semi-implicit Euler method, a step-by-step rule that treats some terms at the old time and some at the new. They prove the scheme is well-posed, meaning each step has a sound solution. They also derive uniform bounds that hold for the step values as the steps shrink. Such bounds are the groundwork for proving the simulation truly closes in on the real system. The setting is a bounded, convex region in three dimensions.
arxiv-2506-05558:
Andreas Meuleman and four co-authors rebuild three-dimensional scenes from photos on the fly, with no wait after shooting. Their method appeared in twenty twenty-five. Viewpoint-free rendering from photos is now easy, but finding camera poses and training the scene model can take minutes to hours.

Their approach estimates poses fast, using learned image features and a small GPU-friendly adjustment step. It then seeds scene blobs directly where needed and grows them during training, which speeds the fit sharply. For large scenes, blobs are grouped into anchors and parked off the graphics card, then merged as work proceeds. Tests across many data sets show the method matches rivals in quality while delivering a walkable scene as soon as capture ends.
arxiv-2506-07058:
Larraín-Hubach, Shapiro, and Vodev wrote in twenty twenty-five about how fast wave energy fades near an obstacle when electric and magnetic fields are present. They prove sharp estimates for a magnetic Schrödinger operator with rough, bounded potentials. The same estimates hold outside a non-trapping obstacle with a wall condition. Magnetic potential must vanish in that obstacle case, they note. Applying the estimates gives exponential decay of local wave energy. The potentials themselves decay exponentially at infinity in their setup.

Low frequencies need cutting off in even dimensions for the result. In odd dimensions, no cut-off is needed under a spectral condition. Zero must be neither an eigenvalue nor a resonance there. Sharp resolvent bounds are the technical core of the paper. Such decay results underpin scattering theory and control of waves. The work extends earlier results to less regular potentials.
arxiv-2506-08458:
Daptari, Montesinos, and Rao study continuity points in dual Banach spaces in this two thousand twenty-five math paper. Banach spaces are complete spaces of vectors with a size measure. Their duals hold all the continuous linear readings of those vectors. On the dual's unit ball, two topologies compete: a weak-star one and a weak one. The authors ask where the identity map between them is continuous.

They find classes of spaces where such points are plentiful, forming a dense set of a special descriptive kind. They also study how the trait passes to higher duals. One result is negative: for von Neumann algebras whose predual has a certain smoothness property, no continuity point exists at all. The paper serves functional analysts who map the fine structure of dual spaces.
arxiv-2506-08558:
William de Vazelhes, Xiao-Tong Yuan, and Bin Gu improve optimization when the answer must be sparse and must obey extra rules, in a 2025 paper. Keeping only a few active variables gives clean, cheap models, but real problems add constraints that the sparse set must respect. Older algorithms demanded a projection formula that may not exist, or promised only local success. Their variant of iterative hard thresholding projects in two steps, tuned to support-preserving constraints.

A fresh trade-off between relaxing sparsity and accepting sub-optimality yields global guarantees on the result. The proof rests on extending a classic three-point lemma to their two-step projector. The guarantees cover plain, random, and derivative-free versions of the problem. Even without extra constraints, the zero-order result beats the prior best, which one author set in earlier work.
arxiv-2506-09158:
Neslihan Alan, Mehmet Alpsoy, and Yücel Kılıç present the first light study of an eclipsing binary star in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. In such pairs, one star passes in front of the other, causing dips in brightness. Those dips let astronomers measure star masses and sizes directly.

The team combined a space telescope light curve with new multicolor observations from a robotic telescope in Türkiye. Their modeling gave masses and radii for both stars in the pair, plus brightness and surface gravity values. They also estimated the system's distance. The secondary star proved larger but less massive than the primary, a clue to its stage of life.
arxiv-2506-10658:
Narges Nemati and Mostafa Haghir Chehreghani make recommender systems tougher against noisy clicks by teaching two cleaned-up views of the same data to agree. Graph-based recommenders pass messages along user-item edges, so junk edges poison them, and they overfit easily. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the pair build two views for each interaction's neighborhood. One view denoises with attention-weighted graph layers. The other comes from a variational autoencoder that regularizes the feature distribution. A mutual learning loss gradually harmonizes the two views during training.

Experiments on several real data sets followed. Predicted ratings grew slightly more accurate. Rankings improved dramatically, by up to about a third on the reported metrics. The contrastive design's common patterns, the authors argue, are exactly what survives noise.
arxiv-2506-10758:
Gutekunst studies a special traveling salesman problem where edge cost depends only on edge length around a ring. Its complexity is a noted open question. A geometric object, the edge-length polytope, offers one attack route. Its corner count turns out to hinge on how n factors. For prime n, corners grow in step with n. For a squared prime, they grow like n to the 1.5 power. For powers of two, the count is superpolynomial.

By contrast, the classic salesman polytope has near n-factorial corners. So brute force over corners is fast for some n and hopeless for others. The split ties a salesman problem to number theory.
arxiv-2506-13158:
Aswathy K R, Udaya Maurya, Surya Teja Gavva, and Rickmoy Samanta study swirling vortices on a doughnut-shaped surface in a 2025 physics study. The setting is a thin, frictionless fluid film wrapped on a torus, whose curved shape and closed topology change vortex motion. A Hamiltonian description covers the vortices, plus a self-force that comes from the geometry.

For two vortices the authors work out the basic motion, finding several classes of paths for a vortex dipole. Random clusters of same-sign vortices show collective behavior shaped by the surface. Comparisons with quantum superfluid vortices highlight subtle differences between the two settings.
arxiv-2506-16458:
Likhitha Annapurna Kavuri, Akshay Mhatre, Akarsh Nair, and Deepti Gupta build SecureFed, a two-phase frame to catch rogue clients in shared learning. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Shared learning guards data privacy, since holders keep their data. But its spread form lets a rogue holder warp the results or wreck the model. In phase one, the frame gathers each holder's update and shrinks its dims to bare odd forms tied to bad acts. Fake data sets score each temp model, to grade how odd it is. In phase two, weights are routed by zones of worth: zones with strong, useful slopes count more in the join.
arxiv-2506-17258:
Jasmin Lim, Dimitrios Pylorof, Humberto Garcia, and Karthik Duraisamy design a twin on screen to run a new type core plant, of the fourth kind. Their test plant cools with fluoride salt and runs at high heat. The twin aims to cut run costs and lift calls. It links the real plant to stand in models, learn by gains, and Bayes calls in a closed loop.

The learn chief sets goal strength while it counts health of parts and wear. A chief named for guide rules holds pump flow and heat caps. Bayes screens fold gauges into the mock runs. Three case works show year long plans for care of the plant. They show truth made more fine with oft gauges. They show real time re set past a shock to the plant. The team claims wide use for more new plants.
arxiv-2506-18658:
Zhang and co-authors teach a model to write pathology reports from slide images in this 2025 paper. Whole slide images are vast and redundant, and their raw features lack medical meaning. Pathologists, by contrast, reason with prior cases in mind.

Their framework, BiGen, copies that habit. It first retrieves relevant knowledge from a medical knowledge bank by matching the slide's most attended patches. Then a two-stream learning setup uses one learnable token for image features and one for the retrieved knowledge, aligning the two. A decoder merges both streams into the final report. On a breast cancer dataset it improved language metrics by 7.4 percent and a key classification score by 19.1 percent over prior methods.
arxiv-2506-19458:
Jacques Desmarais and colleagues resolved a long-standing glitch in spin density theory in a 2025 paper. Simulating magnets whose spins point in varying directions produces a torque from the exchange-correlation term, the theory's catch-all for quantum interactions. That torque should vanish or stay physical, but in plain spin-density theory it comes out spurious, because it secretly depends on the spin current, a quantity the theory does not contain.

Their fix works inside spin-current density theory, whose energy obeys an exact combined gauge symmetry. Nonzero torques on twisted solutions are then fenced by that symmetry and never enter the actual spin dynamics, which involve only physical currents and torques. Two decades of confusion trace to a missing constraint.
arxiv-2506-19858:
Manrique Camacho, Amanda Cedeño, Luis Barboza, Shu Wei Chou-Chen, Mario Gómez, and Hugo Hidalgo wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds a Hurricane Impact Index that scores both the direct hit of a storm and its spread harm, for use in Central America.

Hurricanes rank among the worst natural hazards. Their harm runs past the track line, since heavy rain and strong winds bite far off path, shaped by the lay of the land. The index is built so its parts can be split across time and space. That lets crews map where a storm's force fell hardest and how the harm was spread. The team shows the index at work on the Central American region.
arxiv-2506-22558:
Blaise Bourdin, Jean-Jacques Marigo, Corrado Maurini, and Camilla Zolesi set out a new model of how stuff cracks, which can hold any round strength rule. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Past crack models let a phase field eat the stuff's stiffness. Here it does not. In its place, the spring energy grows in a straight line past the strength zone. That zone shrinks to nil as the field nears its top. The team works out the model on a cube under edge loads. Its answer is a clean cross crack, when load and jump paths meet a test they state by a known circle tool. They sort strength rules by whether cracks can form.
arxiv-2506-23358:
Pawel Renc and co-authors present Federated Timeline Synthesis for training medical AI across hospitals in this 2025 paper. Patient records cannot be pooled freely across institutions. Their method turns each record into a token timeline of clinical events. Each hospital trains a generator on its own timelines and shares only model weights.

A central server uses those generators to synthesize a large shared corpus. A global generator trained on that corpus can simulate future patient paths on demand. Five prediction tasks on the MIMIC-IV dataset tested the approach. Models trained on synthetic data performed about as well as those trained on real data. Privacy, scale, and reuse for trial simulation are the main claimed gains.
arxiv-2507-00358:
Yilie Huang and Xun Yu Zhou study reinforcement learning for control problems in twenty twenty-five. Their class of problems runs in continuous time with linear dynamics and quadratic costs. The costs here are indefinite, and the noise depends on both state and control. States are scalar, and there are no running control rewards.

Earlier work on this class used fixed exploration schedules. Those need heavy tuning and ignore how learning is going. The authors propose a model-free method that adapts exploration as it runs. The critic adjusts entropy regularization while the actor adjusts policy variance. Even with that freedom, the method keeps a sublinear regret bound. It matches the best known model-free results for this class.
arxiv-2507-01358:
Hirao, Nozaki, and Tasaka grade three rare unit groups as ball point sets in this twenty twenty-five paper. The groups count two score, four score, and six score points on the ball. A point set earns design rank when set sums kill all wave forms of set grades.

Inside, wave grades that die on each group are found in full for all three. Each group proves the least and lone set of its rank in their tests. One group's rank tale had no past match in the design lore. Grids built on the groups then host wave sums as sum forms. Those sums prove to be shape forms, with dead spans named by rank.
arxiv-2507-01858:
Hank Chen and Joaquin Liniado introduce a three-dimensional quantum field theory with an endless symmetry, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The symmetry generalizes the famous chiral symmetry of a two-dimensional model, now stretched into three dimensions and graded for supersymmetry. Its algebra is an extended loop-like structure with a central term.

By quantizing the theory in radial shells, they build its space of states. A three-dimensional echo of the state-operator link then shows the local operators form a new algebraic structure named after a pasta shape. The authors expect the setup to carry exact methods from two-dimensional theory into three dimensions, a longstanding goal in the field.
arxiv-2507-04358:
Alfakih writes, in a solo 2025 note, on a cleanup task that sits under GPS fixes. A set of points in space yields a matrix of pairwise distances, and such a matrix must meet strict shape rules. Noise in the raw readings can break those rules. His task: given a sound distance matrix and one noisy row of distances, find the closest row that keeps the enlarged matrix sound at the same embedding dimension.

The task grows out of fault checks in GPS, where a bad reading must be flagged and fixed fast. He gives a criterion that spots when a fault is there at all. He then gives three algorithms to find the fix row. One suits the small case of four points. Two more cover five points and up. The note keeps its scope tight: one matrix, one row, exact dimension held.
arxiv-2507-06158:
Anjelo Gabriel Cruz, Manuel Joseph Loquias, and Jörg Thuswaldner studied addition machines for digit systems built on matrices. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with ways to write vectors as digit strings in a matrix base. The base here is a growing two by two matrix with rational parts. Each vector gets a sole such write, but a tail term from a finite set, the attractor, may stay. When that tail can be set to zero, the system is clean.

The team ties those tails to automata that add digits in the system. Such machines let one check if the clean case holds. Readers in number theory get a bridge between digit writes, tilings, and finite machines.
arxiv-2507-06758:
Simon Thelen and Wolfgang Mauerer present a way to pick the best quantum-classical method for a job, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Hybrid methods promise gains, yet their speed and quality are hard to foresee. Users are left unsure which method fits a given problem.

Their frame reads notes placed in the source code to trace key traits of each method. Statistical models then predict which method and settings best meet stated needs. A case study on optimization problems backs the approach with simulation data. The authors argue the same frame fits other tasks, such as simulating physics systems.
arxiv-2507-08858:
Sami Achour and co-authors test foundation models for time series forecasting in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Conformal prediction wraps a forecast in an interval with a stated coverage rate. It needs held-out data for calibration, which competes with training data for classic models.

Foundation models forecast with no task training, so nearly all data can go to calibration. The team compares them with statistical models and gradient boosting inside this setup. When data were scarce, the foundation models gave more reliable intervals, thanks to better raw accuracy. Their calibration was also more stable. The scarcer the data, the bigger the edge. Code is shared for replication.
arxiv-2507-08958:
Xiaowen Zhang, Zhenyu Bi, Patrick Lachance, Xuan Wang, Tiziana Di Matteo, and Rupert Croft wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents SimAgents, a team of language model agents that pulls simulation settings out of papers and sets up cosmology runs.

Cosmology codes grow ever more tangled, and their settings hide in dense papers with no shared form. Hand translation to scripts is slow and error-prone. SimAgents splits the work among agents that reason on physics, check the software, and run tools, all in set talk. The team built a test set from dozens of past simulations in print. The system scores strongly there. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2507-09258:
Liu, Wu, Pan, and Yang tested in twenty twenty-five a dark energy model where dark stuff and dark energy trade flows. The norm model of the cosmos has small clashes with sky data across its long past. Their model lets the sound scale at an early split time set the start state in a neat way.

As the trade strength grows, their count for the present spread rate rises too. That shift helps the clash on that rate a bit, but not in full. The trade leaves a mark on the early sky glow in a thin time span. Chain tests pin down the free parts of the model.
arxiv-2507-10458:
Morteza Baniasad Azad and Mostafa Arabtash studied a number built from finite groups in twenty twenty-five. Take every element of a group, note its order, and multiply them all: that product is their starting point. They then count its prime factors, with repeats, using the classic omega function, and ask how the count behaves under group operations.

The resulting function mimics the derivative rules of calculus. For a direct product of groups of coprime size, a product rule holds. For a quotient by a central cyclic Sylow subgroup, a quotient rule holds. They also show a non-cyclic group never beats the cyclic group of the same size on this measure. A final bound compares arbitrary groups with a specific linear group at three small primes.
arxiv-2507-11258:
Olivier Gasquet's paper on modal logic carries an unusual and candid notice: the proof it set out to present does not work. The paper aimed to show that quasi-dense modal logics have the finite model property, using a path-filtration technique. The author states plainly that the argument contains a major flaw, and that the flaw is unfixable.

The text is preserved as a record of the attempted proof and its failure. Quasi-dense logics are a family of modal logics whose frame conditions generalize density, and the finite model property matters because it often underpins decidability results. A published admission that a promising route collapses is itself useful to logicians: it warns others away from the same dead end and documents where the argument breaks. Readers should treat the paper as a cautionary artifact, not as an established result.
arxiv-2507-12058:
Konstantin Slutsky, Mikhail Sodin, and Aron Wennman prove, in twenty twenty-five, equivariant Borel versions of classic theorems in complex analysis and partial differential equations. Equivariant means the construction respects translations: shifting the input shifts the output the same way. Borel means the assignment is measurable, though not necessarily continuous. Their starting point is a Weierstrass-type theorem: each pattern of prescribed zeros gets an entire function with exactly those zeros, chosen in a translation-respecting Borel way. They also study right inverses for three operators: the Laplacian, the heat operator, and a complex derivative operator.

Borel equivariant inverses exist on the free part of each operator's range. The freeness conditions cannot be dropped, and Borel cannot be upgraded to continuity. Proofs use approximation theorems and Borel toasts, measurable analogues of ergodic towers.
arxiv-2507-12958:
Yu-Yue Cui, Xiao-Mei Tang, Qi Huang, and Rui Chen predict new two-baryon states built from charm and strange quarks. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Dibaryons with heavy flavor are a frontier of hadron physics. The authors use a one-boson-exchange model of baryon forces. Charm baryons pair with light baryons in P-wave motion. Eight coupled channels enter the analysis.

Several molecular candidates emerge with set quantum numbers. Some pair a charmed baryon with a nucleon, others with hyperons. Coupled-channel effects prove decisive for at least one state. Phase shift analysis confirms bound states and flags resonances. One shape-type resonance stands out among them. Experiments gain a target list for exotic hadron searches.
arxiv-2507-14758:
Luyi Ma and co-authors presented a 2025 conference paper on a new way to recommend items to users. Modern recommendation systems can generate a personal list step by step, much like a language model writes text. The catch is cost and clarity: the standard method pays attention to everything at once, which is slow, and its tokens carry little plain meaning.

Their system, GRACE, first turns each user action into tokens enriched with facts from a product knowledge graph, such as category, brand, and price. A chain-of-thought style layout makes the reasoning behind each token clearer. Then a new attention method looks only at selected chunks of the history: near, far, and current parts of the user's journey. The authors report tests showing the design keeps quality while cutting waste. The work aims at recommenders that are both cheaper to run and easier to inspect.
arxiv-2507-17958:
Daniel Carlstrom Schad and five co-authors present VIBE, a two stage transformer that forecasts brain fMRI response from video input. Features from open models for video, audio, and text feed the system. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

A fusion transformer merges the streams, and a second transformer decodes them over time with rotary position codes. Training drew on dozens of hours of film data from a shared brain set, pooled across many seeds. Scores on a held in TV season beat those on fresh films, as expected. An earlier build won one challenge phase and placed second overall, the authors note.
arxiv-2507-18058:
A team including Qing-Xin Ji and Hanfei Hou reports multicolor pulses from a single optical pump in a microresonator, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. In microcombs, solitons can drive other modes to produce optical gain. Theory predicted multicolor solitons: phase-locked pulses sharing one location at new spectral positions. The needed dispersion conditions, though, do not occur naturally in conventional microresonators.

The pulses observed here are closely related to that concept. Individual soliton pulses share the same repetition rate and could potentially be fully phase-locked. They arise through interband coupling inside a compound resonator. A regenerative secondary pulse forms in time and space with the exciting soliton. The result is multicolor light from one pump in one device. Such sources matter for applications needing several synchronized colors on a chip.
arxiv-2507-20658:
Jesco Talies, Eric Breitbarth, and David Melching present a training method for trustworthy AI in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their test task is marking crack tips in image data used to study how materials fracture. Deep models can be accurate yet hard to trust in high-stakes science.

Their method, attention-guided training, feeds expert checks of the model's focus back into training. Explanations are scored, and known stress field patterns guide where the model should look. Aligning focus with these physical fields improved the model's reach to new cases. The explanations also grew more faithful to the real physics.
arxiv-2507-21958:
Casabella, Kastner, and Vlad sort all the graph shapes of a class of tropical curves in this twenty twenty-five paper. The curves come from where two curved faces cross in a warm-math three-space. Each graph stands for a most-worn form of a loop-shaped curve built that way.

Inside, the team finds just over four thousand such graphs in the full class. Each graph has the same count of points and links, which fits the loop form they stand for. The count rests on a huge sweep of ways to split a four-way shape into neat blocks. That sweep ran past four hundred times ten thousand cases in all. The list gives a firm base for more work on these curves.
arxiv-2507-22458:
Hugo Levy-Falk and a large team study graphene quantum dots on a perovskite crystal in two thousand twenty-five. On this surface the dots clump, unlike in solution or on other bases. That holds even from very thin starting mixes. Small clusters were watched through their spectra over time.

Clusters flip back and forth between a lone dot state and a paired state. On some clusters the glow then jumps up for good. At the same time the glow fades faster than before. The team ties that shift to a shared collective state. Light may drive the dots to organize as they sit on the crystal.
arxiv-2507-22658:
Dimitrios Ntalampekos proves, in a solo 2025 mathematics paper, a test for when a set on the sphere can be reshaped into a Schottky set. A Schottky set is what remains of a sphere when open disks are cut out, no two touching. The reshape may bend and stretch but must keep a fixed bound on how far it skews shapes. Such bounded reshapes are called quasiconformal.

His test is neat. The set passes just when each pair of its leftover pieces maps to a pair of open disks under one sphere map with a fixed skew bound. The result covers famed fractal sets such as Sierpiński carpets and gaskets. For gaskets it gives the first reshape rule of this kind. It also contains a past rule for carpets as one case, and drops a separation condition past works leaned on.
arxiv-2507-22958:
Khrulev introduces in twenty twenty-five a benchmark for judging how well vision-language models can grade handwritten maths work. Most tests check whether AI can solve problems. His test instead checks whether AI can read a student's written solution, spot mistakes, and grade it by fixed rules, as a human examiner would.

The set holds just over one hundred scanned solutions from Russia's national school exam, each with an official expert grade. He tested seven modern models from major labs in three modes of use. Results exposed real limits in maths reasoning and in matching human grading rules. The author offers the set as a spur for work on AI-assisted marking.
arxiv-2507-23358:
Renato Vukovic and co-authors brought in TeQoDO in 2025, a method that lets a language model build the data store schema for a task-oriented dialogue system by itself. Such assistants answer from an outer data store set up by a clear ontology. This keeps them clear and controllable, but writing that ontology usually takes hand labels or supervised training. Language models alone, relying on memory, are hard to trust.

TeQoDO exploits the model's skill at SQL programming. Given concepts from modular dialogue system design in its prompt, the model constructs a working ontology from scratch as a data store design task. The result beat transfer learning methods at ontology building, and the generated ontology performed competitively on the downstream job of tracking dialogue state. Tests on Wikipedia and arXiv substance showed the method also scales to much larger ontologies.
arxiv-2507-23558:
Tsipinakis and Parpas study Newton's method for a subclass of well behaved functions in twenty twenty-five. Newton's method is a classic algorithm for minimization. Its theory is well developed for self concordant functions. A local analysis for strongly self concordant functions, a narrower class, was missing.

The known quadratic convergence for the wider class applies here as well. The authors ask whether the narrower class enjoys stronger guarantees. They show its quadratic rate differs from the general case. For a wide range of objectives, convergence is provably faster. The region where local convergence holds is also larger. The results close a gap in the theory of Newton's method. They clarify what extra structure buys in practice.
arxiv-2508-01758:
Pinaki Chakraborty, Tristan Caulfield, and David Pym wrote a paper in 2025 on a logical framework for causality and decision-making in systems and security modeling. The framework assumes only minimal structure about the systems it describes.

The authors model systems as transition systems, formal accounts of states and steps between them. They then apply modal logic, a language for what can and must hold over those changing states. The key new tool is an intervention operator built into the logic, paired with a separating conjunction. The operator acts on a what-if change: hold part of the system fixed, and one sees how changing a part changes the whole. Together the tools capture real causal links between parts. The authors also align the framework with a well-known counterfactual approach to causality. Examples, including microservices in spread-out systems, show how it guides local choice.
arxiv-2508-01958:
Alejandro Mata Ali introduces QUDO, Tensor QUDO, and HOBO formulations in two thousand twenty-five. These are optimization forms for combinatorial problems with varied alphabets. QUDO is quadratic and d-ary, its tensor form adds structure. HOBO covers higher order binary cases in the family.

Plain encodings between the forms are laid out with their limits. Worked cases span the knapsack and traveling salesman problems. Five puzzle games show the forms in play as well. Some games had QUBO forms before, redone here in broader terms. The forms suit quantum and quantum inspired solvers.
arxiv-2508-03358:
Tiago Canario and co-authors build a 2025 tool called Taggus that maps who knows whom inside Portuguese novels. Pulling a cast of characters and their ties from fiction is a hard language task. Standard tools that spot names and tag grammar were not built for it, and they do worse in languages with little labeled training data, such as Portuguese.

Taggus chains several language steps, led by grammar tagging plus a blend of custom rules tuned for fiction. The authors compare it with ready-made name spotters and with a large chat model. Their pipeline beat both at finding characters and the links between them. Such maps let scholars study plot structure and social worlds in books at a scale no reader could manage by hand.
arxiv-2508-03858:
Charles Wang and co-workers put forth a runtime governance setup for self-running AI agents in a 2025 paper called MI9. Agents that plan and act develop new actions no pre-rollout review can fully foresee. Safety must be supervised while the system runs, not only before it ships. MI9 integrates six parts into one rules that watches and steers agents across varied designs without favoring any vendor's stack.

An agency-risk index scores danger at all times, semantic telemetry records what agents mean, and sign-off is monitored without pause. A finite-state fit engine checks actions against allowed patterns, goal-conditioned drift detection notices objectives sliding, and graduated control steps up responses proportionally. Scenario studies are offered as evidence of full coverage.
arxiv-2508-05958:
Yingzhou Li and Jingyu Liu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. Its text introduces hierarchical matrices whose blocks are Tucker tensors, a data-sparse way to hold matrices that come from smooth interaction kernels.

Classic hierarchical matrices store off blocks as low-rank forms. Swapping in Tucker blocks, built by high-dimensional sampling and tensor squeezes, cuts the store further. The authors give builds for the matrix and for its product with a vector, at near-linear cost. Head-to-head tests against a sampling-based hierarchical code show smaller stores and at times faster builds, at like run cost. The frame also fits near-even grids.
arxiv-2508-07058:
Paul Parsons and Prakash Chandra Shukla study how chart designers frame problems in two thousand twenty-five. Design is often told as solving a fixed problem in a known space. That view stresses craft skill and skips how designers judge and define the task. Work in other design fields stresses framing and joint growth of problem and fix.

The pair ran a mixed study with expert designers. Tasks, diaries, and talks showed how experts frame and reframe their briefs. Tricks used spanned sketching, word images, rules of thumb, and tests of failed tries. Framing went on through the whole task, not just at the start. Results call for models that honor this back and forth.
arxiv-2508-07158:
Shankhadeep Mondal, Deguang Han, and Mohapatra ask which backup description of a signal best limits damage when parts of the signal are lost. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Frames describe a signal with some slack, and dual frames rebuild it. When chunks vanish in transit, the choice of dual sets the error.

The team judges duals by the size of their error operators, under three different size measures. They seek the dual that cuts the average error over all loss patterns of a set size. For the gentlest measure they fully solve the problem for even, tight frames. Rules emerge for when the standard dual is the unique best pick. Links between the three measures are also drawn. The results serve speech, imaging, and any system that must rebuild from partial data.
arxiv-2508-08558:
Imre Bartos and Zoltán Haiman published this study in 2025. It reads the fingerprints of GW231123, the heaviest black hole merger yet detected. The pair sits in or above a mass gap where standard star collapse should not leave black holes. Both holes also spin very fast, which repeated mergers struggle to explain. The authors find the two spin arrows point much the same way. Yet both tilt well away from the orbit's axis.

That pattern, they argue, points to growth by swallowing gas. Shared, steady accretion can raise masses and spins together while keeping the spins mutually aligned. Gas disks around galaxy-center black holes are a prime setting. A past record merger, GW190521, may share the same story. Sustained feasting, the authors conclude, shapes the most extreme binaries.
arxiv-2508-09758:
Denti and Laura D'Angelo present a software package for grouping grouped data, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Data often nest, as with patients inside hospitals or students inside schools. Ignoring that nesting can bias results and hurt prediction on new groups.

Their R package fits Bayesian models that cluster both single observations and whole groups at once, while estimating each group's own distribution shape. The models share a common set of building blocks across groups, a recent idea in statistics. Heavy computation is handled by fast code under the hood, with both sampling and shortcut inference options for large data. The authors aim to make these models practical for everyday analysts.
arxiv-2508-10458:
Pooja Chandravanshi and four co-authors engineer a quantum key system in twenty twenty-five. Quantum key distribution promises future-proof secrecy for communications. It is moving from laboratories into real networks. Device imperfections, not protocol math, are now the main obstacle to secure keys.

Their framework implements the BB84 protocol with broader use in mind. Device calibration, synchronization, and optical alignment are treated systematically. Key post-processing gets the same care. A simple sifting algorithm is given that hardware can run easily. Results stress the choice of temporal window, a humble setting with big effects. It trades key rate against the quantum bit error rate. Readers get a builder's guide for turning quantum secrecy into working hardware.
arxiv-2508-13658:
Faruk Alpay and Hamdi Alakkad build a calibrated theory of diffusion across graphs, with constants they can state exactly. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Diffusion smooths signals over networks, and tuning its speed for each graph is essential but slippery.

Their framework blends three known tools: plain Laplacian smoothing, a nonlinear p-Laplacian flow, and a learnable energy drain. For strong nonlinearity they prove sharper decay bounds than standard templates give. They also prove a limit result: no fixed setting can hit universal targets across graphs with different spectra. A calibration algorithm with guarantees answers that limit. Closed-form bounds for key graph gaps and sharp stability constants round out the theory. Small tests confirm the bounds are tight.
arxiv-2508-17958:
Angelo Passariello's dissertation, from twenty twenty-five, extends a stochastic backscatter model from structured to unstructured flow solvers. The model adds random fluctuations to turbulence simulations, with set correlations in space and time. Those variables come from smoothing a random field, which yields a decaying spatial correlation. The smoothing runs along the three coordinate directions of the grid. That works only for structured solvers, which use regular grids. Unstructured solvers use irregular meshes, common for complex shapes.

Laplace smoothing, a mesh-based averaging, can replace the directional smoothing. But the spatial correlation it produces must be derived by analysis, not assumed. Deriving that correlation is the main goal of the dissertation. The work matters for accurate turbulence modeling in real-world flow codes.
arxiv-2508-18158:
Provakar Datta's doctoral thesis, dated 2025, reports precise measures of how neutrons respond to magnetic fields. When electrons bounce off the parts of an atom's core, the pattern tells where charge and flow sit inside. That response is summed up in form factors. Data at high push, where the bounce is hard, are scarce, since such tests are hard to run.

Datta used the ratio method, which takes the neutron's signal as a share of the proton's and so cancels many errors. Two large detectors at a lab caught the bounced electrons and the struck core parts at once. Data came at five push levels, the last far past the old range. The low points match world data, and the high points stretch the map of the neutron for years to come.
arxiv-2508-18258:
Kegreisz presents a paper from twenty twenty-five on a new optimizer for training neural networks in noisy settings. Popular optimizers lean on momentum to size their steps. Noise and shifting tasks can make those size estimates stale. The new method splits direction from size cleanly. Momentum smooths only the direction of travel. Step size comes from the freshest gradient's magnitude instead. A variant stretches the momentum window over time on a log schedule.

Convergence guarantees match other sign-based methods. Gains show strongly in noisy reinforcement learning tests. Calm tasks stay competitive with standard tools. Simplicity and speed are stressed throughout.
arxiv-2508-18958:
Matteo Contini and co-authors present a drone-based method for mapping coral in a 2025 arXiv paper. Pixel-level labels over wide reef areas are a bottleneck for machine learning in ecology. Their framework trains a segmentation model from weak labels instead.

Underwater photos give fine-scale class calls, while drone images cover broad areas. Point-level calls become coarse masks that supervise training on the aerial views. A second pass trains on the model's own refined output to sharpen edges. On hand-labeled reef zones, the model reached strong pixel accuracy. New coral classes can be added with ease.
arxiv-2509-00058:
Eric Zhang, Li Wei, Sarah Chen, and Michael Wang compare four dysfluency detection models in 2025 on more than raw scores. Dysfluency means breaks in speech flow, such as repeats and blocks in stuttering. Clinics need models that doctors can control and understand, not just accurate ones, before they will adopt them.

Four approaches are weighed on performance, controllability, and explainability across many data sets, with clinician input. Two light models are fast and simple but opaque. One modular model best balances accuracy with clinical clarity. A fourth shows promise but could not be fully rebuilt by the team. The study maps trade-offs that builders must face when speech tools move toward real care.
arxiv-2509-00258:
Erwan Dereure, Emmanuel Akame Mfoumou, and David Holcman assess one-dimensional cluster stability in 2025 by trimming extreme points. Given a sample of independent points on a line, the span shrinks as the most extreme points are removed one by one. The diameter-shrinkage ratio quantifies that relative reduction at each step.

The team derives formulas, with finite-sample corrections, for the expected shrinkage under uniform and Gaussian models. The two curves stay distinct even after moderate trimming. A simple rule assigns each sample to the closer profile, beating the classic likelihood-ratio test in small or noisy samples while staying consistent for large ones. The criterion also plugs into clustering methods to judge stability.
arxiv-2509-00458:
Fabrizio Chinu reports a measurement made with the ALICE detector for the ALICE Collaboration. The work tests perturbative quantum chromodynamics, a method that computes strong-force rates step by step, using beauty hadrons, particles that contain a beauty quark, made in proton-proton hits.

Chinu rebuilds B-zero mesons from their decay into a D meson and a charged pion, using data from LHC Run 3 at an energy stated in the record. The rate he finds, tracked against sideways momentum and rapidity, a measure of direction, is set beside modern calculations. Agreement or gaps here check how well the theory handles heavy quark production.
arxiv-2509-00558: Thibault Damour, writing alone, sums up joint work begun in 2008 with A A Starobinsky. The work was never finished. The pair tried to apply the stochastic approach to quantum gravity. That approach treats long-wave quantum effects as random noise. They focused on infrared effects, meaning effects at very large scales. The setting was an inflationary space-time, an early universe that expands fast. Damour presents the results reached in those first stages. The text preserves ideas from a project that stopped early.
arxiv-2509-00758:
Dongdong Wei, with two co-authors, studies double-layered vacuum bubbles. These bubbles can form during phase transitions in the early universe. The setting has multiple vacua, meaning several stable states. Standard transitions produce single-wall bubbles. Those bubbles expand and collide with each other.

The team uses lattice simulations to evolve the fields on a grid. They show flyover transitions can produce double-layered bubbles. Such bubbles arise by crossing two barriers in a row. The team tracks wall speedup, collisions, and trapped regions. Double-layered bubbles behave quite unlike single-wall ones. The difference bears on signals such as gravitational waves. It also bears on baryogenesis, the origin of the matter imbalance.
arxiv-2509-00858:
Wei-Chun Chen and one co-author, Wei-Hsuan Yu, establish upper bounds for two-distance sets, point sets in Euclidean space or on a sphere whose points use only two distinct distances. Bounding the largest such set is a classic problem in discrete geometry.

Their main recipe is the spectral method: they construct Seidel matrices, matrices that encode the distance relations between points, and apply eigenvalue analysis to derive explicit bounds. For Euclidean space, they bound the cardinality in terms of dimension and the ratio of the two distances. For spherical sets, two bounds are given depending on the sign of a sum of inner products, and one coincides with the relative bound for equiangular lines in one higher dimension.
arxiv-2509-01058:
Health falsehoods spread fast online, and replies that correct them often use words many readers cannot follow. Xiaoying Song, with five co-authors, builds a system that writes such replies at a reading level matched to its audience. Their method joins search-based generation with learning from rewards.

The system first pulls in facts written for a chosen literacy level, meaning how well a reader handles health text. A reward score then blends user likes with plain readability checks, guiding the output toward that level. Tests show the replies were easier to read and more liked than those from rival methods. Song and the team argue this can make public health messages fairer and clearer.
arxiv-2509-01558:
Promotions in online marketplaces do not act on one item alone: treating one product can change the fate of its neighbors. Bram van den Akker studies uplift modeling, a method that estimates the extra profit a promotion causes, under such clustered network interference. Standard uplift methods assume no interference, an assumption whose failure leads to poor policies in real marketplaces.

Van den Akker builds a practical method around an interference-aware estimator, used as a learning objective that gradient methods can optimize directly. Combined with proven response transformation techniques, the framework aims straight at economic outcomes such as incremental profit. Simulations show the approach beats interference-naive methods by a wide margin, above all when interference effects grow. Guidance is also given for adapting profit estimation to settings where items influence each other in clusters.
arxiv-2509-01658:
Zhenyu Wu and seven co-authors present MoTo, an add-on module that lets a fixed robot arm work while its base moves. Fixed arm systems can handle many tasks but cannot travel across a room. MoTo adds travel skill without new training data drawn from moving robots. Vision and language models help the system find where the robot should park.

The method picks docking points near a target object and plans paths for both the base and the arm. Key points on the object and the arm guide the motion so the arm stays in reach. Tests on a standard benchmark and with a real robot beat prior methods on success rate. The gain comes with no extra training examples.
arxiv-2509-02058:
Luca Bianchi, Carlo Marconi, Laura Ares, Davide Bacco, and Jan Sperling join two forms of boson sampling into one scheme. Boson sampling sends light bits through a web of optics to draw hard samples. One form counts single light bits, while the next form uses squeezed light states. A join lets rich states like squeezed light join the more new schemes.

A math frame based on generating functions treats multi bit light under smooth changes in one tongue. Those tools let unlike light based platforms meet and work as one. Code based tests grade the joined sampler on speed, hardness, and scale. Measures of quantum links show the kind of links the mixed scheme can make. The work widens what sampling rigs can try.
arxiv-2509-02458:
Borja Ocejo and nine co-authors wrote a 2025 applied machine learning paper on deciding when to send notifications in a large production system, LinkedIn's. Each message trades user value against fatigue, and choices form a long sequence rather than single steps.

Earlier offline reinforcement learning, such as Conservative Q-Learning, proved unstable and hard to reproduce at scale. The team reframes the learning task with Decision Transformers, which cast policy learning as supervised learning conditioned on target returns. Additions include a multi-reward design for ongoing tasks and quantile-based conditioning on those returns. A production system with circular sequence buffers supports near-real-time decisions. Online tests raised session activity over the older agent while keeping fatigue in check.
arxiv-2509-02558:
Sahel Sharifymoghaddam, Yijun Ge, and Jimmy Lin wrote a 2025 information retrieval paper revisiting BRIGHT, a benchmark of long, reasoning-heavy search queries like those used with retrieval-augmented generation. They supply strong, reproducible baselines inside three open toolkits.

While rebuilding the lexical baseline, the authors found an under-documented detail: BM25 weighting applied to the query side, a variant called BM25Q. On long multi-sentence queries, that variant beat standard BM25 and became the strongest word-based baseline. An audit of the benchmark corpus also uncovered data quality problems, with suggested fixes. Tests on five other benchmarks show the query-weighting gain is mostly specific to BRIGHT. Blending it with standard BM25 gave the steadiest gains overall.
arxiv-2509-02758:
Michael Bouzinier and four co-authors present a 2025 mathematics education paper reviving an ontology-based system for organising Euclidean geometry problems, first built in the 1990s. Geometry trains logical reasoning, yet it has faded from many curricula.

The ontology sorts problems, solutions, and skills into linked facts, objects, and methods, letting teachers track student abilities in fine detail. Its core device is the solution graph, a directed acyclic graph holding multiple solution paths and the skills each step needs. Problem selection can then match teaching goals precisely. The framework was tested in practice by annotating problems numbering in the thousands across three decades. Open problems remain automated annotation and solution checking, which would cut teacher validation time and give self-learners instant feedback.
arxiv-2509-02958:
Kaustuv Mukherji and 7 co-authors introduced a 2025 logic system called LAT Logic for reasoning about events over time. Many real problems are non-Markovian, meaning the future depends on more than the present state. A useful logic must also handle an open world, where unknown facts stay unknown rather than false.

LAT Logic extends an earlier annotated program framework and adds a lower lattice, a ranked scale of truth values that supports that open stance. The authors bound the cost of grounding, the step that turns general rules into concrete ones, even with endless possible constants. Their open-source tool, PyReason, ran far faster and leaner in tests. In game-like simulations it even raised agent win rates by capturing richer time patterns.
arxiv-2509-03158:
Yiyu Tang wrote a 2025 paper in harmonic analysis on Hardy spaces over product domains. A product domain varies in several free directions at once. The topic is how a fractional integral, an averaging tool with a power-law weight, acts on such spaces.

Using vector-valued theory for singular integrals, he proves a Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality in this setting. It parallels a classic result with the same name. The same technique shows the iterated Hilbert transform stays bounded there. As a byproduct, several recent Hardy type results on product spaces get new proofs. Those proofs skip the heavy Calderón-Zygmund machinery and run in a much simpler way.
arxiv-2509-03758:
Alvaro Almeida Gomez turns to interpolating functions over smooth curved surfaces, called manifolds, from scattered measurements in a 2025 research paper. Rebuilding a full function from sparse points is a basic task in data science and geometry. Classical kernel methods use one fixed smoothing width everywhere, which fits unevenly sampled regions poorly.

His method pairs a Gaussian kernel interpolant of Nadaraya-Watson type with a bandwidth set by Voronoi tessellation, a division of the surface into cells around each point. The width adapts to the local sampling geometry, with no training, tuning, or preprocessing. The construction is an explicit closed formula that reproduces every observed value exactly. Its intrinsic gradient vanishes at sample points, and dense sampling smooths away high-frequency wiggles. The formula also matches minimising a total-variation style functional, linking it to compressed sensing ideas. Evaluation at any new point costs time linear in the sample count.
arxiv-2509-03858:
Zizhao He and five co-authors confirm lensed quasar and galaxy candidates with spectroscopy from DESI and the Palomar 200-inch telescope in a 2025 research paper. Gravitational lensing bends light from a distant quasar around a foreground galaxy, multiplying its images. Confirmed lenses probe cosmology, black hole growth alongside host galaxies, and dark matter's distribution.

The team cross-matched over seventeen hundred candidates from earlier imaging surveys with the DESI survey's first data release. Spectra for hundreds of unique systems followed, joined by Palomar Double Spectrograph observations. Two lensed quasars are confirmed outright, with distant sources and measured bending scales. Twelve further likely lensed quasars match a simple lens model, show lens galaxies in imaging, and have at least one spectrum; most need one more spectrum for full confirmation. Eight new static strong lenses, from galaxy to group scale, are also reported.
arxiv-2509-04358:
Atikkhan Faridkhan Nilgar and two co-authors examine what makes people trust a coaching robot with private information in a 2025 research paper. Social robots increasingly support well-being coaching, sometimes beside human professionals, and they hear sensitive disclosures. An online study with two hundred participants varied three factors. One was how openly the robot explains data use. Another was how much control users hold over their information. The third was whether the robot acts proactively or only when asked.

Even after granting general access, participants wanted explicit say over interpretation and sharing during sessions. Conditions offering that control earned significantly higher privacy and trust ratings. Transparency and proactivity alone showed weak or no effects. Robot designers should build real user controls, not just notices.
arxiv-2509-04458:
Daniel B Hier and two co-authors ask why language models fail to attach the right codes to medical terms in a 2025 research paper. Systems like the Human Phenotype Ontology and the Gene Ontology sort medical and genetic knowledge with strict codes. Models often handle medical text well yet mislink those codes. Two strong systems, GPT-4o and LLaMa 3.1 405B, were tested across both systems. Nine possible causes were tested, covering term familiarity, code usage, word shape, and system layout.

One factor dominated: how much exposure the model had to the codes themselves. Single-factor and combined checks agreed on that ranking. Creators of medical AI should ensure code-rich training material, the evidence suggests.
arxiv-2509-04558:
Michael Zhang and nineteen co-authors report a carbon-rich atmosphere with strong winds on a planet orbiting a pulsar in a 2025 astrophysics paper. A few Jupiter-mass objects circle pulsars, the spinning remains of dead stars, and one resembles a hot Jupiter in density and temperature. The James Webb Space Telescope watched that planet's emission across a full orbit. Unlike any planet around a normal star, its air is rich in molecular carbon, with compounds of two and three carbon atoms, and winds blow strongly westward.

Carbon outweighs oxygen by more than a hundredfold, an extreme never seen elsewhere. Black widow companions, stripped stellar cores, were expected to show varied elements instead. Formation theories face a severe challenge from this strange world.
arxiv-2509-04658:
Robots that judge a surface by both sight and touch are the subject of Surformer v2, a 2025 classifier paper by Manish Kansana, lead author with three co-authors. Surface material classification helps robots handle objects more safely and skilfully. The model fuses visual and tactile streams at decision level.

Each branch first works alone: a convolutional network handles images, and an encoder-only transformer handles touch readings. Their output scores are then combined with a learnable weighted sum. Evaluated on the Touch and Go benchmark, the design keeps strong performance while letting each sense contribute on its own strengths.
arxiv-2509-04958:
Poverty in cities has many faces that a single satellite signal cannot capture. Sungwon Park, lead author with six co-authors, learn a multidimensional poverty representation from very high-resolution satellite imagery in a 2025 paper. Models based only on urbanisation traits correlate weakly with poverty, since unplanned growth hides economic inequality.

Their framework fuses three traits: accessibility to essential infrastructure, housing morphology from building footprints, and economic activity from nightlight intensity. A backdoor adjustment uses morphology during training to reduce spurious nightlight correlations. The unified representation aims at precise urban poverty mapping for policy and research.
arxiv-2509-05258:
Training very large language models across hundreds of machines is described from hands-on experience by Alexander Interrante-Grant and four co-authors in a 2025 computing paper. Frontier labs spend heavily on this training, yet they publish little about how the pipelines perform at scale.

The authors focus on distributed training, moving huge datasets across many nodes, and spreading work across graphics processors so the hardware stays busy. Practical advice in this area is scarce in public writing, and working at this scale brings problems that small projects never meet. Their account aims to demystify the pre-training pipeline for other teams. The lessons concern performance tuning rather than model design.
arxiv-2509-05358:
Phone sensors carried by Nigerian drivers supply the data for detecting drink-influenced driving in a 2025 paper by Iniakpokeikiye Peter Thompson and two co-authors. Alcohol-impaired driving is a major safety problem, and enforcement tools are limited in many lower-income settings.

The dataset records motion sensors and satellite positions from real trips in Nigeria. A decision tree model, trained on behavioural and time features, flagged every alcohol-influenced trip in testing, though with moderate precision. Speed variation, course deviation, and time of day were the strongest signs. The long-term aim is a phone app that warns in real time and nudges safer behaviour, offering a cheap, scalable route to road safety.
arxiv-2509-05658:
Keeping an X-ray beam on target for hours is handled with a time-aware optimiser by Aashwin Mishra and six co-authors in a 2025 optics paper. Brighter modern light sources enable intricate experiments, but drift ruins the precision those experiments demand.

Their data-driven method, time-varying Bayesian optimisation, models how the optimum itself moves with time. It is demonstrated on a split-and-delay optical system of six crystals with twelve input dimensions. Simulations cover steady linear drift, rough non-smooth drift, and multi-objective settings under constraints. The approach adapts to other beam guidance hardware, the authors note, aiming at sub-micron and nanoradian stability across long experiments.
arxiv-2509-05958:
A flat electronic band in the layered material yttrium monochloride needs more than the textbook dice lattice model, argue Jianqi Zhong and four co-authors in a 2025 paper. YCl is an electride, a crystal where loose electrons act like anions, and it hosts the first observed dice lattice flat band. A simple three-band picture captured the headline features but misses a coupling unique to this material.

The authors build an ab initio multi-orbital Hubbard model, adding local interactions across the layer, orbital, and valley degrees of freedom. That fuller model predicts a robust ferromagnetic ground state and electrically tunable correlated quantum anomalous Hall phases, effects absent from the single-orbital version. The work opens electride systems as a fresh arena for correlated topological physics.
arxiv-2509-06058:
Scattering amplitudes are computed through paths in phase space in a 2025 paper by Joon-Hwi Kim. The worldline formalism rewrites particle scattering as sums over paths; Kim moves the method from position space to phase space, where position and momentum appear together. The Feynman rules there show shared features tied to the symplectic geometry of the target space.

Noncompact worldline topologies then automate the LSZ reduction steps under phase-space boundary conditions, once the moduli spaces are pinned down. A change to noncanonical coordinates makes the rules cubic and exposes gauge invariance directly. As a test, Kim computes multi-photon Compton amplitudes up to six points in the classical limit, and handles Yang-Mills and gravity Compton scattering in the same uniform way over combined plane-wave backgrounds. The payoff is a cleaner path from setup to answer.
arxiv-2509-06158:
How many particles a jet produces, and with what pattern, is recomputed in a 2025 paper led by Xiang-Pan Duan with four co-authors. The authors revisit Koba-Nielsen-Olesen scaling for quark- and gluon-initiated jets, folding energy conservation into the double logarithmic approximation. The modified theory departs substantially from the standard one and lands closer to recently proposed QCD-inspired formulas.

With its two parameters fixed, the modified approximation describes ATLAS measurements of charged-particle counts in the two leading jets of proton collisions. It does so across a wide energy range, within uncertainties, and matches PYTHIA simulations. Cross-checks against quark and gluon jet samples separated by the jet topics method support the picture, though experimental uncertainties remain sizable.
arxiv-2509-06258:
Making hadrons with two heavy quarks inside collisions that barely touch is the subject of a 2025 paper led by Jun Jiang with seven co-authors. In ultraperipheral heavy-ion collisions, the nuclei miss and interact through their electromagnetic fields. The authors compute production there of heavy quarkonia, doubly heavy baryons, and doubly heavy tetraquarks.

Numerical results say several of these rare states are within experimental reach at the high-luminosity LHC and a future circular collider. The states include the eta-c quarkonium, the doubly charmed baryon, and the Tcc tetraquark. The authors present ultraperipheral collisions as a fresh avenue for producing and studying doubly heavy hadrons, complementing direct collision programs.
arxiv-2509-07158:
Guanzhou Hu and 2 co-authors introduce Bodega in 2025, a protocol that lets computers in a distributed system read the latest data from a nearby copy. Distributed systems keep copies of data on many machines so work can continue if one fails. Linearizable reads must return the newest value, and older systems usually force such reads to travel to a leader machine, which slows distant users.

Bodega solves this with roster leases, an agreement scheme that tracks which sets of copies may answer reads locally. Guards against interfering writes, early accept notices, and light heartbeats keep the scheme practical. In tests on real wide-area clusters, Bodega sped up average reads by about 5.6 to 13.1 times over earlier methods under moderate write traffic. Write speed stayed comparable, and the design layers onto classic consensus without special demands.
arxiv-2509-07658:
Claudia Cancellieri and 4 co-authors analyze the structure of co-sputtered copper thin films mixed with niobium or palladium in a 2025 paper. Co-sputtering two metals at room temperature freezes disorder into the film, and telling the two metal phases apart at the nanoscale is extremely challenging. The cases contrast sharply: niobium barely mixes with copper, while palladium alloys with it readily.

The team presents a model for how the alloy element distributes itself inside magnetron-sputtered copper films. The model is fitted to diffraction patterns from several geometries and checked against elemental distributions from energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. It aims to separate each phase's contribution, locate the second element within the lattice, quantify its content, and assess internal disorder. Reliable structure models underpin thin film design for electronics and coatings.
arxiv-2509-07858:
Training data for code-writing language models can be made by small open models themselves, argue Xinyu Zhang and 7 co-authors in a 2025 paper. Large code models usually learn from examples distilled from costly closed systems. The team instead bootstraps a small model of about seven billion parameters into a data synthesizer, a maker of practice examples.

Their method, SCoder, works in rounds. A few excellent synthesis examples from a strong model first teach the small model how to create good training data. Repeated self-distillation then sharpens that skill, so the model generates better code instructions on its own. Cheaper, self-made data could let open code models improve without depending on proprietary teachers.
arxiv-2509-07958:
Higgs bosons produced alongside two jets are measured without assuming a specific production theory, in a 2025 particle physics paper by the CMS Collaboration. The Higgs decays into two W bosons, whose own decay products, an electron, a muon, and invisible momentum carried off by neutrinos, mark the events. Data come from proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider.

A machine-learned discriminating variable separates signal from background while staying agnostic about which Higgs production hypothesis is right. The result is a differential cross section, showing how often the process occurs across ranges of measured quantities. Model-independent measurements age well: later theories can be tested against them without redoing the experiment's analysis from scratch.
arxiv-2509-08158:
Computing distance across a curved surface sounds simple, but meshes for complex shapes are painful to build. Tony Wong, Shingyu Leung, and Byungjoon Lee introduce the Closest Point Heat Method in a 2025 research paper. Their target is the surface Eikonal equation, which describes distance and wavefront travel on surfaces. The method builds on the classical heat method, known for simplicity and speed.

Closest point techniques free the computation from surface meshes. The surface can instead be given implicitly, as the zero level of a function. That embedding keeps the heat method's efficiency and its respect for surface geometry. Numerical experiments on benchmark shapes confirm accuracy and convergence. The method also handles complex geometries well. It should serve graphics, robotics, and medical imaging tasks that need distances on surfaces given only implicitly.
arxiv-2509-08358:
Synthetic toxic text, generated by language models, turns out to be a poor teacher for detoxification systems in a 2025 study by Sergey Pletenev and 2 co-authors. Detoxification models rewrite harmful text into neutral text, and training them needs toxic examples that are costly and unpleasant to collect from people. Synthetic data looked like an escape from that bottleneck.

Using activation-patched Llama 3 and Qwen models, the team generated toxic counterparts for neutral texts from two datasets. Models fine-tuned on the synthetic data consistently performed worse than those trained on human-written data. The lesson generalises: in sensitive domains, machine-made training data can quietly lack whatever makes real examples instructive, and fluency is no substitute.
arxiv-2509-08658:
Kwok Ho Wan and 2 co-authors show how to simulate magic state cultivation with very few Clifford terms in a 2025 paper. Magic states are a costly resource for fault tolerant quantum computing. Cultivation circuits grow them, but their non-Clifford parts are hard to simulate.

The authors write a key circuit state as a sum of about eight Clifford diagrams on average at a stated noise level. A naive split of all non-Clifford pieces would need millions of terms. Numerical tests with their tsim tool reach millions of shots per second on a laptop for smaller circuits. The method helps simulate the escape stage into larger circuits.
arxiv-2509-08958:
Foam looks stable one day and collapses the next, and evaporation may quietly tip the balance. F. Boulogne and E. Rio review that overlooked factor in a 2025 research paper. Evaporation can stabilize a foam or hasten its bursting, depending on conditions. The review opens with evaporating drops, where cooling drives internal flows through surface tension gradients.

The authors then survey foam films and foams across three systems: pure liquids, non-volatile surfactants, and volatile surfactants. Evaporation can shift film temperatures significantly, changing drainage and rupture behavior. Several open questions remain, and the authors sketch research paths toward answering them. Foam stability matters far beyond soap: firefighting, food, and oil recovery all depend on it. A factor this basic, still this unsettled, marks a genuine gap in soft matter physics.
arxiv-2509-09058:
Ajay Kumar and 2 co-authors optimize variant calling pipelines on human genomes using GPU machines in a 2025 paper. Variant calling finds differences between an individual genome and a reference. It is compute heavy, so workloads often run in the cloud.

Machine learning predicts run times for each pipeline stage from features like sequence size, read quality, and read length. A scheduling method inspired by flexible job shop problems then builds execution plans for the machines. Careful synchronization runs the plans across hardware types. On public genomes, the method doubles speed versus a greedy approach and beats a dynamic method by a clear margin.
arxiv-2509-09158:
Priyanka Rushikesh Chaudhary and 1 co-author present IoTFuzzSentry, a protocol guided fuzzer for IoT devices, in a 2025 paper. Internet of Things devices run light servers for tasks like video streaming. Flaws in their security layers can allow unauthorized access and data leakage.

Crafted transport and application packets are mutated and injected to probe commercial devices. The tool found four vulnerability types, including credential leakage, live video access, image access, and command injection. Exploits are shown on three devices, and findings were disclosed to vendors. Two public CVE identifiers have been published, with one more awaiting. Traffic from six more devices suggests similar flaws may be widespread.
arxiv-2509-09558:
Akshit Achara and 3 co-authors probe demographic bias in brain scan classifiers in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Deep learning systems can diagnose Alzheimer's disease from magnetic resonance images, which remain the standard tool for viewing the brain. Trouble starts when a model leans on shortcut features tied to race or sex rather than to disease, harming groups that are already underrepresented.

The authors first test whether models can read race or sex from three-dimensional scans at all. They then unbalance training data by those traits and watch for performance drops. Attribution maps across brain regions complete the picture. Across several data sets and two model families, both kinds of shortcut were found.
arxiv-2509-09758:
