Using an integral identity of Sekigawa, the authors obtain a global characterization of AH1 from apparently weaker conditions. They then take steps toward a full classification of these manifolds. On four-dimensional Lie algebras they prove a uniqueness result. Exactly one such algebra admits an invariant non-Kähler structure of this class. The work tightens the map of how close non-Kähler geometry can sit to Kähler geometry.
arxiv-2510-05458:
Deo and colleagues built a test for a skill that AI assistants need every day. Social inference means reading a conversation and judging what people likely mean or feel. Models often miss sarcasm, irony, and other quiet social cues in transcripts. Their 2025 dataset, SocialNLI, targets exactly those hard cases.

Each item pairs a short dialogue with a claim about the scene. Human judges scored how plausible each claim is and explained their scores in writing. The dialogues come from the TV show Friends and were chosen for tricky social moments. The set holds about 1,400 human-scored items plus a larger machine-scored split. Tests show current models fall well short of human judgment on these items. Counterfactual tasks, which change one detail and ask again, expose the same weakness. The authors offer the data as a diagnostic tool for building socially aware assistants.
arxiv-2510-05858:
Fu and colleagues adapt language models to phone conversations without labeled data. Summarizers trained on clean text stumble on noisy real-world call transcripts. Fine-tuning needs costly human annotations that businesses rarely have. Their 2025 DACP approach instead continues pre-training on unlabeled business conversations.

The adaptation uses large-scale automatic speech recognition transcripts from real calls. Continual pre-training then improves summarization both in-domain and out-of-domain. Generalization and robustness survive the domain shift intact. Data selection strategy matters, and the paper distills practical guidelines. Quality and diversity in curation beat raw volume for adaptation. Smaller models benefit most because production inference costs favor them. The method is self-supervised, so no annotation budget is required. Privacy concerns rule out annotating customer calls with outside services. Industrial summarization is the deployment target throughout the study.
arxiv-2510-05958:
Rebotier studies random population growth in a 2025 paper on branching processes with interaction. These models track a population whose size changes through births, deaths, and bursts. An added drift term captures how crowding can help or hinder growth. He asks when a population that starts huge quickly drops to finite size. The question is known as coming down from infinity in this field.

He gives clear conditions on the drift and the branching rule for this drop. The result needs no finite mean for the jump sizes, which widens its reach. His proof also rules out blow up of the population in finite time. As the start value grows, paths settle onto one limit path from above. That limit path solves a stochastic equation in the strong sense. The tools are comparison bounds and Lyapunov functions, which he reviews for wider use.
arxiv-2510-06058:
Grabowski builds a Galois theory for maps that symmetry groups cannot see in a 2025 algebra paper. In positive characteristic, purely inseparable morphisms identify points differing only by p-th powers. Automorphisms are blind to such maps, so classical Galois theory says nothing about them.

The replacement dictionary uses differential operators instead of symmetries. Grabowski proves that a purely inseparable morphism corresponds to a finite saturated subalgebra of differential operators. Extending the dictionary to all such subalgebras leads to power towers, layered field structures modeled on foliations. Power towers support versions of core foliation theorems, including a Frobenius theorem whose local form can change from point to point. The theory also yields a formula for pulling back canonical divisors under these maps. From that formula come new not-Lüroth results on which varieties projective space can cover inseparably.
arxiv-2510-06158:
Watanabe and colleagues at Northeastern University examine how wearable heart signals should be cleaned in a 2025 health sensing study. Photoplethysmography sensors yield inter-beat intervals and pulse rate variability, used as markers of stress and mental health. Preprocessing is not standardized, and prior work mostly chased motion artifacts.

Beat-detection errors stay large even in low-motion recordings, so artifact removal alone cannot guarantee accuracy. They tested how a band-pass filter's cutoff frequencies change beat detection. A fixed filter produced substantial errors, and the best settings differed markedly across people and tasks. Tuning cutoffs per person and task raised beat-location accuracy by up to about seven percent. It also cut interval and variability errors by tens to well over a hundred milliseconds. The result argues for adaptive, signal-specific preprocessing in wearable mental-health measurement.
arxiv-2510-06558:
Jiacong Zhu, Eloy de Lera Acedo, Kaan Artuc, and Xuelei Chen design hardware for a space mission called CosmoCube. Their 2025 paper describes a spectrometer that will orbit the Moon. It will listen for the faint global 21-centimeter signal from the early universe. The far side of the Moon shields it from Earth's radio noise and ionosphere.

A satellite leaves little room, weight, or power to spare. So the team built the receiver calibration system around a radio-frequency system-on-chip. That single chip merges converters, processors, and programmable logic. A vector network analyzer module on the chip keeps the receiver's measurements honest. Simulations showed the main error source in detail. Mistakes grow when measuring weak reflections at low power. Lab tests then checked the module's output power, accuracy, stability, and trace noise. The design shows how a full calibration lab can shrink onto one board.
arxiv-2510-06658:
Jiaman He and four colleagues ask whether machine labels can pass as human ones. Their 2025 paper studies annotation, where people tag data for research and industry. Language models now do much of this tagging. Most checks only ask whether model labels match a human gold standard. The authors instead ask whether the two are statistically equivalent.

Their method compares labeling behavior across individuals, not just final accuracy. It needs only a small number of annotated items to run. They tested it on two datasets, MovieLens 100K and PolitiFact. On the movie data, the model's labels were statistically indistinguishable from human labels. On the fact-checking data, the model failed the equivalence test. The contrast shows that machine annotation quality depends heavily on the task. Subjective, context-heavy judgments remain harder for models to mimic. The test gives teams a cheap way to check before swapping humans for machines.
arxiv-2510-07058:
Ori Nizan, Oren Shrout, and Ayellet Tal define a kind of image search based on concepts rather than looks. Their 2025 paper introduces concept retrieval, where a query image should fetch others telling a similar story. Retrieval rewards visual or semantic similarity instead. Two photos can share a concept, like celebration, while looking nothing alike.

Their method studies the neighborhood of the query in embedding space. Each neighbor shares at least one concept with the query, but neighbors need not share concepts with each other. Modeling that neighborhood with a two-humped distribution exposes the concept structure. The approach needs no training data, which matters because ground truth here is elusive. New evaluation metrics tailored to the task accompany the method. In a human study, people preferred their results over classical retrieval results. The preference margin was fourteen percent in the comparison. Retrieved sets showed greater diversity, as intended.
arxiv-2510-07458:
Jung and co-authors test whether language models can grade political speeches for populism as well as trained human coders. Their 2025 paper addresses a measurement bottleneck in political science. Scoring the people-versus-elites framing in speeches is slow, costly, and hard to scale across languages. The team mimicked human coder training with prompts: a rubric and anchor examples guide the model's step-by-step reasoning. The Global Populism Database, a large set of leaders' speeches already graded by experts, supplied both the training materials and the answer key for validation. Multiple commercial and open models were tried.

The best prompting strategy brought model classifications to parity with expert human coders. The models handled the context-sensitive judgments that make holistic grading valuable, rather than counting crude keywords. That parity held across the database's varied leaders and settings.
arxiv-2510-07658:
Fontaine and three coauthors wrote this 2025 quantum optics paper on making special states of light on a chip. Non-Gaussian states of light are essential for photonic quantum computing. The usual recipe measures squeezed light, which works only by chance and needs cryogenic parts. The team proposes a deterministic source instead. Their design uses tiny microring resonators built from a known semiconductor material.

The source relies on cascaded four-wave mixing, where light waves interact inside the rings. Working in a well-understood low-power regime, the design generates photon triplets directly. The authors show it can do so efficiently with realistic ring designs. The light emerges in a single clean set of modes, which makes it easy to characterize. Reaching stronger output also looks possible at practical pump powers. A chip-scale source like this could supply non-Gaussian light on demand for future quantum devices.
arxiv-2510-07758:
Zhang, Sun, Zhang, and Liu wrote this 2025 deep learning paper on why some trained networks generalize better than others. A common clue is sharpness, which measures how steep the loss sits near a solution. Flat minima are thought to generalize well. Many sharpness measures, however, correlate only weakly with generalization. The authors set out to design a measure that tracks it, grounded in the spread of curvature directions.

Their measure, Rényi sharpness, uses Rényi entropy over the eigenvalues of the loss Hessian. Evenly spread eigenvalues score as desirable under this view. The authors prove generalization bounds stated in terms of the measure. Experiments confirmed a rank correlation between Rényi sharpness and generalization. They also turn the measure into a training method, RSAM. It beat rival sharpness-aware methods in their tests, with accuracy gains approaching two and a half points over the standard baseline.
arxiv-2510-07958:
Zhang and nine coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on question answering when a question has several right answers. Standard benchmarks assume one gold answer, so models get punished for valid alternatives. Human labeling of every alternative is too costly to scale. The authors present A2Search, a training framework that handles ambiguity without annotation. An automatic pipeline first detects ambiguous questions on its own.

Trajectory sampling gathers candidate alternative answers, and evidence checks verify them. Reinforcement learning then trains the model with a reward that credits any of the valid answers. On eight open-domain benchmarks, the system set new state-of-the-art results. A seven-billion-parameter version beat a rival more than four times its size on multi-hop tests. Analyses showed the model genuinely resolves ambiguity rather than memorizing one answer. The authors argue that embracing ambiguity is essential for question answering that people can trust.
arxiv-2510-08158:
Yuan and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on language models that refuse harmless requests because a trigger word resembles something unsafe. The authors built two benchmarks. One holds hundreds of single-turn prompts annotated with the keywords that provoke refusal. The other embeds refusal tests in thirty multi-turn dialogue scenarios. Exaggerated refusals persisted across diverse models and grew worse in multi-turn settings.

To fix the behavior without retraining, they used post-hoc explanations to find each refusal's trigger. Three lightweight interventions followed: ignore-word instructions, prompt rephrasing, and attention steering at inference time. Tests on four instruction-tuned models showed compliance on safe prompts improving substantially, while safety stayed robust. The work reframes over-refusal as a diagnosable calibration problem, not an unavoidable cost of safety tuning.
arxiv-2510-08258:
Parinya Karndumri constructs new solutions in a five-dimensional supergravity theory in a 2025 arXiv paper on string theory. Supergravity joins gravity with supersymmetry, a symmetry linking different kinds of particles. His theory has a gauge group combining a circle symmetry with shifts in three directions. It descends from a seven-dimensional theory placed on a curved surface. Holography, the paper's frame, links such gravity theories to quantum field theories.

The setup has a supersymmetric anti-de Sitter vacuum, a space with constant negative curvature. That vacuum matches a superconformal field theory from M5-branes wrapped on the curved surface. Karndumri finds flow solutions that deform this theory toward non-conformal phases in the deep interior. He also builds interfaces between phases and several black string and black hole solutions. All solutions lift to M-theory, the eleven-dimensional parent theory, he shows.
arxiv-2510-08358:
Alexander Belyaev, Pierre-Alain Fayolle, and Michael Cohen introduce SPICE in a 2025 arXiv paper, a simple way to fix dark and hazy photos. Low light, fog, sand dust, and murky water all wash out image detail. Many enhancement tools are complex models that need training data. SPICE instead builds a filter that mimics how the damage forms.

From that damage filter, the method derives an approximate reverse filter that undoes the harm. The same idea serves both dark photo brightening and haze removal tasks. Experiments showed the approach is highly competitive with leading techniques. It often surpassed them on extremely dark images and on hazy ones. A key selling point is simplicity: the core method needs just a few lines of MATLAB code. The authors publish their MATLAB implementations openly for others to use.
arxiv-2510-08458:
Kwanseok Kim and co-authors reframe video summarization as generation rather than scoring, in a 2025 arXiv paper. A good summary is subjective: different viewers keep different moments from the same video. Older systems regress to one averaged frame score across raters, erasing that variety. Their method, SummDiff, learns the distribution of good summaries instead.

SummDiff adopts diffusion models, a first for video summarization, the authors say. Conditioned on the input video, it generates multiple candidate summaries that fit varied tastes. Experiments showed state-of-the-art performance on several standard benchmarks. Its summaries also aligned closely with individual annotators' own preferences, not just averages. The team adds new analysis of the knapsack step, which packs chosen frames under a length budget. That final step had been overlooked in past evaluations, they argue.
arxiv-2510-08558:
Kai Zhang and a large team propose 'early experience' as a middle path for training language agents, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Agents should learn from their own experience, but reinforcement learning stalls where rewards are unverifiable or rollouts are long. Most agents instead imitate expert data, which is costly to scale and generalizes poorly. Expert demonstrations cover narrow scenarios and little environment diversity.

Early experience uses data from the agent's own actions, with resulting future states as supervision and no reward signals. Two strategies use this data: implicit world modeling, grounding the policy in environment dynamics, and self-reflection on suboptimal actions. Across eight diverse environments and several model families, both strategies improved effectiveness consistently. Out-of-domain generalization improved as well, they report. In verifiable-reward settings, results hint early experience can bootstrap later reinforcement learning.
arxiv-2510-08858:
Marvi, Kanwisher, and Khosla pull apart the human visual brain into a few strong components and compare them with machine vision, in this 2025 arXiv paper. High-level visual cortex splits into three streams, loosely serving object recognition, spatial action, and social perception. Yet a single artificial network trained on one task models all three fairly well, which raises a puzzle about shared principles. The team applied a sparse decomposition, a method that explains activity with few active parts, to each stream in turn.

The components matched textbook roles in the recognition stream, with units tuned to faces, places, bodies, text, and food. The social stream favored interactions, implied motion, and hand actions, while the action stream's parts resisted easy labels. The authors then built an alignment score from those components. Standard vision networks, it showed, line up best with the recognition stream and less with the other two.
arxiv-2510-09058:
Santos, Magalhaes, and Santos survey how working programmers actually use language models day to day, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Anecdotes abound, but systematic evidence from practitioners is still thin. The authors gathered responses from one hundred thirty-one software professionals worldwide. Participants described which coding tasks they hand to the models, what they gain, and what worries them.

The reported gains were practical: higher productivity, lower mental load, and faster learning of unfamiliar material. The worries were equally concrete. Models produce inaccurate output, lose track of project context, and raise ethical questions about authorship and responsibility. Most developers said they treat the tools as assistants rather than replacements, keeping a human in charge of the result. The authors call their findings preliminary and frame them as an early practitioner-centered snapshot. They aim to guide both future research and responsible adoption policies inside engineering teams.
arxiv-2510-09258:
Fino and Viana determine when heat spreading through a degenerate material, fed by its own past and present intensity, must blow up rather than settle, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Grushin heat equation governs diffusion that weakens along certain directions, a model for materials with uneven conductivity. Its reaction terms mix a memory effect, where earlier heat feeds current growth, with an ordinary local term. The question is whether solutions exist for all time or explode in finite time.

The authors prove sharp nonexistence results: across wide parameter ranges, no positive solution survives globally in time. The results complete the map separating global existence from blow-up, and pin down Fujita-type critical exponents, the threshold powers where behavior flips, in certain regimes. The proof adapts the test function method to the operator's degeneracy and the memory integral together.
arxiv-2510-09458:
David-Alexandre Duclos and nine co-authors, among them Philippe Giguère, introduce SilvaScenes in a 2025 arXiv paper, a dataset for seeing trees from inside a natural forest. Forestry automation needs machines that can find trees and name their species during field surveys. Working under the canopy is hard: trunks hide behind each other, light varies, and vegetation is dense.

The dataset spans five bioclimatic domains, all sampled in Quebec, Canada. It holds 1,421 trees from 28 species, with pixel-precise masks for trunks and species labels from forestry experts. Benchmarks with modern deep learning methods show trunk segmentation is feasible, reaching about seventy percent average precision. Naming the species while segmenting proved much harder, at about thirty-nine percent. The authors single out species imbalance and occlusion as the most pressing obstacles for the field.
arxiv-2510-10158:
Liu and co-authors simulate user mobility and mobile traffic together in this 2025 arXiv paper on urban computing. Mobility traces and traffic volumes feed urban planning, network optimization, and emergency management. Real data at fine scale is hard to obtain because of privacy concerns and collection cost.

The authors use a multi-scale diffusion transformer, a generative model that works across spatial and temporal scales, to synthesize both patterns jointly. Simulating them together matters because movement drives traffic load. Realistic synthetic data can stand in for private traces in planning studies. The work aims for simulations faithful enough that decisions based on them do not mislead city and network operators.
arxiv-2510-10358:
Velidi and co-authors generalize a Bayes factor for evidence in this 2025 arXiv paper on statistics. Concern over misused p-values has driven interest in alternatives that quantify evidence directly. Jeffreys's approximate Bayes factor can be computed in one line from the p-value, sample size, and test dimension.

The authors define a generalized version and study its model-selection consistency and finite-sample accuracy. They also use it to detect type I errors, false positives, across more than seventy-one thousand clinical trial findings. That large audit shows how often published significance may overstate the evidence. A simple, well-tested evidence measure could help journals and readers judge trial claims more soundly.
arxiv-2510-10658:
Guy Mor-Lan, Tamir Sheafer, and Shaul R Shenhav compare how CNN and Fox News make their reporting sound factual, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Media bias is widely studied, but the epistemic strategies behind factual reporting are not. To separate style from topic choice, they matched articles covering the same events. They applied their FactAppeal framework to more than 470 thousand articles from two politicized periods, the COVID-19 pandemic and then the war between Israel and Hamas.

They find that CNN's reporting contains more factual statements and grounds them in external sources more often. The sourcing styles diverge sharply. CNN builds credibility by citing experts and expert documents, an appeal to formal authority. Fox News instead favors news reports and direct quotations. The authors argue that partisan outlets use systematically different strategies to construct reality, adding a measurable new dimension to the study of media bias beyond topic selection and tone.
arxiv-2510-11958:
Xuan Luo, Weizhi Wang, and Xifeng Yan speed up language models by trusting their middle layers. Studies suggest a transformer's layers divide the labor: early layers understand the input, middle layers do task-specific processing, and late layers turn thought into words. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks why, then, every new word must re-traverse the whole network.

Their answer is Direct Multi-Token Decoding. Once the early and middle layers have built a rich hidden state, the late layers alone generate several tokens in a row. Unlike speculative decoding, the method adds no extra parameters, helper models, or after-the-fact verification. A fine-tuned Qwen3-4B model trained on limited data already reached up to twice the normal speed with only minor quality loss. The authors' scaling analysis predicts further gains as training data grows. If borne out, the trick could cut the cost of running large models substantially.
arxiv-2510-12058:
Chunliu Feng, Geng Tian, and Ran Yi improve a construction at the crossroads of geometry and group theory. A group is called a-T-menable when it acts properly on a Hilbert-like space by affine isometries, motions combining shifts and rotations. Such actions feed proofs of the Baum-Connes and Novikov conjectures. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a new action for any countable discrete group.

The stage is an infinite direct sum of even-dimensional sequence spaces over the group. On it, the authors construct a proper affine isometric action whose cocycles, the shift parts of the action, decay faster than those in the benchmark construction of Haagerup and Przybyszewska. Faster decay means the action's orbits flee to infinity more decisively,. Brown and Guentner had shown such actions exist on mixed sequence spaces; this work sharpens the quality of what can be achieved.
arxiv-2510-12458:
Costa, Zhou, and Granelli build a working digital twin of a real 5G private network and release it openly, in a 2025 arXiv networking paper. A network digital twin mirrors a physical network so operators can analyze and predict behavior, a capability expected to matter for future 6G systems. Despite many theoretical papers, actual implementations remain rare.

The authors first lay out what a network digital twin should be, then describe their deployment. Their twin mirrors a real 5G private network operating in a laboratory and is built on open source network emulation software. The implementation is offered to the community as open source code. Measurements taken on both the physical infrastructure and its twin show high accuracy in matching the state and behavior of the actual system. The paper is offered as a proof of concept bridging theory and practice, giving other researchers a concrete starting point.
arxiv-2510-12958:
Gupta, Muthukrishna, and Audenaert pretrain astronomy models on simulations in this 2025 arXiv paper. Classifying variable stars and transient events from their light curves normally needs large labeled collections of real observations, which are scarce. Simulations, by contrast, can be made freely when domain knowledge exists to build them.

The authors trained classifier models on simulated data from two sky surveys, adding contrastive and adversarial objectives that push the learned representations to ignore which telescope produced the data. Fine-tuned with only minimal real labels, the models beat baselines at classification, redshift estimation, and anomaly detection. Models trained only on current survey simulations transferred zero-shot to simulations of the future LSST survey. They even generalized to variable stars from the Kepler telescope despite training on transient events.
arxiv-2510-13158:
Pan and colleagues represent programs by how they react to optimization in this 2025 arXiv paper. Machine learning for compilers needs good program embeddings, numerical fingerprints of code. Static embeddings built without running the code are cheap but blind to behavior. Dynamic profiling is rich but expensive and non-deterministic.

Their quasi-dynamic framework builds a Program Behavior Spectrum. It probes a program's internal form with many pass sequences and measures how its static features change. Product quantization then compresses those continuous reaction vectors into structured compositional codes. A multi-task transformer called PQ-BERT learns the grammar of those codes in pretraining. On two compiler tasks, picking the best pass and judging whether size tuning will help, the method beat leading static baselines. The code is public.
arxiv-2510-13858:
Biglari and Denil judge whether a model is valid by checking whether it leads to the same choices as a trusted one. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces DOTechnique for model-based systems work. Models are only trustworthy inside their valid region, yet those edges often go unwritten. Ready-made validity frames, when they exist, solve the problem by fiat.

DOTechnique instead compares choices: a cheaper stand-in model stands in for a high-validity reference. Wherever the stand-in's choices match the trusted model's, the model counts as valid there. Domain rules and symbolic logic narrow the search for those regions cheaply. A highway lane-change system shows the method end to end. The method found the model's valid region without any handed-down frame. The authors note one case study cannot prove the method works in general. Broader checks across scenarios are flagged as future work.
arxiv-2510-14258:
Subash Adhikari and Hasan Barbhuiya investigate how energy dissipates at small scales of plasma when electrons and ions sit at different temperatures, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In weakly collisional plasmas, like the solar wind, fluid models cannot account for kinetic-scale energy transfer, but filtered versions of the Vlasov-Maxwell equations can, revealing that the pressure-strain interaction does the accounting.

Running two-dimensional kinetic particle-in-cell simulations of decaying turbulence, the authors vary the electron-to-ion temperature ratio and dissect the pressure-strain interaction into its normal and shear parts, plus pressure dilatation. Across the kinetic range, the interaction is dominated by one component, Pi-D, and within it the shear part contributes most. The normal and shear contributions stay anticorrelated across scales. Their results clarify how disequilibrium between species reshapes the energy budget, a step toward predicting heating in space and astrophysical plasmas.
arxiv-2510-14558:
Ayyam and Sammler, writing on arXiv in 2025, work in formal verification, where software is proven correct rather than merely tested. A popular tool there is the interaction tree, which describes a program's behavior as responses to effects from its environment. But their effects cannot themselves take or return computations, which blocks features like parallel composition and call/cc, a control operation capturing a program's future.

The authors introduce Higher-Order Interaction Trees, or HITrees, the first variant to support such higher-order effects in a non-guarded type theory. Two tricks make it work. Effects are designed so their fixed points can be written as inductive types inside the theory, and higher-order outputs are encoded in first-order form. The team implemented HITrees in the Lean proof assistant, with a library covering concurrency, recursion, and call/cc. They also gave semantics for a small language using these features.
arxiv-2510-15458:
Gabriele Visentin and Patrick Cheridito study optimization that must stay sound when an intervention changes the system itself. Their 2025 arXiv paper works inside causal models, where variables are linked by cause and effect rather than mere correlation. A robust decision should perform well across the shifts an intervention might cause, and the authors measure distance between distributions in a causality-aware way.

They show such robust optimization problems vary continuously under their G-causal Wasserstein distance, yet can jump discontinuously under the standard Wasserstein distance. That contrast warns against augmenting data with generators that ignore causal structure. The team therefore builds a normalizing flow, a flexible generative model, that respects the causal ordering by design. It provably approximates any causal structural model and trains efficiently against their distance. In tests on causal regression and on portfolio optimization with causal factors, it beat standard non-causal generators at data augmentation.
arxiv-2510-15558:
Dongjun Kim, Chanhee Park, Chanjun Park, and Heuiseok Lim build a benchmark for how well language models follow instructions in Korean. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that evaluation has centered on English, missing the grammar and culture of other languages. Korean is a hard case, with honorifics that encode politeness, rich word endings, and two numbering systems.

Their benchmark, KITE, tests open-ended instruction following rather than factual recall or multiple choice. It mixes general instructions with ones that are specifically Korean in character. Scoring combines automated metrics with human judgments, giving a fuller picture of each model's strengths and weaknesses. The evaluations exposed clear performance gaps between models on Korean tasks. Kim and colleagues released the dataset and code publicly. They hope KITE encourages similar benchmarks for other underrepresented languages and pushes model builders toward linguistically inclusive design.
arxiv-2510-15658:
Oscillators that share a rhythm appear in brains, power grids, and superconducting devices alike. Wilfried Segnou and four colleagues study Stuart-Landau oscillators coupled nonlinearly on networks in a 2025 arXiv paper. Earlier theory mostly assumed linear coupling, which keeps the stability analysis autonomous and tractable. Nonlinear coupling makes the linearized system non-autonomous, so new tools are required. The team handles some coupling choices with a complete exact description of synchronization.

For other cases they build a mixed framework using Jacobi-Anger expansion and Floquet theory. From it they derive precise conditions for complete synchronization to emerge. The results extend classical coupled-oscillator theory toward realistic nonlinear interactions.
arxiv-2510-15758:
Natalia Hormazábal and Carlos Martínez-Ranero prove a negative result in a 2025 paper. The result is in mathematical logic. It asks which equation problems a computer can settle. They work with S-integers in an imaginary quadratic field. That field is built from square roots of negative numbers. They ask if an algorithm could test certain equation systems there. The systems pair linear equations with divisibility conditions.

They show no such algorithm exists. This holds whenever the allowed denominator set is finite and nonempty. The ordinary integers behave differently. There, Lipshitz showed a decision procedure exists. The new result extends undecidability results in the style of Hilbert's tenth problem. It covers these richer rings.
arxiv-2510-15858:
MohammadJavad Maarefvand surveys geometric construction in a 2025 article. It asks what can be built as the tools grow stronger. The article starts with ruler and compass. It then adds origami folding and marked rulers. Conic sections and mechanical linkages follow. Certain transcendental curves are added too. Each step widens the set of constructible numbers.

The expansion runs from square roots to cube roots. It reaches all algebraic numbers. With some tools it reaches specific transcendental constants. Field theory explains each level precisely. Computability theory sets the outer limit. No step-by-step method can reach uncomputable numbers. The article closes with the full hierarchy of constructions.
arxiv-2510-15958:
Kaiyu Zhou, Somasekhara Goud Sontti, Joe Zhou, and Xuehua Zhang use microbubbles made inside the flow to pull bitumen residue out of oil sands tailings. Tailings volume is a major environmental burden, and bitumen left in concentrated slurry is both waste and pollutant. Their trick decomposes dilute hydrogen peroxide inside the pipe, releasing gas as microbubbles with no extra device.

Microscope images confirm bubble formation in place, and magnetic particles already in the slurry speed the peroxide breakdown. A high-speed camera watches the flow through a clear window and sees many tiny bubbles after injection. Over seventy percent of the bitumen is recovered from a lab pipeline loop within half an hour. Comparing seven conditions shows total peroxide dosage dominates bubble formation, and real mature fine tailings also bubble rapidly.
arxiv-2510-16158:
Peter Risse and four co-authors rework how we map the proton's inner parts, called partons. They also rework how sure we are of that map. These maps, known as parton distribution functions, say how the proton's push is shared among its quarks and gluons. Past maps leaned on methods whose error bars rest on shaky rules.

Instead the team samples the map's odds directly with a Markov chain Monte Carlo method, a random walk guided by Bayes' rule. Their fit blends data from HERA, BCDMS, and NMC with boson data from the LHC and Tevatron colliders. The method handles clashing or oddly spread data sets with more honest error bars. It also yields a sound rule for when a fit is off, fixing a long-standing weak point of older methods.
arxiv-2510-16558:
Xiaofan Li and Xing Gao map risks in a new AI tool web in their 2025 paper. The web is the Model Context Protocol, or MCP, a shared way to link models to tools. Hosts, servers, and lists of servers each add risk. Weak checks let bad or seized servers slip into hosts. Bad tool notes can then steer a model to do the wrong act.

They study 67,057 servers drawn from six public lists in all. Wide gaps for server seizure and steered calls show up across the lists. Their tool, MCPInspect, scans servers before they join a host. It flagged 833 weak servers, plus 18 with suspect notes. Early scans can block harm before a bad server gets in.
arxiv-2510-17058:
Hassan Hamad, Yuou Qiu, Peter A. Beerel, and Keith M. Chugg redesign number formats for training AI in a 2025 paper. Training still relies on costly floating-point arithmetic. Low-precision fixed-point arithmetic could cut hardware cost sharply. Logarithmic number systems turn multiplication into simpler addition.

Their advance tailors the math approximations to each bit width. A piecewise linear approximation handles logarithmic addition efficiently. Simulated annealing tunes that approximation at each precision level. A bit-exact simulation trained standard image networks successfully. Twelve-bit integer training nearly matched thirty-two-bit floating-point accuracy. The networks were trained on two standard image datasets. Hardware estimates showed sizable area and energy savings. Their multiply-accumulate units used up to half the energy. The work targets future training accelerators.
arxiv-2510-17658:
Anindya Biswas studies special analytic functions and their extreme cases in a 2025 arXiv paper. His setting is the Schur-Agler class, a family of functions generated by a chosen set of test functions. He focuses on Carathéodory extremal functions, which are the boundary cases that shape the class. The central question is which domains such a family can describe.

Biswas shows that, under stated conditions, only two domains allow finitely many test functions to generate the full Schur class. These are the unit disc and the product of two unit discs. He then describes the extremal functions for a well known function space's multiplier algebra. He also gives operator based representations for a broad class of hyperbolic domains.
arxiv-2510-17758:
Alex NieMiera and three co-authors report a first calculation of the gluon content inside a nucleon. A nucleon is a proton or neutron, built from quarks and gluons. Their parton distribution describes how momentum is shared among those parts. The team used lattice quantum chromodynamics, meaning simulations on a space-time grid.

Their method follows large-momentum effective theory with a self-renormalized hybrid scheme. Calculations ran at three grid spacings with high statistics. Results stayed consistent as the grid grew finer toward the continuum limit. The final gluon curve matches some global fits reasonably well. It favors fits with near-zero gluon density at large momentum share.
arxiv-2510-17858:
Xu Cai and five co-authors present a cheap way to make large image-making diffusion models work in far fewer steps. Normal shortcut methods need a special step-size input built in from the start. Adding that later means retraining the whole model, which costs almost as much as the first training run.

Their method teaches the model from its own velocity field, with no step-size input needed. They report turning the Flux model into a three-step version in less than one day on a single high-end chip. The idea can also join pretraining, so new models may learn fast sampling from the start.
arxiv-2510-17958:
Matthias Fabry and Andrej Prša offer a new cause for a long-noted oddity in close double stars. In some contact binaries, the two brightness peaks in each orbit are unequal, a pattern called the O'Connell effect. Spots on the star surface are the usual blamed cause in past work.

Using the PHOEBE modeling code, the authors add a stream that carries mass and heat sideways from the hotter star to the cooler one. A stream with low heat capacity matched a strong case from the Kepler sample. The result gives modelers a second, testable way to explain uneven peaks.
arxiv-2510-18258:
Xiaohan Qin, with Xiaoxing Wang and two co-authors, tackles uneven learning across tasks in a 2025 paper. Multi-task learning trains one model on several jobs at once, sharing what it learns. Some tasks learn fast and crowd out slower ones, a problem called task imbalance.

The proposed method, NTKMTL, studies training through Neural Tangent Kernel theory. That theory tracks how a network's outputs shift as its settings change during training. By comparing the speeds of different tasks, the method rebalances them during learning. A faster variant shares representations across tasks to save time. Tests across supervised and reinforcement benchmarks reached top results.
arxiv-2510-18358:
Firas Gabetni and his five co-authors address a practical worry about neural networks: knowing when a prediction might be wrong. Running many full copies of a model gives good uncertainty estimates, but it costs too much memory and time for large models. Their answer, Hydra Ensembles, builds varied members by pruning attention heads, the parts of a transformer that weigh which inputs matter most.

The pruned members are then merged through a new grouped attention design, so the combined model runs almost as fast as a single network and needs no training from scratch. Careful study showed that careless pruning can damage how well confidence matches reality, while the Hydra design keeps that balance. Across image and text tasks, the method matched or beat full ensembles, and it led on zero-shot image sorting as well.
arxiv-2510-18558:
Yue Wang works with Lixian Zhang, Yimin Zhu, Yangguang Liu, and Xuwei Yang. They design a drone that can fly, grab, and perch. The craft is called Flexbee. It swaps plain propellers for four soft nozzles. The nozzles bend to aim their thrust. One set of parts does all three jobs. That reuse frees the drone's structure. It also lets position and tilt be controlled more apart.

The team built a dynamics model of the craft. A coupling flaw in the turning forces caused trouble. They fixed it by simplifying the moment model. Controllers were then built in layers. They serve the drone's two working modes. Flight tests checked basic motion. Grasping and perching tests checked the rest. All showed the craft moves as planned. The control strategy worked in practice too.
arxiv-2510-18658:
Gabrielle Browne, with Mengfei Liu, Eitan Grinspun, and Otman Benchekroun, improves non-rigid registration, the task of aligning two shapes when one has bent or stretched. Registration matters in medical imaging, robotics, vision, and entertainment. Standard algorithms inch a shape toward its target and easily get stuck in poor local matches, depending heavily on where they start.

MorphModes reframes the problem as matching signed distance functions, which describe a whole shape's geometry rather than just surface points, giving the optimizer richer information. Deformations are expressed through a smooth set of skinning eigenmodes, motion patterns that prevent degenerate, crumpled solutions. An adaptive step then enlarges the pattern set where fine local bending is needed. The result is an algorithm more robust than the standard approach and less touchy about parameter settings than other distance-based methods.
arxiv-2510-19358:
Yejin Kwon and three co-authors present M3-SLU, a benchmark for speaker-attributed reasoning in multimodal language models. Models read speech and text well, yet they still struggle to track who said what, and when, across a multi-speaker, multi-turn conversation, a skill real meeting and dialogue tools need.

Built from four open corpora, the benchmark holds more than twelve thousand checked examples with audio, transcripts, and metadata. Its two tasks ask models to answer questions tied to specific speakers and to match utterances to their speakers. Baselines from both pipeline systems and end-to-end models show where current systems stand.
arxiv-2510-19658:
Laura Meissner-Oszer, Bogdan Cichocki, and Jeffrey C. Everts prove exact results about dissipation in chiral active fluids, materials made of self-spinning particles that constantly inject energy. Such fluids have an unusual property called odd viscosity, an antisymmetric part of the viscosity tensor allowed by the particles' spin. The authors extend the Helmholtz minimum dissipation theorem to cover it.

They show that steady slow flows in three-dimensional odd fluids are unique, and that odd viscosity makes flows dissipate more energy than ordinary Stokes flow when it affects the motion. Working out the flow around single spheres, they find a translating sphere dissipates more with odd viscosity present, while a rotating sphere does not, and they explain why.
arxiv-2510-19758:
Joseph Casale, Andrew Silverschotz, and Joseph DeSimone propose replacing fixed top-K masking with a dynamic top-P version in sparse information retrieval models. Masking keeps only the strongest entries of a representation vector, making search faster and cheaper; keeping a fixed count, however, treats every document the same regardless of how its scores are distributed. Top-P masking, borrowed from nucleus sampling in language models, keeps entries until a cumulative probability threshold is met.

The authors evaluate the idea in cross-language information retrieval, where queries and documents sit in different languages. Their experiments show the dynamic scheme outperforming top-K masking in that setting. The change is a small post-processing swap for existing systems that use masking, such as bilingual expansion models.
arxiv-2510-19858:
Jindi Wang and six co-authors adapt the Interaction Analysis Model to classify knowledge construction in the messy comment streams of online learning. Knowing how learners build knowledge in forums helps designers and teachers, but hand-coding does not scale to unstructured, large-scale discourse. The team distilled the model into four comment-level categories, from non-knowledge construction through sharing and exploring to integrating.

Three trained annotators coded twenty thousand comments from YouTube education channels, reaching strong agreement. A DeBERTa model then automated the coding, beating bag-of-words and other transformer baselines, and it transferred to four further domains with respectable scores, strongest in medicine and programming. The study shows theory-driven analysis of knowledge construction can run at platform scale.
arxiv-2510-19958:
Hugo Méndez-Hernández and fifty-six co-authors describe how targets were chosen for the low-redshift part of the CHANCES galaxy cluster survey, to be observed with the 4MOST spectrograph. Clusters are ideal laboratories for studying how environment quenches and reshapes galaxies. The sub-survey covers fifty clusters and two superclusters nearby, reaching well beyond each cluster's edge and down to faint magnitudes.

Candidate members were picked by matching photometric redshifts against each cluster's known redshift, merging public estimates with custom ones and checking their scatter against spectroscopy. The final catalogs hold more than five hundred thousand candidate members, split into bright and faint sub-surveys, from which roughly three hundred twenty thousand galaxy spectra are expected. The sample will support statistical studies of galaxy evolution in dense environments.
arxiv-2510-20358:
Francesca Padovani and six co-authors ask if a small language model trained just on dialogue can talk well, in the BabyLM style. Their model, llamalogue, learns from talk text alone. Fine-tune steps then push it to make more apt replies in chat. The aim is a small model with both form skill and talk skill.

The talk-trained models lag on most stock BabyLM tests. But they shine at picking the right next line in paired chat tests. PPO fine-tune gives mixed to bad shifts. DPO fine-tune lifts scores on their chat test by more. The team takes this to mean talk data alone, and growth-style training alone, are each not quite enough.
arxiv-2510-20558:
Xiaohan Sun and Carol O'Sullivan gauge how crowds in a scene read at far and near views in screen work. Each crowd form trades image truth for speed in its own way. The forms are mesh builds, flat impostor cards, Neural Radiance Fields, and 3D Gaussians. View range and crowd count of traits shift what a user sees as good or poor.

The study mixes scored tests with free views of the crowds at set ranges. It finds where more traits stop to count for the eye. It also finds where cheap forms start to look weak. The team gives the marks as a guide for trait plans that spend power where the eye can tell.
arxiv-2510-20758:
Alexander Gorsky and Ilya Liubimov map the phase structure of the Russian Doll Model, a compact model of paired electrons in a small system with a twist that breaks time reversal symmetry. The model is prized because its equations match a known spin chain and its growth rule cycles in a log scale.

In the clean version the pair finds a broad region of non ergodic multifractal states, with re entry moves between localized, ergodic, and multifractal phases as settings vary. A global charge drawn from the exact equations shows clumping patterns in the multifractal region that echo ideas from black hole state counting. Quantum shape measures and fractal dimensions fill out the map for both clean and disordered versions.
arxiv-2510-20858:
Nubio Vidal, Naghmeh Moradpoor, and Leandros Maglaras present AIR, a vendor neutral framework for live incident reporting in operational technology networks such as power and plant control systems. As control networks merge with office networks, attacks grow easier and response needs shared facts fast, yet standards say little about what data to capture during an incident.

AIR defines twenty five elements in seven groups covering context, timeline, impacts, and actions, shaped for technical, managerial, and regulatory readers alike. The team maps AIR onto major control standards, marks where it plugs into existing response frameworks, and replays it against the twenty fifteen Ukrainian grid attack. The replay shows AIR turns broad duties into concrete fields that aid awareness and coordination.
arxiv-2510-21258:
Xin Du and Kumiko Tanaka-Ishii propose a new way to judge text produced by large language models, which can repeat themselves or drift into nonsense even when standard scores look good. Common metrics reward accurate next-word guesses but miss the overall shape of a long passage.

Their measure, correlation dimension, comes from fractal geometry and captures how patterns recur across scales in text as the model sees it. In experiments, the measure reveals three phases during pretraining, shifts with context, flags a tendency to invent facts, and detects several kinds of breakdown in generated text. It stays cheap to compute, works even for heavily compressed models, and applies across different model families, from Transformer to Mamba designs.
arxiv-2510-21558:
Dae San Kim and Taekyun Kim write plain polynomials in terms of Bernoulli polynomials that have been given a random twist. The classic Bernoulli family is a standard basis for expanding other polynomials. Here the rules depend on a random variable. Its moment generating function must exist near zero.

A second family bends the classic formulas with a small parameter. Those are the degenerate Bernoulli polynomials. The authors find clear formulas that write any polynomial as a mix of these new ones. They also write polynomials in terms of higher-order versions of the same families. The tool they use treats sequences of polynomials almost like powers of a single symbol. Worked cases cover several discrete and continuous choices for the random input.
arxiv-2510-21758:
Kumater Ter, Abolanle Adetifa, and Daniel Udekwe review how reinforcement learning took over large parts of robotics and control. They organize a sprawling decade into one structured map. Trial-and-error learning suits machines that must act in dynamic, uncertain settings. Yet the field's algorithms and deployments have multiplied faster than any newcomer can survey.

The review starts from the Markov decision process formalism. It covers value-based learning, policy gradients, and actor-critic methods. It then covers the modern deep algorithms that cracked high-dimensional continuous control. A taxonomy sorts applications across locomotion, manipulation, multi-agent coordination, and human-robot interaction. It notes training styles and how close each line stands to real deployment. The synthesis aims to connect theory to practice. It charts where autonomous robot learning is genuinely maturing.
arxiv-2510-22458:
Sen Na, writing alone in a 2025 research paper, tackles nonlinear optimization problems where only rough function values are available. The goal carries random sampling noise, while the equality constraints, meaning conditions that must hold exactly, stay fixed. No slope or curvature information can be measured directly.

Na proposes a derivative-free method that guesses slopes and curvature by random small changes, needing as few as eight checks per step. A momentum style trick, which averages past guesses, reduces the random bias those guesses create. He proves the method settles toward a solution and describes how its final steps behave, then tests the ideas with numerical experiments.
arxiv-2510-22558:
Engineers need to know how a design change affects the chance a structure fails under random shaking. Jianhua Xian, Sai Hung Cheung, and Cheng Su present a surface decomposition method in 2025 for that sensitivity question in linear systems under Gaussian random excitation.

Their method splits the change in first passage failure chance into surface integrals over each part's limit surface. Linear systems give closed form expressions for those surfaces and their changes, making the sums workable. A smart sampling strategy boosts efficiency, needing only hundreds to thousands of evaluations. Three numerical examples show the approach works, especially with many design parameters.
arxiv-2510-22958:
Yuhao Chen leads a team of eleven researchers who ask how fresh magnetic flux near the Sun can bend the path of a solar eruption. New flux often rises beside filaments, the cool strands that can burst outward as coronal mass ejections. That sideways push can spoil space weather forecasts.

The group joins analytic theory with two-dimensional simulations that start at the point where balance is lost. They find new flux can create or remove a higher resting point, causing a failed eruption or a full ejection. In borderline cases a rising filament wobbled in ways that matter for predicting its path.
arxiv-2510-23058:
Rutvij Bhavsar and N D Hari Dass examine quantum trajectories that arise when a single unknown state is measured again and again. They use gentle QND measurements described by POVMs, which disturb the state as little as possible. An earlier Gaussian approach showed the state of one copy cannot be pinned down from such measurement statistics.

The present work avoids stochastic equations and instead uses martingale properties of certain observables. Those properties force convergence results that explain the limit. The paper clarifies a subtle point: repeated gentle looks at one copy still cannot reveal its full state, a fact that shapes quantum measurement theory.
arxiv-2510-23158:
Philipp Gotz and four co-authors address how to fake room reverberation that matches a real recording, for auditory augmented reality. Reverb tells listeners about a space, but plausible real-time rendering is hard when no acoustic measurement of the room exists. The team frames the problem as matching a reverberant signal directly.

A learned embedding captures room-acoustic traits from the signal, guiding a feedback delay network that reproduces frequency-dependent decay and spectral shape. The system estimates parameters blindly from audio alone. Such matching could make virtual sounds sit naturally in real rooms on AR headsets.
arxiv-2510-23358:
Sheri Osborn, Rohit Valecha, H Raghav Rao, Dan Sass, and Anthony Rios benchmark how well large language models forecast changes in job demand, especially in occupations touched by AI. Society lacks tools to predict AI effects on employment in a systematic way. Models can already extract sentiment and summarize economic reports, but forward-looking labor prediction was untested.

Their benchmark joins a high-frequency index of sector job postings with a second complementary data set. By scoring model forecasts against real posting shifts, the study shows where AI predictions of AI jobs can be trusted and where they mislead planners.
arxiv-2510-23458:
Litu Ou leads a team of eleven researchers with BrowseConf, a confidence-guided method for scaling web agents at test time. A language model confidence can signal uncertainty and answer reliability, but most work covers single-turn settings. Multi-turn web tasks, with long action sequences, are far harder for verbalized confidence.

Experimenting on open-source agentic models, they first find that models report much higher task confidence after long sequences. BrowseConf uses confidence to guide extra test-time effort where it helps. Better calibrated web agents could browse, compare, and buy with fewer silent errors.
arxiv-2510-23658:
Vaibhav Jindal and four co-authors align diffusion language models with human preferences without paired comparison data. Diffusion models generate text by gradual denoising rather than word by word, which makes their sequence likelihoods intractable and preference tuning awkward. Paired preference data, the usual fuel for alignment, is also costly to gather.

Their method, ELBO-KTO, swaps the true likelihood for a tractable lower-bound stand-in and plugs it into an unpaired preference objective drawn from prospect theory. The authors analyze the bias and variance this swap introduces and add variance-reduction tricks to steady training. Applied to the LLaDA-8B-Instruct model, the method won about sixty-six and sixty-two percent of judged comparisons against the base model on two datasets. On downstream tests like GSM8K and MMLU it matched or beat the base model, showing unpaired tuning is a real alternative.
arxiv-2510-24058:
Zihan Zhao and three co-authors tackle a common problem for body sensors and robots that learn from many senses at once. The best sensor in a lab is often too costly, weak, or awkward to use in real life. Their framework, PULSE, moves knowledge from that rich teacher sensor to cheaper student sensors.

Each student sensor learns both shared traits and traits of its own. The shared part is matched to the teacher, while the private part keeps details needed to rebuild its own signal. The paper shows this transfer helps the small sensors perform well after the teacher is gone, which matters for wearables and robots used outside the lab.
arxiv-2510-24358:
Lingyue Fu and nine co-authors propose an agent driven pipeline to build benchmarks for code agents automatically. Code agents now develop software at project level with language models, but evaluating them is hard. Good project level test sets need deep expertise, making annotation costly and narrow, while agent judges using plain in context learning often misjudge quality against human standards.

Their pipeline uses agents themselves to annotate and evaluate, cutting the cost of benchmark construction and widening coverage. It also aims to align automated judgments more closely with human standards than generic judges achieve. The work addresses a growing bottleneck in measuring real software engineering ability.
arxiv-2510-24458:
Samuel Talkington, Dmitrii Ostrovskii, and Daniel Molzahn, three authors, tackle network design. Power grids and other networks sometimes need their links reshaped. The goal is to cut congestion while still meeting fixed demands. The exact best design is a hard mixed problem, NP-hard in general. Here NP-hard means no fast exact method is known at all.

Rather than chase one best design, they build a lottery of designs. Drawing from the lottery keeps congestion near the best level on average. A key strain measure has a smooth shape that aids fast search. Simple gradient steps then find good lottery weights quite fast. In tests the method beat a top commercial solver by far. The gap grew to orders of magnitude on large problems.
arxiv-2510-24858:
Ross Silver leads a team with thirty co-authors who report a deep X ray survey of the field the Webb scope watches for change over time. Two X ray scopes have swept that north sky field on a set beat for five years. This is the third report in the set, on the most fresh two years of data.

The new sweep stacks a large dose of time on a field a third of a square degree in size. It found scores of hard X ray sources and more than two hundred soft ones at high trust. Count curves match past sweeps of the same field, on a wider patch. About a third of the hard sources are hid by thick gas.
arxiv-2510-24958:
Guido Ivetta and seven co-authors built LACES, a set of shared views on groups in Latin America, drawn from folks who live there. Bias tests for language tools lack data from this part of the world, so harms there go un gauged. Their set spans fifteen lands in the region.

Near five thousand group views were made and marked by hand, from more than eighty folks in joint work with local teams. Their new build flow folds fresh views and checks of old views into one pass, which yielded more sole views than past fixed flows. Tests show past bias fix tools work less well on this set. That marks the size of the geo gap.
arxiv-2510-25658:
Maximilian Graml and Jan Wilhelm add a many-body optics tool to the CP2K code. Their 2025 paper tests the tool on small carbon-based units. The tool finds how much light a unit takes in, and at what hues. They first check it on a standard test set of such units. The check matches known values to a very fine margin.

They then study nanographenes, flat carbon sheets of growing length. The sums match lab tests of those sheets well. The size of the first light response grows with length, then levels off. That size ends near seven point six angstroms. They also test a cheaper, older tool on the same sheets. No form of that tool matched both the size and the light curves. Full many-body sums seem to be a must for such small carbon sheets.
arxiv-2510-25958:
Lukas Pfromm, Alish Kanani, Harsh Sharma, Janardhan Rao Doppa, Partha Pratim Pande, and Umit Y. Ogras present a simulator for deep learning on chiplet based hardware. A chiplet system builds a processor from smaller dies linked over an interposer, which helps yield and scale as single large chips struggle to meet compute and memory demand. Fast, accurate simulation is needed to design such systems well.

Their framework, CHIPSIM, models compute and communication together, capturing network contention and pipelining that other simulators miss. It also profiles power for each chiplet and link at microsecond scale for heat analysis. Tests with mixed chiplet and network designs show versatility and up to a three hundred forty percent accuracy improvement in their comparisons.
arxiv-2510-27258:
Yifan Zhang, Zhen Qin, Mengdi Wang, and Quanquan Gu introduce higher-order linear attention, a cheaper way for language models to weigh context. Standard attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, blocking long contexts. Linear-time rivals and state space models scale better but usually capture only first-order or kernel-based interactions, limiting expressiveness.

Their mechanism keeps compact running summaries, called prefix sufficient statistics, so second-order interactions are computed in linear time with constant-size state and no large pairwise matrices. Closed-form streaming identities, a strictly causal masked variant, and a chunk-parallel training scheme reproduce serial results exactly. Extensions to third and higher orders are outlined. The design offers attention-like data-dependent mixing with recurrent efficiency for long-sequence models.
arxiv-2510-27558:
Sushil Samuel Dinesh and Shinkyu Park describe a robot control setup in 2025 that needs no task-specific training. The setup joins ready-made foundation models, which are large models trained on broad data. One part handles sight and sound input, while a general model plans the order of steps for long tasks.

Scene graphs, which are maps of objects and their links in space, are kept up to date as the robot works. They give the system a steady sense of place through each step. Tests with a tabletop robot arm show the setup can carry out long tasks in sequence. The work points to robots built from shared, general models.
arxiv-2511-00058:
Paul Alexander Bilokon stands for computation as a two-player game between an Algorithm and Nature, grounded in domain theory and game theory. The Algorithm outputs step by step refined estimates inside a Scott domain, while Nature charges fines matched to the distance from the true value. Correctness becomes balance in the limit of refinement.

Complexity classes such as P and NP are then marked game-in theory, as problems admitting special balances. Theoretical computer science readers get a uniting language for computation, approximation, and hardness. The famous P versus NP question is recast, in this language, as a question about which balances exist.
arxiv-2511-00258:
Salvador Rey Gomez and Tomek Jaroslawski ask how much trust to place in a popular tool for studying turbulence near walls. The tool, resolvent analysis, breaks the flow equations into modes that show which patterns grow strongest. It often runs on measured average flows, but sensors cannot resolve the thin layer right at the wall, leaving the near-wall speed uncertain.

The authors show that the effect of that uncertainty can be measured at little extra computing cost. Tests use artificial disturbances to average profiles and real camera-based flow measurements with different near-wall fits. In one boundary layer case, poor near-wall data flipped the conclusion. Careful uncertainty checks, they argue, should accompany the method.
arxiv-2511-00558:
Blaž Ivšić, Igor Weber, Piotr Nowakowski, and Ana-Sunčana Smith model how single cells crawl. Crawling comes from cycles of protrusion and retraction driven by the cytoskeleton, whose layout is steered by reaction-diffusion chemistry of Rho GTPase proteins shuttling between cell interior and cortex. That chemistry patterns the membrane and sets front-rear polarity, coupling biochemical signals with mechanical feedback.

Their cross-scale framework joins the reaction-diffusion signaling to flows inside the cell and along its cortex, including Marangoni flows driven by surface tension differences. Small parameter changes reproduce a wide range of observed shapes and motility styles, suggesting those styles are self-organized limit cycles. Phase-space analysis shows both the inner flow and the varying surface tension are essential to recover the full spectrum of movement modes.
arxiv-2511-00758:
Hong Su proposes an Active Thinking Model, a cognitive design meant to let AI systems improve themselves in changing real-world settings. Most models execute fixed procedures toward predefined objectives, trained on static data with feedback supplied from outside. That design cannot adapt, reflect, or grow on its own. The proposed design instead integrates goal reasoning, dynamic task generation, and self-reflective learning in one loop.

Inside the loop, the system evaluates its own performance through logical reasoning and environmental indicators, reuses methods that worked before, and invents strategies for situations it has never seen. A math analysis, the author reports, shows the model can evolve on its own from suboptimal to optimal behavior without outside supervision, while keeping tracking regret bounded as conditions change. It is a theoretical proposal for truly adaptive intelligence.
arxiv-2511-00858:
Yu Liu and colleagues propose an occlusion aware diffusion model for predicting whether a pedestrian is about to cross the street. Drivers and robots need that forecast, but people are often partly hidden behind cars or other obstacles, and most earlier models ignore the missing information.

Their model reconstructs the hidden motion patterns and uses them to guide the forecast. A diffusion transformer estimates noise features tied to the occluded parts, A reverse process guided by the occlusion mask keeps the reconstruction faithful to what was seen. That limits error build up. On the PIE and JAAD benchmarks, across many occlusion levels, the method proved more robust than current approaches.
arxiv-2511-00958:
Khoat Than offers a theoretical explanation for why normalization layers, a standard part of deep neural networks, help training so much. These layers are known to steady training and improve generalization, but the mechanism, especially in very deep networks with many such layers, has stayed unclear.

Than frames the issue as capacity control. Without normalization, a network's Lipschitz constant, a measure of how sharply its output can change, can grow exponentially, and such over flexible networks are everywhere. Adding normalization layers cuts that constant at an exponential rate per layer. Two benefits follow: the loss landscape smooths, easing optimization, and the effective capacity shrinks, improving guarantees on unseen data.
arxiv-2511-01058:
Michael Howes studies how quickly a random sampling process settles into uniformity. The Burnside process is a Markov chain on the symmetric group used to sample Sylow p-double cosets evenly. Its mixing time tells users how many steps to run before trusting the output.

Howes derives sharp estimates in the regime where the group size is a prime times a smaller factor. The main result gives the limit profile of the distance to the stationary distribution as the prime grows. Two regimes emerge. With the smaller factor fixed, order p steps are necessary and sufficient, and no sharp cutoff occurs. If that factor also grows, a cutoff appears at a stated time, with a window of size p. The bounds stay accurate even for primes as small as eleven.
arxiv-2511-01858:
Quentin Noraz, Mats Carlsson, and Guillaume Aulanier dissect how the Sun's chromosphere gets heated under quiet conditions. This layer, the interface between the solar interior and space, decides how energy becomes heat and escapes upward, yet which process dominates its heating has stayed controversial.

The authors use a radiation-magnetohydrodynamics simulation from the Bifrost code. They apply physics-based criteria to identify individual shock and current-sheet events in space and time. Then they tally each kind's contributions to viscous, ohmic, and mechanical heating. Shocks dominate the lower chromosphere. They supply up to about 59 percent of the mechanical heating there. Current sheets take over higher up, as plasma beta and Mach number fall. Together the two mechanisms power about 66 percent of the mechanical heating, supporting a multi-process picture of the quiet chromosphere.
arxiv-2511-01958:
Eleonora Villa, Golam Mohiuddin Shaifullah, Andrea Possenti, and Carmelita Carbone study how to speed up data analysis for pulsar timing arrays. These arrays time pulses from many pulsars and pool the results into one shared data set. The work rests on Bayesian inference, a way to weigh how well a model fits noisy data. The standard tools for that task can be slow and hard to scale.

The team adds a sampler called i-nessai to the Enterprise software framework. The sampler uses normalizing flows, a machine learning method that reshapes simple distributions into complex ones. On realistic simulated data sets, it gave accurate results and sound evidence estimates. It also cut run time sharply, by up to three orders of magnitude in some setups, next to single core parallel tempering Markov chain Monte Carlo runs. The authors present the method as a faster, stable path for array analysis.
arxiv-2511-02158:
Wilfried Kuissi-Kamdem studies a saver who must invest, consume, and still meet a fixed liability at the end, without being able to see one key driver of the market. The market price of risk is unobservable, interest rates move randomly, and preferences follow Epstein-Zin recursive utility, which separates attitudes to risk from attitudes to shifting consumption over time. Adding the terminal liability changes the mathematics fundamentally, demanding a new guess for the shape of the value process.

The problem becomes a coupled forward-backward stochastic differential equation outside the reach of standard existence results. Exploiting its special structure, Kuissi-Kamdem reduces it to an explicit solution under mild assumptions. Malliavin calculus then expresses the optimal investment rule through conditional expectations that Monte Carlo methods can approximate. The framework also prices the loss from ignoring what could be learned about the hidden market price of risk.
arxiv-2511-02358:
Wongyu Kim, Hochang Lee, Sanghak Lee, Yoonsung Kim, and Jaehyun Park teach a search embedder to decide for itself whether a query needs help. Expanding a query with extra produced information often improves retrieval, but doing it for every query is slow, and for some queries the expansion actively hurts. Prior work had also never tested the idea in multimodal search, where queries and documents mix text and images.

Their embedder, M-Solomon, learns the decision during training: queries are split into those that benefit from augmentation and those that do not. Synthetic augmentations are produced for the first group with a multimodal model. At run time the system prefixes its generation with a marker that either triggers an augmentation or goes straight to embedding. It beat both the never-augment and always-augment baselines while embedding much faster than the latter.
arxiv-2511-02458:
Giulia Iadisernia and Carolina Camassa test two trendy ideas at once: whether a large language model can forecast the economy like a professional, and whether dressing it in a persona helps. They drew 2,368 economics profiles from a public corpus. They had a leading model, GPT-4o, mimic the European Central Bank's Survey of Professional Forecasters across fifty quarterly rounds, predicting inflation, core inflation, growth, and unemployment at several horizons.

The model's accuracy landed very close to the human panel's, with differences that showed in tests but were small in practice. It stayed competitive on genuinely unseen recent data. The persona experiment, though, was a clear negative: dressed-up prompts gave no measurable advantage over plain ones, so the profiles can be dropped to save computing cost. A side observation was that varied prompts produced strikingly uniform forecasts compared with the diversity of human experts.
arxiv-2511-02758:
Nizar Demni, Nicolas Gilliers, and Tarek Hamdi compute key polynomials for the Hermitian Jacobi process, a random matrix model that evolves over time. Their 2025 paper finds the averaged characteristic polynomial at any fixed time, along with its finite S transform. That transform, a tool from free probability, tracks how such polynomials combine under multiplication of random matrices.

They prove directly that these polynomials solve a backward heat equation. That equation is tied to the one-dimensional Jacobi operator. Expansions in Jacobi polynomials follow from a dual Cauchy identity and orthogonality. The S transform obeys its own finite difference and differential equations. In the high-dimensional limit, those yield an equation for the free Jacobi process. A general lemma on convergence of finite differences supports the passage to the limit.
arxiv-2511-02858: Alexandra Antoniouk and Anatoly Kochubei introduce a p-adic version of the Kelvin transformation, a classic trick that flips a function through a sphere to study its behavior far away. Their version is tied to the Vladimirov-Taibleson operator, a key operator in p-adic analysis. The setting is functions over a non-Archimedean local field, where distance follows rules unlike the real numbers. The 2025 paper defines the new map and studies its main traits, carrying a tool of classical potential theory into this very different geometry.
arxiv-2511-03058:
Martina Conte and Nadia Loy introduce a transport equation where a particle's speed and direction are scattered by two different mechanisms. Each runs on its own time scale and strength. The twist is that each scattering rule depends on the current spread of the other quantity, through its marginals. So the gain terms are not tied to a fixed equilibrium, as in classical kinetic theory.

That twist breaks the standard toolbox. Entropy methods, spectral analysis, and Fredholm theory do not apply in their usual form. The 2025 paper analyzes the new operators directly, including their unusual pseudo-inverses and long-time behavior. It also derives the large-scale limits under different balances of the two scattering rates. Those limits show how speed and direction relaxation interact.
arxiv-2511-03158:
Changqing Lu, Ganggang Xu, Junho Yang, and Yongtao Guan report a surprise in geostatistics. When sampling sites are chosen preferentially, near the values being mapped, some simple methods that ignore the bias still work. Since a landmark 2010 paper, the field has built likelihood methods that model the sampling scheme to fix the bias. Those fixes are costly and can misfire if the scheme is misspecified. The 2025 paper looks again at ignoring the problem.

Under the standard framework and its extensions, certain non-likelihood estimators stay unbiased and consistent even with preferential sampling. The authors give conditions for when sampling can be safely ignored. They also give estimators for regression and covariance that never name the sampling rule. Simulations showed smaller errors, better interval coverage, and far lower cost. A tropical forest data set shows the practical use.
arxiv-2511-03258:
Mohit Thakre, Praveen Kumar Dhankar, Behnam Pourhassan, and Safiqul Islam test whether a sticky cosmic fluid can explain why the universe speeds up. Their fluid mixes a Chaplygin gas idea with bulk stickiness inside the standard expanding space picture. They solve how density, expansion rate, and slowdown change over time, with and without stickiness.

Stickiness calms a known flaw of the gas idea, where structure growth would otherwise wobble too much. The team then fits the model to sky data with a sampling method that maps allowed values. Expansion history and the shift from slowing to speeding come out of that fit. The work weighs whether one thick fluid could play the roles usually split between dark matter and dark energy.
arxiv-2511-03358:
Alexander Alecio studies how randomness can steady, as well as shake, a model of system-wide financial risk. Banks or firms are pictured as particles in a double-well landscape, pulled by their average state and buffeted by noise of two kinds. Uncertain barrier heights stand in for shifting firm strength.
