Such systems are known to flip between an ordered, stable phase and a disordered, unstable one as noise grows. With both noise kinds varying separately, Alecio finds far richer behavior than a single flip. How the random integral is read changes which phase wins in parts of the range. Noise-driven stability matters because real markets live with mixed, uneven shocks rather than one clean dial of randomness.
arxiv-2511-03558:
Anu Sreedevi and co-authors test a century-old pattern in how paired sunspot regions tilt on the Sun. Bipolar magnetic regions lean away from the equator by an amount that grows with latitude, a rule called Joy's law. One leading story credits the Coriolis effect twisting a thin magnetic tube as it rises through the Sun's churning outer layer.

If that story holds, the tilt pattern should already appear at first emergence, before surface flows can reshape the region. Fresh emergence data show the law present at birth, backing the thin flux tube picture. Support has been thin until now, so direct emergence evidence carries weight. Solar activity forecasts lean on how these regions tilt, since tilt shapes the next cycle.
arxiv-2511-03858:
Walter Quinonez, Maria Jose Sanchez, and Diego Rubi study memristor-based neural networks trained with the Manhattan update rule, a simple hardware-friendly method, and weigh learning quality against energy use. Realistic models of how memristor conductance rises and falls drive the tests on a single perceptron and a deep network trained on MNIST.

Single perceptrons tolerated modest device nonlinearity, while deep networks needed far stricter limits to keep accuracy. More conductance levels improved convergence, acting like a finer learning rate. Fixing one memristor in each differential pair cut training energy by nearly half with little accuracy loss. Device and algorithm must be designed together, the authors conclude.
arxiv-2511-04258:
Balagopal Komarath, Anant Kumar, and Akash Pareek study the space cost of counting graph patterns inside degenerate host graphs, where pattern counting by dynamic programming over decomposition trees traditionally needs polynomial space. Their new parameter, DAG treedepth, unlocks divide-and-conquer algorithms that run in constant space.

Building on the induced-minor characterization that separates treewidth one patterns by forbidden long induced cycles, the team characterize patterns of DAG treedepth at most two through induced minors. Every pattern graph on at most nine vertices can be counted within their constant-space framework as well, extending a recent subquadratic-time result. Memory, not just time, becomes a design axis for pattern counting.
arxiv-2511-04358:
Claudia Núñez, Miguel Pardina, Manuel Asorey, José Ignacio Latorre, and Alba Cervera-Lierta ask whether quantum information can explain gauge invariance. Their study links two resources, entanglement and magic, to the rules that govern basic forces. Magic here means the non-Clifford part that makes universal quantum computing possible.

The authors study gluon-gluon and graviton-graviton scattering in the high-energy limit. There, mass terms fade and conformal symmetry holds, so particles act as massless. They argue that limits on entanglement and magic together restrict how such particles can interact. The work offers a fresh route from quantum information principles toward the symmetries of fundamental physics.
arxiv-2511-04458:
Akhil Ambekar and two colleagues built TRAECR, a tool that prepares PET brain scans for statistics. PET imaging helps study cancer and Alzheimer's disease, including whether new drugs cut amyloid. Raw scans, though, need careful preprocessing before any model can use them.

TRAECR handles that preparation and adds views that help users check each step. The authors explain the background statisticians need when they first meet PET data. Good preprocessing matters because later claims, like links between amyloid loss and thinking scores, rest on it. The tool aims to make those pipelines clearer and easier to repeat.
arxiv-2511-04658:
Adam Bouyamourn, writing alone, offers a method for choosing sites in multi-site experiments. Such studies test interventions across varied populations in medicine, education, and social science. The catch is that deployment groups may differ from the study groups in set directions.

His method picks sites with minimax guarantees against those directional shifts. Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization supplies the machinery for the choice. A new cutting-plane algorithm implements it, and optimality is proved for the worst-case goal. Researchers gain a principled way to protect outside validity before the first site is enrolled.
arxiv-2511-04858:
Ali Mohamed, writing alone, recalculates B-meson decay rates inside the Mesogenesis framework. That framework tries to explain both baryogenesis and dark matter through meson decays. Heavy Quark Expansion supplies the rate calculation, carried to dimension-six terms.

The Darwin term is the last piece included in the systematic expansion. Mohamed finds regions where the suppressed terms actually beat the leading free-quark rate. There, the expansion itself nears breakdown, echoing the standard model only under heavy charm masses. Updated bounds on a key exclusive decay follow, tightening what Mesogenesis parameter space remains viable.
arxiv-2511-05258:
Liding Xu and co-authors extend semidefinite optimization from matrices to tensors, where the tensor case matches separable quantum states. The matrix cone is a workhorse of convex optimization, but its tensor cousin is far less tame.

The tensor cone can be re-shaped smoothly by factorization, yet it is not self-dual. No fast method is known to test membership or project onto it, and the optimization task, though convex, is NP-hard. The authors develop new ways to compute with this cone, which links convex methods to the study of quantum entanglement.
arxiv-2511-05358:
Jeff Murugan proposes a way to use on-shell scattering methods, a staple of particle physics, on strongly linked Dirac materials. Many such materials host low-energy excitations that act like massless relativistic spinors, the same form those methods were built for.

He shows that traits like nonlinear optical and Hall responses can be read from compact on-shell amplitudes, with no need to grind through Feynman diagrams. As a proof, he derives the nonlinear Hall conductivity of a Dirac semimetal from one parity-odd amplitude. The frame could ease hard sums across quantum matter.
arxiv-2511-05458:
Yukuan Tao and co-authors set a trade-off between complexity and energy cost in quantum phase estimation. In that task, a phase is read by applying a channel to a probe again and again until it is measured. Energy cost is a growing gauge of whether quantum tools can scale.

Their frame links the total energy spent to how complex the process is. The sequential protocol gives a clean test case. A firm trade-off tells builders that sharper phase reads cannot be had for free. They must budget energy as they budget qubits and time. That is a check on bold sensor claims.
arxiv-2511-05658:
Steve Bryson leads a team asking why estimates of Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars disagree so wildly. The quantity at stake counts rocky planets in the habitable zone, where liquid water could exist. The Kepler telescope was built to measure it, yet published values differ by more than a factor of ten.

The team traces the spread to two sources. Studies differ in definitions and input data, and Kepler's own limits force hard inference, since its detection edge sits right in the regime of interest. Extrapolating from easier planets risks large bias. The authors suggest reprocessing Kepler data for cleaner catalogs and look ahead to future telescopes that can measure the rate directly.
arxiv-2511-05758:
Anirudh Satheesh and co-authors design a learning algorithm for decisions that must stay safe and robust on average over time. Their setting joins three hard features: costs counted as long-run averages, hard constraints, and a world that may differ from the model. Standard primal-dual methods fail here because strong duality does not hold.

Their actor-critic algorithm works with the primal problem only. Theory shows it reaches near-feasible, near-optimal policies, with sample needs comparable to the easier discounted setting. Rates are given both with and without a slackness assumption. The work speaks to reinforcement learning for systems like power or traffic control, where average cost and safety limits both matter.
arxiv-2511-05858:
Chuanyu Li and co-authors build a handheld rig for teaching robots two-handed skills by demonstration. Handheld tools can gather many high-quality demonstrations fast. But existing rigs often lack firm touch sensing or steady pose tracking, which contact-rich, two-handed tasks demand.

Their system, ViTaMIn-B, centers on DuoTact, a soft visuo-tactile sensor that withstands large contact forces while capturing fine contact shape. The sensor's deformation is rebuilt as a 3D point cloud, which becomes the policy's input and helps it transfer across sensors. Pose tracking uses game controllers, avoiding the drift of camera-based methods. User studies with novices and experts found the rig efficient and easy to use, and it beat prior systems on four tasks.
arxiv-2511-05958:
Stepan Vanecek and co-authors present MT4G, a tool that maps the inner layout of graphics chips on its own. Knowing a chip's cache sizes, speeds, and layout is key to fast computing, yet that knowledge is scattered, patchy, and split by maker. Unlike CPUs, these chips had no standard mapping tool.

MT4G pairs the makers' own software hooks with more than fifty small test probes. Stats tests then settle traits that no hook reports outright. The team checked the tool on ten chips from both big makers. They show it feeding three jobs: speed modeling, bottleneck hunting, and live splitting of chip resources. The tool is open source and maker-neutral, aimed at AI and large-scale computing.
arxiv-2511-06058:
Jacob Fields and David Radice simulate two magnetized neutron stars spiraling together and merging, with a state-of-the-art relativity code. The stars carry initially dipolar magnetic fields extending outside them, and the matter follows a realistic nuclear equation of state that depends on temperature and composition. Three grid resolutions test whether the results can be trusted.

The two finest runs stayed in phase agreement through merger to a tight tolerance. The magnetic field grew during the merger, and a magnetized funnel formed over the remnant's poles. Yet the merged object failed to launch a magnetically dominated outflow, because stray baryonic matter polluted the funnel. The authors discuss which numerical and physical effects might change that verdict.
arxiv-2511-06558:
Akshay Revankar, Charan Renganathan, and Sartaj Wariah hunt for shared overhead work inside data centers that could move onto accelerator hardware. Modern data centers run varied workloads that repeat the same low-level functions, nicknamed tax components. Speeding up a tax pays off across the whole fleet, but offloading everything to accelerators is impractical.

The team profiles MongoDB, a database common in data center applications, running inside a standard benchmark suite. They identify its tax components and trace what those components demand from the processor. From those observations they suggest which groups of tax components could be offloaded together for the broadest performance gain.
arxiv-2511-06758:
Kohei Fujiu and colleagues pack surface code patches tightly together to save qubits in future quantum computers. The surface code leads the race toward fault-tolerant machines, but its appetite for physical qubits is enormous. Fusing several codewords into one connected, densely packed layout can cut the qubits per logical qubit to roughly three quarters.

Concrete deformation procedures for reaching that packed shape were missing, along with hard error-rate numbers. The authors supply both, plus a gate schedule for stabilizer measurements that suppresses hook errors. Noise simulations show the packed code's logical error rate beating the standard layout as distance grows and physical errors fall, but only with the protective scheduling in place.
arxiv-2511-07258:
Brayan M Shali and Rodolphe Sepulchre extend the notion of reciprocity to systems that vary in both time and space. Reciprocity, a symmetry familiar from acoustics, elasticity, electromagnetics, and thermodynamics, reveals deep internal structure in plain linear systems that do not change with time and ties closely to passivity and relaxation. The authors carry these ideas to linear time-and-space-invariant systems, an infinite-dimensional class with spatio-temporal dynamics.

They argue that, as in the finite case, combining reciprocity with impedance passivity forces the system to admit physical state-space forms. That matters most for such systems, where unbounded operators can otherwise destroy well-posedness, the guarantee that the model behaves sensibly at all. A physical example drives and shows the results, connecting abstract systems theory back to concrete physics.
arxiv-2511-07558:
Tomotaka Kuwahara, Marius Lemm, and Carla Rubiliani bound how fast boson energy can pile up in one spot. In Bose-Hubbard lattices, particles hop and repel on site, and local energy growth controls how quickly information spreads. Older estimates allowed faster than ballistic growth.

The new bound caps on-site energy growth at a ballistic rate for translation-invariant systems, even with long-range hopping. The proof uses adiabatic space-time localization operators rather than tracking particles directly. Sharper energy bounds feed into Lieb-Robinson limits on signal speed in quantum matter. Extending the result to higher moments could strengthen those fundamental speed limits further.
arxiv-2511-08058:
Steven De Keninck, Martin Roelfs, Leo Dorst, and David Eelbode rethink mesh representation using plane based geometric algebra. Meshes are built from simplices such as points, edges, and faces, and from complexes that join them into clouds, lines, and surfaces. The authors find compact ways to write these objects as joins of vertices and sums of joins.

One formula then gives size measures like length and area from the algebra norms. Unified coordinate free formulas follow for volume, centre of mass, and moments of inertia in any dimension. Worked real world examples show the approach is practical, opening a multi part cleanup of mesh foundations.
arxiv-2511-08258:
Jae Joong Lee and Bedrich Benes introduce Top2Ground, a diffusion model that generates ground level views from aerial images. The viewpoint gap is extreme, with heavy occlusion and a narrow field of view at street level. Rather than building depth maps or voxel models first, the method generates the ground image directly from the aerial input.

Denoising is conditioned jointly on spatial features from the aerial image and an estimated height map, plus semantic embeddings from CLIP. Geometry and content therefore guide the result together. On three data sets covering wide and narrow views, structural similarity improves by about seven percent on average over rivals.
arxiv-2511-08458:
Sanchita Chakraborty, Jeremy Hoskins, and Alan Lindsay present a high order numeric method for the Neumann Green function in two dimensions, for a general closed planar curve. The Green function gives the response to a point source with no flux through the edge. The method resolves interior and exterior versions. The source may sit in the bulk or on the surface, giving four functions in total. Singular and regular parts are separated so the singularity is represented exactly.

An integral constraint fixes the interior answer uniquely, and a fast integral method handles the regular part at high order. Accuracy is checked on disks and ellipses with known closed forms. Applications target capture of Brownian particles, including how small traps or boundary windows should be arranged to maximize capture.
arxiv-2511-08558:
Cedrick Kinavuidi, Luca Peres, and Oliver Rhodes pair spiking neural networks with hyperdimensional computing to read out network activity. Spiking networks promise low energy use, but standard readouts based on firing rates or spike timing trade away accuracy, speed, or both.

On gesture and animal-action datasets recorded with event cameras, their SNN-HDC model classifies more accurately and faster than comparable designs. Estimated energy use drops by factors ranging from just over one to more than three, depending on the dataset and baseline. The decoder can also flag samples from a class it never saw in training. On one dataset it caught every unseen-class sample, a useful safety trait for open-world sensing.
arxiv-2511-08658:
Stanislav Selitskiy tests a simple question with neural networks: does a model trained on one stock index forecast a different country's index just as well? The study tries several network designs, from standard architectures to more exotic ones, on long-term forecasts of indexes from different global markets.

The answer is mostly yes. Cross-trained models often match or beat models trained on the target index itself, suggesting the indexes share deep behavioral patterns that networks pick up. Selitskiy reads this as fresh evidence for the Efficient Market Hypothesis, the long-debated idea that prices already reflect available information. If markets process information alike everywhere, a model that learns one market's habits may genuinely carry those habits abroad.
arxiv-2511-08858:
Shou-I Tang and four co-authors rebuild the thermodynamics of information processing as a fully autonomous quantum system. The cast is a principal system, a heat bath, a memory, and a work source, all evolving under one Hamiltonian with no outside controller. Initial correlations between the parts are allowed, generalizing an influential earlier formulation.

The team derives the conditions the total Hamiltonian must obey so the work source acts as a true catalyst, keeping its randomness unchanged. That requirement turns out to be equivalent to a commutativity condition on the joint operators. From there they generalize the quantum speed limit into a thermodynamic speed limit for system and memory together. A dynamical version of Landauer's bound falls out, and the speed limit is reinterpreted through quantum hypothesis testing.
arxiv-2511-08958:
Md. Tanzeem Rahat and two co-authors study a sequence puzzle with a mountain shape. Given two ordered lists, the goal is the longest subsequence common to both whose values strictly rise and then strictly fall. Either slope may be empty. Such bitonic patterns appear wherever data climbs before it turns.

Reformulating the problem through the endpoint values at matching position pairs yields a constructive quadratic-time baseline. A match-sensitive algorithm then runs two dominance-maximum passes, its cost governed by the number of matches times a squared logarithmic factor. The authors state the interface that lets standard increasing-subsequence algorithms be reused, and they are careful to separate that reuse from any new range-searching machinery. A padding reduction imports a conditional hardness result: strongly subquadratic algorithms are unlikely, matching the known barrier for the increasing case.
arxiv-2511-09258:
Mirko Degli Esposti and five co-authors measure urban quality across six Italian cities using street-level imagery and computer vision. Rome, Bologna, Florence, Milan, Naples, and Palermo were scored with an urban vision intelligence system. Key metrics include a pavement condition index and a façade degradation score.

Quality varies widely within each city, with Milan showing especially large dispersion in pavement condition. The classic expectation that quality falls steadily with distance from the center proved weak everywhere, suggesting polycentric, fragmented city forms. Façade quality and greenery move together modestly but consistently across cities. The authors argue such vision-based diagnostics can scale to a national analysis of urban structure.
arxiv-2511-09658:
Ujjaini Das and four co-authors co-design ways for blind and low-vision learners to learn dance from videos they cannot see. Dance instruction online relies on visual demonstration, while audio description struggles to convey mechanics, orientation, speed, and timing together. Three workshops brought together blind dancers, instructors, and sound, haptics, and description experts.

Twenty-eight participants designed eight candidate systems across the workshops. Common themes emerged: staged learning that dissects routines piece by piece, shared vocabularies for movements, and selective modality use. Narration carried movement structure, sound carried expression, and haptics carried spatial cues in their designs. The authors distill design implications for accessible asynchronous dance instruction that scales beyond simple movements.
arxiv-2511-10058:
Shiqi Chen and Xuesong Chen speed up a class of control problems where a system ruled by a partial differential equation must be steered to a target. They recast the task as one nonlinear equation through a variational route and lay it out on a grid with a second-order scheme. Their solver is a Newton method that does not need smoothness, and it solves each Newton step only roughly, with a Krylov method called GMRES.

Solving the steps roughly cuts the work per step by a lot, and a slanting form of derivative gives the Newton steps their aim. A line search that need not improve at each step adapts the step size and keeps the method from stalling. Theory gives faster-than-linear closing speed near the best point, and numeric tests bore the claims out.
arxiv-2511-10358:
Zhiqiang Wan and Heng Zhang characterize which sets are observable for Schrödinger equations evolving on combinatorial graphs. The question asks whether watching the solution on a subset over time determines the whole state. On 1D lattices with a potential settling to a constant at infinity, they prove a set is observable at some time, equivalently at any time. That holds exactly when it satisfies a local arithmetic condition.

That arithmetic obstruction has no analogue in the continuous theory, where mere thickness of the set decides the question. The same criterion governs the heat equation on the integers. In higher-D lattices, everything outside any finite set is observable, while on discrete tori positive density alone does not guarantee observability. The result gives a clear test for when watching part of a network is enough to know the whole state.
arxiv-2511-10758:
Saheli Mukherjee, Bivas Mallick, and Pratik Ghosal devise a way to certify that a quantum channel truly preserves high-dimensional entanglement. Channels that store or transmit entangled subsystems are only useful for high-dimensional information processing if they keep that dimension intact. The most a channel can preserve is called its effective dimensionality.

Their method checks whether a channel's effective dimensionality exceeds a chosen threshold. It works for any channel without the usual crutches: no need to prepare entangled states, add auxiliary channels, or trust the measurement devices perfectly. The approach extends to certifying other non-resource-breaking channel classes, and the authors discuss how the scheme could be realized experimentally through explicit examples.
arxiv-2511-10958:
Gunho Jung, Heejo Kong, and Seong-Whan Lee address reading feelings from faces in video when only the whole clip has a single label. A clip has many frames, but just one emotion tag, so the model must guess which frames matter most. Treating the task as learning from grouped examples helps, but wide facial variety and change over time still make it hard.

Their TG-DFER method adds text guidance from a model trained on both pictures and words. Text prompts link rich emotion words to frame features, and a network reads both brief moves and long flow. Tests show gains in broad use, clarity, and sense of timing under weak labels.
arxiv-2511-11058: V. Bach, A. F. M. ter Elst, and J. Rehberg revisit the Birman-Solomyak theorem. The theorem concerns Hilbert-Schmidt operators. These are operators whose size can be summed in a square sense. The authors give a new short proof that uses only basic steps. They also widen the result beyond its first form. As a use case, they apply it to a Schrödinger-Poisson system. That system couples quantum particles with their own field.
arxiv-2511-11458:
Xenofon Chiotopoulos, Miriam Lucio Martinez, and their colleagues present TrackHHL, a quantum algorithm for reconstructing charged particle tracks at the LHCb experiment. The coming high-luminosity era will flood detectors with events whose reconstruction strains classical computing. The LHCb vertex locator serves as the case study. The method recasts tracking as minimizing an Ising-like energy through matrix inversion. The Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd quantum algorithm could in principle speed that job up exponentially.

Their version restricts phase estimation to one bit, which slims circuit depth by up to ten thousandfold and eases the readout problem. A classical post-processing step then rebuilds the primary vertices where collisions occurred, completing the event picture.
arxiv-2511-11658:
J. W. Moffat and E. J. Thompson link two famous spacetimes through a complex space. The two are anti-de Sitter space and de Sitter space. A smooth passage, called analytic continuation, joins them. Key geometric values stay intact on the way. No singularities appear during the crossing.

Gravity and gauge forces sit inside one complex symmetry group. Bulk unitarity is kept for both spaces. On the boundary, unitarity holds for anti-de Sitter space but fails for de Sitter space. That boundary is spacelike there. Holographic tools tie the picture to black hole heat and entropy. The work offers one angle on quantum gravity and the cosmological constant.
arxiv-2511-11758:
Michael Sun and four co-authors introduce GeoBPE, a tokenizer that turns protein shapes into discrete tokens a language-style model can read. Multimodal protein models need to reason over sequence, structure, and function together, but structure has lacked a principled alphabet: earlier tokenizers fixed token size or hid structure in continuous vectors.

Borrowing byte-pair encoding from text, GeoBPE merges frequent geometric pairs step by step into a hierarchy of shape primitives, enforcing global constraints as it goes. The vocabulary's resolution can be tuned, and the tokens stay interpretable. Better structure tokens could help models predict function, design proteins, and transfer across architectures more cleanly.
arxiv-2511-12258:
Ju Gao and Fang Shen derive Bell correlations for a physical state more general than the ideal spin singlet usually used in textbooks. Bell tests probe whether quantum correlations can be explained by local hidden causes. In the ideal case the key value does not depend on how far apart the detectors are.

Here the state is a pair of entangled Dirac wavepackets whose amplitude and phase coherence are set at the source. Local detectors sample the propagated branches, giving a value that changes with separation. At zero separation the maximal quantum value returns, while at large separation the surviving value is fixed by the coherence prepared at the source.
arxiv-2511-12458: O. V. Kaptsov examines the steady equations for a polytropic gas in three dimensions. He uses symmetry methods to build exact solutions. For a Chaplygin gas the analysis gives a very general solution family. It depends on three free functions. For a general adiabatic index, the work gives explicit solutions. Those are described by several constants.
arxiv-2511-12858:
Hao-Song Li calculates axial charges and magnetic moments for a family of ten hidden-charm molecular pentaquarks. Pentaquarks are exotic hadrons made of five quarks, and the hidden-charm molecular states are thought to bind a charmed baryon and a charmed meson loosely together. Working inside the constituent quark model, Li computes two properties that experiments and other theories can compare against: axial charges. They govern weak transitions. Magnetic moments reflect the internal arrangement of charge and spin.

The axial charges come out comparable in size to the nucleon's. More notable is a pattern in the magnetic moments: they obey sum rules, named the Hao-Song sum rules in the paper. These hold for states sharing the same spin-flavor configuration. Such relations give experimentalists cross-checks, since measuring a few members of the family constrains the rest.
arxiv-2511-12958:
Dhiren Panda, Manas Kumar Mohapatra, and Rukmani Mohanta ask how quantum decoherence distorts what physicists extract from B meson decays. Neutral B mesons oscillate and decay in ways that reveal Standard Model parameters such as the CKM angles, but real systems interact with their surroundings and lose coherence. The authors model that loss with a single decoherence parameter and re-examine key measurements in its presence. They include the CKM phase beta and penguin contributions.

Using simulated pseudo-experiments and flavor-symmetry analysis with a partner decay, plus a separate charmless decay mode, they track how decoherence moves the CP-violating observables. Their findings show the shifts can be crucial: ignoring decoherence risks mis-measuring the very parameters these decays are prized for. Environmental effects, they argue, belong in the error budget.
arxiv-2511-13658:
Jiaming Qu, Mengtian Guo, and Yue Wang use language models to explain why odd words such as a city name can flag deceptive reviews. Classifiers separate fake from genuine reviews well, but the word cues they learn are subtle and hard for people to grasp. Unexplained cues leave users unable to judge reviews where no classifier is at hand.

Their conjecture-then-validate method asks a language model to propose plain-language phenomena behind the cues, then checks each proposal against data. Phenomena found this way were grounded in the data, carried across similar domains, and predicted better than those drawn from model priors or in-context tricks alone. The output reads as rules a shopper can actually use.
arxiv-2511-13858:
Jaden Lopez and Stefano Profumo study how a hidden companion could weaken the search for dark matter at the center of our galaxy. Theory predicts a dense spike of dark matter around the central supermassive black hole, which should boost signals from dark matter particles destroying each other. A heavy companion object orbiting nearby could stir that spike and carve out its inner part.

Combining a simple scouring model with full numerical runs, the authors map how the signal drops with companion mass, orbit size, age, and spike steepness. For shallow spikes even a modest companion can cut the expected flux by ten to a hundred times. A simple fitting formula captures their results well.
arxiv-2511-14358:
Kai Ren and Maryam Kamgarpour work back from play to hidden costs in a noisy game. Two or more players act over a set time span in a linear quadratic Gaussian game. Each player's Nash play, the point where no one gains by a lone change, comes from cost weights that shift over time and stay hidden. The authors first mark out the full set of cost weights that could yield a given Nash play.

They then give a back-stepping method that finds the time-shifted costs, with a bound on the error when only a few play paths are seen. Tests on the computer, plus drive tests, show the method finds costs that copy both the Nash play and the seen paths.
arxiv-2511-14558:
Adam Bajger and six co-authors present a clustering method to explain digital pathology models. Pathologists use convolutional networks to flag disease in slide images, but need to trust model logic. Common saliency tools explain one slide at a time. The new method instead groups internal activations to show global model behavior, with finer detail.

Resulting clusters can be visualized to reveal what patterns the model relies on. The team test the technique on an existing prostate cancer detection model. It proves useful for understanding that model in practice. Clearer global explanations could speed safe adoption in clinics. The method complements per slide tools rather than replacing them.
arxiv-2511-14658:
A. Crespo Gómez and 21 co-authors examine a distant galaxy whose light left when the universe was young, magnified by gravitational lensing. The galaxy, RXCJ2248-ID, stands out for holding far more nitrogen than expected. Using sharp data from the James Webb Space Telescope and the ALMA array, the team maps its hot ionized gas.

The gas proves very hot and clumpy, with densities that vary widely from cloud to cloud and a complex pattern of motion. Broad components point to dusty outflows pushing material out of the galaxy. Such detailed views of an early, chemically odd galaxy help test how the first galaxies formed stars and enriched their surroundings.
arxiv-2511-14758:
Dawn Lawrie and eight co-authors present NeuCLIRBench, a modern test collection for retrieval across languages. Good test collections need judgments that can separate strong systems from weak ones. Documents are written natively in Chinese, Persian, and Russian, plus machine translated English versions. Scenarios cover monolingual, cross language, and multilingual search.

Queries come from three years of a shared evaluation track. Hundreds of thousands of relevance judgments support the tasks. Monolingual and cross language tasks use about one hundred and fifty queries. Multilingual search uses one hundred queries with relevant items in all three languages. The scale gives strong statistical power for measuring real progress in cross language retrieval.
arxiv-2511-14958:
Alessa I. Wiggins, Jamie R. Quinn, and twelve co-authors use galaxy simulations to explain the odd orbit of Berkeley 20, an old open star cluster. Open clusters carry a chemical fingerprint and a known age, so their present paths record the Milky Way's past pushes and pulls. Berkeley 20 is unusually distant, metal-poor, and far above the galactic disk for its kind.

In the FIRE-2 simulation suite, the team finds a look-alike cluster and follows its life story. The simulated cluster wanders outward and climbs high above its home disk, much like the real one. Tracing how it got there shows which galactic events can lift a cluster onto such an extreme path.
arxiv-2511-15658:
Naomi Simumba, Nils Lehmann, and ten co-authors present GEO-Bench-2, an evaluation framework for geospatial foundation models, the large pre-trained models now used to analyze Earth observation data. Testing such models lacked standard protocols, making fair comparison hard. The new bench spans classification, segmentation, regression, and detection tasks across nineteen openly licensed data sets.

Instead of a single score, models are ranked inside capability groups that share traits like resolution, spectral bands, or time structure. Experiments show no single model wins everywhere. Models pre-trained on natural images lead on high-resolution tasks, while Earth-specific models lead on multispectral uses such as farming and disaster response, so the best choice depends on the task.
arxiv-2511-15758:
Miguel M. Valero and Marcello Meldi combine data assimilation and machine learning to predict flows that oscillate over time. Data-driven fluid methods work well on simple, steady cases, but many real flows vary cyclically and challenge a single learned model. Their approach starts from sparse, high-quality measurements plus a cheaper low-fidelity simulation of the same flow.

Data assimilation merges those sources into a complete, accurate flow history. Multiple learning tools are then trained on separate phases of the cycle, using a sliding window, so each model specializes in one part of the motion. Applied to flow around an oscillating cylinder in a smooth regime, the phase-resolved method captured transient features a global model would miss.
arxiv-2511-15958:
Zhenyu Bi, Gaurav Srivastava, and five co-authors benchmark how well small language models can judge whether an answer is correct. Small models are cheap and promising for reasoning tasks, but their skill as evaluators was unclear next to large models. Earlier judging setups compare candidate answers indirectly against reference labels or each other, which resists fine-grained, automated scoring.

Their JudgeBoard pipeline asks models directly to assess answer correctness, then ranks them as judges with accuracy and an Elo rating system borrowed from chess. Leaderboards span math and science or commonsense reasoning across five data sets. A multi-agent judging method, where several small models with distinct reasoning styles interact, lifts lightweight judges toward large-model accuracy.
arxiv-2511-16658:
Vedran Brdar and four co-authors assess whether neutrinos from binary neutron star mergers could ever be observed, and what their timing would reveal about neutrino mass. Attention has focused on the diffuse supernova background, expected to give about a hundred events in Hyper-Kamiokande over the next decade. Merger neutrinos went largely unstudied with modern inputs.

Updated simulations and the lowered merger rate from gravitational wave observatories make detection infeasible for current and near-future detectors; a megaton-scale detector with a low energy threshold would be needed. The authors use energy-dependent time windows, since a nonzero neutrino mass delays events after the gravitational wave signal and widens the search window. That timing sensitivity to the lightest neutrino mass could exceed both laboratory bounds and supernova projections.
arxiv-2511-16858:
Toufique Ahmed, Jatin Ganhotra, Avraham Shinnar, and Martin Hirzel carry out the first broad study of test overfitting in tools that fix code issues. Overfitting here means code that passes the tests it was shown but still misses real cases or breaks other parts of the program. The risk grows when tests are made by machine from the issue text itself, since those tests can be flawed.

Some repair tools even revise code and tests together, which can hide the flaw further. The authors set out how often this happens in the SWE-bench setting and what signs mark it. Their work gives tool builders a clear warning: passing the given tests is not the same as fixing the issue, and checks need to look past the test set.
arxiv-2511-16958:
I. Sebastian Buhai models how artificial intelligence firms time their product releases, treating each release as a strategic option the firm can choose to exercise. In his setup, a firm privately watches its technology improve, and can issue a cheap reversible patch or a costly, hard-to-reverse pivot. It also controls how often it shares noisy public signals about performance and safety.

Buhai shows that when staying silent is cheap, the best strategy includes quiet windows around close-call moments, which collapse release behavior into a simple two-rung ladder of patches and pivots. Debt, he finds, barely affects patch timing but can distort pivots, though only within a bound set by switching costs. The model predicts patterns in release timing and disclosure that data on real firms could test.
arxiv-2511-17258:
Omer Rochman and Gilles Louppe tackle a flaw in neural solvers for partial differential equations, the equations that govern many physical systems. Such solvers are fast, but their outputs often break the very rules the equations impose, like conservation laws. Easy rules can be enforced cheaply, while curved, nonlinear rules are much harder to respect, above all when effects stretch across time.

The authors test two fixes applied after the solver runs, with no retraining. One solves a small optimisation problem to pull the output back to the allowed set, and the other uses a local straight-line shortcut built from derivative products. Across sample equations, both fixes cut rule breaks sharply and improve accuracy over standard physics-guided baselines.
arxiv-2511-17358:
Daniil Ignatev and three co-authors argue that natural language inference, judging whether a hypothesis follows from a premise, should be grounded in pictures rather than learned from text alone. Text-only systems often pass inference benchmarks by exploiting surface heuristics and dataset biases instead of meaning. The authors' zero-shot method instead generates a visual representation of the premise with a text-to-image model, then compares that representation against the textual hypothesis.

Two comparison techniques are tested: cosine similarity between representations, and visual question answering over the generated image. Without any task-specific training, the method reaches high accuracy and proves robust against the textual biases that trip up conventional systems. A controlled adversarial dataset, built by the authors, confirms the robustness. Their conclusion is that visual grounding offers a promising meaning representation for more trustworthy language understanding.
arxiv-2511-17458:
Ismail El Mellas, Juan J. Hidalgo, and Marco Dentz simulate fluid flow through pipes whose walls wave in a sinusoidal pattern, from smooth laminar flow up to turbulence. Direct numerical simulations span bulk Reynolds numbers from one to over five thousand. The waviness changes the physics early: at quite low speeds, flow can reverse in the troughs. Recirculation zones form and sharply raise friction, an effect classical formulas based on bulk geometry fail to capture.

The authors define an effective hydraulic radius that does capture it. Wall modulation also triggers turbulence far below the classical threshold for smooth pipes, with a critical Reynolds number that falls as the wall amplitude grows, following a power law. In the turbulent regime the flow behaves as fully rough, and the wall amplitude, read through the hydraulic radius, estimates the equivalent sand roughness. The Moody chart, they conclude, cannot describe such pipes.
arxiv-2511-17858:
Isabelle Ye, Philip Bull, Caroline Guandalin, Chris Clarkson, and Ainulnabilah Nasirudin forecast whether a subtle effect in galaxy images can be measured with two major surveys. Galaxies moving toward or away from us look slightly larger or smaller, an effect called Doppler magnification, which is strongest at low redshift.

They combine planned size measures from the Rubin Observatory survey with redshifts from a spectroscopic survey. Simulated images show that natural variation in galaxy sizes, not measurement error, limits precision. Even so, the effect should be detected clearly in several distance slices, opening a new test of how galaxies move.
arxiv-2511-18158:
Abdelrahman Abdelmotlb, Abdallah Taman, Sherif Mostafa, and Moustafa Youssef reduce the survey effort behind indoor localization by fingerprinting, which normally requires collecting signal data tagged by location at every target spot. Their LocaGen framework instead generates realistic new fingerprints for locations nobody visited.

A conditional diffusion model, guided by a spatially aware tuning, makes fingerprints from a subset of visited locations. Rules of thumb augment the visited data, and a density based rule picks which spots to visit for a robust spread. On a real WiFi data set, exactness holds even when a large share of locations is unseen, and it beats leading rival methods by a clear margin.
arxiv-2511-18458:
Chrysafis Hartonas builds one relational frame that can serve as semantics for many sentence logics at once. Logics differ in what they allow — some drop rules that classic logic keeps — and each has often needed its own model story. A shared frame would ease comparison across that whole range.

The frame grows from a known duality for Boolean algebras with operators, spread to posets, semilattices, and lattices with loose operators. Completeness proofs use a choice free build of canonical extensions for the algebras tied to each logic. For logics of implication, results move through a full translation into modal companions, with a generalized algorithm to compute matches. One kit thus covers classic and non classic systems alike.
arxiv-2511-18558:
Genoveva Vargas-Solar examines gender, diversity, and inclusion gaps in data science and artificial intelligence across academia and industry, in both majority and minority world settings. These fast growing fields shape hiring and technology, yet men dominate them, and the pandemic hit women and minorities hardest, deepening current inequality.

The chapter maps who is present by sector, job type, and skill level and traces root causes, from unequal access to education and funding to views of elite fields. It argues that imbalance feeds bias in machine learning systems themselves. It closes with workable plans for building a fairer and more supportive setting.
arxiv-2511-18758:
Judah Van Zandt and five co-authors blur the line between giant planets and brown dwarfs with a fresh census of companion masses. Doppler surveys track both kinds well over orbits to thirty years, but Doppler data give only a minimum mass, tilted by the unknown orbit angle. A purported planet may in truth be a brown dwarf or a star.

The team join legacy Doppler data with absolute sky position measures to refit orbits for a large companion set from the California Legacy Survey. Near half of the refit brown dwarfs cross into star mass once the true angle is known. Folding in sensitivity maps gives an occurrence spread that runs smooth from planets to brown dwarfs. Formation lines drawn at a set mass look less sharp.
arxiv-2511-19058:
Han Luo and eight co-authors raise the current-carrying capacity of an iron selenide superconductor simply by squeezing it. The critical current density sets how much current a superconductor can carry before resistance returns, and standard boosts, doping and irradiation, add foreign atoms or defects that change the material itself. Their method applies compressive strain through a plastic substrate that shrinks unevenly as it cools, straining the crystal without altering its chemistry.

At low temperature the critical current rises about fourfold with no field, and tenfold under a strong field. Analysis of the pinning that holds magnetic vortices in place shows strain strengthens it and shifts its character from point-like pinning toward a mix with surface pinning. The work offers a clean route to stronger superconducting tapes and magnets.
arxiv-2511-19258:
Antonis Psistakis reports thesis work on making remote memory access work across computer nodes. In the Unimem system, many nodes share one virtual address space, and each node's IOMMU hardware must translate addresses correctly for direct memory transfers. ARM's version of that unit, the SMMU, has sparse and unclear Linux documentation.

Psistakis wrote custom kernel modules to insert address mappings into the SMMU on a Xilinx Zynq chip. Transfers sent to virtual addresses, from both the main processors and the programmable logic, passed through the SMMU and were translated as intended. The tests confirm the hardware path that Unimem's shared memory design depends on.
arxiv-2511-19458:
Jeongeun Lee, Ryang Heo, and Dongha Lee build a reward model that judges text-to-image output by one user's taste at a time. General scoring tools miss how personal visual preferences are, since people read the same prompt in different ways. Their model, PIGReward, invents user-specific judging dimensions on the fly.

With little reference data, a self-bootstrapping step reasons over the few examples to build a rich picture of the user's taste, needing no per-user training. Step-by-step reasoning then scores each image and gives feedback that rewrites prompts toward the user's intent. A per-user benchmark, PIGBench, supports tests showing gains in accuracy and clarity.
arxiv-2511-19858:
Farzad Ahmed, Joniel Augustine Jerome, Meliha Yetisgen, and Özlem Uzuner test whether language models can find and fix errors in clinical notes. Such notes can contain factual, diagnostic, and treatment mistakes that put patients at risk. The team compares plain zero-shot prompting, fixed example prompts, and retrieval-based dynamic prompting.

Using the MEDEC dataset, they test nine instruction-tuned models on flagging errors, locating the faulty sentence, and correcting it. Retrieval-based prompting, which pulls in similar examples, cuts false positives and raises recall compared with the other methods. It also produces corrections that fit the context better, though the authors still study where model reasoning differs from clinicians.
arxiv-2511-20258:
Wang, Cheng, Zhong, Chen, and Zhou balance fast and slow senses in multi-modal learning. Their 2025 paper proposes MBCD for domain generalization. Models must work on unseen domains, not just training ones. Weight averaging usually helps by finding flat minima. In multi-modal setups it backfires early though.

Fast modalities dominate averaging before slow ones mature. The fused model then leans on one sense too much. MBCD starts with adaptive modality dropout in the student. Randomly muting strong senses curbs the early bias. A gradient consistency rule aligns branch learning signals. Uni-modal and fused gradients are pushed to agree. A weight-averaged teacher then distills fused knowledge back. Each single-sense branch receives cross-modal teaching. Convergence steers toward flatter, sturdier solutions. EPIC-Kitchens and HAC benchmarks tested the framework. Accuracy and robustness beat prior methods across settings. Balanced fusion survives domain shift better.
arxiv-2511-20658:
Ashlae Blum'e argues in 2025 that the pictures scientists use for sound quietly shape what they can learn from it. Waveforms, spectrograms, and editing screens modelled on recording-studio software dominate audio research, yet each carries design assumptions from the era and industry that produced it. Because a display steers how people group and connect patterns, Blum'e warns that tools built for older jobs may no longer fit today's research questions.

The argument walks through a long history of sound tools. It starts with the phonautograph of 1857, which etched sound onto glass, and the phonograph of 1877. It reaches the Fast Fourier Transform of 1965, the maths still underpinning digital sound processing. Studio software followed, from the Soundstream editing system of 1977 and the Fairlight CMI synthesiser of 1979 to Steinberg's Pro-16 in 1986, whose layout resembles modern editors. Blum'e urges designers to add dimensions back into sound displays, so analysis and creative work both gain.
arxiv-2511-21458:
Guilherme Inacio and four coauthors switch on a forbidden solar effect with an electric field, in a 2025 condensed matter paper. The bulk photovoltaic effect lets some crystals generate current from light with no junction, but only when their structure lacks a center of symmetry. Many layered semiconductors are centrosymmetric, so the effect is ruled out, unless something breaks the symmetry from outside.

Inacio and his coauthors bake a static out-of-plane electric field, a gate bias, directly into the material's quantum ground state using a Wannier-based Hamiltonian dressed by the field. Applied to molybdenum disulfide, the method produces a genuine shift current in centrosymmetric bilayers where none should exist. The response grows linearly at small fields, then saturates as the field weakens the coupling between bands. Polar stackings, which already respond, become tunable instead, and a Taylor expansion ties the whole picture to the third-order optical response.
arxiv-2511-22058:
Burke, Macheras, and Strauss, measure theorists, develop the theory of vector liftings for products of probability spaces. A lifting picks one concrete representative function from each equivalence class of functions equal almost everywhere. Vector liftings keep linearity without demanding positivity, which lets them exist on all L^p spaces rather than only L-infinity. The paper asks how liftings on two factor spaces combine into liftings on their product, a question with a long, murky history.

The authors establish existence of strong product vector liftings for two-factor products. Vector liftings that behave as 2-marginals yield a characterization of stochastic processes admitting a measurable modification, along lines discovered by Musiał. The paper gives a proof of that characterization avoiding liftings altogether. Machinery for extending measures by new null sets, with weakened completeness assumptions, powers several of the improvements over earlier results.
arxiv-2511-22158:
Patra, Anurag, Sai Shankar, and colleagues run quantum chemistry for drug-like molecules on quantum hardware by combining two size-cutting tricks. Density matrix embedding theory fragments a molecule into impurity problems. Sample-based quantum diagonalization builds the solution space from configurations sampled on the quantum processor, repaired on a classical computer. Applied together, the pipeline computes ground-state energies for natural ligand-like molecules in a minimal basis.

The embedded Hamiltonians were executed on IBM's Eagle R3 superconducting processor, the Sherbrooke device. For every system studied, the energies matched classical density-matrix-embedding full-configuration-interaction benchmarks within chemical accuracy, one kilocalorie per mole, the threshold chemists care about. The authors present this as evidence that sample-based quantum methods inside an embedding framework can handle chemically relevant molecules. It is a concrete step toward quantum-assisted drug discovery rather than a toy demonstration.
arxiv-2511-22458:
Al Khansa and Bahannis improve radar target detection inside future wireless networks combining sensing and communication on one platform. Their setting is OFDM-based integrated sensing and communication, where a periodogram scan looks for several targets at once. Window functions used before the scan trade sharpness against sidelobes, ghost echoes that can mask weak targets. Standard systems commit to one fixed window plus one fixed detection routine, either cheap or accurate.

Their dual-window algorithm runs two complementary windows in parallel, one tuned for resolution and one for sidelobe suppression, applies a cheap cancellation routine to both, and compares the answers. When the two agree, the sharp estimates are accepted directly. When they disagree, a costlier coherent routine is triggered to settle the ambiguity. Simulations show it matches the expensive routine's accuracy while cutting complexity, especially at high signal-to-noise ratio.
arxiv-2511-22758:
Rantzer extends his exact adaptive control solutions to systems whose states live on cones. Positive systems, states and inputs nonnegative, arise in chemistry, biology, and economics. Recent work on control over cones found problem classes where the Bellman equation admits explicit solutions like classical linear quadratic control. Rantzer brings minimax adaptive control into that framework: the controller must perform against worst-case disturbances and unknown parameters simultaneously.

The payoff is exact solutions to Bellman equation instances for dual control, where a controller must learn the system while controlling it. Because the solution is explicit, the tradeoff between exploration and exploitation can be optimised exactly rather than approximately. The controller's law compresses past data into one accumulated sum, and as data accumulate, attention focuses on the shrinking set of consistent models. The result enlarges the small catalogue of adaptive problems with provably optimal solutions.
arxiv-2511-22858:
Ishihara and colleagues design a legal AI assistant obeying courtroom rules, not just answering questions. In Japanese litigation, expert commissioners, physicians, accountants, engineers, supply specialist knowledge helping judges clarify disputed points. Replacing those experts with a retrieval-augmented language model runs into strict legal norms; the authors work out what such a system must satisfy to be trusted in that role.

Three requirements emerge. First, retrieval must gather knowledge relevant to the disputed issues while honouring the ban on private knowledge: only properly sourced material. Second, responses must originate from the retrieved context and remain faithful to it, with attribution. Third, referenced knowledge must carry appropriate timestamps, since what facts were available when matters legally. The paper lays out a design meeting these requirements for medical litigation support; implementation and experiments follow. The framing generalises: any professional RAG system inherits its profession's norms.
arxiv-2511-22958:
Shen and colleagues build a reusable AI backbone for solar images from NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory, a satellite that has watched the Sun since 2010. Its instruments record the solar atmosphere in ultraviolet light and map surface magnetic fields at the same time. But most learning systems are trained from scratch for one task or borrow features from ordinary photos, which fit solar data poorly.

Their framework, SolarCHIP, pretrains image encoders by contrast. It teaches them that views of the same solar moment should match across instruments and at matching locations, at three levels from whole image down to patches. On two jobs, translating between instrument views and classifying full-disk solar flares, it reached state-of-the-art results. The biggest gains came when labeled training data was cut to as little as 5 percent of the full set. And the team released the weights for others to reuse.
arxiv-2511-23158:
Cao and colleagues build a detector for AI-generated images that must show its work, because explainable detectors mostly rationalize a verdict after the fact instead of reasoning from checkable evidence. Their contribution starts with REVEAL-Bench, a benchmark in which each image comes with a chain of evidence assembled from lightweight expert models. It also has step-by-step reasoning traces and justifications recorded for every judgment.

On top of the benchmark sits REVEAL, a multimodal model trained with an expert-grounded reinforcement learning method. Its reward scores detection accuracy, explanation fidelity, and logical coherence against the evidence at the same time. In their experiments it set a state of the art for explainable image forensics, improving detection accuracy and explanation quality. It generalized better to images from generators it was not trained on, the out-of-domain setting where surface pattern matching usually fails.
arxiv-2511-23358:
Moine and colleagues replace hand-written proofs with a new type system for disentanglement. The property that parallel tasks stay oblivious to each other's memory allocations. Disentanglement lets a runtime like the MaPLe compiler do garbage collection locally inside each task with no synchronization, a large performance win. But the only static check before was a full separation-logic proof per program, demanding expert effort every time.

Their TypeDis annotates every type with a timestamp naming the task that allocated the value, supports recursive types and polymorphism over both types and timestamps. And lets timestamps change at join points through a subtyping rule they call subtiming. Any well-typed program is then automatically disentangled for programmers, and the soundness of the system, plus all its worked examples. Is mechanized in the Rocq proof assistant using an improved version of the earlier DisLog logic.
arxiv-2511-23458:
Powell reviews the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season. An odd season that produced fewer storms than average yet above-average accumulated cyclone energy, concentrated in three distinct bursts of activity. Broad-scale conditions were often hostile, with no La Niña to help. But above-average sea surface temperatures meant that storms which did form could intensify strongly, yielding five hurricanes, three of which reached category five in the basin.

Powell attributes the quiet early and mid season to a strong upper-level trough driving wind shear, plus high sea-level pressure causing sinking. Dry air, while later clusters followed windows of weak shear and favorable equatorial wave activity from the Madden-Julian oscillation and Kelvin waves. Just four strong storms, Erin, Humberto, and Melissa among them, produced most of the season's energy, fitting the predicted trend of fewer but more intense tropical cyclones in coming decades.
arxiv-2512-00258:
Mixed polynomials involve both a complex variable and its conjugate, which complicates their geometry. Davi Lopes Medeiros, José Edson Sampaio, and Eder Leandro Sanchez Quiceno study the Lipschitz geometry of such polynomials in 2025. They work with two-variable polynomials satisfying a Newton inner non-degeneracy condition.

The authors investigate bi-Lipschitz equivalence, which asks when two singularities have the same shape up to controlled stretching. They show conditions under which families of perturbations stay trivial in a precise sense. Singularity theory uses such results to classify the possible local shapes of algebraic objects. Bi-Lipschitz maps distort distances by at most a fixed factor in both directions. Newton non-degeneracy ties the polynomial's geometry to its Newton diagram. The work is pure math, and its worth lies in clean lines. It tells us which forms can match, and which can not, when we stretch space in tame ways.
arxiv-2512-00458:
The method of image charges solves electrostatic problems by replacing a conductor with imaginary mirror charges. Farhang Loran and Saman Moghimi-Araghi, at Isfahan University of Technology, ask whether a curved mirror honestly reflects identity in 2025. Their setting is a multipole placed before a grounded conducting sphere.

Standard problems treat single charges near conductors, while multipoles have received less attention beyond the flat plane case. Multipole images reveal how the sphere distorts a structured charge distribution, not just a point. The study is a careful piece of classical electrostatics, useful for teaching and for boundary-value problems in physics. Grounded spheres are a textbook geometry, so the multipole extension is a clean next step.
arxiv-2512-00858:
Saiful Mondal and Ahmad Al Abdulaali study special classes of analytic functions in a 2025 math paper. An analytic function can be written as a power series, and its shape can be sorted into families. One family, lemniscate starlike functions, is defined by how the function's values relate to a figure-eight curve called a lemniscate.

The authors derive conditions on the power series coefficients that place a function in this family. Their tools include the Cauchy product of series and inequalities involving the Pochhammer symbol and the Gamma function. They also apply the results to special functions. Coefficient tests make membership in such families easy to check.
arxiv-2512-00958:
Vladimir Dzhunushaliev and Vladimir Folomeev build a charged object out of a wormhole in a 2025 physics paper. A wormhole is a tunnel-like shortcut through spacetime, usually an exotic idea. Within Einstein-Dirac-Maxwell theory, they study an asymmetric wormhole held open by a complex spinor field.

The spinor field has a bare mass near the Planck mass and gives the system its topology and an intrinsic spin. An electric field supplies the charge, and a magnetic field completes the setup. Their goal is a realistic classical model of charge, where charge and spin arise from spacetime structure rather than a point particle.
arxiv-2512-01058:
Youssof Abdullah, Violet Hart, and Moumita Das model how neurons fire in a 2025 biophysics paper. An action potential is the spike a neuron uses to signal, and voltage-gated sodium channels drive its rise. These channels come in several isoforms, versions with slightly different behavior.

Their conductance-based model pairs a six-state Markov description of sodium channels with a first-order potassium channel model. They vary the maximal sodium and potassium conductances and compare nine sodium channel isoforms. The stability analysis shows which settings let a neuron generate spikes reliably. Such models link channel mutations to excitability problems in disease.
arxiv-2512-01858:
Jakub Czartowski, Adam Sawicki, and Karol Zyczkowski extend quantum pushforward designs to approximate forms. Pushforward designs average quantum states or channels in a structured way. Exact averaging is often out of reach. Approximate forms settle for finite precision.

Using Schatten norms and Lipschitz arguments, they bound the approximation traits. Builds come from complex projective spaces, simplices, mixed states, and channels. Bounds tell users how close an easy build sits to the ideal. That helps in tomography and benchmarking of quantum devices. Projective builds are explicit, so a user can construct the design rather than merely know that one exists somewhere in theory.
arxiv-2512-02058:
Language models can be dressed up as personas, a man, a woman, a Muslim, a political supporter, and asked to answer as that person would. Tabia Tanzin Prama, Christopher Danforth, and Peter Sheridan Dodds test in 2025 how well such personas match real people in a low-resource setting, Bangladesh.

They compared human answers with those of eight model-generated personas on culturally specific questions. The models' shallow grasp of local context, culture, and emotion is the suspected weak point, and the study measures the gap quantitatively. Findings like these warn against using synthetic personas as cheap stand-ins for surveying real communities.
arxiv-2512-02558:
Yufei Xiao and Shangfei Wang work on predicting empathy, the felt sense of sharing another person's state. Most past methods read text alone, which misses tone of voice and facial cues. They also ignore extra documents that describe a scene and could enrich the reading.

Their 2025 method joins video, audio, and text in one multi modal system. Supervisory documents, holding privileged extra information, assist training as well. Richer inputs should help machines judge empathy in settings like counseling, education, and care, where missing a cue can change the right response. A judge who can hear, see, and read at once is far less prone to miss a key cue.
arxiv-2512-02658:
Teresia Stranden and five co-authors build a bridge between light flying free and light guided in chips. Free space beams are easy to shape into many spatial modes, while waveguides on chips are compact and stable. Joining the two worlds is key for larger multi mode communication networks.

Their multimode interface passes several spatial modes between the two domains at once. A good interface loses little light and keeps modes separate and clean. Such links could let chip based processors handle the rich beams used in high capacity optical communication and sensing. A clean bridge lets chip gear tap beams that roam free, which is how most light based links start out.
arxiv-2512-02758:
Klaus Jansen, Lis Pirotton, and Malte Tutas show that optimal bin packing can need a surprising variety of bin layouts. In the classical problem, items of a few different sizes must fill as few bins as possible. The support of a solution counts how many differently filled bin types it uses.

The authors prove the needed support can grow exponentially in the number of item sizes. Even an optimal plan may mix a huge range of layouts. That lower bound limits how compactly optimal packings can be described, guiding algorithm designers who compress solutions for huge inputs. Wide bins are not a flaw of one code; they are a trait of the task that plans must own up to.
arxiv-2512-02858:
Mahrokh Ghoddousi Boroujeni and three co-authors control noisy nonlinear systems with guarantees attached. Stochastic nonlinear optimal control seeks plans that minimize cost under random disturbances. The true expected cost is usually intractable, so practice averages over a finite sample of disturbance scenarios.

That empirical shortcut needs proof it will generalize to unseen noise. Their PAC-Bayesian approach comes with stability and generalization guarantees in the title's promise. Guaranteed control matters for robots, vehicles, and medical devices, where a plan that works only on sampled noise is not safe enough. A plan with a proof is a plan a board can sign. That mark of trust is what moves such plans from labs to streets and wards.
arxiv-2512-02958:
Rajat Adak and L. Sunil Chandran count cliques, the tightly linked groups inside a graph. For a simple graph, the key count records how many copies of a complete graph on t vertices appear inside it. Complete graphs, where every vertex joins every other, are the densest possible patterns.

Their generalized Zykov theorem extends a classic result about such counts. Zykov's theorem long tied clique counts to edge counts in extremal graph theory. A broader version gives sharper bounds for networks where dense clusters drive behavior, from chemistry to social graphs. Dense groups drive much of graph life, from pals to parts, so sharp counts for them pay rent in more than one trade.
arxiv-2512-03058:
How word pieces move inside a Transformer model is the focus here. Duy-Tung Pham and six co-authors study trained Transformers in this 2025 work. They look at self-attention, the step that lets each piece weigh the others, and at codes that mark word order.

The team treats the model as a system that flows over time. They describe how its paths settle in the long run. Knowing that behavior could help builders make models more stable and clear. It may also guide small changes that lift how well these models work. Model builders can use these long-run patterns to judge training choices with more confidence.
arxiv-2512-03158:
Sewage can reveal which virus variants move through a town. Adele Chinda, Richmond Azumah, and Hemanth Demakethepalli Venkateswara work on that task in this 2025 work. Wastewater checks give a broad view of health across a whole community.

The data are messy, with high noise, low virus coverage, and broken reads. Worse, there are no labels to train on. The authors use contrastive deep learning, which learns by comparing samples, to spot variants. Better tools could warn health teams earlier when a new variant spreads. Communities could gain earlier warnings than clinic reports alone can give, since sewage reflects whole neighborhoods at once.
arxiv-2512-03258:
New satellite data show the ocean surface in fine detail, plus noise. J. W. Skinner, J. Callies, A. Lawrence, and X. Zhang work on cleaning that data in this 2025 work. The SWOT satellite measures sea surface height over wide swaths.

The team isolates the balanced part of the signal, which reflects steady ocean flow. They use a Bayesian method based on Gaussian processes to fill the gap under the satellite. The method pulls out flow structures at medium and small scales. Cleaner maps help track currents, eddies, and ocean heat. Balanced flow is the part tied to currents, while waves and noise must be set aside first.
arxiv-2512-03858:
Shining light through a single cell and watching how it scatters can reveal the cell's dry mass, volume, and inner structure. Cael Warner compares the tools for interpreting such scattering in a 2025 computational physics preprint. The Born-Rytov approximation estimates a cell's effective refractive index from scattered intensity, polarisation, and phase, but its accuracy against fuller methods needed checking.

Warner benchmarks the approximation against an exact analytical solution, a finite-difference time-domain method on a Yee lattice, and a discrete-dipole method, all solving Maxwell's equations. Test cases cover a simple sphere and a tomographic reconstruction of a yeast cell, scored on accuracy, memory, and compute time. Against a commercial time-domain package, Born-Rytov and discrete-dipole approaches matched the yeast cell's far-field pattern better. The comparison gives experimentalists a practical guide to choosing a method.
arxiv-2512-04158:
The Higgs boson's mass is oddly light. Dark matter's favourite candidate happens to sit near the same scale. Maximilian Detering, Thomas Steingasser, and Tevong You argue the two facts explain each other. Their 2025 particle physics preprint links the hierarchy problem to weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs, the classic thermal dark matter candidate.

In their scenario, the Higgs mass is dynamically driven toward the WIMP scale, because the true vacuum lies near a phase transition boundary. That arrangement destabilises the Higgs potential just above the weak scale. Rescuing it requires the new physics naturalness expects: light fermions, heavy bosons, and a WIMP whose Higgs couplings set the boundary. A higgsino-like model shows the mechanism working. If the WIMP proves heavier than a threshold value, the scenario tightly bounds the Higgs mass and the stabilising physics scale.
arxiv-2512-04358:
Ao Xu and a team of co-authors built MAFNet, a network that judges depth from two camera views fast enough for phones. Stereo matching pairs points across left and right images to build a depth map. Older designs lean on heavy three-dimensional filters or slow step-by-step refinement. Both strain small devices and block real-time use. Their 2025 arXiv paper takes a leaner route built on two-dimensional filters alone.

MAFNet splits its cost data into high and low frequency parts and treats each with its own attention filter. Fine edges live in the high part, broad surfaces in the low part. A low-rank attention block then blends the parts with care for context. The result is a crisp depth map at real-time speed on modest hardware. That opens stereo vision to mobile robots, drones, and phones that cannot carry server-grade chips.
arxiv-2512-04558:
Yue Yu, Qiwei Di, and Quanquan Gu probe the limits of spending extra compute at answer time to make language models smarter. Test-time tricks include sampling many answers and keeping the best, or revising drafts in sequence. Their gains are real, yet their ceilings were unclear. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies a model where answers are drawn from a mix of reference policies, and proves the popular best-of-many rule is inherently short of optimal.

The authors then study a simple upgrade: reward-filtered sequential inference. Only generations with high reward join the working context, so compute piles onto strong candidates and weak ones fade. Theory shows this rule earns strictly stronger guarantees than standard test-time methods. Experiments across varied tasks back the math. The lesson guides labs that must choose where each extra unit of inference compute goes, a choice that now shapes both cost and quality.
arxiv-2512-05158:
Byung Gyu Chae reformulates a neural network design built on reentry — signals looping back into the network — as a continuous-time system of differential equations. In the Fast-Weights Homeostatic Reentry Network, a fast associative memory works alongside a global control that keeps activity near a set level, like a thermostat for the population. Casting the update rule in continuous time reveals the coupled system underneath.

The analysis shows the dynamics settle onto attractors organized by an energy-like quantity, forming ring-shaped structures. A study of the system's stability identifies a reflective regime in which the reentry produces stable oscillations rather than runaway growth or collapse. Unlike continuous-time recurrent networks, which stabilize through fixed wiring, this design holds steady through population-level gain control. Liquid networks adapt neuron by neuron instead. The result is a distinct class of self-referential dynamics that computes recursively without blowing up.
arxiv-2512-05658:
Pietro Ferrazzi, Aitor Soroa, and Rodrigo Agerri aim to make medical question answering by language models work across languages, not just English. Most systems borrow their knowledge from general models by distillation, which raises doubts about reliability. Their 2025 method instead grounds the reasoning in medical text drawn from Wikipedia. From it, they generate reasoning traces for questions from two known medical exam sets.

The traces number about five hundred thousand and appear in English, Italian, and Spanish. The question sets were also extended into Italian and Spanish. Used as examples in the prompt, or as training data, the traces lifted scores on medical tests inside and outside their home domain. Among models of their size, results reached the best reported level. The team releases the traces, the translated sets, the medical Wikipedia corpus, and tuned models. The hope is more open, checkable support tools for doctors in many languages.
arxiv-2512-05958:
Sara Patel, Mingxun Zhou, and Giulia Fanti tackle the money question inside generative search: who gets credit when the answer is assembled from other people's pages? Language model search engines read sources, then write. The fair yardstick, the Shapley value, costs exponentially to compute exactly. MaxShapley is their way out: a special case built on a utility that splits into a sum of maxima.

That structure makes fair attribution computable in polynomial time. On three multi-hop question answering datasets, MaxShapley matched the exact Shapley attribution's quality while consuming a fraction of the compute. It cuts resource use up to ninefold against prior methods at the same accuracy. The stakes are the economics of the open web. Search once paid in clicks. A credit system that is both fair and cheap enough to run is the missing plumbing for paying the sources the answers stand on.
arxiv-2512-06258:
Chaoyang Wang and eight co authors uncover a flaw in models that answer questions about images: they often land on the right answer by a wrong path. The model may know the facts it needs, yet it picks shaky or tangled chains of steps, so results jump around from run to run. Tests that allow many tries show the right answer is in reach far more often than single tries suggest.

The team answers with a two stage fix. First, the model is trained with rewards for neat step by step work and for right final answers. Next, it samples its own paths, grades them, and learns to favor the sound ones, while bad paths are kept in a store of hard cases to learn from. The work shifts the goal for these models: not just knowing more, but picking the sound route to what they already know.
arxiv-2512-06358:
Mingjia Li and six co authors tackle a stubborn photo problem: wiping window reflections out of a picture taken through glass. A single photo mixes the scene behind the glass with the scene bouncing off it, and past tools often guess the layers wrong, so they fail on real shots. The team reframes a large image editing model, built on diffusion, to reason about such stacked images.

They argue the core snag lies in the model's inner code, which was never built to read one picture as the sum of two layers. Their fix has three parts. An encoder is reshaped so the code honors how reflections add up. A learned text cue guides the model without vague words. A depth guided sampling plan branches early toward good results.
