Chatbots have become a popular gateway to information, yet most handle news-related trending queries poorly, and user experience suffers when a breaking topic is treated like an ordinary question. Trending detection built for traditional search engines underperforms here, because conversational queries differ radically in distribution and expression from typed search queries.

Their multi-stage method, based on generative query indexing, runs from raw events to trending hotspots suited to dialogue traffic. Detecting a surge early lets a conversational system route it to fresher sources or special handling. The work targets a gap the authors note is largely unexplored for dialogue systems specifically.
arxiv-2601-05758:
Miguel Camarillo and 4 co-authors used molecular model runs in 2026 to ask what makes a surface good at starting ice formation. Ice nucleation from supercooled water matters for climate, cryobiology, geology, and food storage. Predicting a substrate's ability to trigger freezing remains difficult.

The team compared simple cubic, body-centered cubic, and face-centered cubic model lattices, plus several orientations of the last. Hexagonal symmetry, surprisingly, did not guarantee stronger nucleation. The crystal plane beneath the surface mattered greatly, and efficient nucleants made the adjacent liquid more structured. A new method based on standard nucleation theory estimated contact angles, energy barriers, and critical cluster sizes from the modeled rates, matching microscopic measurements of nucleus size. In short, what sits under the water matters as much as the water itself for the first step of freezing.
arxiv-2601-06258:
Ordinary matter reshapes dark matter, and Matthew Gebhardt and 15 co-authors measure that back-reaction in a 2026 simulation study. Cooling gas and feedback from stars and black holes move baryons around. The changing gravity then drags the invisible dark matter with it, complicating efforts to read cosmology from galaxy surveys.

Using thousands of CAMELS simulations across four galaxy formation models, the team matched halos to dark-matter-only counterparts. Feedback ejected baryons and lowered halo masses. Dark matter density rose in halo centers from cooling and fell farther out from feedback, with effects varying strongly by model. Clustering changed by up to about a fifth in some runs. The results demand accounting for baryonic uncertainty in lensing surveys.
arxiv-2601-07358: Raphaël Ruimy and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers pro-étale motives and solid rigidity. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. The authors introduce coefficient systems of pro-étale motives and pro-étale motivic spectra with coefficients. In any condensed ring spectrum and show that they afford the six operations. Over locally étale bounded schemes, étale motivic spectra embed into pro-étale motivic spectra. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07758:
R. Benbrik and colleagues ask whether a future muon-proton collider could reveal a heavy partner of the top quark. They study single production of a vector-like top partner. The setting is the type-II two-Higgs-doublet model, which adds a second Higgs doublet. Within that model, a produced top partner can signal charged Higgs bosons. Their 2026 preprint assesses discovery prospects at high-energy muon-proton colliders.

Muon-proton machines are proposed as a possible next step after current colliders. Knowing which signals they could see guides their design. A vector-like top is a favored target because many theories predict one. Tying its production to a charged Higgs gives two discoveries for one signal. The paper serves collider phenomenologists who map the reach of future machines. It links a concrete channel to a concrete model.
arxiv-2601-07858:
Nina Peire, Yupei Li, and Björn Schuller test whether continual learning methods suit EEG-based emotion classification. Generalizing to unseen subjects is hard because brain signals vary greatly between and within people. Continual learning promises progress by learning tasks in sequence without catastrophic forgetting. Regularization-based methods are the common baselines here. They include Elastic Weight Consolidation, Synaptic Intelligence, and Memory Aware Synapses.

Despite their popularity, these methods' suitability for EEG emotion data remains underexplored. The authors examine that gap directly. EEG signals are noisy and personal, which stresses any method that protects old knowledge by freezing important weights. Knowing the limits of standard baselines guides better method choice. The paper speaks to affective computing and brain-computer interface scholars. It checks a default assumption before the field builds further on it.
arxiv-2601-07958:
Surya Subramani, Hashim Ali, and Hafiz Malik build a varied corpus for catching fake speech and tracing its source. Speaker-specific anti-spoofing needs data that systematically vary how fakes are made. Progress was hampered by datasets lacking such variety. Their 2026 preprint introduces LJ-Spoof, a speaker-specific, generatively diverse corpus. It varies prosody, vocoders, generative hyperparameters, prompt sources, training regimes, and post-processing.

Tracing a fake to its synthesis pipeline helps investigators and platform moderators. Detectors trained on one generator often fail on the next. A corpus that varies the generation recipe stresses detectors properly. LJ-Spoof builds on the well-known single-speaker LJ Speech base. The paper serves audio forensics and speech security scholars. It supplies training and test material the subfield has lacked.
arxiv-2601-08158: Yuqing Zhou and co-authors present WISE-Flow, a way for service agents to learn from their own workflow history. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that language model agents in user-facing services stay error-prone on new tasks. They repeat the same failure patterns and vary a lot between runs. Fixing failures with task-specific training or manual patches costs much and scales poorly. WISE-Flow instead induces structured experience from workflows themselves. The aim is a self-evolving agent that improves from past service runs without constant human repair.
arxiv-2601-08358: Hilde Hummel and co-authors test underwater acoustic target recognition with pre-trained audio embeddings. Their 2026 arXiv paper starts from ship noise, which adds to underwater sound pollution and risks marine ecosystems. Passive acoustic monitoring systems record years of sound across diverse soundscapes to track that impact. The authors probe what linear methods can extract from general audio embeddings. Their title gives the verdict shape: the features are decodable but not structured. The study guides marine monitoring teams choosing models for ship detection.
arxiv-2601-08658: Rachael Boyd introduces the geometric and combinatorial group theory of Artin groups. The 2026 arXiv paper gives a brief entry point to these groups, which generalize braid groups. A central topic is the K(pi,1) conjecture for Artin groups, a major open problem in the field. Boyd surveys known results on the conjecture as of January 2024. New readers get the main definitions and the state of the art in one short account. The survey serves graduate students entering geometric group theory.
arxiv-2601-08758:
Juntao Jiang and nine co-authors build a test for AI that reads health scans. Good care needs step by step thought, not just a fast call. New large models can think in steps and can also look at images. The team asks if that step thought helps on hard health image tasks, and where it fails.

Their test is called M3CoTBench. It holds health image tasks that need both sight and step thought. Each task lets staff grade the steps, not just the last call. That makes it clear if a model saw the right clue. A reader in health AI gets a strict test set. It can show which models think in a way a doctor can trust.
arxiv-2601-08858:
Tejaswini Bollikonda sets out trust scores for teams of chat models in strict fields. Such fields are health, banks, and law. In them, a wrong reply can cause real harm, and rules demand proof of care. One trust score for one model is not enough when models pass work to each other in a chain.

She gives a frame where trust scores shift as facts shift. A model that was sound last month may drift on new data. Scores must track that drift and flag it fast. The frame also ties scores to the rules of each field. A reader who runs AI in a strict field gets a plan to watch trust live, not just at launch.
arxiv-2601-09358:
Paul Pružina, Nathanaël Schaeffer, and David Cébron study fluid motion deep inside giant gas planets. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with semi-convection in rotating spherical shells. In these regions, heat pushes the fluid toward motion, while a gradient of heavy elements holds it back. The clash of the two gradients drives slow, layered flows.

The team asks how such flows organize into layers and whether they can drive a dynamo. A dynamo is the process that builds a planet's magnetic field. Semi-convection may help sustain those fields, so its behavior matters for models of Jupiter-like worlds. The paper links fluid physics to the magnetic life of gas giants.
arxiv-2601-09758:
Austin Talbot and Yue Ke hunt for hidden batch effects in genomic tests. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents likelihood clustering to detect batch heterogeneity. Batch effects are a major confounder in genomic diagnostics, especially in copy number variant detection from sequencing.

Many detectors compare a sample's read depth against a reference built from its processing batch. That works only if the batch truly matches. Reagent changes, sample quality, or multi-site processing can break the match quietly. A wrong reference creates false variant calls or hides real ones. Detecting mixed batches early protects patients from bad calls.
arxiv-2601-09958:
Zhongyang Li studies spread on flat graphs that go on with no end. Each site is open with chance p. At low p, open clumps stay small. Past a key point, one vast clump can form. Two key points mark the start of spread and the start of one vast clump.

A known guess links these points to the end shape of the graph. The guess is the Benjamini Schramm claim. Li brings the end shape of the graph into the test. Flat graphs have ends that can be one, two, or vast in count. His work probes when the two key points must match.
arxiv-2601-10058:
Renpu Liu and Jing Yang show that free text can boost how models learn in context. A model can learn a task from a few shown cases in its prompt. But marked cases cost time and funds. Few can fit in one prompt. That caps how well the model does.

Raw text with no marks is vast and grows each day. Some of it links to the task at hand. The pair show that such text can help for sure, not just by luck. They give a proof based claim. It says raw text can lift in context grades past the cap set by marked cases.
arxiv-2601-10358:
Jay Nandy, Arnab Kumar Mondal, Anuj Rathore, and Mahesh Chandran shrink large graphs for fast training. Graph nets learn from vast nets of nodes and links. Training on the full graph costs much time and power. A shrunk graph can stand in for it. That shrink is named condensation.

Past shrinks lean on clean hand marks. Real graphs have few marks, or marks with noise. The team add fake marks to guide the shrink. Their plan is named PLGC. It makes a small graph that trains a net well. It holds up when true marks are thin or flawed.
arxiv-2601-10858:
Sébastien Kuchly and co-authors measure the mechanical traits of sea ice with fiber-optic sensing. Ice mechanics drive processes from meter scales to hundreds of kilometers. Polar ice is changing fast, so models need accurate values for thickness, density, Young's modulus, and Poisson's ratio. Distributed Acoustic Sensing turns a fiber cable into a dense line of vibration sensors.

With it, the team takes high-resolution readings of how sea ice bends and rings. Dense data can separate traits that sparse gauges blur together. Better trait values feed forecasts of ice drift, breakup, and shipping risk. The work shows how a telecom-born tool can serve polar science in a time of rapid change.
arxiv-2601-10958:
Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas and Mingzhe Chen set fundamental limits for quantum semantic communication. Semantic communication sends meaning instead of raw bits, saving bandwidth in multi-agent systems. Agents may hold very different inner representations, shaped by their sensors and AI designs. Perfect bit transmission then no longer guarantees mutual understanding.

The authors use sheaf cohomology, a tool from geometry that tracks how local data glue into global data. It fits the question: when do local meanings compose into shared meaning? Their limits mark what no quantum semantic system can beat. The work guides engineers who want agents that swap understanding, not just signals.
arxiv-2601-11258:
Pingzhi Tang, Yiding Wang, and Muhan Zhang argue that facts alone do not teach. Their 2026 preprint deals with large language models and new facts. A model's built-in memory is frozen at a cutoff date. New facts must be added by extra training runs.

The usual add-on is supervised fine-tuning on the new facts. That step can store the facts in the model's weights. Yet the model may fail to use them when asked. The team says the gap is one of skill, not storage. They inject skills trained with reinforcement learning instead. The skills teach the model to apply new facts in answers. That blend aims at models that keep learning over time.
arxiv-2601-11358:
Bernd Finkbeiner, Martin Franzle, Florian Kohn, and Paul Kroger guard runtime monitors. Their 2026 preprint deals with stream-based health checks. Such monitors read sensor streams and give a verdict stream. Safety-critical systems lean on those verdicts to stay safe.

Sensors are flawed, though monitors treat their data as exact. Calibration and measurement errors ride along with each value. Errors grow as the monitor's math runs on the stream. The final verdict can warp far from the truth. The team uses zonotope abstractions to track the doubt. A zonotope is a shape that bounds where values may lie. Tracking bounds keeps verdicts honest about sensor error.
arxiv-2601-11458:
Five years of Mini-EUSO results are summed up in this 2026 report. Mini-EUSO is a detector that flies on the space station. It is the first space-borne unit of the JEM-EUSO program. That program hunts extreme-energy events from orbit above Earth.

The detector has run on the ISS since October 2019. It seeks ultra-high-energy cosmic rays past 10 to the 21 eV. Such rays are the most energetic particles ever seen. The team logged more than 150 observation sessions. Total data come to near 750 hours over five years. The runs set a strict upper limit on the rare flux. That limit paves the way for bigger space observatories.
arxiv-2601-11558:
Nilesh Rijhwani bridges two fields of medicine with a DICOM frame. The 2026 preprint maps both data kinds in one view. Sound diagnosis depends on specialties working well together. One side reads scans; the other reads tissue under the scope.

Departments often use distinct systems and proprietary formats. That split hinders joint study of data that fit together. Separate viewers for each modality restrict collaboration further. DICOM is the standard frame for medical imaging data. Extending it to tissue maps could unify the two worlds. The frame supports joint mapping and merged views. Clinicians could then read scans and slides side by side.
arxiv-2601-11758: Arnab Das Utsa studies early signs of anxiety in posts on social media. Anxiety touches a vast share of people round the world. Yet large scale checks for it stay rare. Word use in posts may give a cheap way to spot risk at scale. His method rests on word traits that a human can read and check. He tests it with care for word bias and for clean splits of users. Tests cross more than one data set and domain.
arxiv-2601-11958:
Zefeng Chen and Darcy Pu ask if a fully agentic AI can nowcast stock returns. They run a state-of-the-art large model each day to rate each stock in the Russell 1000 index. The run starts in April 2025, when AI web tools gained live search.

Each stock gets a daily score for how attractive it looks. The team then check if those scores track later returns. Their data set is new in three ways, which they set out in the work. The study tests AI stock calls in real time, not on past data alone.
arxiv-2601-12058:
David Dos Santos Ferreira and Benjamin Florentin solve two inverse problems for a magnetic field case. They work on closed Anosov manifolds with a simple length spectrum. The data are the eigenvalues of a magnetic Schrödinger operator.

From those data, they recover an electric potential. They also recover a magnetic potential, up to a natural gauge choice. They use trace invariants of the wave flow as the key tool. Such results show how much of a system its spectrum can reveal.  Gauge choice is part of the result, not a flaw in it.
arxiv-2601-12158:
Isaak Mengesha and Debraj Roy measure growth and convergence at the mesoscale, between city and nation. Global gaps have shifted inward, with more spread now inside countries than between them. They use 8,790 harmonised Functional Urban Areas, which are labour-market regions.

Those areas hold 3.9 billion people and about 80% of global GDP. At that scale, national means hide the true dynamics of growth and structural change. The pair show how that hiding has grown. Policy based on national means may thus miss where growth truly lags.  City scale data show trends that nations hide in means.
arxiv-2601-12458:
Nils Dencker, at Lund University, works on preparation theorems in analysis. The classic results of Weierstrass and Malgrange let one rewrite a function in a clean local form near a point. Dencker extends those results to systems whose values are symmetric matrices. The systems in view are analytic or smooth, and they vanish to first order.

A symmetric version of preparation is more than a cosmetic change. Matrix valued systems show up in partial differential equations and spectral problems. A clean local form can turn a hard system into one that is easier to solve or classify. The work sits in several complex variables and related fields. It gives analysts a sharper tool for symmetric systems.
arxiv-2601-12558:
Alan Muniz bounds a key invariant of a foliation, a way of slicing a space into sheets. The invariant is the second Chern class of the tangent sheaf of the foliation. He works with foliations of codimension one. Chern classes are numbers that capture global twists in a geometric object.

The bound has a concrete form for projective space. For a foliation of degree d there, one part of the singular scheme must have degree at least d plus one. Singular points are where the sheets fail to be smooth, so their size matters. Bounds of this kind limit which foliations can exist at each degree. They are core tools in the classification of foliations.
arxiv-2601-12758:
Shenyan Zheng and five co authors work on pluralistic alignment of language models. As models enter high stakes domains, outputs should reflect a range of human perspectives. Reflecting only average preference flattens real disagreement. Achieving pluralism remains challenging, though. Existing approaches consider limited values or rely on prompt level tricks.

Prompt tricks lack real value control and representation, the team argue. Their system, VISPA, works by automatic value selection and activation. It aims to select fitting values for a context and activate them in the model. Pluralistic systems could serve diverse users without erasing minority views. The work speaks to alignment research beyond one size fits all preference.
arxiv-2601-13558:
Mehrab Beikzadeh and co-authors mine social and dating app text for risk and guard acts in men who have sex with men. That group faces high rates of sex passed ills and harm from drink next to peers. Text from apps they use may hold early marks of risk or of guard acts, such as test or safe sex talk.

The team uses ChatGPT and other text tools to tag such acts at scale. Auto tags could let health teams aim help to a person, not a crowd. Care is need, though, since app text is private and tags can err. The work weighs that gain and risk in one frame.
arxiv-2601-13658:
Arthur Amalvy and Hen-Hsen Huang work on pulling time-stamped facts from text for the web in 2026. Big knowledge bases like Wikidata need facts that say when things held true. Temporal knowledge graph extraction pulls such facts as quadruples: subject, relation, object, and time. The hard part is facts not seen in training data.

Their work, framed by its title as going beyond known facts, makes new unseen temporal knowledge. Fresh facts help test large language models without data contamination. Contamination occurs when test items leaked into training data. Clean tests give a truer read on what models know.
arxiv-2601-13858:
Guixiang Zhang, Yiyuan Wang, and Marius Hoggenmüller design drone interfaces to help people cross risky roads in 2026. The roads in focus have no crosswalks or traffic lights. Drones can watch traffic in real time from above. Past work shows drones can aid navigation and street-level tasks.

The team explores how a drone's interface should guide a person on foot. It could signal safe gaps, warn of fast cars, or show its intent. Good design must be clear at a glance in a tense moment. Such help could cut risk at crossings that cities have left unmarked.
arxiv-2601-14058:
Joe Barton and co-authors prove a splitting theorem for curved spaces that mimic relativity in 2026. The spaces are Lorentzian pre-length spaces with global non-positive timelike curvature. A splitting theorem says such a space must break into a product of simpler parts. The team also extends a key tool, the first variation formula.

That formula now works for spaces with any timelike curvature bound. The bound can be from above or below, and different from zero. Splitting results reveal rigid structure hidden in weak assumptions. They help math models of spacetime stay close to physics.
arxiv-2601-14358:
Christian Ecker, Florian Ecker, and Daniel Grumiller solve a gravity problem in closed form in this 2026 paper. Their topic is critical gravitational collapse, the borderline case where matter is just strong enough to form a black hole. Discretely self-similar solutions govern that borderline. Since Choptuik's pioneering work, those solutions were known only from numerical runs.

The team constructs an infinite family of such solutions in analytic form. The system is the Einstein-massless-Klein-Gordon system, gravity plus a light scalar field. Their tool is the large-D expansion, which treats the number of space dimensions as large. Readers get exact formulas where the field long had only computer output.
arxiv-2601-14758:
Injin Kong, Hyoungjoon Lee, and Yohan Jo look inside a model conversion in this 2026 paper. Post-training pretrained autoregressive models into masked diffusion models has emerged as a cost-effective strategy. It aims to overcome the limitations of sequential generation. Autoregressive models write one token at a time. Masked diffusion models can fill many blanks in parallel.

However, the internal algorithmic transformations induced by this paradigm shift remain unexplored. It is unclear whether post-trained masked diffusion models acquire genuine bidirectional reasoning capabilities. They might merely repackage autoregressive heuristics. The title calls the question a mechanism shift. The test is strict. It asks what the net does, not what score it gets, so a fake gain can be caught. Looks can fool. A smooth text may hide a plain trick, and this work digs for that gap. Readers get a probe of what truly changes inside a converted model.
arxiv-2601-15158:
Yuval Ran-Milo, Yotam Alexander, Shahar Mendel, and Nadav Cohen ask when reward alone can teach a transformer to reason. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with reinforcement learning that pays only for final outcomes. Trained this way, transformers can start to produce chain-of-thought steps on their own.

Yet how sparse rewards steer the training to find such reasoning stays unclear. The authors study a single-layer transformer on a synthetic graph traversal task. The task cannot be solved without chain-of-thought but has a simple iterative fix. Their results hinge on the training data being right.
arxiv-2601-15458:
Emily G. Light, Morgan E. Prior, Noah M. Daniels, and Najib Ishaq speed up a core task in biology. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with multiple sequence alignment, lining up many DNA or protein sequences so matching parts sit in columns. The problem has been studied for years.

Sequence data now grows faster than the classic tools. Fast and accurate aligners that scale to large datasets are in demand. The authors present MuSAlS, an alignment approach based on hierarchical clustering. It groups similar sequences first, then aligns the groups, cutting the work sharply.
arxiv-2601-15558:
Man Luo and a large team test language models as editors for empathy in a 2026 arXiv paper. Clinical empathy is essential for patient care. Doctors must balance emotional warmth with factual precision. They do so under heavy cognitive and emotional strain. The study asks whether a model can refine a doctor's written replies. The edit should raise empathetic tone while keeping the medical content intact.

The framing shifts the model's role. It is not the author of the reply, but a collaborator who polishes it. That keeps the physician's judgment in charge of the facts. The risk is plain too: a warmer tone must not soften needed candor. For health systems, such editing could ease the burden of patient messaging. Clinicians write many replies a day, and tone is hard to sustain.
arxiv-2601-15658:
Aiswarya T and Srijanani Anurag Prasad build a fractal function in a 2026 arXiv paper. Fractal interpolation functions pass through given data points. Unlike smooth curves, they keep detail at every scale. The team's version is a hidden variable function. It uses Edelstein contractions inside an iterated function system. The system starts from a finite set of data points.

Variable functions act as vertical scaling factors in their construction. That yields a generalized vector-valued fractal interpolation function. The authors also compute its box-counting dimension. Dimension measures how rough the graph truly is. Such functions model jagged data, from signals to rough surfaces. A construction with a known dimension gives users control over the roughness they create.
arxiv-2601-15958:
Zihao Wu and a large team clean a blemish from space telescope images in a 2026 arXiv paper. The work belongs to Data Release 5 of the JWST Advanced Deep Extragalactic Survey, JADES. Wisps are scattered-light artifacts in JWST's NIRCam imaging. They haunt certain detector regions. They contaminate observations at brightness levels that matter for faint sources. Photometry of dim galaxies suffers when wisps add false light.

The team removes wisps with nonnegative matrix factorization. The algorithm models the artifact pattern, then subtracts it. JADES images the early universe in deep fields. Faint-source science is its core mission, so artifact control is not cosmetic. Cleaner images mean truer brightness for the most distant galaxies the survey can see.
arxiv-2601-16258:
Sriram Akella, Abhijit Gadde and Jay Pandey build tools to sum join traits of firm states. Their 2026 preprint deals with states shared by more than two parts. Two part join is well known, but multi part join is far less clear. A class of sums, called multi invariants, gives join marks for such states. Past sums of them were slow and hard to run.

The team gives a fast code sum for firm states. Firm states, called stabilizer states, have a clean maths form. That form lets the code sum marks for big states. Fast sums open multi part join to wide study. The work aids teams who build and test quantum states.
arxiv-2601-16358:
Aref Farhadipour and three coauthors build a clean speech set for voice checks in many tongues. Their 2026 preprint, named TidyVoice, deals with voice ID tools. Strong voice tools need big, open sets in many tongues. Such sets are scarce, most of all for read speech. Read speech counts for guards against fake voice use.

TidyVoice draws its clips from the Common Voice pool. The team cleans and sorts clips for voice check use. A clean open set lets teams train and test on shared terms. Shared terms make scores fair to weigh side by side. The set serves voice guard work world wide.
arxiv-2601-16458:
Wenbo Guo and coauthors guard code packs with expert facts in a search frame. Their 2026 preprint deals with bad packs in NPM and PyPI stores. Such stores face more supply chain hits each year. Past guards rest on hand rules or thin data traits. Both miss new hit tricks as they shift in form.

The frame, named IntelGuard, joins expert facts to model search. Facts guide the hunt for hit signs in each pack. Search pulls proof spans that back each flag call. Clear proof helps teams act fast on true bad packs. The work aims to cut both miss and false flag rates.
arxiv-2601-16558:
Wang and a large team study a super flare on the RS CVn star HD 22468. Their 2026 preprint uses more than one wave band for the flare. The flare was first caught in hard X rays by the SVOM craft. RS CVn stars are close pairs known for strong flare acts. A super flare sheds huge power in a short burst.

Joint views trace the flare from birth to fade in each band. Band by band acts test how loops of gas drive the burst. Hard X ray catch at the start is a rare, prized fact. Such facts pin the first steps of the flare maths. The work adds a full case to flare studies.
arxiv-2601-16658:
Sima Amirkhani, Mahla Alizadeh, Farzaneh Gerami, Dave Randall, and Gunnar Stevens study couples and phone privacy. Their 2026 paper asks how partners set limits with each other. Phones are both private and shared tools in daily life. That mix makes shared rules hard to fix.

Past work looked at how partners share or block phone access. It also looked at hard talks about rules, and at spying. Far less is known about quiet ways couples cope. The authors focus on hints, habits, and acts done with no words at all. Their study shows how trust can rest on small signs. It speaks to design of phones and apps for pairs.
arxiv-2601-16758:
Mirko Legnini and Julian Berberich test if a key quantum tool can shrug off noise. That tool hunts the low energy state of a system. It blends a quantum chip with a plain PC in a loop. Noise in the chip can throw the hunt off course. Their 2026 preprint seeks proofs that the hunt still lands true.

The team gives bounds on how noise bends the path. They also show when the loop pulls back to truth. Such proofs matter for drug and stuff design by chip. Firms need trust that noisy chips give sound states. This work helps mark where that trust is earned.
arxiv-2601-16958:
Paolo Bassani tests if bent space forms can ape dark matter's pull. Dark halos are vast clouds that hold galaxies in spin. Their pull shows in how stars move and light bends. His 2026 preprint builds halo forms in a bent space-time. The base form joins space chunks in the LTB style.

He tracks how shape rules of the core math form dark-like wells. Those wells rise in plain gravity and in a tweaked kind. The tweaked kind is Hořava-Lifshitz gravity. If bent forms can ape halos, dark stuff may be less key. Or the ape may fail, which firms the dark case.
arxiv-2601-17058:
Wei Zhou and a team of seven co-authors survey how chatbots prep raw data for use. Raw data oft comes dirty, split, and hard to join. Prep cleans it, links it, and mines it for worth. Need for app-ready data keeps on the rise. Chatbot tools and agent kits now make prep more flex. Their 2026 preprint maps that fast field in full.

The survey sorts prep tasks and the tools for each. It weighs where chatbots shine and where they slip. Dirty data wastes much pro time in all fields. Sound maps help teams pick prep tools with proof. They also mark gaps for the next wave of work.
arxiv-2601-17358:
Zbigniew Fiedorowicz and Muthu Veerappan Ramalingam link two classic curve families in a broader way. One family is sinusoidal spirals, curves set by a cosine power law. The other is Lamé curves, closed shapes that range from ellipse to near-square. A known tie joins the squircle to the lemniscate. The authors extend that tie to full families.

They relate arc length of the spirals to area of the Lamé curves. The link also reaches Keplerian dynamics, the math of orbits. Such ties let one hard problem borrow answers from another. Geometers gain a cleaner map of special curves. The orbit link hints at uses past pure geometry.
arxiv-2601-17458:
Shuhao Zhang and four co-authors design real-time VR training for novice doctors. Surgical crises can overload a new doctor's mind. Stress inoculation training uses practice stress to build calm skill. VR can stage such crises safely. Current systems, though, give weak help at peak stress. Help must come in real time, at the moment of overload.

The team designs interventions for those peak moments. The goal is support that steadies choice, not noise that adds load. Better timing could turn VR drills into true readiness. Hospitals could train rare crises without patient risk. The work links stress science to interface design. It asks what help looks like when seconds count.
arxiv-2601-17658:
Bich Ngoc Doan and three co-authors map the relational harms of QAnon radicalization. Conspiracy theories erode trust and fuel polarization in public life. The authors look past that public toll. They study harm to friends and family of believers. That personal toll is often missed in large-scale research. Their title frames the work as going beyond the rabbit hole.

Mapping relational harm shows what belief costs at home. Strained ties, lost trust, and family splits are part of that cost. Support groups and counselors need such maps. Policy that ignores home harm misses half the picture. The work gives a name and shape to quiet damage. It can guide help for affected families.
arxiv-2601-18658:
Max Behrens and seven colleagues build a tool to help teams choose how to fit a health model: one fit for all, or one fit per person. A fit for all is firm and cheap but may miss what makes one case stand out. A fit per person can catch those traits but may chase noise. The choice is made in most wards by gut feel, with no clear test.

Their tool turns both fits into one smart net so they can be set side by side. The net shows where the per-person fit parts from the joint fit in a strong way. Those spots mark where a ward may need its own fit. A clear tool could help teams spend their fit work where it counts. It could also stop waste on fits that add no gain.
arxiv-2601-18958:
Ramón Herrera and Carlos Ríos rebuild the early universe's fast growth phase inside a modified gravity theory. The theory, Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity, adds extra terms to Einstein's rules. The pair work backward: given measures of how smooth the early cosmos was, they rebuild the background values that must have held.

Two key numbers guide the rebuild, both tracked against how much the cosmos grew. Fresh data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope set the test the rebuild must pass. The work shows which forms of this gravity can still match what the sky shows about the first burst of growth.
arxiv-2601-19058:
Arantha Ranu shows a classic bound can break when the rules soften just a bit. The Gibbs inequality says a certain ratio stays trapped between two positive bounds. It holds for steady states of potentials that meet a smoothness test called Hölder continuity, on shift spaces.

For merely continuous potentials, Ranu shows the bound can fail. The gap between the two smoothness levels turns out to matter a great deal. Results of this kind map the true edge of theorems in dynamics, telling users exactly which assumptions carry the weight.
arxiv-2601-19158:
Qijiong Liu and ten co-authors squeeze user histories so generative recommenders can run in real time. Such recommenders get better as they read longer histories of what a user did. But reading long histories live is costly, which blocks their use in fast feeds.

Their fix compresses each user's sequence into a simple categorical form before the model reads it. A shorter input that keeps the key signals cuts cost while holding quality. Tricks of this kind decide whether lab grade recommenders can survive the speed demands of real products.
arxiv-2601-19258:
Minkyu Kweon and five co-authors surface the hidden gestures inside mobile apps. Modern apps hide key actions behind long presses and swipes that leave no mark on screen. Hidden actions keep screens clean, but users who never stumble on them lose real features.

Their study, GhostUI, unveils how these hidden interactions work and where they hide. It asks which users find them, and which never do. Designers face a balance: clean screens versus features people can find. Naming the hidden layer is a first step toward tools that reveal it gently.
arxiv-2601-19358:
Swarnali Datta, Arunava Mandal, and Ravi Tomar carry classic group theory tools into a broader, wilder setting. Totally disconnected locally compact groups, TDLC for short, generalize the discrete groups that geometers know well. The team studies graphs of such groups and a local convexity property inside them.

They also study Cannon-Thurston maps, which extend maps from a subgroup's edge to the larger group's edge. Moving these notions over tests which parts of the classic theory are robust. The payoff is a firmer base for the geometry of groups that are not discrete.
arxiv-2601-19558:
Weronika Buczyńska and Jarosław Buczyński work in algebraic geometry, on ways to write a point as a combination of simple pieces. Their tool is apolarity, a method that links points to ideals, which are special sets of equations. An earlier technique, border apolarity, handled secant varieties over the complex numbers. This paper extends the theory further.

The extension covers cactus varieties of toric varieties over any algebraically closed field. A border cactus decomposition is an ideal in the variety's coordinate ring. That ideal witnesses that a given point lies in a specific cactus variety. Such decompositions certify how complex a point is. The results give algebraic geometers a broader toolkit for decomposition problems.
arxiv-2601-19758:
Felipe Flores and three colleagues prove results about a family of algebras built from groups. Reduced twisted group C-star algebras encode a group together with a twist, a phase rule for multiplication. Two prized properties are pureness and having stable rank one. Both say the algebra is, in a precise sense, clean and simple inside.

The note proves these properties for algebras from certain group extensions. One step uses groups with a property identified by Ozawa. Such groups give algebras that are completely selfless, a strong simplicity trait. The authors extend Ozawa's theorem from the untwisted to the twisted case. These results feed the classification program for C-star algebras, a major thread in modern analysis.
arxiv-2601-19858:
José Barrientos and four colleagues construct new spacetimes that carry a baryonic charge. Two classical exact solutions frame the work: the Melvin-Bonnor universe, held together by a magnetic field, and the Bertotti-Robinson spacetime, a uniform electromagnetic world. A recently found dictionary translates between two theories of gravity with fields.

One side of the dictionary is the simpler Einstein-Scalar-Maxwell theory. The other is a gauged Skyrme-Maxwell-Einstein model, where baryonic charge appears naturally. Using the translation, the authors build setups with both a magnetic field and a real baryonic charge. Such solution-generating tricks expand the catalogue of exact spacetimes. They also test how robust the dictionary between the theories is. The math is dense, but the aim is plain. New worlds of this kind are rare finds. Each one is a small win. The trick is to trade one hard task for a known one.
arxiv-2601-20358:
Chen-Hsuan Hsu and Anna Ohorodnyk review the coupled-wire approach to quantum states in twisted nanostructures. The approach describes strongly correlated quantum matter by joining many one-dimensional wires, giving bosonic descriptions of hard states. Early uses covered cuprate superconductors and quantum Hall states.

The review covers recent work in nanoscale systems, where the wire picture is not just theory but a tunable physical platform. Twisted layers of materials create patterns where such states can be engineered. The authors show how a method built for pencil-and-paper theory now guides the design of real quantum devices.
arxiv-2601-20558:
Kyota Kamamoto, Asuka Hosokawa, and Yoshiyuki Tagawa study jets of viscoelastic liquid that stretch and snap back like a bungee jumper. An impulsive force launches the jet, which extends to a peak and then retracts. Despite the strongly stretched, far-from-equilibrium motion, the jet shows simple, uniform rheological responses.

The authors investigate this uniform extension and stress. A jet that stretches evenly is easier to predict and control than one that thins at a neck. The findings bear on printing, spraying, and fiber spinning, where elastic liquids are pulled into threads.
arxiv-2601-20658:
Qian Gao and Ruikang Zhong design an integrated sensing and communication system for segmented waveguide pinching antennas. The design exploits the low propagation loss inside segmented waveguides. A hybrid segment selection and multiplexing protocol is used to gain good performance at lower hardware cost.

Pinching antennas can be activated at chosen points along a waveguide, placing radiators close to users. Segmentation extends that reach. A system that senses and communicates through the same array could serve factories and streets where both radar-like awareness and data service are needed. Less gear for the same reach is the gain the design is built to give. It is a neat fit of form to need.
arxiv-2601-20758:
Lixiang Zhao and four co-authors build a tool for exploring huge point clouds in virtual reality. Their 2026 paper presents ScaleFree, a GPU-accelerated method based on kernel density estimation. A point cloud is a set of points in space, such as particles in a simulation. Kernel density estimation turns those points into a smooth density field. The method adapts as the user zooms across scales.

The target users work with massive scientific data. Cosmological simulations, for example, can hold billions of particles. Their structures span many scales at once, from voids to dense clumps. ScaleFree aims to keep exploration interactive at that size. It lets researchers move through data in VR and see structure at each scale. That speed turns a static dataset into a place one can inspect up close.
arxiv-2601-20858:
David Tan and three co-authors show how a test set can leak into a model in a subtle way. Their 2026 paper studies contamination in machine translation evaluation. Large language models can be benchmark-contaminated. They score high by recall, not by skill. In multilingual settings, the memorization can even cross into clean languages. The team uses the FLORES-200 translation benchmark as a diagnostic.

They study two multilingual models of similar size. Bloomz was trained on FLORES; Llama serves as an uncontaminated control. Comparing the two exposes cross-direction contamination. Scores inflate in language pairs the test was not meant to touch. The paper warns evaluators that clean test sets may not stay clean. It also gives a method to check for this hidden leak.
arxiv-2601-20958:
Jessica Zebrowski and six co-authors set the first limits on a non-inflationary source of cosmic ripples. Their 2026 paper uses B-mode polarization data from five experiments. BICEP/Keck, SPTpol, SPT-3G, Planck, and WMAP all contribute. B-modes are swirl patterns in the cosmic microwave background. They can carry the imprint of primordial gravitational waves. Non-inflationary sources predict a causality-limited spectrum at low frequencies.

Causality caps how large the ripples can be on the biggest scales. That cap gives the spectrum a universal shape to test. No such constraints existed before this work. The combined data now bound how strong causal sources could have been. The result trims the space of early-universe theories. It shows the value of pooling many sky surveys into one test.
arxiv-2601-21258:
Wei Minn and eight co-authors examine a weak spot in Android banking apps used across East and Southeast Asia. Mobile banking lets people handle money from their phones, which is fast and handy. The same apps draw criminals who hunt for flaws that expose private financial data.

The study uses virtual setups to test the apps the way an attacker would. It focuses on abuse of features built to help users with limited vision or movement. Those access features can open side doors into an app if they are not guarded well. The work shows banks where such flaws hide and how they can be found.
arxiv-2601-21358:
Jiecong Wang, Hao Peng, and Chunyang Liu rethink how language models reason step by step. Writing each step as words works, but it costs a lot of compute. Forcing thought into single tokens can also collapse the range of paths a model considers.

Newer methods let the model think in smooth hidden states instead of words. The authors frame that hidden thinking as planning, split apart from speaking. Keeping the plan separate from the wording should keep more options alive longer. It also promises faster reasoning, since the model skips needless text. The work points toward models that think quietly, then answer once.
arxiv-2601-22058:
Arata Ishige builds string dualities that drop a beloved crutch: supersymmetry. Classic dualities equate a Type II string theory with a heterotic one in six dimensions, but they rely on a large amount of supersymmetry. Ishige seeks analogues with none.

The construction starts from Type II strings on a K3 surface, a standard compact geometry. A quotient by an involution of that surface yields an Enriques surface and orbifold theories without supersymmetry. He extracts the massless and tachyonic spectra and identifies the moduli spaces locally. His 2026 preprint matters because realistic string constructions lack supersymmetry at low energies. And duality is one of the few tools that can check such theories for consistency.
arxiv-2601-22358:
Matteo Nerini and Bruno Clerckx test a new way to make radio smarter: signals that can move. Their 2026 preprint sets this idea beside two known ones, smart surfaces that bounce waves and antennas that flex. They study the simplest shared case, with just two users.

The team map the full set of rates both users can reach at once. They do this for the shared up-link and the shared down-link. The maps show what moving signals add over fixed gear. Such gains could shape next-wave wireless design. The two-user case sets a base line for larger nets.
arxiv-2601-22658:
A. Murphy and a team use fine new telescope data to read the jet of the young star Th 28. Jets and accretion are two sides of one act: gas falls in, and a beam shoots out. Their 2026 preprint notes that this jet is lopsided, and its ejections come in bursts.

The MUSE near-field data let them trace how outflow and inflow link, knot by knot. That link can reveal how jets are launched. It also shows how the disc that feeds a star evolves. The work is a close read of one telling case. Rare clarity makes it count.
arxiv-2601-23158:
Jean-François Burnol presents new series that compute the Riemann zeta function in its region of convergence. The zeta function sits at the heart of number theory and the study of prime numbers. His series come with remainders that shrink geometrically, step by step.

The formulas are easy to implement, using only polynomial and power functions. They can deliver dozens or hundreds of correct digits when the imaginary part is moderate. Fast, simple zeta evaluation serves both research and high-precision numerical work. Remainders that shrink geometrically make the series practical, since each added term buys a predictable gain in digits.
arxiv-2601-23258:
Mikael Møller Høgsgaard and Chirag Pabbaraju study language identification without assuming the data fit a known language. Recent work set tight statistical rates for identifying and generating languages. Those results rest on realizability: the input is drawn from some language in a given collection.

Their agnostic setting drops that comfort, so the true source may sit outside the collection. Identification must then pick the closest match and still generate sensibly. Agnostic guarantees matter for messy real text, from dialects to mixed-language posts. Dropping realizability changes the statistics fundamentally, since the best available language may only approximate the true source.
arxiv-2602-00058: Md Min-Ha-Zul Abedin and Tazqia Mehrub compare classifiers for Android malware on the CICMalDroid2020 set. The set holds 17341 apps across benign, adware, banking, SMS, and riskware types. They build a 564 trait hybrid vector from static and dynamic traits. They test seven classifiers under raw traits, principal component analysis, and linear discriminant analysis, with a 70 to 30 train test split. Gradient boosting on raw traits wins, with XGBoost on top, while component analysis hurts all models.
arxiv-2602-00158: Ziqi Gao and colleagues propose RAPTOR, a ridge adaptive logistic probe for reading frozen language model layers. Probing trains a light predictor on layer states to reveal encoded information. Probe then steer pipelines use the learned concept vector to steer later passes. Success hinges on concept vectors that are accurate, stable under ablation, and cheap to obtain. RAPTOR uses L2 logistic regression with a tuned ridge strength, drawing concept vectors from normalized weights, at far lower training cost.
arxiv-2602-00758: Ali El Lahib and colleagues show search-engine date filters cannot be trusted to enforce pre-cutoff retrieval for retrospective forecaster evaluations. Checking Google's before filter and DuckDuckGo's date-range filter, they find major post-cutoff leakage in at least one retrieved page for most questions on both engines. Answers are given away outright in a large minority. The authors conclude date-restricted search on these engines cannot support credible retrospective evaluation, recommending stronger safeguards or frozen, time-stamped snapshots.
arxiv-2602-00958: Baoqi Shi and colleagues build a mid-infrared spectrometer that joins broad tuning, strong output, and lab-grade frequency truth. Driven by tunable near-infrared diode lasers tied to atomic standards, it reaches a frequency accuracy of 7.2 MHz. The team uses it to find and strip hydrogen-linked loss in silicon nitride rings, cutting optical loss 88-fold. It also spots multi-phonon loss in silica cladding as the limit for chip photonics. They show fog-piercing LiDAR and a dual-mode sensor that reads both range and makeup.
arxiv-2602-01058: Dylan Zhang and co-authors warn that a stronger first-stage tune can make the later reward stage worse. First-stage data comes from a fixed set, while reward learning uses the model's own fresh runs, so the two data worlds drift. Their PEAR fix re-weights first-stage loss by odds ratios, at token, block, or full-run level, with little extra cost once old odds are known. In tight game and math tests, PEAR lifted post-reward scores time and again, with gains up to 14.6 percent on AIME2025.
arxiv-2602-01758: Francois Deloche and colleagues correct membrane admittance in time domain TL models of the cochlea. One dimensional models suit wave motion, but real cochleas add higher effects. They are focusing and viscous damping. The authors offer a 2D correction for membrane admittance using filtering and regression. In a gerbil model with damping nonlinearities, the model compressed too little at higher levels. The corrected model, made level dependent by feedback, decouples gain and selectivity, adding five decibels of gain and widening the compressive range by ten decibels.
arxiv-2602-02258: Gaurav Bhatt and others propose an match-aware fine-tuning method keeping foundation models aligned while adapting them to downstream tasks. The method integrates feedback from an outside match signal through policy-gradient regularization, with adaptive gating balancing supervised and match gradients per sample. Uncertain or misaligned cases receive priority, well-aligned cases follow standard updates, and fully misaligned inputs learn abstention. Tests show fewer harmful and hallucinated outputs without task loss, plus robustness to hostile fine-tuning and unsafe initializations.
arxiv-2602-02358:
Yikun Zhang and 3 co-authors propose a way to borrow data from related domains when the target domain has little, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is regression, meaning predicting a numeric outcome. Each source domain first gets its own generative model, which learns to produce realistic responses for given inputs.

The borrowed data is then adjusted to match the target domain through conditional quantile matching. That step lines up the spread of generated values with the target's spread, without assuming only inputs or only labels shifted. Theory shows a model trained on the adjusted data can beat one trained on target data alone. Simulations and real datasets confirm steady gains over rival transfer methods.
arxiv-2602-02958:
Long videos generated by artificial intelligence run out of memory, and Haocheng Xi and 15 co-authors attack that bottleneck in a 2026 paper. In autoregressive video models, a key-value cache stores past context and grows with every new frame. It can exceed the memory of common graphics hardware and weakens consistency over long horizons.

Their framework, Quant VideoGen, compresses that cache to two bits per value without training. A smoothing step exploits redundancy across space and time in video. A progressive scheme then quantizes residuals in stages, trading quality against memory smoothly. Tests on three video systems follow. Cache memory fell by up to seven times, with small latency cost and better quality than baselines.
arxiv-2602-03058:
Sharp bounds for sums of random exponential quantities are proved by Silouanos Brazitikos and 2 co-authors in a 2026 mathematics paper. The variables are independent, each exponentially distributed, with fixed total variance. The authors bound the size of their sum in a strong averaged sense, extending a positivity theorem of Hunter from nineteen seventy-six for completely homogeneous polynomials in several variables.

Beyond the lower bound, the paper determines exactly where such sums enjoy Schur-monotonicity. That property describes how the sum's size responds when the individual variances become more or less spread out while their total stays fixed. The results complete a picture that earlier work, referenced as CHS, had left open for these sums.
arxiv-2602-03358:
Prompt search is treated as posterior use by Junmo Cho, leading a team of 7 others, in a system called GFlowPO. Finding effective prompts is critical yet difficult, because the prompt space is combinatorially large and evaluating each option on the target model is expensive, making rewards sparse. Reinforcement learning optimizers that sample on-policy from a fixed meta-prompt spread explore inefficiently and waste those costly reviews on unpromising regions.

Their method fine-tunes a lightweight prompt model with an off-policy generative flow network objective, reusing past reviews through replay for sample-efficient exploration. A dynamic memory update then refreshes the meta-prompt with diverse replay prompts and top performers from a priority queue, concentrating search on high-reward regions without extra training. Across classification, instruction induction, and question answering, GFlowPO beat recent discrete prompt tuning earlier methods.
arxiv-2602-03458:
Warm dense matter sits between solid and plasma, and it matters for both planet interiors and fusion research. Luc Revello and 5 co-authors model an experiment that creates this regime by Joule-heating thin metal foils with pulsed power. Their 2026 paper describes foils confined in a sapphire cell, driven to an expanded warm dense state.

Designing such shots requires predicting the driver's electrical behavior and the foil's fluid motion together. The authors couple an electrical circuit model of the driver, switches, and load to a one-dimensional hydrodynamics code. Material conductivity links the two halves consistently. The combined model reproduces measured expansion velocity, current, and voltage well, giving a practical tool for planning future experiments.
arxiv-2602-03558:
Rating AI-generated images is a moving target: each new generator raises the quality bar and stale human labels mislead. Xinyue Li and 7 co-authors present ELIQ in a 2026 paper, a framework that assesses generated image quality with no human annotations at all. It judges both visual quality and how well the image matches its prompt.

ELIQ automatically builds positive pairs and aspect-specific negative pairs covering ordinary distortions and AI-specific defects. Those pairs teach a pretrained multimodal model, through instruction tuning, to act as a quality critic. Lightweight gated fusion and a query transformer produce a two-dimensional quality score. Across benchmarks ELIQ beats other label-free methods and transfers to user-generated content without modification.
arxiv-2602-04158:
Christopher D. Hacon and 2 co-authors study how positivity survives deformation in families of Kähler manifolds. Their 2026 paper asks whether pseudo-effectivity of canonical divisors, a key positivity notion, stays stable as the complex structure varies across a family.

Using recent advances in the Kähler minimal model program, they prove global stability when one fiber is projective, and for threefolds even without that assumption. Volumes of adjoint classes stay locally constant in smooth families with a big adjoint class. For Kähler threefolds, deformation invariance of volumes and plurigenera follows, confirming a famous conjecture of Siu in dimension three.
arxiv-2602-04358:
Engineering organizations need a way to grade the risk of using language models before rollout. Stefan Otten and 6 co-authors propose the LLM Risk Assessment Framework in a 2026 paper on AI in systems engineering. Current uptake is uneven, with unknown failure modes and limited room to scale.

The framework sorts each use by autonomy, from help to automated decisions, and by impact, how bad it gets if outputs mislead. Joining the two axes yields steady risk levels across the whole life of a system, from requirements work to decision support. A shared scheme lets organizations set controls matched to risk instead of improvising per project.
arxiv-2602-04458:
Yaxin Hu's 2026 paper, written with 7 co-authors, asks how a mobile robot could help blind people join group tours. Group activities depend heavily on visual cues, such as who is speaking or where others are standing, which can shut blind visitors out.

The team interviewed blind people and museum experts, then built a robot prototype for mixed tours of blind and sighted visitors. In a science museum field study, blind participants joined tours with a guide and sighted visitors. Users valued the robot's navigation help and its information about surroundings. They also raised concerns about joining group interaction. The paper closes with design lessons for future systems.
arxiv-2602-04758:
Gianluca Galletti and 8 co-authors compress huge plasma simulation data without losing its physics in a 2026 paper. Gyrokinetic runs of plasma turbulence take weeks and yield tens of terabytes, forcing researchers to discard valuable output.

The team first built a test pipeline checking structural patterns and multi-scale shifts over space and time. Common compression methods failed to keep both the spatial mode structure and the temporal turbulence character. Their physics-informed neural compression adds loss terms tailored to gyrokinetic physics. It reached extreme compression ratios, and entropy coding pushed compression further still. The authors argue such methods make later study of data once thought unkeepable feasible. That could change how large simulation campaigns are planned.
arxiv-2602-04958:
The three-dimensional Ising model is a cornerstone problem in statistical physics. The paper comes from Giulia Fardelli and 2 co-authors. Modern conformal bootstrap work needs precise data about the model's primary states and the numbers, called OPE coefficients, that describe how they interact. The fuzzy sphere method turns the problem into a quantum system that computers can diagonalize.

The authors use a special conformal generator, called K, to pick out primary states cleanly. A gap in the generator's spectrum protects primaries from mixing with their descendants, which sharpens the results. For states up to a moderate scaling dimension they recover all known primaries and identify several fresh ones, including in the parity-odd sector. The improved states then give better OPE coefficients, which they compare with expectations from the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis.
arxiv-2602-05058:
Learning an unknown quantum operation from queries is a basic task for calibrating quantum hardware. Aria Christensen and Andrew Zhao revisit it for fermionic linear optics in this 2026 quantum information paper. These operations, also called fermionic Gaussian unitaries, describe non-interacting fermions, and earlier learning schemes needed many queries plus operations that violate the rules real labs must obey.

The new protocols respect fermionic superselection rules, need at most one extra mode, and reach Heisenberg scaling, the best possible dependence on the target precision. Query counts improve on earlier work for both general and number-conserving operations, with a further gain available if more ancilla modes are allowed. A side result speeds up tomography of Slater determinant states, which may interest researchers beyond this problem. The paper runs to 56 pages.
arxiv-2602-05158:
A future muon collider could uncover particles behind neutrino mass. Xue-Xin Zhang and 3 co-authors study one such signal in this 2026 particle physics paper, 24 pages with eight figures. In models with an extra gauge force, a heavy partner of the Z boson and a heavy Higgs can be made together, echoing the standard Higgs-strahlung process.

If heavy neutral leptons exist to give neutrinos mass through the seesaw mechanism, that chain can end in striking final states. They are four same-sign muons plus four fat jets, or three same-sign muons with extra jets, from the heavy leptons decaying through W bosons. The authors work out these tetralepton and trilepton signals for muon colliders running at 3 and 10 tera-electronvolts. Such same-sign patterns are rare in the Standard Model, which makes them promising flags for new physics.
arxiv-2602-05258:
Extending a language model's context window usually means retraining or fiddling with its position encoding. Haoran Li and 3 co-authors offer a lighter touch in this 2026 paper with CoPE, a modification of rotary positional embeddings, the standard scheme that encodes position by rotation. Two schools of fixes exist, one fighting out-of-distribution positions, the other protecting semantic attention patterns.

CoPE unifies both aims with one minimalist move: softly clipping the low-frequency components of the rotary encoding. Soft clipping removes the outlier positions that break generalization and sharpens semantic signals, while avoiding the spectral leakage that hard clipping causes. Experiments showed significant gains that held up to contexts of 256 thousand tokens, which the authors take as validation of their theory. They bill the method as a free lunch, near-zero cost for state-of-the-art length generalization, and release code, data, and models.
arxiv-2602-05358:
How many hops of a graph should a graph neural network look at? Paribesh Regmi and 2 co-authors make that choice Bayesian in this 2026 machine learning paper, published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research. Searching over fixed hop counts by training and validating repeatedly is slow and biased by which scopes the designer thought to try.

Their scheme treats message passing as a stochastic process, with the count of hops ruled by a beta process. The most plausible neighborhood scope is inferred jointly with the network's own parameters, rather than before training begins. Theory shows the scope inference increases the model's expressivity. Tests on benchmark graphs where neighbors tend to share labels, and on harder graphs where they tend to differ, show the method working with leading network variants. It matches or beats them at node classification while giving well-calibrated predictions. Code is available.
arxiv-2602-05458:
Local fixes inside a software system can keep each part healthy while the whole service still fails its users. Anatoly Krasnovsky presents Emergence-as-Code, a framework that ties system-level reliability goals to the parts that carry them. A declared user journey duty stays fixed, while the system keeps a working guess about which running parts fulfill that duty at any time.

That guess decides which measurements feed a combined reliability score, and the strength of the evidence decides whether a numeric score is justified at all. In a proof of concept on a sample application, the method found the exact change in part states in all twenty test runs, with no false alarms in twenty control runs. When evidence was mixed or unclear, the system reported the case as unassessable rather than guessing. The paper lays out a research program on keeping these links current over time.
arxiv-2602-05658:
Riemann ellipsoids are spinning fluid bodies with an oval shape, a classic model for stars and planets. Joris Labarbe studies their linear stability, asking whether small disturbances die away or grow. He works in two regimes: no viscosity at all, and weak viscosity added as a fix.

For the ideal case, he derives a broad Poincaré equation for small fluid wobbles and builds polynomial solutions that extend classical results by Cartan. The method gives a plain wave-speed rule for three dimensional shifts and stays cheap to compute at any harmonic degree. Viscous effects enter through a boundary layer analysis in the style of Prandtl, yielding first order corrections to the inviscid spectrum. Stability diagrams over the space of allowed ellipsoids show how rotation, internal strain, and diffusion each shape stability. The author points to uses in rotating shear flows in geophysics and astrophysics.
arxiv-2602-05758:
Long documents defeat language models not at reading but at reasoning, since a single reward at the end gives little guidance through thousands of tokens. Qize Yu and 8 co-authors propose LongR, a reinforcement learning framework for long context reasoning. It pairs a think and read mechanism, which interleaves reasoning steps with fresh looks at the document, with a dense reward based on relative information gain from the passages consulted.

That reward measures the utility of relevant documents without needing evidence annotations. On the LongBench v2 benchmark the framework gained clear ground, with consistent improvements on the RULER and InfiniteBench suites as well. Gains held across several reinforcement learning algorithms, which suggests the benefit sits in the framework rather than one optimizer. The authors also analyze how reasoning chain length affects efficiency and how the model handles distractors.
arxiv-2602-05958:
Growing germ groups change shape as they expand, and Benjamin Evert Himberg and Sanghita Sengupta ask whether simple shape math can track their motion. Using time lapse close-up photos, they follow area, edge length, and edge aware shape tags across the growth history of groups. Their approach is shape first and time tracked, rather than a snapshot sort of final shapes.

For long stretches, groups show tight area edge scaling run by a single true length scale. That scaling breaks at pinned times during ongoing growth, and the breakdowns match passing edge shifts while bulk growth goes on. Different looks can therefore arise inside one shape zone. The authors argue the shifts show inner remake, not growth arrest. More broadly, they offer time tracked shape math as a rough frame for spotting when growth leaves single scale ways. The study runs to twelve pages with eight figures.
arxiv-2602-06358:
Adapting a language model to new material normally means fine-tuning, but Yewei Liu and 5 co-authors built a machine that skips that step. Their system, SHINE, is a hypernetwork that reads a context and, in one forward pass, writes a ready-made LoRA adapter for the model. LoRA adapters are small add-on weights that steer a big model cheaply.

SHINE reuses the frozen model's own parameters inside its design, keeping its own size modest. Training included a pretraining stage and an instruction stage. After generation, the model answers questions about the context without seeing the context again: knowledge moved from the prompt into the weights. The authors report strong results with large savings in time, compute, and memory.
arxiv-2602-06658:
Matching two point clouds that may be rotated versions of each other is a basic problem in data science. Guillaume Houry, Jean Feydy, and François-Xavier Vialard take it up through the Gromov-Wasserstein framework. That framework compares the inner distances within each set, so rotation does not fool it. Solving it is usually slow and memory-hungry, though.

The authors spot a wide family of distortion measures for which the matching task turns into an alignment task in a lifted feature space. Building on that, their solver uses memory that grows only in step with the data. It runs far faster than the usual cubic-time methods. It handles hundreds of thousands of points in minutes, carries theory-backed guarantees, and can map out the energy landscape whose low points reveal symmetries of the match.
arxiv-2602-06758:
Rong-Sheng Hu, Ze-Chun Hu, Zhen Huang, and Mu-Xuan Li study a probability question with roots in three conjectures of modern probability theory. For families of random variables with a shape parameter, they ask for the smallest possible value, over that parameter, of three probabilities that compare a variable with its mean and spread. The two distributions treated are the Laplace distribution and Student's t distribution.

The three functions cover being at most a multiple of the mean, staying within a multiple of the standard deviation of the mean, and straying beyond it. The authors trace their motivation to Chvátal's conjecture, Tomaszewski's conjecture, and the Hitczenko-Kwapień conjecture, which ask related questions about symmetric distributions. Their results give exact lowest values for these probability functions across the parameter range.
arxiv-2602-07058:
Natnael Mola and four co-authors tackle unlearning for text-to-image diffusion models. The goal is to strip out the influence of specific data or concepts while keeping overall quality, a need driven by data protection rules and responsible AI practice. Yet unlearning in diffusion models costs a lot, and it is hard to balance forgetting against keeping unrelated concepts intact.

Their method, SPARE, runs in two stages. First, gradient-based saliency finds the weights most tied to the unwanted concepts. Updates then pass through sparse low-rank adapters, keeping edits light and local. Second, a self-distillation objective swaps the unwanted concept for a user-chosen surrogate, while other behavior stays put. A timestep sampling trick targets only the diffusion steps that matter for a given concept. SPARE beat the current top method on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark, with fine control over the forgetting-retention trade-off.
arxiv-2602-07358:
Unlearnable cases protect images from unauthorized training by making them unlearnable. Tabular data in finance and healthcare resists the same tricks because features mix types and learning concentrates on few dimensions.  Jiaming He and seven co-authors extend the protection to tables with UTOPIA.

Under a spectral dominance setting, they show certified unlearnability is possible when a poison spectrum overwhelms the clean meaning spectrum.  UTOPIA then decouples tuning into two channels: high-salience features for meaning obfuscation and redundant low-salience features for a strongly correlated shortcut, preserving tabular constraints.  Data owners get a principled way to share tables that models cannot profitably learn from.
arxiv-2602-07758:
Layered magnetic materials can change their behavior with how their sheets stack, a knob that matters for future electronics. Brandon Pedroza-Rojas and two co-authors study Bernal-like stackings of MA2Z4 monolayers and bilayers, a family related to molybdenum disulfide, using first-principles calculations and a spin model.

They extract exchange couplings between neighboring magnetic moments within and between layers, then show how stacking and the choice of metal atom can tune magnetic order and symmetry breaking. The analysis maps a route to designing magnetic states in atomically thin materials by stacking alone. Physicists working on two-dimensional magnets will find a detailed microscopic guide.
arxiv-2602-08358:
Spin-triplet superconductors pair electrons with aligned spins, a state with promise for quantum technology, but how those spins react to magnetic fields is poorly known. Hiroki Matsumura and eighteen co-authors probe the material UTe2 with Knight-shift and susceptibility measurements. Their arXiv paper tracks the spin response as the field grows along the crystal's c axis.

Below the transition, spin susceptibility dips slightly, then climbs back near normal values by about 5 tesla, well under the upper critical field. The critical field also grows when the pair spin lines up with the applied field. Comparing field directions, the authors link the pair-spin layout to the critical field and to anisotropic pinning. Readers get a distinctive fingerprint of triplet pairing, with echoes of superfluid helium-3.
arxiv-2602-08758:
Roman domination assigns values to vertices so that undefended vertices neighbor a strong defender, and bondage asks how few edges must be cut to raise the domination number. Fahimeh Khosh-Ahang Ghasr and Sakineh Nazari-Moghaddam study the total Roman bondage number, where the defended set itself has no isolated vertices. Their arXiv paper proves deciding the bondage bound is NP-complete for arbitrary graphs.

Sharp bounds relate the bondage set's effect on domination number, and a lower bound ties bondage to minimum degree and ordinary bondage when the domination number equals three times the independence number. Graphs with infinite bondage are characterized, and a condition for bondage equal to one is given. Exact values follow for complete, bipartite, broom, wheel, and spider families. Readers get a complete complexity and structural picture.
arxiv-2602-08958:
Plants grow by adding new material, which breaks most tools for filming changing 3D scenes. Weihan Luo and five co-authors introduce GrowFlow, a representation that couples 3D Gaussian blobs with a neural differential equation, so growth becomes a continuous flow over each blob's position, size, and orientation. Every blob keeps its identity over time, preserving correspondence from seedling to mature plant.

To start, the team reconstructs the full-grown plant, then learns growth in reverse to recover its history. On a new multi-view timelapse data set, GrowFlow beats prior methods on image quality and geometric coherence. It is the first temporally consistent appearance model for growing 3D structures.
arxiv-2602-09258:
Graph neural networks ship frozen, yet must handle clean data, spread shifts, and jolts at once. Xiaoguang Guo and seven co-authors show fixed guessing forces a trade-off: steadiness demands down-weighting shift-touchy traits, leaving a hard worst-case learning floor. Case-based routing could break that ceiling, but shifts can mislead routing and jolts can make it jitter.

Two splits part reach from picking and base touchiness from wobble growth, lighting up the failure modes. Their STEM-GNN setup answers with a mix-of-experts coder for varied math paths, a vector-quantized token link steadying coder-to-head signals, and a Lipschitz-tamed head capping output growth. Across nine tests, it balances toughness to degree and homophily shifts and to damage while staying rival-ready on clean graphs.
arxiv-2602-09958:
In first-year calculus, l'Hôpital's rule rescues limits where both top and bottom of a fraction vanish. A 2026 paper by Albert Chern and Sadashige Ishida asks what survives when the functions are complex-valued and live in higher dimensions. The answer, they show, is far subtler than the familiar real-valued case.

The authors give a complete characterization of when such a quotient can be defined continuously at points where both functions vanish. They also explain why pushing the result to smoother quotients stays an open challenge. The paper thus draws a sharp line between a classroom rule and its higher-dimensional cousin.
arxiv-2602-10058:
Music generation systems split sound into controllable parts, such as structure versus timbre, yet whether those parts truly separate is rarely checked. A 2026 paper led by Laura Ibáñez-Martínez, with four co-authors, evaluates disentangled representations in music audio models with a probing setup that reaches past standard downstream tasks. The models span varied unsupervised strategies, from inductive biases to staged training.

Analysis runs along four axes: informativeness, equivariance, invariance, and disentanglement, across data sets, tasks, and controlled transformations. The findings show gaps between intended and actual embedding meanings. Current strategies, the authors conclude, fall short of true disentanglement, and controllability in music generation needs rethinking.
arxiv-2602-10158:
Reading molecular structures from NMR spectra is fundamental chemistry, yet interpreting experimental spectra at scale is slow and expertise-heavy. A 2026 paper led by Liujia Yang, with eleven co-authors, builds NMRSpec, a large corpus of experimental proton and carbon spectra mined from chemical literature. It proposes NMRTrans, which treats spectra as unordered peak sets. The model is the first NMR transformer trained only on large-scale experimental spectra.

On experimental benchmarks, NMRTrans leads the field, beating the strongest baseline's top-ten accuracy by nearly eighteen points. The result underscores how experimental data and structure-aware design matter for reliable structure elucidation, closing the gap that retrieval and computed-spectra methods leave on real measurements.
arxiv-2602-10358:
