Linear-time preprocessing builds a structure that answers each call in log time. The method extends to strings compressed by straight-line programs, with the same prep cost. Complex edits on the compressed form also update in log time. The access step beats a recent result by a log factor.
arxiv-2603-13258: Yi-Xuan Deng and co-authors propose MemCoder, a framework that lets code agents grow through structured memory. Most code agents work from static snapshots and miss the history inside a project. Past commits hold reasoning paths and intent-to-code mappings worth reusing. MemCoder structures that history, then refines agent behavior in real time with verification feedback. Human-validated solutions are internalized as long-term knowledge for later tasks. On SWE-bench Verified, MemCoder reached state-of-the-art results and beat the base model by a clear margin.
arxiv-2603-13358: Zongze Li and co-authors rethink prefill-decode disaggregation for multi-turn LLM serving. Each new turn now forces a fresh prefill and repeated KV transfers, which clog bandwidth. Their key insight is that append-prefill, which reuses cached KV states, slows decoding far less than full prefill. That makes local routing to decode nodes a good option for later turns. No fixed routing plan meets all service goals at once, they show. Their PPD system routes by dynamic weights and cut time-to-first-token by about 68 percent.
arxiv-2603-13458: Evgeniy Khain, Baruch Meerson, and Pavel V. Sasorov study speed fluctuations of a stochastic Huxley-Zel'dovich front. The front is an invasion of A-particles into an empty region, driven by fast random walks and reversible on-site reactions. Shot noise from reactions and diffusion makes the empirical front speed fluctuate over time. Typical fluctuations act like front diffusion in a frame moving at the mean speed. Monte Carlo simulations support the predicted scalings for speed shift and diffusion. Large deviations are dominated by optimal histories.
arxiv-2603-13558: Arsenios Scrivens presents Holographic Invariant Storage, a safety contract for LLM context drift that is set at design time. It builds on known traits of bipolar Vector Symbolic Architectures. The contract gives three guarantees, each in closed form, that can be checked before a system ships. One covers how well a single signal can be recovered, and it holds at any noise depth. The other two cover robustness to steady noise and how capacity falls as more signals are stored. Monte Carlo tests back the bounds.
arxiv-2603-13758: Yue-Tong Dong, Jack F. Douglas, and Wen-Sheng Xu study tunable cooperative motion and glassy dynamics in knotted ring polymer melts. Their molecular dynamics work varies knot complexity and molecular mass to tune glass formation on cooling. They test prevalent glass formation models, including the string, localization, and shoving models, against the data. All three models quantitatively describe segmental relaxation as a function of knot complexity, mass, and temperature, despite distinct foundations. The authors also discuss dynamic and elastic heterogeneities tied to fragility and stiffness variations.
arxiv-2603-14258: Rehman and Friesecke put flow-based sampling of Boltzmann distributions on firm math ground. A 2019 method by Noé and co-authors samples such distributions by learning a transport map with a normalizing flow. The authors prove a flow exists that matches the true distribution to any set error in Wasserstein distance. The proof covers rough molecular cases with Coulomb and Lennard-Jones forces. Tests on a toy system and the alanine dipeptide molecule confirm the closeness in practice.
arxiv-2603-14458: Kietkajornrit, Tarifi and Asgharbeygi split planning from fact lookup to make language models more reliable. Fact questions fail when answers need fresh or disputed information. Search tools cut errors, but vague plans waste tool calls. Their design trains a small student planner with a teacher model. The planner outputs ordered reasoning steps plus fact requests, with no answers shown. Separate modules then search and write the reply. On the SEAL-0 test set, the authors report gains in both accuracy and speed.
arxiv-2603-14558: Vyas, Chakraborty and Gupta present JobMatchAI, a job matching platform with explainable scores. Most hiring search acts as a keyword filter. Such filters miss skill synonyms and nonlinear careers, and scores stay opaque. JobMatchAI mixes Transformer embeddings with a skill knowledge graph. A clear reranking step weighs skill fit, experience, place, pay and firm preferences. Each score comes with factor-wise reasons. The team also releases JobSearch-XS, a benchmark for skill generalization tests.
arxiv-2603-14958: Okada and Nishio adapt closed split computing systems per user with SALT, a lightweight tuning frame. Split inference divides a network between edge device and cloud. User data shifts and noisy links erode accuracy in the field. Closed systems hide the model weights from any retraining. SALT adds a small client-side adapter after the frozen head network. Intermediate features get refined before the server tail runs. No extra communication load appears. ResNet-18 tests on CIFAR sets beat retraining baselines at lower cost, they report.
arxiv-2603-15158: Rahiminasab and co-authors tackle robust prediction when hidden confounders shift between domains and proxies are imperfect. Older proxy methods need a completeness assumption that imperfect proxies break. The team groups confounders into latent equivalent classes that yield the same proxy distribution. Point identification still works if domains mix these classes in varied enough ways, a weaker rank condition. Their PQAL framework actively queries a few well-chosen domains that meet the condition. It beat prior methods on synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets.
arxiv-2603-15358: Xu and co-authors present FuXiWeather2, an end-to-end neural system for global weather analysis and forecasting. Older machine learning models copy reanalysis products, which bakes in their biases and delays. This system trains on a mix of real observations and reanalysis data, so it can correct reanalysis errors. Recursive unrolling training keeps its own generated backgrounds stable in use. It produces high-resolution global analyses and ten-day forecasts within minutes. Its forecasts beat the ECMWF HRES system on most scored metrics, with strong typhoon track skill.
arxiv-2603-15658: Gaikwad studies how memory-augmented agents should pick which memory store to query. Most systems search every store for every question. That habit wastes tokens and pulls in off-topic context. He frames the choice as a store-routing problem. Scores cover coverage, exact match, and token efficiency. An oracle router beat uniform retrieval on question answering while using far fewer tokens. He also casts routing as a cost-sensitive choice that trades accuracy against retrieval cost.
arxiv-2603-15958: Shulgin and co-authors derive tuning rules for modern optimizers from fresh theory. Hyperparameter transfer across batch size and horizon leans on folklore rules. Their lens is the Linear Minimization Oracle family of methods. That family covers normalized SGD, signSGD, and Muon. Recent convergence bounds serve as the object to minimize. Closed power-law schedules drop out for key knobs. Learning rate, momentum, and batch size each get a budget law. Momentum and batch size interact in ways worth care, they note.
arxiv-2603-16158: Kumar, Kumar, and Gupta pin GRPO credit to the exact tokens where code goes wrong. One pass-fail signal smears blame across whole programs in GRPO. Their EGCA method runs candidate and reference code side by side. Matching traces reveal the earliest semantic split point. Advantage then lands only on the matching token span. Later tokens stay masked out of that update. No critic, extra loss, or learned verifier joins the loop. HumanEval pass-at-1 hits 82.1 percent, up 3.1 on GRPO. MBPP gains 1.5 points at 18 percent more time.
arxiv-2603-16758: Chigurupati and Garyfallidis present SuCor, a tool that fixes susceptibility warping in echo planar brain scans. SuCor uses optimal transport along the phase encoding direction. It treats each column of the distortion field as a shift between two scans taken with reversed encoding. A spectral penalty smooths the field, and its strength is set on its own. On human connectome data, SuCor scores 0.341 in mutual information with a structural scan, above 0.317 for FSL TOPUP. It runs in about 12 seconds on one CPU core.
arxiv-2603-17058: Rabbani, Mojahed, and Nazari study Nash equilibrium seeking when the two players hold unequal information. Many methods assume each player knows the other's objectives and constraints, which is often unrealistic. Here, player 1 knows only its own problem, while player 2 is reachable through a best response map. The authors propose an iteration that mixes projected gradient descent with that map. They prove existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium, plus global linear convergence when the map is exact. When the map is inexact, iterates still land near the true equilibrium.
arxiv-2603-17158: Wadud, Golpayegani, and Afraz propose a new way to optimize handovers in open radio access networks. User mobility patterns vary widely, and radio conditions change fast. Existing learning schemes sit at the near real time layer and miss longer term context. Their framework puts all predictive intelligence inside an rApp: mobility mode classification, trajectory forecasts, and a PPO policy. The rApp sends ranked neighbour cell recommendations to the handover xApp, which decides using live measurements. On mobility traces, the approach cut ping pong handovers and raised reliability.
arxiv-2603-18158: Escalona and co-authors study two-component dark matter in the type-I two-Higgs-doublet model. The dark sector holds a real scalar and a Dirac fermion, kept stable by a Z4 symmetry. The scalar links to the visible sector through Higgs portals; the fermion links through the scalar. They scan masses, mixing angles, and couplings under theory and experiment bounds. Viable regions survive, but collider limits squeeze the scalar sector hard below the TeV scale.
arxiv-2603-18258: Luo and co-authors show that sharpness-aware minimization in logit space improves direct preference optimization. DPO can suffer a squeezing effect, where preferred response odds fall during training. Their logit-space analysis ties this to negative-gradient growth along high-curvature directions. Logits-SAM perturbs only the output layer, adding almost no cost. Tests on Pythia, Mistral, and Gemma models show steady gains, and the method pairs with other DPO variants.
arxiv-2603-18558: Ben-Ami and co-authors present HiMu, a frame picker for long video question answering. A fixed frame budget forces models to choose which frames to see. HiMu splits a question into a logic tree of small predicates. Light tools for vision and audio score each part on every frame. Fuzzy logic then joins the scores while keeping time order and cross-modal links. With 16 frames, HiMu beats rival pickers on three benchmarks. It matches uniform sampling that uses four times the frames.
arxiv-2603-18858: Moradi, Popoli, Shallit, and Vukusic study automata that read shifted Fibonacci word terms. The Fibonacci word is a classic object in combinatorics on words. A five-state machine computes each term from Zeckendorf digits, least significant first. A two-state machine works most significant first. For a shift by c, the machine size grows like the log of c. That growth nearly matches the least possible for an aperiodic sequence. The proof blends state complexity tools with Diophantine approximation.
arxiv-2603-19058: Lunde and Ramgraber adapt nonlinear data assimilation to pick its own level of complexity. Linear methods are too crude for skewed data, while full nonlinear ones cost too much. Their transport method maps data in a flexible triangular form. Too much freedom overfits, and too little misses structure. Their algorithm uses spline bases and a score that tracks complexity as a smooth dial. Gradient steps then tune the map with no hand-set knobs. Tests include a large groundwater model with skewed, nonlinear behavior.
arxiv-2603-19158: Lee and co-authors present a way to keep text-to-image models on target when the prompt names a rare concept. Their method blends the main prompt with helper anchor prompts at each step. A closed-form rule, drawn from Tweedie's identity, sets how much weight each prompt gets. The blend gives semantic support for rare ideas and shape support for edits. Tests on RareBench and FlowEdit beat fixed blends and prior training-free methods. The team reports gains in both meaning and structure.
arxiv-2603-19258: Chien and co-authors make private synthetic text that starts closer to a target domain. Private Evolution builds such data through model APIs, but a poor start wastes calls and hurts quality. Their MAPLE method first pulls private table-style facts about the source data. Those facts ground the first synthetic batch through in-context learning. On domain text tasks, MAPLE reaches a better privacy and utility balance. It also converges faster and cuts API costs by a wide margin.
arxiv-2603-19358: Li and co-authors sort all tree-level ways to complete a class of dimension-nine operators. These operators drive a short-range form of neutrinoless double beta decay. The team works in the SMEFT J-basis and splits cases by their topology. Of 505 mediator blends found, 440 are minimal in heavy parts. Twelve cases need only two distinct heavy species. The list adds 324 minimal cases with vector resonances, a class not mapped before. Prior scalar and fermion results are matched and extended.
arxiv-2603-19458: Ahmed and co-authors work out what a magnetically charged anti-de Sitter black hole would look like. The model comes from string-inspired Euler-Heisenberg theory. They derive photon paths, the photon sphere, and the shadow size for the hole. Both radii shrink steadily as the magnetic charge grows. Stable orbits and their key frequencies shift from the Schwarzschild case as well. Twin-peak oscillation data from many hole sizes are then fit to the model. The best fit sits at zero charge, with an upper bound near 0.2.
arxiv-2603-19558: Guo and co-authors benchmark whether step-by-step reasoning really helps text classification. Their TextReasoningBench compares seven reasoning strategies across ten language models and five data sets. Simple chain-of-thought gives small, steady gains of about 1 to 3 percent on big models. Richer methods like tree and graph search often fail to beat simple baselines. They can even hurt small models. Many strategies use 10 to 100 times more tokens for tiny gains. New cost-aware metrics track gain per token spent.
arxiv-2603-19658: Qiu and co-authors present ProHunter, a system that hunts advanced persistent threats in system logs. It models audit logs as a whole-system provenance graph. Attack patterns from threat intelligence reports become query graphs to match. Huge graphs, tangled benign activity, and semantic gaps make matching hard. ProHunter stores long-term graphs in a compact encoded form. A heuristic sampler extracts precise attack patterns from the graph. Adaptive features align query and provenance graphs at local and global levels. On DARPA data sets, it beats prior hunting systems.
arxiv-2603-20058: Gurgel and co-authors estimate time delays between signals with the Wigner-Ville distribution. Common tools build cross spectra from linear time frequency maps like wavelet transforms. Those maps blur frequency detail and need extra smoothing to act as similarity measures. The quadratic Wigner-Ville form reaches near the joint resolution limit. It also gives a proper measure of likeness between signals. On two wave physics test cases, it gave sharper delay estimates. The gains were largest in the most energetic frequency bands.
arxiv-2603-20458: Milivojević and Gmitra propose a gate-tunable synthetic antiferromagnet built from graphene and MnS. They sandwich a type-A antiferromagnetic semiconductor between two graphene layers. Gate tuning breaks the balance between the top and bottom graphene sheets. That induces opposite magnetic proximity effects in the two layers. The result is nonrelativistic spin splitting right at the Fermi level. Transport calculations show matching conductance dips in graphene nanoribbons. The effect appears as giant magnetoresistance within a narrow energy window. The platform suits low-dimensional antiferromagnetic spintronic devices.
arxiv-2603-20558: Breitner and co-authors grow and study single crystals of CrRhAs. This metal has a kagome lattice and orders as an antiferromagnet near 150 kelvin. They measure transport, heat capacity, and magnetization. The Hall signal stays linear in field, with no extra nonlinear part. Its sign flips between two current and field setups. Below the ordering point the Hall signal grows a lot. They link this to changes in the Fermi surface or added magnon scattering.
arxiv-2603-20958: Acosta-Pareja and co-authors simulate the magnetic behavior of ferromagnetic nanoscrews. These are long, thin magnetic membranes with a helical shape. They vary curvature, torsion, eccentricity, thickness, and inner diameter. The screws show bistable behavior, with vortex domain walls moving during reversal. They find four forms of a stable mixed remanent state. The coercive field grows with eccentricity but stays largely flat as torsion changes. They explain the trends through surface magnetic charges on the membrane.
arxiv-2603-21058: Hu and co-authors detect smart contract flaws in Vyper using models trained only on Solidity. Smart contract bugs pose major security threats, yet Vyper lacks the tools and labeled data that Solidity enjoys. Their Sol2Vy framework transfers knowledge across the two languages. It needs no large labeled Vyper data set to work. They test it on reentrancy, weak randomness, and unchecked transfer flaws. Despite Solidity only training, it performs strongly on Vyper contracts and beats prior state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin.
arxiv-2603-21358: Xiao and Shen test how well personality-driven student agents match real learners in mathematics education. Real teaching experiments face ethical limits and cannot be repeated on the same student. Their agents carry Big Five personality traits and run through teacher interaction, self-study, and exams. They gathered thirteen empirical studies on traits and learning and distilled them into fourteen criteria. About seventy one percent of agent behavior aligned with human learners. The study checks agent credibility before such simulations are used at scale.
arxiv-2603-21558: Zhang tackles a failure mode in self-training, where a model learns from its own solutions over many rounds. Checking only final answers lets lucky guesses with flawed reasoning slip into the training data. Zhang's Verified Self-Improvement framework checks each reasoning step instead, using a computer algebra library and consistency rules. On grade-school math problems, it rejected about a third of correct-answer solutions as lucky guesses. Accuracy climbed from 80.5 to 91.0 percent across five rounds, while unverified training collapsed.
arxiv-2603-21658: Chen and co-authors compare how model families memorize training text, in output stats and in inner signals. Past work used single model lines, so shared and unique traits stayed unclear. They gather six lines, including Pythia, OLMo, and StarCoder. Memorization grows log-linearly with model size, and memorized text compresses more than expected. Families share frequency and domain patterns yet keep their own marks. Inside the models, memorized text reacts more to injected noise, and key attention heads sit in different spots per family.
arxiv-2603-21858: Kelly and Tang study splitting methods for stochastic delay differential equations with two correlated noise sources. Such equations mix a fast linear part with a delayed nonlinear part, and splitting solves each in turn. They bound the mean-square error of Lie-Trotter splitting. With uncorrelated noises, the method converges at order 0.5. With correlation, a stubborn error term appears that does not shrink with step size. Tests confirm the clean case and the rapid loss of accuracy as correlation grows. Reordering the split recovers some range, they find.
arxiv-2603-22058: Sekine's thesis builds asset pricing models for markets with many unlike agents. The tool is mean field game theory, and markets are incomplete. Agents differ in wealth, risk aversion, and unspanned liability, and all use exponential utility. Sekine derives the equilibrium risk premium from inside the model. He characterizes equilibrium with a new mean field backward stochastic differential equation. He proves solutions exist and clear the market for large populations. Later parts add consumption with habit formation, plus markets where agents infer the premium from prices.
arxiv-2603-22158: Gögl and Yau study survival prediction that mixes three kinds of patient data. The inputs are clinical text, tabular variables, and genomic profiles. Their method runs on local language models, not cloud services. That suits hospitals with tight budgets and strict privacy rules. The method estimates calibrated survival chances for each patient. It also writes short prognosis text grounded in the evidence. Training uses teacher-student distillation and a principled fusion of the three inputs. On a TCGA cohort, the authors report it beats standard baselines.
arxiv-2603-22558: Pachet and Zucker tackle the problem of building synthetic populations that match many stated statistics at once. Planners need fake populations for simulations and privacy-safe data release. The targets can mix one-way, two-way, and three-way counts drawn from surveys or expert notes. Exact matching scales badly as targets pile up. Their fix borrows from statistical physics: match the counts on average under a maximum-entropy rule. On benchmarks with up to forty traits, their method pulls ahead as the targets grow more tangled.
arxiv-2603-22658: Gatti and co-authors build a large-scale method to map snow avalanches from radar satellite images. Avalanches threaten lives, roads, and ecosystems, and they are growing more common. The team uses change detection on Sentinel-1 image pairs. Tests across several alpine regions use hand-checked records. Using only pre- and post-event radar images works most steadily. Their pipeline reaches an F1 score of 0.8061 in a strict setup. A recall-focused setup finds over 80 percent of mapped avalanches. They also release an annotated dataset as a benchmark.
arxiv-2603-22758: Moon, Seong, and Heo tackle a flaw in video object-centric learning. Such models split video into object slots, but one object often takes many slots. Their method, SlotCurri, starts training with a few coarse slots. New slots are added only where reconstruction error stays high. A structure-aware loss sharpens slot boundaries by keeping local contrast and edges. A cyclic pass rolls slots forward and back for stable tracking. The method gains 6.8 points on YouTube-VIS and 8.3 on MOVi-C in FG-ARI scores.
arxiv-2603-22858: Basu introduces an architecture for persistent memory in neural networks and draws two lessons from it. The network routes sparse attention through a lasting pheromone field over latent slots. The core finding: lasting memory needs a stable coordinate system. Any coordinate system learned with the model proves unstable. Fixed random Fourier features give stable outer coordinates, but routing bias alone does not transfer. Using the pheromone as a learning-rate prior removes negative transfer. Basu names coordinate stability and graceful transfer as two separate needs.
arxiv-2603-22958: Merluzzi and co-authors propose triple-functional networks that share one wireless infrastructure. The same resources would serve sensing, communication, and edge AI inference. Sharing opens gains, such as joint resource use across services. It also brings cross-talk and hard allocation choices. The authors argue compute resources and model access must enter allocation choices directly. They link the performance bounds of the three services. Their joint optimization beats a disjoint allocation plan in the cases shown.
arxiv-2603-23458: Ranchal-Pedrosa and Marsh present SNARE, a consensus protocol for players who act in their own interest. It adapts their TRAP design to the n equals 5f plus 1 setting. One key trick adds a single broadcast round after predecisions. That round alone secures agreement against coalitions near 60%, with no deposits. The players may even be deceitful, not just rational, and the result still holds. A baiting layer with tiny deposits pushes tolerance to about 73%. Valid candidacy, which blocks reward front-running, holds with no threshold strings attached.
arxiv-2603-23558: Vu, Destercke, and Pichon study how to compute upper entropy for set-based uncertainty models. In credal methods, belief comes as a set of probabilities, not one number. Upper entropy gauges the uncertainty inside such a set. The team focus on 2-monotone lower probabilities, a tractable family. They give a full algorithmic and complexity study of the task. The problem, they show, has a strongly polynomial solution. They also add sharp speedups over the older algorithms for this family and its special cases.
arxiv-2603-23858: Niu and co-authors build a stable way to interpolate at high order on the Grassmann manifold. Standard maps based on singular value decomposition cost much and can make derivatives unstable. Their method first maps data into maximum-volume coordinates, a well-conditioned flat domain. It then builds polynomial bases with an Arnoldi process, avoiding ill-conditioned linear systems. A confluent version handles derivative data for Hermite interpolation. They prove stability bounds for the mapping and the approximation, and tests show high accuracy at high degree.
arxiv-2603-24158: Bellucci and co-authors study how field mass changes the entanglement entropy of a massive scalar field. They use a spherical shell lattice model and vary both mass and region size. For the ground state, entropy falls exponentially as mass grows, while area-law scaling holds for all masses. Excited states behave differently. Their excess entropy breaks the expected universal scaling in the combined variable mR. A second length scale, the width of the wave packet, explains the break. They discuss links to black hole entropy.
arxiv-2603-24358: Jamalifard and co-authors present a neuro-symbolic system that detects human fatigue from body signals. It combines eye tracking with functional near-infrared spectroscopy of the forehead region. Attention encoders learn four readable concepts, such as gaze stability and prefrontal blood flow. Differentiable reasoning rules then combine the concepts with learned weights and soft thresholds. In leave-one-subject-out tests on 18 people, accuracy reaches 72.1 percent, close to tuned baselines. The system also exposes concept scores and rule strengths, and a per-subject audit metric tracks accuracy well.
arxiv-2603-24858: Wolter and co-authors propose context-mediated domain adaptation in multi-agent sensemaking systems. Experts hold tacit knowledge they cannot state as explicit rules. When they edit AI-made artifacts, fixing terms, reworking arguments, and shifting emphasis, those edits reveal latent domain understanding. Current systems treat edits as mere endpoint corrections. Their system, Seedentia, instead treats user edits as implicit specs that reshape later reasoning. Links between artifacts and reasoning support knowledge transfer from edits. Agent behaviour also adapts in context from edit patterns.
arxiv-2603-25158: Ni and co-authors turn agent work logs into reusable skills with Trace2Skill. Hand-written skills do not scale, and skills dreamed up by a model miss real pitfalls. This system reads many run traces side by side and reasons over them as a group. It can deepen skills a person wrote or grow new ones from weak drafts. The distilled skills compress repeat failures into standard steps. They travel well: skills from one model's traces lift a bigger model by up to 58 points on table questions.
arxiv-2603-25258: Pscherer and co-authors build a superconducting resonator tuned to hear a single electron spin. Their stacked parallel-plate design has very low impedance, which boosts coupling to one spin. The shape also shrinks the stray magnetic field, giving a Purcell factor above ten to the fifteenth. They show several ways to make the device. Built units hold quality factors past twenty thousand at the single-photon level. Tests run in fields up to 500 millitesla, and the team weighs photon counting against dispersive readout for spin sensing.
arxiv-2603-25458: The CMS Collaboration measures the angles between jet pairs in proton smashes at 13 TeV, hunting for new physics. The sample holds 138 inverse femtobarns from the LHC. Cleaned data meet quantum chromodynamics forecasts pushed to a new order of precision, plus electroweak tweaks. Shape gaps show in two mass bands, but the broad match is good. The curves then bound many wild ideas at once: quark insides, extra dimensions, quantum black holes, and dark mediators. Quark contact forces are ruled out below 17 to 37 TeV.
arxiv-2603-25658: Aubert's lecture notes survey the theta correspondence over finite fields of odd characteristic. The notes expand a mini-course given in Paris in March 2025. They cover the main properties of the correspondence in this setting. Topics include its fit with Harish-Chandra series and with Lusztig series. The notes also treat the Jordan decomposition of representations. They end with a full explicit description of the correspondence. The goal is a clear map of a central tool in representation theory.
arxiv-2603-26158: Hou and co-authors prove new results about groups acting on CAT(0) spaces. First, every torsion subgroup of a CAT(0) group is finite, settling a question from the 1990s. The proof uses random walks with zero drift plus a fixed-point rigidity principle. Bounded-exponent torsion groups must fix a point under broad conditions. A Kazhdan-type principle links almost fixed points to true fixed points. For amenable groups, an alternative holds: fixed points for all actions, or a nonzero virtual first Betti number.
arxiv-2603-26358: Wu and co-authors build a mixed time series model to track Covid-19 viral load and deaths together. Case counts suffer from delays, bias, and missed infections. Cycle threshold values from PCR tests offer a proxy for viral load, but they form a bounded continuous series beside a count series. Their MixTSQL model needs only a mean-variance spec, with no full distribution assumed. Applied to weekly data from São Paulo, it orders viral load and deaths in time and tests Granger causality.
arxiv-2603-26458: Liu asks whether a costly AI model can direct a cheap one through software tasks. He builds ManagerWorker, a two-agent setup where a text-only manager plans and reviews while a worker model edits code. Tests cover 200 SWE-bench Lite cases in five setups that vary pairing and pipeline shape. A strong manager with a weak worker scores 62%, matching a strong solo agent at 60% with far fewer costly tokens. A weak manager guiding a weak worker does worse than the worker alone.
arxiv-2603-27358: Zeldes and co-authors pilot an annotation scheme for graded proposition salience in real texts. Summarization research assumes some propositions matter more than others. Yet graded salience for propositions lacked an operational definition on natural data. The authors adapt a summarization-based metric first built for salient entities. They define the annotation task and apply it to a small multi-genre dataset. Agreement between annotators is measured and reported. A preliminary analysis links their salience scores to discourse centrality. That comparison follows Rhetorical Structure Theory's notion of central units.
arxiv-2603-27658: Pham and Gupta measure entropy production in networks that change over time. Real interaction networks rarely stay fixed. They model shifting links as colored noise with a memory time. Dynamical mean field theory gives an exact entropy rate formula. The formula holds at any transient time. Simulations of the full system confirm it. Noise shifts the chaos threshold to higher link variance. Chaos fades, but dissipation grows in exchange.
arxiv-2603-27858: Amico cuts the cost of quantum phase estimation with uncontrolled gates. Phase kickback usually needs a controlled unitary. Knowing that unitary lets him swap in an uncontrolled one. Controlled state preparation pays the small extra cost. The trick fits cases where eigenstate preparation is known. Two-qubit gate counts drop exponentially for fine estimates. Other kickback-based algorithms can adapt the same idea. Assumptions are stated with care.
arxiv-2603-27958: Du and three co-authors present CARV, a test of analogical reasoning for multimodal language models. Unlike older tests, CARV asks a model to draw rules from several image pairs and combine them into new changes. The set holds 5,500 samples. Even the best model tested, Gemini-2.5 Pro, scored only 40.4%, while humans reached 100%. The authors trace the gap to weak rule extraction and poor robustness in complex settings.
arxiv-2603-28358: Hao proves a Wiener-type test for p-massiveness on weighted graphs, a boundary question at infinity for the graph p-Laplacian. Under volume doubling and a weak Poincaré inequality, he shows every infinite p-massive set passes a capacity test in nested balls. With one more condition, the test also runs in reverse. He further links massiveness to nonuniqueness of outside Dirichlet problems. Bounded p-harmonic functions turn out to hinge on two disjoint massive sets.
arxiv-2603-28458: Xu and co-authors speed up the indexer inside fine-grained sparse attention for long texts. Models like DeepSeek's sparse attention still scan every past token for each query, and that scan grows with context. HISA swaps the flat scan for two stages: quick block scoring to drop dead regions, then exact scoring inside what survives. The downstream attention sees the same token picks, and no retraining is needed. At 64K context it ran much faster, with quality near the original on haystack and LongBench tests.
arxiv-2603-28558: Laabs compares three t-norm operators for judging EU AI Act compliance. The test uses a neuro-symbolic system called LGGT+ and 1,035 labeled AI system descriptions. Systems fall into four risk groups, from prohibited to minimal risk. The Gödel operator reached 84.5 percent accuracy and the best recall on borderline cases. It also gave eight false positives. The Łukasiewicz and Product operators gave no false positives, but missed more borderline cases. Laabs concludes that rule completeness matters more than operator choice. A mixed system is the suggested next step.
arxiv-2603-28758: Hakobyan and co-authors propose a robust planning framework that joins robust control with L1 adaptive control. Safe autonomy must handle model error and shifts in the environment. Their planner uses distributionally robust model predictive control over a receding horizon. The adaptive controller supplies online bounds on the Wasserstein distance between nominal and true state spreads. Those bounds certify the ambiguity sets used for planning, without distribution samples. Sets for the setting come from finite data samples. Theory and numerical tests show proven safety under both kinds of uncertainty.
arxiv-2603-28958: Davidson and Byers study geofence surveillance as a dynamic spatial sampling problem. Police must pick a site, set a geofence perimeter, and seek suspects through reverse location warrants. Courts must also limit how far that surveillance can reach. Fixed boundaries ignore how people move near a site, which raises privacy risks. The authors propose optimal radius estimators that adapt perimeters to local context. Given a site and a privacy constraint, the perimeters change size with local population density. That gives magistrates a way to quantify trade-offs in warrant proposals.
arxiv-2603-29658: Zanotta and co-authors present SCORE, a statistical way to certify regions of attraction for dynamical systems. Exact checks give hard guarantees but stall beyond about twenty dimensions. SCORE instead bounds the worst safety violation with high statistical confidence. It pairs stochastic gradient Langevin sampling with extreme value theory. The Lyapunov derivative falls in a Weibull domain, giving a finite endpoint to estimate. On a Van der Pol test case, tightness rivaled exact methods. The method scaled to a dense 500-dimensional system.
arxiv-2603-29958: Kakariadis and co-authors recast a classic extension problem through operator systems. The question asks if positive definite functions on part of a group extend to the whole group. Since Rudin's work, it has tied to sums of squares in group algebras. They show the extension property matches a quotient map on the Fourier-Stieltjes algebra. The factorization side matches a complete order embedding into the group algebra. Examples connect the frame to nuclearity and C-star envelopes.
arxiv-2604-00158: Jing Lu and eight colleagues model near-peak optical and near-infrared spectra of supernova 2014L, a Type Ic event, to settle whether helium hides in its ejecta. Optical spectra alone cannot tell absence from invisibility, but near-infrared helium lines blend less with other ions. A deep-learning emulator stands in for radiative-transfer simulations, with a mean fractional error of 1 percent, feeding Bayesian inference of ejecta. The spectra require 0.018 to 0.020 solar masses of helium above the photosphere near peak light, and a statistical test rules out zero helium.
arxiv-2604-00258: Islam and three colleagues argue that flawed student demonstrations in e-learning carry patterned signal, not noise, if their quality is ranked. Their HALIDE system models student actions across several layers of abstraction, reading higher-level goals and plans from suboptimal actions while tracking how reward functions evolve. By folding demo quality into hierarchical reward inference, HALIDE tells apart transient errors from suboptimal plans and genuine progress toward goals. Tests show HALIDE predicts student teaching choices better than methods relying on perfect paths, fixed rewards, or unranked imperfect demos.
arxiv-2604-00758: Chechelnitsky and colleagues interview 19 translators spanning 11 languages and as many domains about translation technology in the age of large language models. Translators prove cautious. They worry that machine translation and language models erode the human judgment and checking their craft requires, with harmful knock-on effects. The authors argue tools should assist translators and honor the uncertain, social character of translation, rather than replace human work.
arxiv-2604-00958: Gnatenko and Kaczmarek study multi-qubit variational quantum states that stand for vertex- and edge-weighted graphs. Built as one-layer variational circuits using RX rotations and RZZ entangling gates, these states cover graphs of any structure. They work out the geometric entanglement measure and test quantum correlators, showing both relate to edge weights around vertices. They test the star graph K1,4 on a noisy simulator with results matching theory.
arxiv-2604-01058: Ballesteros, Fernandez-Silvestre and Gutierrez-Sagredo revisit universal T-matrices, the Hopf algebra dual forms of quantum groups, and build contraction theory. They work out the (1+1) timelike kappa-Poincaré T-matrix first. Spurred by the Galilei group's role in non-relativistic quantum reference frames, they obtain a deformation of the centrally extended (1+1) Poincaré algebra and present its T-matrix. Contracting that Poincaré T-matrix gives the Galilei T-matrix for reference frames, so the form is a candidate for the symmetry structure of relativistic quantum reference-frame changes.
arxiv-2604-01258: Remaki derives an efficient analytical formula for choosing the radial basis function kernel parameter in data classification. That parameter strongly shapes performance in methods such as support vector machines, yet it is usually set by costly training procedures that may lack robustness. His approach optimizes the diameter of mapped classes in feature space while maximizing distances between classes. Tests validate the formula on support vector machines and on a proper orthogonal decomposition subspace method, for two-class and multi-class problems.
arxiv-2604-01558: Sun argues that patient voice in interactive health research is an inclusion issue and an epistemic one, about how experiential accounts are seen and shared. Patients' lived stories are usually treated as data rather than knowledge in their own right. Methods, author rules, review rules, and print formats tend to place patients as subjects rather than authors of evidence. Looking to patient-partnered work in journals like The BMJ and JAMA, Sun sketches a path for patient-authored or patient-led pieces. Sun presents this as a design probe.
arxiv-2604-01658: Qu and colleagues present CORAL, the first framework for self-run multi-agent evolution on open problems. Current methods rely heavily on fixed heuristics and hard-coded search rules, limiting agent freedom. CORAL replaces rigid control with long-running agents probing and collaborating through shared memory, asynchronous execution, and heartbeat-based interventions. Evaluated on diverse mathematical, algorithmic, and systems tasks, CORAL sets new state-of-the-art results on 10 tasks, achieving 3-10 times higher improvement rates. On Anthropic's kernel task, evolving agents improve the best known score from 1363 to 1103 cycles.
arxiv-2604-02158: Oztop, Kulkarni, Zhao, Coskun and Konate predict GPU power and use for supercomputing jobs before they run. Mining Slurm logs and GPU manager metrics for the VASP materials code on Perlmutter, they build a two stage forecaster: first from submission features alone, then enriched with profiling history. Submission features alone predict peak GPU use with up to 97 percent accuracy, and runtime power predictions reach up to 92 percent. The results support smarter scheduling and power aware operation of heterogeneous clusters.
arxiv-2604-02858: Hu and four colleagues study random reshuffling for distributed Nash seeking in noncooperative games. The game is framed as a finite-sum problem from a stochastic game. Unlike methods that sample with replacement, their approach updates components without replacement across networks. A full-information benchmark introduces a reference trajectory and shuffling variance over epochs. The method then extends to partial information, where players use local estimates of joint actions. For the distributed case, the algorithm converges in a straight line to near the equilibrium under constant parameters.
arxiv-2604-03058: Cheng and colleagues trace chat-model flattery to false beliefs about what users want. Their Verbalized Assumptions method draws those beliefs out of a model, then uses probes built from them to steer flattery in fine steps. They also find an expectation gap: people want straighter answers from machines than from people, but models trained on human talk miss that difference.
arxiv-2604-03358: Tassopoulos and Sarkar show that increments of the KPZ fixed point share the same null sets as Brownian motion with diffusion parameter 2 on compacts. Additive Brownian motion is absolutely continuous against the centred Airy sheet on compacts, but not mutually so globally. Applications include record times with probability strictly between zero and one, plus dimension results for random intersections and Airy sheet images.
arxiv-2604-03658: Reza Rahimi Baghbadorani and colleagues proposed two solvers for a broad class of math problems in which the goal is a point where no move can improve the result. Such problems show up when players seek a stable outcome, when choices unfold over time, and when competing aims must be balanced. Building on the adaptive Golden Ratio Algorithm, the team pushed its momentum past the golden ratio and switched between small and large momentum to reach the answer faster. Tests across several problem classes showed gains over existing methods.
arxiv-2604-03758: Ragib Shahariar Ayon and Shibbir Ahmed built AutoReSpec, a system that writes formal software specifications with language models and repairs its own failures. It picks a model pair and prompt setup from the program's shape, then calls a partner model with validator feedback when the first attempt fails. On 72 Java programs it passed 67, beating SpecGen and FormalBench on success and completeness.
arxiv-2604-03958: Ziyuan Guo and team solved distributed optimal consensus for general nonlinear multi-agent systems, spanning leader-free and leader-led cases as one. The key move recasts agreement as optimal control, with each agent shrinking a global shared cost. A spread-out method based on the optimal control principle plus two look-ahead upgrades handles broad systems of this kind. The team proved convergence and faster-than-linear settling rates, with tests backing the method's worth.
arxiv-2604-04258: Calboreanu offers Context Engineering, a set way to gather all the facts an AI tool needs next to a prompt. The method sorts facts into five roles, Authority, Exemplar, Constraint, Rubric and Metadata, and runs them through four stages from Reviewer to Auditor. In a study of 200 logged tasks, gaps in facts went with 72 percent of repeat cycles. That approach cut repeat cycles and raised first-try passes from 32 percent to 55 percent. The author notes the results come from watching one user, with no test group.
arxiv-2604-04358: Guest and Ho study a space of meromorphic connections with wild singularities, proving it is a symplectic Lie groupoid. The links carry physical meaning: they match answers to the tt* fusion equations, hence to changes in supersymmetric quantum field models. The groupoid shape arises because the authors stick to tt* equations of Toda type, whose monodromy data admits a Lie account. To reach these results, they show the universal centralizer of a Lie group is a holomorphic symplectic groupoid over the Steinberg section.
arxiv-2604-04558: Telatin presents NBI-Slurm, a Perl package offering a simplified panel for submitting and managing jobs on SLURM high-performance computing clusters. It gives a library of Perl modules for programmatic job management plus command-line tools that cut the load of SLURM's panel. Distinctive parts include terminal panel apps to view and cancel jobs, and wrappers for bio tools. An energy-aware scheduling mode called eco mode alone defers flexible jobs to off-peak periods. Eco mode helps research institutions shrink their compute carbon footprint without manual send planning.
arxiv-2604-04858: Souligne and Subbian offer FairLogue, a Python toolkit that checks fairness in clinical machine learning beyond single traits such as race or gender alone. It measures parity, odds, and opportunity gaps for combined groups, then tests fairness under treatment settings and under imagined changes to group membership. In a glaucoma surgery prediction test on All of Us health records, the toolkit found large combined-group gaps even though the model itself performed only moderately.
arxiv-2604-05158: Ewais, Hashish, and Ali propose Just Pass Twice, a method that lets causal models do classification with bidirectional context for named entity recognition. Causal attention lets tokens see only preceding context, blocking disambiguation that needs context. Generative approaches that list entities suffer slow decoding and errors. The key insight: concatenating the input to itself lets each token in the second pass attend to the sentence. With definition-guided entity embeddings, it beats the best by 7.9 F1 on average across CrossNER and MIT, running over 20 times faster than methods.
arxiv-2604-05658: Beltrão and three colleagues give practitioners a practical way to read Human-Computer Trust Scale scores. Their empirical study builds an evidence-based guide for interpreting trust propensity, stressing that scores need reflection within each interaction's context. The scale works well as a first check on propensity to trust, not as a standalone verdict.
arxiv-2604-05858: Tiwari and five colleagues model quark-gluon plasma heat and flow traits at finite baryon chemical potential with a deep-learning quasi-particle model. Neural nets fit heat- and potential-linked thermal masses to lattice QCD equations of state. Sound speed, heat, viscosity, and conductivity estimates agree well with lattice and rival models.
arxiv-2604-06058: Cherenson and Panagou present staggered integral online conformal prediction. It is a data-driven uncertainty bound for adaptive systems whose dynamics change without state-derivative measurements. The standard method falls short there. So their 2026 algorithm scores the lumped effect of disturbances and learning error with an integral score. The result carries long-run coverage guarantees. That yields long-run safety when paired with robust tube model control. A deep-neural-network quadcopter test under such control backs the approach.
arxiv-2604-06258: He and Panchekha improve floating-point debugging by computing residues (ideal-versus-actual values) better without losing speed. Fast error-free methods report many false issues; slow high-precision methods are accurate. Their approach splits residue computation into rounding and evaluation steps. On workloads, it eliminates false reports on 10 benchmarks and reduces them on 3 more. Residue override handles absorption, where one run cannot compute two residues well, by re-executing to compute different residues per run into a patchwork execution. Across 169 benchmarks it means 3.6 re-executions.
arxiv-2604-06358: Li and seven colleagues introduce GS-Surrogate, a Gaussian Splatting ensemble surrogate. Exploration trades raw data storage against viewing settings tuning. Stand-ins work in image space without explicit 3D representation, or use radiance fields. Those fields cost too much for exploration and encode all parameter shifts in one field. GS-Surrogate builds a Gaussian field, then adapts it through setting-shaped warps. Splitting simulation shifts from viewing changes enables adaptation to surface and transfer function work. On sim sets, it enables real-time exploration across sim and viewing spaces.
arxiv-2604-06458: Sadek, Mikuni, and Ploskon build a fast generative model for heavy-ion collision events. Such collisions spray thousands to tens of thousands of particles, among nuclear physics' heaviest simulations. Their score-driven diffusion model uses the Point-Edge Transformer in OmniLearn. Training runs in two stages: first on lower-multiplicity oxygen-oxygen collisions, then fine-tuned on lead-lead collisions. Closure checks cover event- and particle-level observables, flow consistency, jet finding with FastJet, and classifier fidelity tests. The compact model yields realistic high-multiplicity events, making local generation practical.
arxiv-2604-06558: Cheng and Zhang study when context helps prediction. They test conditioning across 10 families, 4 architectures. Using NestDrug, a FiLM-based architecture conditioning on targets. First, fusion dominates: FiLM beats concatenation by 24 points and additive by 9. Second, context enables impossible predictions: on CYP3A4, transfer succeeds where forests collapse. Third, context can hurt: mismatch costs 10 points on BACE1. They expose benchmarking flaws. Tanimoto reaches near-perfect DUD-E scores without learning, and half the actives leak. Their temporal split shows no degradation. It shows context-conditional representations generalize.
arxiv-2604-06858: Chaudhuri weighs how quantum memory burden reshapes neutrino signals from dying primordial black holes. Treating backreaction as an energy-linked change to Hawking emission, he shows the high-energy tail falls while infrared light stays the same. The change cuts total light output and stretches evaporation lifetime by a mass-free factor set by the suppression setting. Folding in cosmic redshift, he computes the diffuse flux and compares it with IceCube's observed spectrum, finding suppression onset inside its window, which weakens inferred dark-matter fraction bounds.
arxiv-2604-07258: Lin and Fukuyama compare how SHAP analysis, a popular way to explain model predictions feature by feature, behaves across machine-learning models and datasets. Black-box models earn trust only when their decisions can be explained, yet SHAP values are model-dependent, so no single analysis recipe fits all cases. Their detailed investigation maps the nuances analysts face in practice. They also generalize the waterfall plot, a standard SHAP display, to multi-class problems.
arxiv-2604-07358: Khawaja, Hernandez Marcano, and Jacobsen improve satellite DVB-S2 and S2X links with external synchronization from GPS-disciplined oscillators. Standard synchronization leans on headers, pilots, and optional superframes, but offers no defined implementation method. They test the idea in a hardware-software loop model of low Earth orbit channels, with and without Doppler shifts and radio interference. External synchronization improves bit-error, frame-error, and signal-to-noise ratios, cutting the frames needed for reliable lock and raising throughput.
arxiv-2604-07458: Ferreira fixes fermion field transformations for two-Higgs-doublet models under a new class of symmetries, dubbed GOOFy, from an unorthodox transformation of scalar, gauge, and spacetime fields. Earlier work showed Yukawa matrix textures can respect those symmetries up to two loops. This paper sets out how fermion fields transform under the new symmetries. New parameter regions invariant under renormalization to all orders emerge, including scalar-fermion interactions, widening the symmetry's reach for model building.
arxiv-2604-07558: Bhattacharjee and four colleagues offer live experience for digital mental health care tools. The feel is made at runtime, not just custom in content. Their GUIDE system makes own content and multimodal formats through rubric-guided making of modular parts. In a study with 237 people, GUIDE reduced stress and gave better user ratings against an LLM-based cognitive reframe control. GUIDE also aided diverse thought and action through varied flows.
arxiv-2604-07658: Cao traces weak long-range memory in linear recurrent models to their decay spectrum. Random starts collapse the smallest gap in that spectrum. Evenly spaced rates also fade over long contexts. His Position-Adaptive Spectral Tapering pairs geometrically spaced decay rates with scaling that stretches the spectrum to the true dependency range. Tests on Mamba-2, RWKV-7, and related models show steadier language modeling and better long-context retrieval.
arxiv-2604-07958: Xu and eight colleagues propose ImVideoEdit, a video editing framework that learns entirely from image pairs instead of costly paired video data. Most editing tasks decouple into preserved temporal dynamics plus selectively modified spatial content. By freezing pretrained 3D attention modules and handling images as single-frame videos, the method separates 2D spatial learning from temporal behavior. Its Predict-Update module pulls out and feeds in spatial differences. Rather than rigid external masks, the module adapts to content, keeping edits precise while motion stays faithful to the source.
arxiv-2604-08058: Celiberti and three colleagues investigate the Jahn-Teller phase transition in LaMnO3 near 750 Kelvin. Runs use machine-learning atomic motion trained on ab initio data. The transition is driven by ordering of the Q2 Jahn-Teller distortion of MnO6 octahedra. That distortion acts as the order marker and sets its order-disorder nature. Local shifts keep moving above that temperature. Results match the experimental temperature trends of structural and phonon traits and highlight anharmonic effects at finite heat.
arxiv-2604-08158: Paspaliaris and 10 colleagues show DustPedia and Local Volume Legacy samples serve as benchmarks for dust change in galaxies. Combined, the samples hold 1011 objects of all shapes, spanning varied stellar masses and star-forming rates, with spectral coverage far UV to far IR. The samples span matching ranges of stellar mass and shapes, ideal to pin down the main drivers of galaxy dust change. Using multi-band survey data, the team fitted spectral energy distributions and estimated real traits, including stellar mass, dust mass and star-forming rate.
arxiv-2604-08358: Gu, Bonilla Ataides, Lukin, and Yelin build a neural decoder for quantum error correction that uses the geometric layout of low density parity check codes. It reaches the tiny logical error rates needed for large fault tolerant programs with modest code sizes at present physical error rates. It also runs fast enough for leading hardware. On the Gross code it cut logical errors to about 17 times below rival decoders, reaching around one in ten billion at a physical error of one tenth of a percent.
arxiv-2604-08658: Baumann and three colleagues uncover a combinatorial pattern behind the rules for wave numbers of massive scalar fields in de Sitter space. Writing the Feynman sums as twisted sums of simple functions, they show the sums reduce to a finite master integral set obeying a first order system. The rules admit a simple graph based picture through graph tubings. That gives a fast way to derive them and an edge view of massive cosmic links, shown in small and large mass limits.
arxiv-2604-08958: Kim and Sreenath address a robotics bottleneck, where gathering real-world training data is costly and risky, by moving experience from a source task to a new target task. Their WOMBET framework learns a world model in the source task and generates prior data from it. That data moves to the target task under an uncertainty-penalized objective that lower-bounds the true return. Tests on continuous control benchmarks show better sample efficiency and final performance than strong baselines, with theory separating mismatch from approximation error.
arxiv-2604-09058: Baeg and Kim tackle long-range guessing, where piling errors, noise growth, and missing real-world fit defeat current models. Diffusion models offer a chance-based frame for doubt but usually rely on mean squared error and miss motion ruled by nature's laws. Their PDYffusion system brings PDE-based controls into a motion-aware model with doubt filter. It settles under the new loss. Tests on several data sets show better CRPS and MSE scores with stable doubt, giving an even, robust answer to the score-doubt trade-off.
arxiv-2604-09158: Güreş and three colleagues compare structuring and problematizing in language-model help for diagnostic reasoning. Novices face biases like jumping to conclusions early and leaning on rules of thumb, and struggle to apply diagnostic methods to new cases. Case-based learning with data tracking and language models pairs lifelike cases with tailored help. Results were driven mainly by case hardness, not prior knowledge or help style. Structuring was linked to more accurate Active and Interactive work, while problematizing drew out Constructive work. Mixing methods best builds diagnostic reasoning.
arxiv-2604-09458: Özyılmaz, Thareja, and Nasser revisit nonlocal games through a representation-theoretic path from Bell locality to quantum pseudo-telepathy. Nonlocal games unify classical, quantum, and wider no-signaling correlations. The authors link the Bell view to math views of nonlocal games and quantum plans. They start from hidden-variable models, the CHSH inequality, and Bell nonlocality as a witness of entanglement needing no device trust. They present nonlocal games via predicate and checker rules, looking at XOR, GHZ, coloring, magic square, and Hardy cases, then compare four views.
arxiv-2604-09558: Hu and nine colleagues introduce VTC, a compiler framework that removes needless data movement from neural-network workloads. Its virtual tensors track movement between compute steps through index maps, instead of shuttling data to and from global memory. A new search routine picks the profitable virtual-tensor plan automatically, and the design works with existing compute kernels across arbitrary operator mixes. On graphics processors it beats current compilers by up to about 2 times, averaging about 1.3 times, while cutting inference memory by up to 60 percent.
arxiv-2604-09758: Zanineli and five co-authors ask whether odors share molecular drivers or emerge from distinct regimes, a question at the heart of the shape-versus-vibration debate. Clear machine-learning models trained on basic markers spanning electric, vibrational, and shape traits reveal odor-wise patterns of feature weight. No single marker class always rules odor guessing. The mix holds across models, hinting no single code captures smell; instead, receptor- and odor-tied links govern it. The results constrain rival theories and offer a guide for mapping odor space.
arxiv-2604-10158: Lin and nine colleagues open up Leela Chess Zero, a top chess transformer whose inner workings are largely opaque. They take apart its MLP and attention modules with sparse stand-in layers that capture the main work. A close case study shows these pathways expose rich, checkable tactical ideas. Three numeric metrics further show side-by-side reasoning matching the policy head's built-in bias. This is the first breakdown of both module types for clarity, and causal tests complete the picture of super-human tactical reasoning.
arxiv-2604-10658: Seck proposes Cognitive Core, a governed decision system for institutional choices like compliance, triage, and authorization appeals. Ordinary AI agents can silently execute wrong calls without flagging them for review. Nine typed reasoning steps, a four-tier governance model with human review as a condition of execution, and a tamper-evident audit ledger structure the design. On an 11-case appeals test it scores 91 percent, against 55 and 45 percent for two baselines. It makes zero silent errors while the baselines make 5 to 6 each.
arxiv-2604-11058: Ren and three colleagues investigate the nonlinear response of flow harmonics to initial eccentricities in the Gubser-flow model. By extending small answers, they derive analytic relations linking them to flows. Their results match the well-known large transverse momentum limit result. They further study a mismatch between the participant and fixed planes. They find standard values acquire a factor set by plane angles, often treated as random noise. This factor can modify the strength and even the sign of the coefficient, making it tied to first crashing nuclei setup.
arxiv-2604-11158: Katoch, Sarkar, and Sen take timelike entanglement rules from one interval to two in a changing holographic model. This extends their earlier work on a single timelike region, now with two regions in play. Where regions do not overlap, timelike mutual information stays positive and a weak monotone rule holds. Subadditivity and the Araki-Lieb rule still hold when intervals overlap. Strong subadditivity, though, generally fails for timelike intervals, as their worked examples show.
arxiv-2604-11358: Klausner and five colleagues update Bayesian inference of a Skyrme energy density functional for neutron star structure, using a Gaussian emulator of the Milano HFBCS-QRPA code to explore a wide parameter space. The calibration adds data sensitive to isospin from calcium and tin chains plus updated giant monopole resonance constraints. Posteriors are further tightened by ab initio neutron-matter calculations and NICER observations, giving consistent crust and core properties for catalyzed neutron stars. Bulk matter parameters come out nearly Gaussian, while several finite-nucleus parameters look clearly non-Gaussian.
arxiv-2604-11458: Stolte, Rahnenführer, and Bommert compare methods for measuring how similar categorical datasets are, judging both detection power and resource use. Edge count tests do well for two datasets, and the constrained minimum distance does even better in some settings. For variables with five categories each, the best method depends on the difference type, with graph-based tests or classifier tests winning. For two samples they recommend the Friedman-Rafsky test; for many samples, the Multi-Sample Mahalanobis Cross-Match test.
arxiv-2604-11658: Gaspari and three colleagues study brain-like computing with optomechanical oscillators. Phase oscillators suit machine learning through built-in nonlinearity and joint sync when coupled. The authors study a network of oscillators pumped in the blue-detuned regime for self-sustained oscillations, propose a theory for their motion, and show how such systems serve brain-like computing. They discuss training and a drum-resonator platform for a real build. Results from modeling an XOR gate with 5 nodes in an all-to-all setup round out the work.
arxiv-2604-11858: Härkönen sets out a scheme for finding which quantities in non-relativistic many-body quantum theory count as truly physical, for molecules and crystals. Two new postulates add: the states that matter are normalizable and stationary. A quantity counts only if unchanged under a chosen symmetry group and Galilean boosts. Superselection rules and quantum reference frames fit in the same scheme. Each truly physical quantity must then draw on more than one quantity that alone fails the test, linking the account to relational quantum theory.
arxiv-2604-11958: Saha conjectures a description of the Chow ring for the universal moduli stack of bundles over hyperelliptic curves, and proves it for rank two and genus two. The proof yields explicit generators and relations, showing the Chow ring is tautological. He also computes the Chow rings of products of universal Jacobians over genus-two curves.
arxiv-2604-12158: Hammoud gives one variational frame joining Kalman-type methods, KL-regularized control, Bayesian filtering and smoothing, and variational data assimilation. He proves identities showing the evidence is the global infimum and the true posteriors are the unique minimizers when they belong to the allowed classes. The frame clarifies targets often mixed up. Strong- and weak-constraint 4D-Var count as MAP estimators under Gaussian assumptions, and the ensemble Kalman filter is exact only in the limit of linear-Gaussian dynamics with infinite ensembles.
arxiv-2604-12358: Jiwan Kim and four colleagues study why cutting visual tokens harms multimodal models on hard reasoning. They trace the failures to a shift in what visual detail matters as answers form. Their training-free add-on, DSTP, keeps pruning matched to those changing needs during decoding. Tests show it recovers much lost accuracy on reasoning tasks and helps simpler image tasks too. The gains come at little extra computing cost.
arxiv-2604-12658: Muhammad Junaid simulates a massive black hole binary in the Leo I dwarf galaxy. Dark matter and stars shape the binary's long-term fate. N-body simulations track the orbit in a realistic Leo I model. Separation shrinks from 300 parsecs to roughly 1 parsec in about 2 billion years. Dynamical friction and stellar hardening drive the shrinkage. The orbit then stalls, illustrating the final parsec problem. Eccentricity grows while inner mass profiles shift modestly. Gravitational-wave models suggest no merger within a Hubble time.
arxiv-2604-12758: Mykyta Kliapets and 30 colleagues catalog variable stars in PLATO's first long-term field, LOPS2. PLATO launches in January 2027. The team sorted 38 million TESS light curves for 6 million sources. Two frameworks did the work: a neural network and a boosted tree ensemble. Combined predictions form the first LOPS2 catalog. Vetting and analysis validate the method. About 72 percent of curves show instrument or pipeline signals. The rest are 3.6 million variables: pulsating, rotating, and eclipsing types.
arxiv-2604-13058: Lee and six colleagues introduce KMMMU, a Korean-native benchmark of 3,466 questions across nine disciplines and nine visual modality types, built from Korean examination materials. The strongest open-weight model reaches 42.05 percent, while the best proprietary model scores 52.42 percent on the harder KMMMU-Adv set. Korean-specific questions show gaps up to 13.43 percent, with failures tied to local conventions and knowledge recall more than to reasoning depth.
arxiv-2604-13258: Pramanik, Maliha, Bastian, and Jha propose Hessian-Enhanced Token Attribution, an explanation framework tailored to decoder-only language models. It combines a semantic shift vector tracking token-to-token effect across layers, Hessian-based response scores catching second-order effects, and KL gap gauging information loss when tokens are masked. The unified design yields context-aware, causally faithful, meaning-grounded credit, and tests show it beats current methods on truth and match with human labels.
arxiv-2604-13358: da Silva and Vassilevich extend the Atiyah-Singer index theorem to non-Hermitian Dirac operators. When an operator anticommutes with a chirality operator, its null space splits into positive and negative parts, and the index is their size difference. For Hermitian operators the theorem keeps this index fixed under smooth changes. Using heat-kernel methods, the authors prove the same fixed index for diagonalizable non-Hermitian operators under ellipticity rules, with the index given by a local integral.
arxiv-2604-13458: He presents the first around-the-clock analysis of jump risk, combining market data with news narratives behind jumps. An open-source reasoning model sorts those narratives. Jump categories show risk premia vary widely, and macroeconomic news carries the largest premium. An annually rebalanced Fama-MacBeth portfolio isolating the most priced jump risk achieves a high Sharpe ratio and significant alphas over standard models. In short, news about the wider economy moves jump risk the most, and a portfolio built on that insight earns well out of sample.
arxiv-2604-13958: Al Ezzi and colleagues show that twisted monolayer-bilayer graphene hosts two kinds of band flattening at once. Global flat bands stabilize states at whole-number fillings, while local flattening lifts degeneracy and breaks symmetry at fractional fillings without opening a global gap. The metal stays conducting, yet anomalous Hall signals reveal broken time-reversal symmetry and valley polarization, making transport a probe of gapless correlated states.
arxiv-2604-14058: Stafford and the CMS collaboration present a first search for new resonances in events with four top quarks in the two-lepton channel. Using 138 inverse femtobarns at 13 TeV and 35 at 13.6 TeV, they find no significant excess. Limits cover vector Z-prime, scalar, pseudoscalar, and ALP mediators, with Z-prime mediators at 50 percent width excluded up to 850 GeV.
arxiv-2604-14658: Koroleva proves a fresh weighted Hardy-type inequality for functions in the Sobolev space W1p, under the assumption that small alternating boundary pieces are where the functions vanish. That classical family is thus widened to functions whose vanishing set consists of small alternating boundary pieces. Hardy-type inequalities relate a function to its derivatives through weights, and this result extends that classical pattern to the alternating-piece setting.
arxiv-2604-14858: Yang and eight others extend ATBench, a benchmark for trajectory safety testing and diagnosis of agent systems, to OpenClaw and Codex. The adaptation analyzes each setting, customizes a 3D safety taxonomy of risk source, failure mode, and harm, and feeds it into the ATBench pipeline as the spec. ATBench-Claw covers OpenClaw chains over tools, skills, sessions, and external actions. ATBench-Codex covers Codex trajectories over repos, shells, patches, dependencies, approvals, and policy boundaries. Emphasis falls on taxonomy tuning, domain risk coverage, and design under one framework.
arxiv-2604-15058: Yang and others study how people share place memories by jointly making heritage objects in VR. Pairs built 3D objects and scenes in VR heritage sites, using GenAI to give shape to memories you cannot touch. Watchers saw partners merge prompts and spots while settling clashing views, and use space itself to show how a place felt in the body. When the AI fell short, people reused its output in new ways rather than stopping.
arxiv-2604-15158: de la Cruz develops a projector-based way to study additive left group codes over finite fields. Classical idempotent codes describe images of projectors that must be linear over the bigger field, too narrow a frame for additive codes. He separates restricted idempotent codes from projector codes built from any projectors, showing the two kinds differ as a rule. The projector view thus widens the theory to cover additive codes the classical frame misses.
arxiv-2604-15658: Mei and five colleagues pin down how far away 56 gas clouds sit in sky from 10 to 20 degrees in Galactic longitude, using the MWISP carbon monoxide survey. For 47 of them, no distance was known before. Clouds picked out by DBSCAN get their range from a color-based method tuned on models and fed by 2MASS and Gaia EDR3 star data, giving 275 to 2,118 parsecs. Dust dimming rises with carbon monoxide glow, but only in a middling way.
arxiv-2604-15858: Ming-Xing Luo gives the first unconditional proof of Weber's conjecture for k up to 12, a claim from 1886 that governs lattice-based cryptography. The conjecture covers the Principal Ideal Problem, freeness of modules over rings of integers, and tight worst-case-to-average-case reductions in Ring-LWE and Module-LWE. Earlier checks for k at 9 and above leaned on the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. Luo's method joins the Fukuda-Komatsu sieve, the inductive structure of the cyclotomic Z2 tower, and Herbrand's theorem.
arxiv-2604-15958: Bodea, Meisenbacher, and Matthes study where anonymization should sit in a RAG pipeline, the chain of steps behind retrieval-augmented answers. Privacy worries arise when RAG insights risk exposing private data to the model or the end user. Anonymization strips private markers and other sensitive tags, but no prior work asks where along the pipeline it belongs. Testing anonymization at the dataset and at the generated answer, they find privacy-utility trade-offs differ by placement, showing that placement itself matters for risk mitigation.
arxiv-2604-16058: Dihan and Muhtasim present LLMSniffer, a detector that tells AI-generated code from human-written code. It fine-tunes GraphCodeBERT with a two-stage supervised contrastive pipeline, comment removal preprocessing, and an MLP classifier. On GPTSniffer, accuracy rises from 70 to 78 percent and F1 from 68 to 78. On Whodunit, accuracy rises from 91 to 94.65 percent and F1 from 91 to about 95. Plots confirm fine-tuning yields split, compact embeddings. Model checkpoints, data, code, and a live demo are public.
arxiv-2604-16258: Alharbi, Tamma, Payne, and de Berardinis study competency questions generated by large language models, the natural-language questions an ontology should satisfy. Such questions traditionally come from engineers and domain experts working by hand, while generative AI now creates them at scale. The authors build quantitative measures to compare generated questions across domains and models, open and closed, and assess their intrinsic properties such as readability and structural complexity.
arxiv-2604-16658: Sole challenges stories of tempo change in Beethoven performance, arguing for coexisting traditions. Past studies fit regression lines to tempo against year, imposing stylistic evolution. K-means clustering of bar tempo data from over one hundred recordings of five sonatas finds traditions. Every movement holds two, three traditions: slow and fast, each stable across decades. The mid-range cluster dominates each movement with 55 to 70 percent. No slow cluster appears in fast movements, and one drifts, slowing near 3.2 beats per minute. Membership shows no link to performers' backgrounds.
arxiv-2604-16758: Shepherd presents a system detecting, localizing and scoring arrow punctures on archery target faces from only 48 photographs. The pipeline rectifies distorted photos into a standard system, then pairs a frozen DINOv3 transformer with guided upsampling. Only about 4 million of 308 million parameters are trainable, yet F1 reaches about 89 percent with localization error of one point four one millimetres. An ablation shows the CenterNet offset head adds negligible detection gain while degrading localization. Per-image scores return with median error of one point eight percent, and group centroids land within 4 millimetres.
arxiv-2604-17058: Liu links three traits of a memory kernel for open quantum systems: delayed support, upper-half-plane holomorphy, and Hardy boundary control. He gives conditions linking them for the Nakajima-Zwanzig kernel when the system space is finite-dimensional. The paper also derives Kramers-Kronig formulas, treats a perturbative force-fit equation, and proves them in Lean 4, closing with a Jaynes-Cummings check.
arxiv-2604-17258: Yan, Liao, and Ye present a pipeline that cuts onboarding for a new object from one to two days to about 30 minutes. Roboflow annotation trains a YOLOv8 detector, SAM 3D rebuilds the object without a scanner, and FoundationPose tracking uses the generated mesh as its template. The pose drives a Unity planner whose joint commands stream via UDP to a Unitree G1 humanoid. Tests show detection mAP of 0.995, pose precision under about 1 mm, and successful grasps at five positions, with generality confirmed on an automobile-window glue task.
arxiv-2604-17358: Lee, Song, Lee, Kim, and Yoon study voice assistants interrupted by third parties, a case where models confuse a bystander with the main user. They build TPI-Train, a set of 88,000 examples with speaker-aware hard negatives that force attention to voice cues over meaning. Their TPI-Bench then measures interruption handling and speaker discrimination in deceptive settings. Experiments show the design curbs shortcut learning from semantics alone, laying groundwork for sturdier multi-party spoken interaction.
arxiv-2604-18058: Delaney and five colleagues introduce Sonata, a compact latent world model for six-axis trunk inertial sensing under clinical data scarcity. Clinical cohorts often hold only tens to hundreds of patients, a poor match for web-scale training. Sonata, at 3.77 million parameters, pretrains on nine public datasets covering 739 subjects and 190,000 windows, predicting future state, not rebuilding raw traces. Against a matched autoregressive baseline it shows stronger frozen-probe clinical tests, fall-risk prediction, and cross-cohort transfer, while fitting wearable use.
arxiv-2604-18158: Lu, Qian, Jiang, and Zhou ask where prompt-based control of a language model actually lives. They test whether a behavior learned in one routing task can transfer through a fixed interface to another.
