CodeThinker combines stepwise reasoning training data, dynamic beam sampling, and a consistency reward that curbs hacking. It beats the baseline by 4.3% on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct and gains on math and code tasks across 17 languages.
arxiv-2605-18558: A. Egorov and A. Vesnin study, in a 2026 paper, spectra of normalized volumes of right-angled hyperbolic polyhedra, the volume divided by vertex count. For ideal polyhedra they find sharp bounds and show the spectrum splits into discrete and dense parts. For compact polyhedra they obtain estimates with a sharp upper bound and numerical intervals where the spectrum is discrete and dense. Interval endpoints use volumes of the regular ideal tetrahedron and octahedron.
arxiv-2605-18858: Zhaohui Wang shows pooling predictors that are each well calibrated can still give a badly calibrated group decision. When agents are scored by the Brier rule and their beliefs move together, each best report understates the chance of a positive case. In one setup the false-negative rate grows more than sevenfold, with no planned coordination, from shared training data alone. A VCG-style rule rewarding added value instead lines up incentives, stays near-optimal on three real datasets, and holds up when data are scarce or hostile.
arxiv-2605-19058: Dmitri Kharzeev and Krishna Rajagopal track plasma heat as it cools into protons. Big Gibbs heat can not just fade; it shifts into plain hadron gas heat plus quantum links in each hadron. Bound bit tangle heat homes this shifted heat, squaring the drop with the second law. Three counts, from deep probe hits, proton wave shapes and Hagedorn tones, put proton tangle heat near its plasma drop heat.
arxiv-2605-19458: Jacobs and Montufar study max-margin solutions reached by mirror flow in deep networks with homogeneous activations. Building on past gradient-flow results, they derive a balance equation from convex duality. It characterizes the horizon function behind the induced margin, with rates and norm growth bounds. Tests on synthetic and standard vision tasks show three points. Distinct mirror maps can reach the same answer, and convergence can run very slowly. All maps learn features yet yield varied representations from sparse to dense.
arxiv-2605-19658: Lucatelli and team characterize multiscale radio emission in 15 luminous infrared galaxies, where star formation and nuclei mix. Using e-MERLIN and the VLA at 1 point 4, 6 point 0 and 33 point 0 GHz, they probe 10 to 250 parsecs and 0 point 5 to 3 point 0 kpc. Emission splits into nuclear and diffuse parts. Nuclear emission averages half total radio power, while diffuse star-birth light gives about 80 percent. Nuclear components track radio and IR glow, rising with mergers, while diffuse light shows no link. Radio-excess sources show less high-end light, hinting active-nucleus rule.
arxiv-2605-20158: Guangzhi Xiong and four co-workers test whether visual attribution for chest X-rays reflects the visual evidence behind a vision-language model's decision. Their evaluation framework keeps only samples where the region is verified by counterfactual editing as responsible for the prediction. Across eleven methods, six models and two modes, they often fail to identify the evidence the models use. Their MedFocus method finds meaningful anatomical regions with unbalanced optimal transport, measures their causal effect through interventions, and beats methods on spatial, concept and token attributions.
arxiv-2605-20258: Sangwoo Park and eight co-workers set out SELFCI, a self-taught frame steering private flows by setting norms in LLMs. Agent aides must choose what to share well, yet top models choose poorly, and fixes blunt their work. SELFCI splits the job in two reverse KL teacher tracks, one guarding task facts, one keeping sharing small and apt, joining skill and restraint as one Product-of-Experts aim. With no outside supervision, it beats GRPO and holds up on new agentic jobs with piled-up private context.
arxiv-2605-20358: Mortier and seven co-workers model phase separation in polymer-derived silicon carbonitride ceramics. They train a machine-learning interatomic potential on over 9000 varied setups, from amorphous models to hot states, surface models and crystal predictions. The potential reproduces pair distribution functions with high fidelity and explains the mix of ceramic and graphitic traits. Defective five- and seven-member carbon rings mediate the shift to stable six-member aromatic rings.
arxiv-2605-20658: Jun-Feng Yang and three colleagues settle classification questions for generalized quaternion groups as NCI-groups and related types. A Cayley graph is CI when isomorphic copies must come from group automorphisms, and a group is NCI when all its normal Cayley graphs are CI. Earlier work left the NCI status of generalized quaternion groups open, though the digraph case was known. The authors prove every generalized quaternion group of order four n is NCI, and none is an NNN-group.
arxiv-2605-20858: Alberto Merici, Kay Rulling, and Shuji Saito construct tame sheaves and tame de Rham-Witt cohomology. They weigh an algebraic form of the tame site of a pair consisting of a scheme and its compactification. With that definition, they provide broad machinery to construct a tame sheaf from an etale sheaf plus a family of local tame sections. Applying that construction to big de Rham-Witt sheaves bearing tame sections from log poles, and over a field toward reciprocity sheaves, they compare tame syntomic cohomology with the Nygaard filtration.
arxiv-2605-21058: Yan Li and six colleagues open a dialogue between causal and traditional representation learning toward shared gains in one setup. Causal and traditional learning have largely grown along separate paths. Old learning has been driven mainly by uses and data-based goals, whereas causal learning has centred more on theoretical questions, particularly identifiability. That difference in emphasis has created a gap in terminology, problem setup, and evaluation, curbing communication and often leading to disconnected or redundant efforts, which the authors argue should be bridged.
arxiv-2605-21258: Yicheng Jiang and colleagues propose structural latent points for robot vision. Implicit neural fields are rich but give no clear structural cues. Explicit geometric primitives keep shape but hit resolution limits and generalize weakly. Their pretraining adds a point-wise latent variational autoencoder inside a point-cloud autoencoder, pulling features and coordinates toward a Gaussian prior. The compact latent keeps rough shape and meaning without precise geometry, blending the strengths of both styles.
arxiv-2605-21358: Yihan Hu and Cemil Selcuk track a shift in US housing market seasonality from summer to spring. Prices and sales once rose through spring, peaked in summer, and fell through autumn and winter. Since 2021, the pattern has moved earlier, with spring strengthening at the expense of the summer peak. Viewed through the search-and-matching model of Ngai and Tenreyro, which links cycles to household mobility through thick markets, the shift raises whether move timing changed. Using SIPP data, they find residential mobility did shift earlier after 2021.
arxiv-2605-21458: Harsh Parikh and co-authors study the sim-to-real gap, urging researchers to think like scientists when re-tuning simulators. Randomized trials set the standard for causal measurement, but are costly. Calibrated to historical data, they offer a cheaper alternative that can become suboptimal under drift. They ask if, when, and how to gather data for recalibration. They weigh multiple units running in parallel managed by a single operator. The real system is partly seen with a latent variable, but the simulator is fully seen and Markovian.
arxiv-2605-21558: Hao Chen and co-authors present From Parameters to Data, a task-guided fine-tuning method for language models. Adapting large language models to niche domains often incurs high data and compute cost, while prior efforts treat data selection and lean tuning as separate processes. Their Strong Map Hypothesis: a small set of attention heads plays a main role in task tuning, acting as keys opening data patterns. Their method uses task-tuned heads for sample mining and shape pruning. It uses the same heads to guide both steps.
arxiv-2605-22058: Chengyan Ma and co-authors present SymTEE, a system that finds missing input validation in trusted execution environments using language-model-assisted symbolic execution. These isolate sensitive code and data in hardware, yet analyzing their apps is costly and limited by hardware isolation. SymTEE lets language models autonomously generate mock environments, enabling auto security analysis without complex setup. Tests report 92.3 percent recall in detecting missing input validation flaws at an average cost of only 0.05 dollars, showing a practical, scalable path for trusted computing security.
arxiv-2605-22158: Luo and co-authors present ST-SimDiff, balancing similarity and difference for video understanding with multimodal large language models. Long videos impose heavy overhead from massive token counts, and existing methods prune or merge tokens by importance or similarity. Those methods overlook changes and turning points, lacking a model for static and dynamic content. ST-SimDiff pairs similarity selection for static information with difference selection that locates changing points, preserving static and dynamic content with minimal tokens. Tests show it beats top methods while cutting costs.
arxiv-2605-22558: Miao and others argue that vision language models need shape detail matched to each image piece, not one shared shape signal. Their GeoWeaver system builds a layered bank of shape facts from a frozen shape encoder. Each visual token then pulls the shape facts that fit its own spatial role. The chosen facts join the token through a small add on step before language work starts. Tests on spatial reasoning tasks show steady gains while broad multimodal skills stay intact.
arxiv-2605-22658: Lu and others close a gap in reasoning segmentation, where language model reasoning rarely links clearly to what the model sees. Their SegCompass model first writes a chain of thought trace, then maps thought and visual tokens through a sparse autoencoder into a shared sparse concept space. A query codebook picks key concepts, and a slot mapper grounds them as a multi slot heatmap guiding the mask decoder. Trained jointly with reinforcement learning and mask supervision, SegCompass matches or beats state of the art results on five benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-22758: Āboliņš and Ambainis pin down a degree threshold for classical simulation of QAOA on two local cost functions. At degree 3, even approximate depth 1 sampling within a generous multiplicative error would collapse the polynomial hierarchy down to its third level. At degree 2, exact sampling from depth p QAOA runs in polynomial time whenever depth grows at most logarithmically. The hard degree 3 instances carry trivially optimizable costs, so sampling hardness alone does not imply a quantum optimization edge. The threshold thus separates easy and hard simulation regimes cleanly.
arxiv-2605-22958: Heering, Kaspers, and Taranchuk link kth-order sum-free functions to Reed-Muller subcodes. A function is kth-order sum-free when its outputs over any k-dimensional affine subspace sum to a nonzero value. For k between 2 and n minus 2, they prove an equivalence. Such a function exists when a codimension m linear subcode of RM(n-k,n) exists. That subcode has minimum distance 3 times 2 to the k minus 1. This yields new subcodes avoiding all minimum-weight codewords. It gives a partition of the Grassmannian into codes.
arxiv-2605-23158: Fan and three coauthors examine privacy leakage from large language models in split inference. There, models split between client and server, so only activations travel. They introduce ActInv, which matches activations to rebuild client inputs. It rebuilds well even against Gaussian noise and activation thinning. They develop the Perturbation Amplification Factor, a metric for a layer's defense to rebuilds. Weakness varies strongly by layer. Tuning noise angles to raise rebuild error improves defense. Their PriPert design is tested on privacy, utility, and compute cost.
arxiv-2605-23258: Lin and five coauthors present VECTOR, a plug-and-play add-on for KV cache pipelines. Existing methods rely on binary dropping or approximation, which may underuse tokens not critical but still rebuildable. VECTOR offers three-way token routing: retention, approximation, and dropping. By using rebuildability, VECTOR recovers useful value information. On LongBench, RULER up to 128K tokens, and SCBench, VECTOR gains over base dropping methods under high shrinking. At 90 percent shrinking, SnapKV augmented with VECTOR beats six competing methods, including D2O and RocketKV.
arxiv-2605-23858: Daniel Ciganda and colleagues forecast world fertility with NeuralTFR, a neural network that pools birth histories from 196 countries and territories. It learns shared demographic momentum across nations. Tested on 2009 through 2023, it beats both a naive drift baseline and the United Nations BayesTFR model on point forecasts. Its uncertainty calibration stays competitive. Looking to 2040, it sees low and very low fertility spreading wider than BayesTFR suggests. That implies weaker backing for a near term leveling off, though not the steepest decline paths in circulation.
arxiv-2605-24058: Fujisawa and four co-authors offer LoRDBA, a small adapter for tuning large language models on devices in unmerged mode, where it stays a live side branch. Both low-rank factors become binary sign carriers, sized by light per-channel scales. The dense floating-point branch thus becomes two sign-accumulation products with scaling between them. Tests show it beats low-bit rivals at matched size and matches fp16 LoRA quality in some cases. Prefill delay rises at most 8 percent at rank 16, despite a tenfold smaller footprint.
arxiv-2605-24158: Markus and Gambar build a theoretical frame for the quantized thermal Hall effect, the quantum cousin of heat bending sideways in magnetic insulators where electrons barely conduct. Like skyrmions, which owe their toughness to protected spin patterns, the effect roots in the geometry of the underlying space. Using Sommerfeld flux quantization, they argue for dissipationless thermal current vortices, swirling heat flows that lose no energy. Such vortices could steady and shape other topological patterns such as skyrmion lattices, tying heat transport to magnetic texture in a fresh way.
arxiv-2605-24358: Lin, Bao, and Kashima address treatment-effect guessing from graph data, where knock-on means outcomes depend on neighbours' traits. Older methods model knock-on but miss differentiated networked effect, the effect of neighbours mixed in weight and scale. Missing it yields off guesses, risking wrong choices. The team offers a tool with two partial focus tools plus a message booster: focus weighs weight, while the booster adjusts for scale. Tests on three real-world graphs show their method beats older methods, showing that catching mixed effects matters.
arxiv-2605-24458: Ekanayake, Naghizade, and Chan propose a multi-job rival model juggling fairness, privacy, and scores. Current methods rarely handle all three at once, and the goals conflict: lifting one often hurts others. Their model treats fairness and privacy as core goals, learning a code that hides private traits while keeping needed data. A tuned cost function juggles the three goals on the fly, with tiny score loss even under strict rules. Broad tests show high fairness and privacy standards without big score loss, and tests show stronger nimble tuning.
arxiv-2605-24558: Ling Zhan, Xiaoyao Yu, and Tao Jia argue that measurement-to-dataset pipelines in AI for science do inference work, not fixed data. Treating shared data as given freezes an observation model and hides uncertainty over pipeline choices. They name three failure modes: hidden hypothesis spaces, uncertified transportability, and ungoverned multiplicity. A brain-science audit found a survival rate of roughly 0.0004 percent under a cross-dataset stability check, and the authors call for pipelines to become computable, auditable objects.
arxiv-2605-24958: Han Liu leads SEP-Attack, a simple paradigm for text attacks transferring across models. Such attacks build hostile examples on surrogate models, yet text transfer work is thin. Submodels often get equal weight, or importance scores mislead. SEP-Attack draws diverse ensemble weights from a determinantal point process. It builds a confidence metric from those weights to score word importance and draft candidates. Each candidate gets a transferability score, and only the top ones become final examples, beating baselines on four data sets and two real-world APIs.
arxiv-2605-25158: The CMS Collaboration studies Z bosons decaying to four charged leptons, electrons and muons, in proton-proton collisions at 8 and 13 teraelectronvolts. Data from the CMS detector total 19.7 inverse femtobarns at the lower energy and 138 at the higher one. The inclusive branching fraction comes out at 4.67 times ten to the minus six, with about 3 percent precision. Separate rates for four muons, four electrons, and two of each are also given. Angular distributions and triple-product asymmetries that probe charge-parity violation are reported too.
arxiv-2605-25258: Alberto Díaz-Álvarez and colleagues add a safety layer to media recommenders that otherwise trap vulnerable users in loops of harmful clips. Their RankAid method demotes risky items and promotes calming material, with the strength of the shift tied to the user's current distress level. In simulations built from a million-rating movie dataset annotated for clinical risk, the system blocks harmful suggestions at crisis peaks. It also steers feeds toward de-escalation. The safety gain costs only a modest dip in standard accuracy scores.
arxiv-2605-25358: Thomas Stephan Juzek extends the study of AI-flavored wording from scientific English to news in 34 languages. Using a split-halves test comparing model continuations with matched human text, he ranks words each language overuses. Related meanings recur across unrelated languages, with emphasis verbs appearing in 24 of the 34 languages. Tracking overused words to 2023-2024, he finds rises in 26 languages averaging about 15 percent, while ordinary words show no such rise. Longer histories in ten languages confirm post-2022 jumps beyond earlier shifts, suggesting AI habits may be homogenizing news language.
arxiv-2605-26058: Bézard and seven colleagues define and measure helicity, a twist measure for fields and objects, in a nanoscale light system. Helicity matters from particle spin to chiral molecule safety, yet it stays ambiguous for chiral photonic systems. Watching circular-polarisation effects, the usual shortcut, does not in fact measure it. The authors excite a model system of two plasmonic dipoles with a focused electron beam in the near field, then read the emitted circularly polarised light. Theory and experiment agree that this route gives a rigorous absolute value.
arxiv-2605-27158: Brückmann and two co-authors learn the rules that drive a system from its observed paths, rather than just forecasting its next states. Each unit in their network stands for a complex monomial, and the output is a sparse mix of such terms. The terms, with fractional or negative powers, are learned from data, so no preset list of candidate functions is needed. The method recovers the exact rules for four chaotic test systems in most trials, and it gives stable paths for real human gait signals.
arxiv-2605-27358: Yanbei Chen and colleagues present MobileMoE, a family of on-device mixture-of-experts models under a billion active parameters. A scaling law tuned to mobile memory and compute picks moderate sparsity with fine-grained shared experts. The models match or beat leading dense on-device rivals with far fewer inference FLOPs and up to 60 percent fewer parameters.
arxiv-2605-27658: In their 2026 review, Zhang Chen and Chen Kay trace probability measures in asset pricing from state prices to modern pricing kernels. Pricing theory builds, transforms, or selects measures so prices read as discounted averages, covering risk-neutral valuation, martingale measures, stochastic discount factors, and benchmark pricing. Landmarks run from Bachelier and Arrow-Debreu through Black-Scholes-Merton to Delbaen-Schachermayer and Cochrane's summary.
arxiv-2605-27858: Shubhashis Roy Dipta, Ankur Padia, and Francis Ferraro build a claim checker that shows its work instead of only giving a verdict. DecomposeRL learns to split claims into checkable parts with reinforcement learning, trained on a distilled set of five thousand claims from a pool of a hundred fifteen thousand. It matched much larger baselines while keeping every step inspectable.
arxiv-2605-27958: Sachin Kumar stress-tests linear probes proposed to detect deception in language models, finding headline scores collapse under simple style changes. No single direction or subspace captures deception, he shows, yet probes trained across styles recover near-perfect detection. Fragility, the paper argues, reflects narrow training data rather than a deep architectural limit.
arxiv-2605-28158: Zhou and colleagues benchmark optimization agents on full industrial workflows, not one-shot problem translation. OR-Space gives agents persistent multi-file workspaces with documents, data, code, and solver outputs, across build, revise, and explain tasks. The design tests whether agents sustain reliable optimization work through a task's whole lifecycle, exposing failure modes one-shot tests hide.
arxiv-2605-28358: Alon Helvits and Eliya Nachmani recast error-correcting decoding as gradual denoising, with a neural network steering a noisy received signal toward a valid codeword under parity checks. Their SB-ECC decoder needs no estimate of the noise level and trades speed against accuracy through its solver budget. Across 42 code and noise settings it gave the best error rate in 39, beating the strongest rival by a modest average margin.
arxiv-2605-28458: Qiang Hao and nine colleagues build a dual-channel spectrometer that records circular dichroism and circular differential scattering from the same sample at once. A spectral matching method fixes the zero line for scatter spectra. Tests on a camphor-sulfonate mix with polystyrene nanoparticles and on gold helicoid nanoparticles check the tool. In the gold case, absorption and scatter share resonance wavelengths and favor right-handed light, showing both arise from the same plasmonic modes.
arxiv-2605-28758: Chandan Watts, Sudhanshu Barway, Mousumi Das, and Ewa L. Lokas study how the environment of the unrelaxed galaxy cluster Abell 2199 shapes stellar bars. From 578 confirmed members, including 325 galaxies with homogeneous stellar mass and star-formation data, they identify 39 barred galaxies and measure bar size and pattern speed. Early-type spiral barred galaxies show larger bars toward the cluster center and smaller bars at intermediate radii, with matching pattern-speed variation with distance. The trends support a split near half the virial radius, inside which morphology-dependent environmental signatures grow clearer.
arxiv-2605-29158: Gabrielle Cohn and colleagues introduce ProtoCol, a model for remote protein homolog search in the twilight zone, where broad sequence likeness is weak and alignment loses power. Instead of pooling protein model vectors into one vector, ProtoCol keeps proteins as sets of residue vectors and scores candidates with MaxSim late interaction, in the style of ColBERT. Codes stay ready to compute, and proteins are encoded alone. On SCOPe superfamily and Pfam clan benchmarks, ProtoCol beats composition, alignment, pooled, and single-vector baselines, backing late interaction as a retrieval layer.
arxiv-2605-29258: Rei Murakami proves that weak solutions exist and are unique for the general Monge-Ampère equation and the supercritical deformed Hermitian-Yang-Mills equation. The classes lie on the boundary of the solvable region. Also, the flows tied to them converge to them in the sense of currents. The proof mixes viscosity ideas and pluripotential ideas. These results cover edge cases for both.
arxiv-2605-29358: Adly Templeton and colleagues show that sparse autoencoders can extract clear features from Claude 3 Sonnet, a production language model. The authors trained them with up to thirty four million features on the model's middle hidden stream, using scaling laws to guide choice. The features are many language and many mode, working on images despite text only training, respond to cases and talk, and can steer the model. Features cover names, concepts like sarcasm or errors, and harms, like lies, power seeking, praise, and bias, which shape outputs when tweaked.
arxiv-2605-29458: Ruoxi Su and colleagues test what a one-hour interview tells a model about a person's value decisions. Forty-six adults completed an adaptive interview, then answered twenty-five dilemma questions. The authors predict answers, compare adaptive follow-ups with fixed ones, and benchmark against a no-information model and the majority answer, but nothing beats either baseline. For eighty-five percent of errors, no evidence distinguishes the person's choice from the alternatives. The same transcripts improve personality type recovery, so interviews of this kind elicit traits, not decision policies.
arxiv-2605-29658: Yi Xu, Gaohang Yu, and Liqun Qi study limited augmented Zarankiewicz numbers in incidence graphs, using zero-one models. Integer programming settles small instances, while search plus exact checks settle larger ones, giving two exact values and three lower bounds. A weak global problem is formulated; on larger cases the exact problem is out of reach, but computations give lower bounds. On fourteen grid benchmarks, the weak problem is solved exactly, never worse than strong and better in several cases. These computations improve classical Zarankiewicz numbers and strengthen BSR bounds.
arxiv-2605-29858: Fengshun Wang, Zhengbo Zhang, and Zhigang Tu adapt masked diffusion models to action localization in video. Autoregressive decoders write in order, so later meaning evidence cannot revise earlier ones. Their masked diffusion approach keeps semantic and boundary tokens open through denoising with two-way attention, refining boundaries and content. Two gaps remain: uniform masking ignores that time tokens grow reliable with meaning, and token cross-entropy misses overlap. An objective with edge-aware masking plus a step-level reward closes gaps, with gains over rivals strongest under strict criteria.
arxiv-2605-29958: Ohad Vilk and Baruch Meerson extend Brownian bees to team reproduction, where each birth adds a particle and removes the farthest from the origin. In the large-population limit they build a free-boundary picture and pin down steady densities for every team size. Steady states hold for small team sizes and fail for larger ones, with a middle case giving a family of steady states at one critical ratio. Above that ratio it collapses to the origin in finite time; below it spreads while births still matter.
arxiv-2605-30058: Weihan Peng and nine colleagues ask whether language-model agents can hold coherent human-like psychology, not just complete tasks. Their HEART-Bench builds 11 characters from orthogonal Big Five traits, each fleshed out with 1000 structured life memories spread across theory-based life stages. A suite of 64 decision scenarios, organized by the DIAMONDS list of situation types, tests whether agents decide in line with their character and memories. After human checks, the benchmark offers 673 quiz questions for studying steady personality and values-based choice in agents.
arxiv-2605-30158: Herman Tesso and Georges Nguefack-Tsague review statistical methods for high-dimensional regression when covariates are measured with error. When predictors outnumber data points, standard methods assume clean inputs, yet real data are often noisy and ignored errors distort conclusions. They compare four penalized methods, ridge, lasso, Dantzig selector and Elastic-net, with corrected versions, under linear additive and uncorrelated models. Simulations and a medical genetics case show the best correction depends on the problem, and the paper offers guidance.
arxiv-2605-30258: Sneheel Sarangi and five co-authors advance reproducible language-model social simulation with EASE, splitting simulators into setting, agent, engine and metric parts. Current simulators are often ad hoc and monolithic, blocking reproducible research. EASE setup is wrapped in a study schema for workflows around explicit research questions in made scenarios. The authors offer SiliSocS, an open-source Silicon Society Sandbox implementing study-structured EASE setups. Three case studies assess, deepen and expand current studies, exposing modelling limits and isolating design effects.
arxiv-2605-30358: Zhenxiao Fu, Lei Jiang and Fan Chen introduce QASM-Eval, a full data set to train and test LLMs on OpenQASM 3, aimed at hardware code. This needs hardware skills past gate lists: mid-circuit checks and feedback, timing, and pulse wave control. QASM-Eval holds a test set of 1,200 tasks and a train set of over 4,000 tasks, covering logic, timing, pulse control, and more. Tuned Llama-3-8B beats zero-shot GPT-5.6-Terra, while tuned Llama-3-70B hits about 61 percent pass@1 and nears few-shot GPT-5.6-Terra.
arxiv-2605-30558: Cattaneo and Mnev prove the BV pushforward map is a quasi-isomorphism of BV complexes. Given a BV theory on fields split into infrared and UV parts, the pushforward sends observables to the IR theory. They realize the map inside a retraction built with the perturbation lemma. Two proofs are given: one comparing Feynman diagrams with cable diagrams, the other using topological quantum mechanics. The construction yields a formula for the quasi-inverse lifting objects to the full theory, with a path-integral form and classical limit.
arxiv-2605-30858: Chang and colleagues build a memory aid for agents that must forecast before outcomes are known, working from patchy clues. Old agent memories store chats, notes, or facts, but not forecast drivers or calibration rules. Their ForecastCompass sorts forecast tasks in a taxonomy and keeps two stores: factor memory for reusable drivers, and reasoning memory for odds updates, doubt handling, and calibration. Past forecasts are re-read to revise both stores. Tests on two forecast arenas with two models show better odds accuracy and calibration.
arxiv-2605-31058: Zheng and colleagues scale code reward learning via atomic splitting and rebuild. Proven-reward learning has shaped coding skills, but growth is limited by lack of hard tasks near the edge. Prior seed growth limits novelty and toughness, so training value fails to scale with making size. Their Atomic Decomposition and Recombination framework makes proven code tasks by splitting into atoms and rebuild, giving novel and hard tasks. Tests show ADR tops baselines in originality, toughness, and diversity, raising code ability across programming, tool usage, and data science.
arxiv-2605-31258: Sultan and colleagues simulate a droplet wetting a thin elastic sheet, where the droplet sinks in and takes a lens shape. Their boundary element method is tested under three sheet conditions: clamped, stretched evenly, and stretched in one direction. For a clamped sheet, lens shape hinges on sheet thickness. Even stretching adds a control knob for shape and tension, tuning the liquid lens focal length. One-direction stretching elongates the droplet and wrinkles the sheet with folds and dimples.
arxiv-2605-31358: Rahlff and colleagues grow Ge-modulated silicon wells with periods down to 0.49 nanometres for spin qubits. Periodic Ge patterns in strained silicon wells enhance valley splitting, a key need for spin qubits. Enhancement needs patterns near the valley wavevector, plus growth control near one atomic layer. The team uses nuclear-spin-free epitaxy with silicon-28 and germanium-72. Wells span periods down to under half a nanometre, including valley-wavevector and two-thirds patterns. Microscopy shows Ge patterns across micron scales, and models suggest valley splitting gains on slopes.
arxiv-2605-31458: Ogundare, Ekpo and Wiggins tackle translating ladder logic for factory automation, where changing PLC vendors is hard. Vendor tools differ in setup, ladder parts and meaning, and black-box tools block the move. The team sets out the maths and a well-built pipeline. It pulls XML, tidies structure, uses a guarded LLM step, and links into Siemens tools through the TIA Portal Openness API. It turns Rockwell ladder code into Siemens S7 code. Tests show the new code keeps its meaning across instruction types.
arxiv-2605-31558: Urrutia and team study how attention heads learn in transformers. They train a decoder-only model on two equivalent multi-hop tasks: a number task needing positional work and a letter task needing symbolic work. A metric sorting each head as positional or symbolic shows successful learning tracks pure heads. The number task needs both kinds of heads, while the letter task needs only symbolic heads. Symbolic methods stretch more reliably to longer sequences, while positional methods face sharper limits.
arxiv-2606-00058:
Sangal and co-authors survey the tangled ties between quantum computing and cybersecurity in this 2026 arXiv review. Quantum machines promise to solve problems beyond classical reach, yet today's noisy devices suffer decoherence, gate drift, and readout errors that hurt accuracy and may open security holes. The survey organizes the field into three parts: security problems inside quantum computers, threats they pose to others, and defenses built using quantum tech.

Coverage includes flaws in quantum hardware and software stacks, plus the danger quantum algorithms pose to current cryptography. Countermeasures reviewed include post-quantum crypto, quantum-safe communication methods, and quantum intrusion detection systems. The authors also survey quantum tools applied to malware hunting, network defense, and Internet of Things security. Error mitigation and fault tolerance receive attention as foundations for trustworthy machines. The paper closes with open challenges and future directions, offered as a reference for building quantum-ready secure systems.
arxiv-2606-00158:
Tatsumi and Watanabe offer a way to tune image codes with no fresh training. Scaled image coding serves both human eyes and machine tasks. Each side needs its own data rate. Smooth rate control for both sides has seen scant work so far.

Their frame shifts step sizes for squeezing based on guessed scale values. This lets each layer set its own rate on a smooth scale. Key traits of each layer stay safe in the shift. Tests show the frame works well in use. They also stress that the split of bits across the two layers holds great weight. The work points to lean, flex-rate codes for mixed use.
arxiv-2606-00258:
Davis and co-authors take sharp Webb views of ten Little Red Dots in the deep sky. These dots have drawn wide study since Webb first showed them. Their OCEANS run uses a fine light tool to split their glow. The aim is hydrogen lines in a set that spans far back in time.

Four of the ten dots show hydrogen soak lines in their glow. That share tops past counts from coarser views. Two dots show such lines for the first time here. Most dots fit line shapes with broad wings. Soak marks tend to sit blue-shifted, with a set mid strength. The team reads this as gas spread round the core in shells. Gas near the core flows in, and gas far out flows off.
arxiv-2606-00358:
Tathed and co-authors fix hum-synced steer slips in quantum bits through code alone. Steer tests can face smooth flaws that shift as a run goes on. When a flaw tracks a trigger beat, it can be read and paid back. Their test bit is a trapped barium ion in a lab.

Mains hum in the lab bends the bit's tune in step with its beat. Code-based tweaks to rate and phase pay that bend back. The hum's part in tune drift drops by a wide span. Its phase mark sinks past the floor the tools can see. Gate tests with scant order show top marks for one-bit gates. The fix grows to 16-grade units, where a test task's win rate leaps.
arxiv-2606-00458:
Greenwell, Wang, and Hill solve a two-asset price law on quantum gear through a block build. The Black-Scholes law prices deals by a no-free-lunch rule. Grid steps turn it to a matrix flip task. That matrix is not of the matched form quantum tools want.

Their block build wraps the flipped matrix in a matched shell. A broad quantum signal tool can then work on that shell. It acts through curve-based turns of the shell form. Sims price two-asset call deals with the new route. Marks tie the stock curve-fit route with back-step grid math. The shell is shown to hold the true push of the raw form. Stock-law tasks in more dims thus open to quantum tools.
arxiv-2606-00658:
Du and co-authors work on cheap video generation in this 2026 paper. Big video diffusion models make fine clips, but each clip needs many steps and a large model in memory. The team shrinks the Wan2.2 model, which creates video from text with two expert branches.

Their recipe mixes two tools. Few-step distillation trains a small student to mimic the big model in far fewer steps. Low-bit quantization then stores its weights with very few bits. They tune each expert branch on its own and shield the first layers, which are touchy. The small model is tuned after distillation, not before, so its values match real use. The authors report that the shrunk model beats the full one at 8 and 20 steps on average. The 20-step setup gives the best mix of quality and speed.
arxiv-2606-00758:
Chan, Cionca, and Van De Ville extend a testing method to directed graphs in this 2026 paper. Graph signal processing studies signals that live on a graph's nodes. One use is hypothesis testing with surrogate data: fake signals that mimic the real one's structure. Past surrogate work covers graphs whose edges run both ways. Directed graphs, where edges run one way, lack such tools.

The team first reworks what a stationary graph signal means for directed graphs. They use the eigendecomposition of the graph shift operator to define it. They then build a way to make surrogate signals that keep the covariance structure under that definition. Test scores from real data can be judged against a null spread built from the surrogates. In guide cases and one real-data use, they report, their method beats undirected tools and naive shuffling. The work opens directed graphs to this style of test.
arxiv-2606-00858:
Zhang, Zhu, and Shao hunt for breaks in streams of object-valued data in this 2026 paper. Object-valued data live in a metric space: networks, distributions, and shapes, not plain numbers. Past change-point tools handle lone data or spot shifts in mean or variance alone. Time-linked streams need more.

Their test rests on self-normalization. It looks for a shift in the whole marginal distribution of the series. The test needs almost no tuning, has a clean limit law, and uses pairwise distances alone. It also tolerates weak links across time. Paired with Wild Binary Segmentation, it can count and place many change points. They prove its traits under null and near-null cases. For the first time, they show segmentation of this kind is consistent for broad object-valued series. Wide tests and a real-data case back the claims, they report.
arxiv-2606-01258:
Zeris gives transformers a new way to mark token position. Standard codes use sine waves or rotary turns. They mark where a token sits, but not its reach. Each spot is treated as just as local as the next. Zeris bases the code on the Morlet wavelet. That wavelet balances position and frequency at once. Each embedding dimension learns its own frequency and reach.

Known codes emerge as special cases of his scheme. When locality is switched off, sine codes appear. The rotary kernel also falls out in that limit. Phase matches the rotary angle exactly. A learned amplitude adds a local kernel that old codes lack. With energy-gated attention, scores rise on TinyShakespeare text.
arxiv-2606-01358:
Germain, La, and Menegaki review the kinetic theory of oscillator chains. These are one-dimensional chains of linked nonlinear oscillators. The Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou system is the most famous case. Kinetic theory links tiny motion to large-scale behavior. The review walks through that chain of limits in detail. It is careful, though not fully rigorous throughout.

Readers get the kinetic wave equation derivation step by step. The hydrodynamic limit gets the same close treatment. The state of the art in the math theory follows, with proofs. Links to the FPUT paradox and Fourier's law are drawn. Many open problems close the survey. It maps where future research may go next.
arxiv-2606-01458:
Kim and co-authors train humanoid robot policies without human teleoperation. Teleoperation demos are costly and complex to collect. Simulator-trained policies transfer poorly to humanoid loco-manipulation. LEGS is a hybrid simulator built to close that gap. A mesh foreground holds the robot, objects, and props. A photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting background sits behind it. That background comes from a handheld scene capture. A procedural generator synthesizes labeled demos at scale.

Color calibration aligns renders to the deployment camera. Tests run on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Three pick-and-place tasks rise in whole-body difficulty. Pure LEGS training matches or beats teleoperation training throughout. Re-rendering demos for new scenes costs 15 times less. Policies also hold up when objects and scene both change.
arxiv-2606-01558:
Sinha and co-authors fix chain-of-thought reasoning in multimodal models. CoT prompting often degrades visual reasoning versus direct prompting. Their analysis spans three modern MLLM families and scales. Datasets require step-wise visual evidence to solve. Two failure modes recur across the models. Models commit to answers too early in the rationale. They also access visual tokens too little while reasoning. Standard CoT fine-tuning helps only in part. It can raise reliance on textual priors instead.

Their Attentive-CoT objective guides attention during fine-tuning. It delays answer commitment in the trajectory. It also sustains visual-token access through the rationale. The objective plugs into any CoT-SFT run with no architecture change. Tests on three benchmarks and six models favor Att-CoT.
arxiv-2606-01858:
Chen and co-authors build a system for personal image styles at huge scale. Users want image models to match diverse personal tastes. Fine-tuning per style is costly and hard to scale. A large pool of tuned modules now exists. Each module serves a narrow set of style needs.

Their Polaris system picks and blends modules per request. It reads a user's instruction to guide the search. The hard part is finding the right few modules. Thousands of mixed candidates fill the pool. The picked parts must also align for the task. Tests are reported on generation and editing jobs. The design aims to reuse the pool, not retrain models.
arxiv-2606-01958:
Wang and Ge turn web text into a survey of economists' views on AI. Classic surveys cost a lot to run in the field. They are hard to rebuild for past periods too. Fast-moving or sensitive topics suit them poorly. Web text is plentiful but noisy and weakly structured.

Their TaDaS method projects raw text into survey-like evidence. Structured side text serves as semantic anchors for that map. Data cover 1.25 million job market forum posts. Posts link to 53,585 top economics and finance papers. Early AI research talk shows low openness, they find. Curiosity also fell fast in the first years. Views grew more open over time, shifting near 2018.
arxiv-2606-02158:
Guo and co-authors propose a new way to detect text that was written by AI models. Machine written text now blends with human writing, which raises risks such as misinformation, academic misuse, and contamination of text corpora. Statistical detectors are appealing because they are efficient and generalize well, but they suffer from two key limits. Boilerplate tokens shared by human and machine writing can swamp the signal that sets them apart, and single score estimates prove brittle under attack.

Their estimator, called Uncertainty, looks at low probability tokens across several scales, since those tokens expose gaps between the two kinds of writing more clearly. Locally, it averages the log probabilities of those rare tokens to ease the boilerplate problem. Globally, it pools evidence across scales to reduce brittle decisions. The design targets steadier detection of generated text.
arxiv-2606-02358:
Leone and co-authors present CHIMERA, a low-power chip for AI at the edge. The chip runs transformer models in real time. It draws only a few hundred milliwatts. CHIMERA is built in 22 nanometer FDX technology. Its compute cluster holds nine general-purpose RV32IMA cores beside a transformer accelerator.

A new shared L2 memory system links the clusters. It moves 563 gigabits per second in total. It also gives firm timing promises for urgent traffic. Latency for that traffic drops up to 16-fold. Peak efficiency reaches 3.1 trillion operations per second per watt. Area efficiency reaches 281 billion operations per second per square millimeter. The authors report gains over top system chips on both counts. The design stays flexible as transformer models keep changing.
arxiv-2606-02558: Weiss Behar and co-authors solve a decision problem in group theory. The setting is free products of finitely generated free abelian groups. The automorphisms in play are Dehn twists of those groups. The conjugacy problem asks whether an algorithm can decide if two elements are conjugate. The authors show that this problem is soluble for Dehn twist automorphisms. The summary gives no detail on the method used. The result adds these maps to the cases where conjugacy can be decided by machine.
arxiv-2606-02858:
Cao and co-authors report a surprise in the physics of magnetic bilayers. Gilbert damping sets how fast a magnet settles and how much energy it wastes. In simple metals it grows with heat and spikes near the Curie point. The team studied bilayers of permalloy and neodymium, called Py/Nd.

Both atomistic simulations and lab measurements show the opposite trend. Damping falls as temperature rises in these bilayers. The cause lies at the interface, where spin pumping boosts damping at low heat. As heat climbs, the interface and bulk magnetizations pull apart during relaxation, and the boost fades. Changing the neodymium layer's thickness tunes the effect. The authors suggest the effect could help design spintronic devices. Such devices could switch faster or waste less energy.
arxiv-2606-03158:
Campbell, Capponi, and Parashar study a household that saves for two goals at once. One goal is precautionary, with a random deadline: a medical emergency, say, that must be paid in full when it hits, if funds allow. The second goal has a fixed deadline, such as a retirement lifestyle target, and can be dropped at that date.

The authors show that saving for the emergency crowds out growth-focused investment. Deadline pressure grows stronger when the emergency claim competes for the same funds. They pin the value function as the unique viscosity solution of an HJB equation. Fund it, the rule says, when its direct gain at least offsets the drop in the value of a funded emergency goal. Tests with a calibrated model show flexibility and fungibility are worth most at mid-level wealth. Locking in a goal early costs flexibility, while split accounts cost fungibility.
arxiv-2606-03558:
Lhost, Ruta, and Semay ask whether an observer could survive falling into a rotating black hole. They compute tidal forces for general trajectories toward a Kerr black hole. The analysis narrows to the polar axis, farthest from the ring singularity. Tidal stretching is the danger during such a plunge. It can tear an infaller apart before crossing the horizon.

Survival turns out to depend on black hole mass. Above a critical mass, set by the spin, the observer is not tidally disrupted during the fall. Any supermassive black hole qualifies as safe on this test. Stellar-mass rotating black holes fail the mass condition. An observer plunging into one faces extreme tides and destruction. The result separates gentle giants from deadly small rotators. Readers get a clear picture of one famous thought experiment, grounded in exact tidal calculations.
arxiv-2606-03858:
Ouyang and co-authors benchmark how well language models mix number skill with math reasoning. Numerical reasoning anchors math ability across applications. Few benchmarks join number processing and reasoning in one test. Failures in math tasks thus stay hard to interpret. PyraMathBench fills that gap with a hierarchical design.

The benchmark holds 32,505 questions drawn from 7,404 word problems. Four cognitive aspects and fourteen subcategories organize the set. Two modalities add range. Experiments expose two weak spots. Raw number computation is poor, and abstract number questions are handled weakly. Two fixes follow: SOLVE, a module for smart tool calls, and IRPO, a training method. Tool calls use fuzzy matching and reject low-quality attempts. With both fixes, one Qwen model gains five points. Math evaluation gains a diagnostic lens, not just a score.
arxiv-2606-04358:
Yuancheng Luo speeds up in 2026 the simulation of room acoustics by the image-source model. The model mirrors a sound source across a room's walls again and again. The mirrors build the room's impulse response.

For rectangular rooms, the count of image sources grows fast with response length. The growth caps practical work at three dimensions. Luo ties the counting to the classic Gauss circle problem, the count of lattice points inside a circle. He extends the bookkeeping to sources with frequency-dependent weights, and links dimensions through convolution. The new bound grows far more gently. Two constructions realize the responses, with time-frequency controls, error and runtime analysis, and response statistics.
arxiv-2606-04958:
Weerda, Syljuåsen, Rizzi, and Burrello hunt numerical fingerprints of an exotic superconducting phase where charge moves in fours, in a 2026 arXiv condensed matter paper. Superconductivity mediated by Cooper quartets matters for understanding exotic superconductors and for engineering quantum memories. Josephson junction arrays shaped as the dice lattice are a leading candidate platform. The authors frustrate the arrays by inserting one third of a flux quantum per rhombic plaquette and simulate Monte Carlo, and tensor networks.

They find the peaks of critical current and temperature correspond to a superconductor-insulator transition compatible with the deconfinement of half-vortices, while low-temperature correlation functions confirm the onset of quartet-mediated superconductivity. They also address Josephson energy and flux disorder. The multi-method agreement strengthens the case that dice arrays really can host quartet superconductivity.
arxiv-2606-05058:
Jingyuan Chen and colleagues introduce UniCAD in this 2026 arXiv paper, a unified benchmark and universal model for computer-aided design learning. CAD software underpins engineering and manufacturing by producing precise, editable 3D models, but research usually treats each CAD task in isolation, and no shared benchmark covered multi-modal, multi-task learning. UniCAD fills that gap.

The benchmark spans point cloud to CAD reconstruction, text and image to CAD generation, and CAD question answering across varied input types. Alongside it, UniCAD-MLLM is a single multi-modal large language model that accepts text, images, sketches, and point clouds and handles all these tasks end to end in one framework. Experiments on the UniCAD and Fusion 360 benchmarks show it reaching state-of-the-art results on every task, ahead of both task-specific and multi-task baselines. The team plans to release the dataset, code, and pretrained models.
arxiv-2606-05358:
Michael Turner and Dragan Huterer examine how the DESI results shift the locally measured Hubble constant in this 2026 arXiv paper. DESI's baryon acoustic oscillation measurements have produced evidence that dark energy evolves over time rather than staying a cosmological constant. The Hubble constant inferred from the distance ladder is analyzed under the constant-dark-energy model, and that assumption is not innocent.

If distance measurements are analyzed with the evolving-dark-energy models that DESI prefers, the Hubble constant can be as much as 2.5 kilometers per second per megaparsec smaller than the standard-model value. Constraining those models with cosmic microwave background data shrinks the shift to 1.1, and adding type Ia supernova data shrinks it to 0.5, in the same units. Local determinations depend on the background cosmology, and the low-redshift cosmology is not well constrained, so part of the discrepancy may live in the modeling rather than the measurements.
arxiv-2606-05458:
João Alves and colleagues automate the detection of eye blinks in horses in this 2026 arXiv paper, aiming at objective pain and welfare assessment. Half and full blinks are recognized indicators of pain and stress, but as micro-expressions they are easily missed by the naked eye and require frame-by-frame video inspection.

The team developed and evaluated three methods on a publicly available dataset. They are a frame-based YOLOv12 object detector, an optical-flow thresholding approach that tracks motion between frames, and a fine-tuned VideoMAE model that reads video clips directly. Their best results reached a macro-F1 score of 0.898 on the harder task of classifying blink type and 0.926 on binary blink detection. A human baseline study underlined why automation matters: even human observers agreed only 73 percent of the time on half-blink labels.
arxiv-2606-05658:
Maharjan, Kaur, and Molyet compare agent-style search pipelines on two contrasting tasks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Search-augmented generation grounds model answers in fetched documents. Standard pipelines fetch once with the raw query, which falters on tangled questions. Their framework splits queries into parts, fetches in rounds, and reflects on results within a bounded loop. Two testbeds check the design: a DevOps knowledge base and a multi-hop reasoning set.

Query splitting gave steady gains on the structured DevOps data, lifting both overall score and ranking quality. On the multi-hop benchmark the same move hurt ranking precision instead. The reflection loop improved citation accuracy but cost substantial response time. Gains in one setting became losses in the other. The authors argue for cost-aware control that turns agentic steps on only where they pay. Uniformly aggressive pipelines, they conclude, waste effort and can even backfire.
arxiv-2606-06058:
Salmani-Zarchi, Rahimi, Faili, and Dousti diagnose why a reinforcement learning method wobbles on instructions in a 2026 arXiv paper. Multi-constraint requests, exact endings, casing rules, word counts, suit verifiable rewards. Yet group-relative policy optimization destabilizes when rewards are discrete and groups score alike. The authors formalize three pathologies of z-score normalization: zero-variance collapse, mean-centering blindness, and low-variance amplification.

MDP-GRPO answers with four stabilizers. Multi-temperature sampling spreads rewards out. Dual-anchor advantages restore gradients when a group is homogeneous. Prospect-theoretic shaping, borrowed from Kahneman and Tversky, bounds updates and punishes violations asymmetrically. An asymmetric KL term completes the package. On FollowBench, IFEval, and a curated set, strict constraint satisfaction improved by up to five points on a Llama model. Training stayed stable with small groups, and abilities held on standard benchmarks. Careful advantage bookkeeping, not bigger models, fixed the instability.
arxiv-2606-06158:
Kevin Dave and co-authors present a cheaper way to compress video for machine use in this 2026 arXiv paper. Video tokenisation turns frames into tokens, compact units that later models process. Adaptive methods spend tokens where a scene changes and save them where it stays still, but many need extra decoder passes or learned estimators to decide. The authors show the needed signal is already visible inside a frozen continuous tokeniser.

Positions whose internal representation barely changes between frames carry almost no new information, so a fixed threshold on that change drops them with no learned allocation network at all. Static scenes then compress steeply while busy scenes keep more tokens, and the rate follows the content itself. A small transformer, LIT, paints the dropped positions back in from those kept. On TokenBench and DAVIS, the method matched continuous-regime rivals at equal keep rates with much lower inference cost.
arxiv-2606-06258:
Shenwei Huang, Yiao Ju, and Yidong Zhou push a famous graph conjecture to two new cases in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Erdős Hajnal conjecture says that any graph avoiding one fixed pattern as an induced subgraph must contain a large clique or independent set. A clique is a set of vertices all joined to each other, while an independent set has no edges at all. The conjecture was recently proved for the five vertex path.

They prove it for two larger patterns built from that path and from the bull graph. One adds a pendant edge to the middle of the path, forming the E graph. The other adds a pendant edge to one horn of the bull. Their proof generalizes the iterative sparsification framework behind the path result, and extends the older Chudnovsky and Safra theorem on the bull.
arxiv-2606-06458:
Alexander Möllers and co-authors teach a model to learn classification tasks from a handful of examples in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multiple instance learning trains on bags of items with only a bag level label, common in pathology slides and satellite images. Labels are scarce in exactly those fields, and ordinary models either overfit or cannot adapt. Their answer is in context learning: pretrain once, then solve new tasks in a single forward pass.

The learner, built on a Perceiver style architecture, was pretrained entirely on synthetic bag data. The team designed several data generators, each encoding a different bias about how bags relate to labels. A model trained on a mixture of the generators inherited their separate strengths. Across twelve multiple instance benchmarks in the low label regime, it achieved the best average ranking, beating supervised baselines that needed task specific training for every problem.
arxiv-2606-06658:
Bhargav Sriram Siddani and co-authors give coarse grained physics a memory in this 2026 arXiv paper. Simulating every particle in a fluid is costly. Modelers instead use stochastic equations for the density, like the Dean Kawasaki equation. Those equations are Markovian, memoryless, and Gaussian. They miss short time behavior and sparse regimes where real systems remember their recent past. The authors learn the distribution of fluxes directly from particle data with flow matching, a generative technique.

Their test case is the Kramers first passage problem, timing how long Brownian particles take to escape. The learned model captured the short time dynamics accurately. It predicted the density's statistical moments better than the Markovian baseline, including higher order statistics at early times. Predictions drift at later times, a limitation the authors state plainly.
arxiv-2606-06958:
Before birth, doctors watch the fluid spaces inside a baby's brain for dangerous swelling. Sayem automates one key measurement in this 2026 arXiv paper. The condition is fetal ventriculomegaly, enlargement of the lateral ventricle. Clinicians judge it by atrial width, measured from ultrasound images.

His network, MVSegNet, first outlines the ventricle, then estimates that width. Manual measurement varies between observers, so consistency matters. Ultrasound also fights back with shadowing, speckle, and weak contrast. The model pairs multi scale feature extraction with boundary aware refinement. It trained on five hundred eighty four expert labeled frames. Against six rival segmenters, it won on boundary and measurement scores. Its overlap score reached about eighty one percent. Width error averaged about three point four millimeters. The model is small, with about two point three million parameters, and runs very fast.
arxiv-2606-07158:
Defenders name attacker groups by their habits, but AI attackers may not keep steady habits. Francesco Balassone and a large team test that idea in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their AI agents posed as five famous state linked hacking groups, including APT28 and Lazarus. They attacked two defended test networks, one business style and one military.

A binary pattern emerged across twenty experiments. All ten enterprise attacks ended in compromise. All ten military experiments were defended or stalled, whatever the persona. In eight enterprise cases, attackers independently turned the defender's own endpoint platform into their control channel. That trick appeared in no threat intelligence profile. Yet checks against official profiles still matched the fake attack chains with fifty five to eighty percent precision. The personas mimicked state tradecraft well enough to fool attribution. If machines can wear any group's fingerprint, habit based attribution collapses.
arxiv-2606-07458:
Israeli and co-authors observe collective light emission from disordered solid-state atom arrays, against expectations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum metasurfaces made of subwavelength atomic arrays promise strong light-matter interaction for quantum devices. Solid-state emitters were thought unfit here because inhomogeneous broadening, the spread of emitters' frequencies, exceeds their natural linewidth hugely and should destroy the photon-mediated cooperation behind emission. The team used silicon-vacancy centers in diamond, whose broadening is about 100 times the natural linewidth.

Collective effects survived: resonance shifts, changed decay rates, and coherent emission all appeared. The trick was placing many silicon ions at each array site, creating superatoms, local groups where some emitters match across the array and amplify the response. Theory explains how cooperation survives the disorder. The authors argue the result opens subwavelength emitter arrays to any solid-state platform, easing use with nanophotonic devices.
arxiv-2606-07658:
Cepeda and co-authors tackle brain shift, the movement of brain tissue during surgery that makes pre-operative scans misleading, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is glioma surgery, where removing as much tumour as safely possible improves survival, yet navigation maps drift once the skull is opened. Operating-room MRI can correct the drift but is rare and costly, while ultrasound is cheap and repeatable.

The pipeline turns intra-operative ultrasound into a synthetic MRI, then uses that image to anchor a deformable registration, a warping that aligns the old scan with the patient's current anatomy. In fourteen patients scored against two hundred fifteen expert landmarks, the anchored warping cut mean alignment error from about six point three millimetres to about five point nine. The real gain is the updated whole-brain volume itself, which shows the resection cavity that registration alone cannot represent.
arxiv-2606-07958:
Xin Peng and co-authors rank three candidate shapes for early-universe inflation energy, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Inflation models give the inflaton field a potential energy curve. The simplest family is monomial, rising as a power of the field: quadratic, cubic, or quartic. In cold inflation these are squeezed by the observed limit on gravitational waves. Warm inflation, where the inflaton leaks energy into radiation, relaxes that squeeze differently per power.

The team computes a Bayesian evidence score for each power. They solve the warm background equations with radiation back-reaction and integrate over the parameter ranges. With fifty-five e-folds, the quartic potential wins clearly. The quadratic branch is disfavoured by about thirty-two log-evidence units, a crushing margin, and the cubic by about seven. If low-temperature warm inflation with this dissipation law is right, the data already point strongly to the quartic shape.
arxiv-2606-08458:
Gonzalez, Shovo, and Ayub design a household robot that predicts what its human needs next, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Proactive assistance requires predicting human activities and object usage under noisy conditions. People move things, pets wander through, toddlers rearrange the home. Existing approaches often rely on complex spatio-temporal models that are expensive and sensitive to this noise. Their framework, GLOBE, instead pairs a lightweight statistical predictor with a large language model consulted only when needed.

The predictor is an n-gram Markov model, which forecasts the next activity from recent activity sequences, running efficiently on the robot. Uncertainty guides the language model's involvement. When confidence is low, the model reasons about the situation. When high, the cheap predictor acts alone. To test robustness, the authors introduce HOMER-Noise, a noisy extension of a household dataset simulating disturbances such as objects moved by humans, pets, and toddlers.
arxiv-2606-08558:
Yingcheng Li and Zou construct a universal theory of an exotic phase of matter from measurable ingredients, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Symmetry-enriched topological quantum spin liquids are phases where spins refuse to order conventionally. They form a liquid with topological order, patterns of long-range entanglement, enriched by symmetries.  The authors present exactly that: a microscopic universal theory for these phases in two spatial dimensions.

The theory is deliberately general. It covers Abelian and non-Abelian phases, chiral and non-chiral ones, internal and lattice symmetries, unitary and anti-unitary symmetries, discrete and continuous ones, with or without spin-orbit coupling. The input is concrete: microscopic states containing anyons, the exotic quasiparticles of the phase, plus operators and symmetry actions. The output is a set of data characterizing the universal properties.
arxiv-2606-08658:
Hila surveys how formal knowledge structures meet neural embeddings, and proposes a hybrid future, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ontologies and knowledge graphs model knowledge explicitly, with named concepts and relations that support crisp logical inference, but they are brittle and hand-built. Dense embeddings, the vector representations behind large language models, capture similarity and context probabilistically but lack explicit, inspectable structure. The paper reviews the ways ontologies and knowledge graphs have been integrated with dense embedding algorithms.

Hila proposes a new frontier: knowledge representation systems that accommodate both kinds of inference in the same representation. The proposal is neuro-quantum-fuzzy systems, which combine neural learning, fuzzy logic's graded truth values, and quantum-neural networks whose contextual behavior models how meaning shifts with context. The paper is a position and survey piece, arguing that the probabilistic-crisp trade-off is a limitation of current representation choices.
arxiv-2606-08758:
Dentelski tests whether a neural quantum decoder's confidence can be trusted like a classical score, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum error correction requires a decoder to infer the logical state of protected information from error syndromes. Beyond a hard decision, some decoders give soft information estimating reliability of the call. For the standard matching decoder, a common confidence measure is the complementary gap, the cost difference between the chosen correction and the best alternative. Dentelski asks whether a graph neural network decoder's output logit can serve as a learned proxy for that gap.

Using a pretrained graph network for the rotated surface code under circuit-level noise, the study compares the network's output with the matching decoder's gap. Post-selection on the network's confidence yields a lower logical error rate than post-selection on the classical gap here. The network assigns higher confidence to many correctly decoded shots.
arxiv-2606-09158:
Junnila, Laihonen, Lehtilä, and Padavu Devaraj count exactly how many strings lie in several error balls at once, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Hamming ball collects strings within a set number of substitutions of a center, over an alphabet of size q. Intersecting balls matters for DNA data storage and the Levenshtein reconstruction problem, recovering a stored string from noisy copies. Center distances alone were known not to determine the size.

They derive an exact formula for the intersection size of any number of Hamming balls, any radii. It reveals which center properties determine the size. Asymptotics for long strings follow. For 3 balls they give necessary and sufficient conditions, every alphabet size at least 2 except 6, long strings, for the maximum intersection size at a given minimum center distance. The maximum is computable from the formula. The q equals 6 exception is a real arithmetic obstruction: the 3-ball characterization is complete.
arxiv-2606-09558:
Mikele Milia and his co-authors build known gene regulation into a Transformer model for single-cell data in this 2026 arXiv paper. Single-cell RNA sequencing records which genes are active in each cell. Most models treat genes as lone features, so the model must learn all links from data alone. Known biology says which regulator genes switch which target genes on or off.

Their model, scTransformer, limits attention flow to paths that match those known links. Attention is the step where the model weighs links between features. The team tested it on disease-linked single-nucleus data, sorting cells by type. Accuracy reached about ninety-one percent, close to the ninety-two percent of a free-form model. With just one percent of the training data, the guided model won clearly. Its chosen gene sets also stayed far more stable across repeat runs.
arxiv-2606-09658:
Tianyu Ruan and his co-authors ask whether the Muon optimizer teaches models better internal features than Adam in this 2026 arXiv paper. Optimizers steer training by setting each update step. Muon, which reshapes gradient matrices, trains big models fast. Its speed edge is known, but whether its features are better was not.

The team tested models trained each way on bent inputs: smudged images and warped text. Muon-trained models held up best across image nets and transformers alike. Probes on each layer showed wider logit margins, a sign of firmer class splits. When the features were reused on fresh tasks, Muon again won, by direct transfer and by full fine-tuning. Hidden states from Muon models also spanned more directions, a trait called effective rank. A toy proof in a clean setting backs both edges.
arxiv-2606-09758:
Quinn Pfeifer and his co-authors fix a weak spot of learning by copying, without new data or expert help in this 2026 arXiv paper. Behavior cloning trains a robot policy on expert demos, then drops the data at run time. Small slips then pile up, pushing the robot into states the demos never showed. Their DARP method keeps the data in play.

At each step, DARP fetches the nearest demo states to the live one. It feeds the model those states, their actions, and the gap vectors between them and the live state. The policy thus reads local structure, not a blunt global map. No fresh demos, feedback, or task tricks are needed. Gains over plain cloning ran from fifteen to forty-six percent. The wins spanned control tasks and arm work, and held for rich image inputs as well.
arxiv-2606-10158:
Balloli and colleagues explore what different stakeholders need before trusting AI tools for pregnancy-related information, in a 2026 arXiv paper on human-computer interaction and health. AI systems increasingly promise to fill information gaps in maternal health, where timely, accurate guidance matters and preventable deaths show stark racial disparities in the United States. The study centers those social questions instead.

The team ran four synchronous focus groups with twenty-four participants spanning birthing people, clinicians, and health workers such as doulas, social workers, and community health workers. Discussions covered information seeking, experiences with current clinical infrastructure, misinformation, and reactions to an AI factual answering tool used as a design probe. The title question, asking where an answer comes from, captures the trustworthiness ideals participants voiced. Findings aim to guide AI peripartum tools that respect how trust is actually built among the groups who support pregnancy care.
arxiv-2606-10258:
Wang and his team extend a background-removal technique so researchers can test whether tiny collision systems create quark-gluon plasma, in a 2026 arXiv paper on nuclear physics. In particle correlations, collective flow signals the plasma, while nonflow, links from other sources, contaminate the signal. Their method extends the subtraction to multi-particle cumulants, built on how nonflow scales with multiplicity in a many-source picture.

Correlators with the dipolar flow component serve as clean nonflow estimators, since its total value nearly vanishes. Using a nonflow-only test setting as ground truth, they test the subtraction on three targets in oxygen-oxygen and deuteron-gold collisions at two energies. Most nonflow is removed, with residual fractions usually within twenty to thirty percent when mapped to the two-particle level, though the best measure differs by target. The method pushes genuine collectivity tests into the smallest collision systems.
arxiv-2606-10458:
Xu studies a design question in signal processing in this 2026 arXiv paper: how should a quantizer be built when its output must follow a distribution chosen in advance? Quantization squeezes a continuous value into one of a few allowed labels, how signals are stored and sent digitally. Designers usually only minimise distortion, the average error between a value and its label. Here the labels must also appear with specified frequencies, for compression, channels, and privacy.

Xu derives the optimal quantizer and shows it has an explicit form built from cumulative distribution functions, curves tracking how probability accumulates. The best labelling is found by choosing a permutation of the output labels, and the proof leans on majorization, a way of comparing how spread out distributions are. When either the input or the required output is uniform, the optimal rule simplifies to one direct mapping, a closed answer where search is usual.
arxiv-2606-10758:
Cristian-Teodor Neamtu and colleagues trace synthetic speech back to its maker in this 2026 arXiv paper on audio forensics. Detecting fake audio is half the forensic problem; investigators want to know which text-to-speech system made it, including systems never seen in training. The framework learns an embedding space with proxy-anchor metric learning over Wav2Vec2-BERT representations, so samples from one system cluster tightly while unknown systems fall away from every cluster. An architecture-merging step groups system versions into unified classes, cutting confusion between near-identical generators.

On the MLAAD v9 benchmark, spanning 140 systems in 51 languages, attribution accuracy reaches 99.76 percent across 110 classes, and unknown systems are flagged with a false positive rate of 2.04 percent. On the MLAAD v5 splits it doubles the best prior out-of-distribution accuracy and cuts the false alarm rate. Well-clustered embeddings serve attribution and rejection at once.
arxiv-2606-10858:
Fjeldstad, Bueie, and de Wijn rework kinetic theory for dense fluids in this 2026 arXiv paper. Chapman-Enskog theory predicts transport properties such as shear viscosity, but its extensions lean on effective hard-sphere diameters that fit poorly for soft, long-range forces. The authors build a framework around an exchange function tied to the fluid's thermodynamics, and show two existing extensions fit inside it.

Their alternative adds the potential interaction energy that modified Enskog theory omits. Tested on simulated Weeks-Chandler-Anderson and Lennard-Jones fluids across wide density and temperature ranges, mean prediction errors stay between 2 and 4 percent at low and middle densities. The worst cases reach 4.4 percent and 8.1 percent for the two fluids.
arxiv-2606-10958:
Khalatbari investigates the hidden life of graphics cards in this 2026 arXiv paper. Over four years the author combined social science with hands-on research-creation: dismantling, dissolving, rebuilding, and remixing some fifty acquired graphics cards. Fieldwork reached liquid-nitrogen overclockers in Taiwan and urban miners in Ghana, two ends of the same device's world.

Miniaturization, the paper argues, is what lets AI look abstract and placeless, hiding rare metals, assembly labor, and the communities that inherit the waste. Taking cards apart made those material ties tangible in ways reading could not. The work presents making itself as a rigorous way of knowing, aimed at ICT sustainability.
arxiv-2606-11358:
Pandit and Koranga expose a hidden systematic error in neutrino physics in a 2026 arXiv paper. Long-baseline analyses often treat Earth matter effects with a constant-density approximation. Using exact propagation through realistic PREM density profiles, they show this mismodeling does not merely shift the standard appearance probability. It generates correlated biases across all oscillation channels at once, as PMNS unitarity dictates.

Their stochastic analysis finds the muon-to-tau neutrino channel is the most volatile carrier of the geophysical error. At baselines like 5,000 and 7,000 kilometers, the tau channel always carries larger mean bias and variance than the electron appearance channel. Below roughly 4,000 kilometers the CP bias is negligible, under one degree, but grows sharply beyond. A multi-channel joint fit does not help, since the coherent errors favor the same wrong CP minimum. They conclude spatially resolved density treatments are a necessity for future precision facilities.
arxiv-2606-11858:
Yiwen Zhang and four colleagues speed up control of virtually coupled trains in this 2026 arXiv paper. Virtual coupling lets trains run close together, coordinated by radio rather than physical links, raising line capacity. The controller must track a target speed profile while respecting comfort limits and guaranteeing no collisions, all in real time, which makes ordinary predictive control expensive.

Their approach lifts the curved train dynamics into a Koopman space, a transformed space where the dynamics become nearly linear, using closed-form observable functions.
