Clinicians usually grade apnea by one number, the apnea-hypopnea index, which counts breathing pauses. The team suspected other measures, such as oxygen dips and sleep time, might predict risk better.

Records from adults first tested between 1994 and 2010 were linked to provincial health data. Over a median follow-up of 68 months, 11.5 percent had a major cardiovascular event or died from related causes tracked in the study. The pause count alone lost its predictive power once other factors were counted, while several other apnea-related measures stayed significant. A scoring chart built from those measures improved risk estimates.
europmc-pmc3989058:
Ewa K. Paluch and Erez Raz review blebs, small round bulges that cells use to move, in Current Opinion in Cell Biology in 2013. A bleb grows when fluid pressure inside the cell pushes the outer skin outward. A tight, shrinking cell cortex, built from actin and myosin, creates that pressure.

Blebs work in a way quite unlike the flat, actin-built sheets called lamellipodia that many cells push forward. Some cells, such as early germ cells in zebrafish, move by blebs alone. Others, among them some cancer cells, can switch between the two forms. The review covers how blebs form, what controls which form a cell picks, and how blebs drive motion with weak or no grip on the surface below.
europmc-pmc3995458:
Daisuke Hishikawa, Tomomi Hashidate, Takao Shimizu, and Hideo Shindou review how cell membranes gain their wide mix of fats, in the Journal of Lipid Research in 2014. Membranes are built largely from a fat family called glycerophospholipids. Each carries a head part and two tail chains, and the pairings vary a lot by cell type and by membrane layer.

Cells first build these fats by a direct route, then reshape the tails in a second, remodelling route. Two enzyme groups do the reshaping, cutting tails off and fitting new ones on. The cycle creates much of the membrane's diversity and also yields signal fats that carry messages in the body. Carrier proteins that move set fats to set places add a further layer of order. The review sums up recent gains in grasping how this mix is built and kept.
europmc-pmc3996658:
Huili Li, Katherine B. Chiappinelli, and a large team of co-authors study a drug that may wake the immune system against common cancers, in Oncotarget in 2014. The drug, 5-azacitidine, blocks enzymes that add methyl marks to DNA. Such marks can silence genes in tumours of the breast, bowel, and ovary.

The team treated sixty-three cancer cell lines from those cancers with low doses of the drug. They then read gene activity and DNA marks across the lines. Immune pathways lit up in all three cancers, covering signal sets for interferon, for showing tumour parts to immune cells, and for call signals called cytokines. A set of silent testis antigens also switched on. From the shifted genes the team built an immune score that split tumours into high and low groups. Biopsy samples from treated patients showed the same rise, hinting at a broad immune role for such drugs.
europmc-pmc4001358:
Trygve Nissen and Rolf Wynn weigh the worth of the clinical case report, in BMC Research Notes in 2014. A case report tells the story of one patient or a few. The form long held a central place in medical writing. Stronger study designs pushed it aside last century, and scholars still debate its worth.

The pair searched databases and textbooks for views on the form. Its strengths include spotting new diseases or drug harms, sparking ideas for study, and deep insight into one case. It also serves where other designs cannot run, and teaches well. Its limits are plain too: findings may not extend to others, cause and effect cannot be proven, and rare cases can draw undue focus or be over-read. Reports also skew toward striking cases. The form still earns its place beside other methods, with online case databases as a fresh use.
europmc-pmc4005958:
Scott J. Webster, Adam D. Bachstetter, Peter T. Nelson, Frederick A. Schmitt, and Linda J. Van Eldik review mouse models of Alzheimer's disease, in Frontiers in Genetics in 2014. Such mice carry faults in a gene for a protein called APP, tied to the brain plaques of the human disease. Labs use them to study how memory fails as the disease builds.

The review first sets out the brain changes and thinking tests used in patients. It then rates the mouse tests that mirror them, from water mazes that probe place memory to tasks for learning, recognition, and attention. Strengths and gaps of each test are weighed against the human measures. Last, the authors chart when thinking and non-thinking deficits appear in ten named mouse models. The guide aims to help researchers pick a model and test set that fit the side of the disease they study.
europmc-pmc4010758:
Yael Leitner reviews what is known about children who show both autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2014. The two conditions were long kept apart by rule. The main diagnosis manual once barred an ADHD diagnosis in a child with autism, which held back study of a common overlap.

Both conditions start early, affect boys more than girls, and can involve weak attention, impulsivity, and restless behaviour. Studies find ADHD signs in a large share of children with autism, and autism traits in many children with ADHD. Having both goes with lower quality of life and weaker daily skills than either alone. Shared gene risk may help explain the pairing. The new manual now allows a dual diagnosis, opening the way for better study. Leitner sets out the rates, the shared traits, and the gaps that work on causes and care must fill.
europmc-pmc4016258:
Kristine Sørensen and nine co-authors describe how a European survey tool for health literacy was built, in BMC Public Health in 2013. Health literacy is the skill set people need to find, grasp, judge, and use health information. Several tools measure it, but few cover it in full for whole populations.

The team built their questionnaire from a clear model of what the skill set holds. Steps ran from drafting items through pilot and field tests, expert review, and a plain language check. The tool was then translated from English into six other languages. The final form pairs a core section of forty-seven items on hard tasks in care, prevention, and health promotion with a second section on habits, health state, and service use. The paper lays out each step so users can judge the tool's limits.
europmc-pmc4028858:
Rochelle M. Eime, Janet A. Young, Jack T. Harvey, Melanie J. Charity, and Warren R. Payne review the mind and social gains of sport for adults, in a 2013 journal paper on activity and health. Health covers body, mind, and social life, yet activity guidance speaks mostly to the body. Proof for the mind side of sport in adults was scattered.

The team searched fourteen databases for studies since 1990 on sport, mind health, and social health. From thousands of hits, eleven studies met their bar. Reported gains were wide, with wellbeing and lower stress most common. Club and team sport stood out: its social fabric tied to better outcomes than solo exercise. Solo players still gained, through self-awareness and personal growth. The authors build the findings into a model, Health through Sport. Most studies cannot prove which way the link runs.
europmc-pmc4067058:
Maria Kuklisova-Murgasova, Gerardine Quaghebeur, Mary A. Rutherford, Joseph V. Hajnal, and Julia A. Schnabel presented a method for building a clear 3D image of a fetal brain from 2D MRI slices. Their paper appeared in Medical Image Analysis in 2012. A moving fetus blocks direct 3D scanning, so clinicians rely on stacks of slices.

Their reconstruction alternates between correcting slice motion and sharpening the image beyond normal slice resolution. Corrupted or misaligned slices are found and dropped automatically. A new step matches brightness between slices, which the authors show is essential for quality. They report excellent results on both clinical scans and optimized data. Better fetal brain images could support measures of growth and earlier spotting of abnormal development.
europmc-pmc4104458:
Mirjam Eberhardt, Peter Reeh, Milos R. Filipovic, and a large team traced how two gas signals, hydrogen sulfide and nitric oxide, jointly relax blood vessels. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2014. Their meeting product, nitroxyl, helps the heart but its route to releasing a vessel-widening peptide was unknown.

The gases are produced next to a sensory channel called TRPA1 in nerve endings around vessels. Nitroxyl switches that channel on by forming bonds in the channel, letting calcium flood in for a sustained period. The nerve then releases CGRP, a peptide that widens vessels locally and across the body. Most widening from hydrogen sulfide depended on this chain. The authors call the pathway an essential element of vascular tone control.
europmc-pmc4130658:
Jane Kaye and colleagues presented dynamic consent, a digital interface that keeps research participants in control of how their data and samples are used. Their paper appeared in the European Journal of Human Genetics in 2015. Biomedical data sharing has gone global and digital, while consent stayed static, paper-based, and bound by national rules.

Dynamic consent gives each person a personalised communication channel with researchers. Participants can set and change their own consent choices over time, and stay informed and engaged. Technically, the system encrypts sensitive data and lets a person's preferences travel with their data when shared with third parties. First built within a biobank project, the approach aims to make consent match twenty-first century research networks.
europmc-pmc4238058:
Sudeep Banjade, Michael K. Rosen, and Anthony A. Hyman rebuilt membrane protein clusters in a dish in eLife in 2014. Many cell signals begin when receptors bunch into patches on the membrane, gathering partner proteins inside the cell. Each known case seemed to follow its own rules, and a general physical picture was missing.

The team fixed the kidney protein Nephrin to an artificial membrane and added its partners Nck and N-WASP. The partners' many-armed binding let them link into a web that separated out of the membrane surface like oil droplets, forming patches a micrometre wide. Patch behaviour shifted with the arms' number and grip strength, as phase physics predicts. Adding the actin-building Arp2/3 complex let patches grow actin fibres, tying the physics to a real cell output.
europmc-pmc4323058:
Lucas B Sullivan and Navdeep S Chandel review reactive oxygen species made inside mitochondria and their double role in cancer. Their review appeared in Cancer and Metabolism in 2014. These molecules leak from the energy chain and were once seen only as damage, but cancer cells make more of them than normal cells while also raising their antioxidant shields.

In the right amounts the molecules act as signals that switch on growth programs and rewire metabolism. Cancer linked mutations and stressed tumor surroundings both push production up, and the cell balances the load with antioxidants to avoid poisoning itself. The review explains this balance and how tipping it might be turned against tumors in therapy.
europmc-pmc4358658:
Yansheng Liu and a team of co-authors measured how much blood proteins vary between people, in Molecular Systems Biology in 2015. They used twins, whose shared or half-shared genes help split nature from nurture. With a precise mass spectrometry method, they measured 342 plasma proteins in 232 samples taken over time from twin pairs, and split the variation into genetic, outside, and time-based parts.

Proteins differed hugely in how much they varied from person to person. Genes, daily life factors, and drift over time each mattered more for some proteins than for others. The team also found 13 gene variants that clearly moved the level of a specific protein. Because blood protein levels shift with genes and time, tests that use them as disease markers need to allow for both, the study argues.
europmc-pmc4363358:
Nehmé Saksouk, Elisabeth Simboeck, and Jérôme Déjardin reviewed tightly packed DNA regions in mammals, in Epigenetics and Chromatin in 2015. Constitutive heterochromatin forms mainly near chromosome centers, in gene-poor zones built from repeated DNA stretches. Those zones help chromosomes split evenly during cell division. The review asks how this packed state is built and kept, and how its parts connect.

The authors describe the chemical marks and pathways that set up and maintain the packing, and note that backup pathways can step in when a main one fails. That flexibility makes the system more plastic than once thought. The second half tackles a surprise: these packed zones are not fully silent. Controlled transcription does occur there in many species and settings, and the review weighs what that activity may do.
europmc-pmc4371858:
Young Seok Ju and a large team analyzed mutations in mitochondrial DNA across cancers, in eLife in 2014. Mitochondria run energy production and help control cell death, and each cell holds many copies of their small genome. Cancer studies had focused on the main nuclear genome, leaving mitochondrial changes unclear. The team gathered mitochondrial sequences from 1,675 tumors and catalogued the changes not present at birth.

They found 1,907 such changes, with a strong bias tied to which DNA strand was copied: certain letter swaps dominated on one strand. That pattern matches the process that shaped primate mitochondrial DNA over evolution, not outside mutagens. Changes that merely swap one building block often drifted toward filling all copies. Changes that break proteins were selected against and stayed partial. The copying process itself seems the main source.
europmc-pmc4390258:
Colin Combe, Lutz Fischer, and Juri Rappsilber built xiNET, a tool for drawing cross-link maps, in Molecular and Cellular Proteomics in 2015. Cross-linking with mass spectrometry ties together amino acids that sit close in space, revealing how proteins interact inside large complexes. One study yields thousands of such links, and tables hide the patterns. xiNET turns the results into interactive node-and-link maps in a web browser, drawn at the resolution of single residues.

The maps show linkage sites and linked peptides, all product types of the cross-linking reaction, and ambiguous results rather than hiding them. Protein domains and other sequence features can be layered onto the same picture. Maps export as vector graphics that can be polished in drawing software for publication. The software is open source, usable online or locally. Visual clustering makes domain-level structure stand out.
europmc-pmc4465158:
Alycia Halladay and eleven co-authors summed up knowledge gaps on sex and gender in autism in Molecular Autism in 2015. Autism spectrum disorder is diagnosed far more often in males than in females, one of the field's most consistent findings. Yet little research has asked why, though understanding the gap could improve prevention and treatment for both sexes.

In October 2014, two autism organizations brought together clinicians, researchers, parents, and autistic adults to take stock. Their meeting asked whether girls are missed by current diagnosis, whether biology protects females or exposes males, and how symptoms differ by sex. The article reports the discussion and names priority areas for future work, including better screening tools for girls, studies of protective factors, and research that includes gender as well as biological sex.
europmc-pmc4479058:
Steven Barrett, Peter Wang, Julia Salzman, and Douglas Black uncovered a new route by which circular RNAs are made, in eLife in 2015. Circular RNAs, loops formed from gene transcripts, are widespread in complex organisms, but their function is largely unknown. The standard model held that a loop forms by backsplicing, helped by repeated sequences flanking the looped piece, yet such repeats are rare in simpler organisms.

Working in fission yeast, the team mutated splice sites systematically and caught splicing intermediates in the act. A loop could form through a lariat precursor, a lasso-shaped intermediate that still contains the looped exon, without any flanking repeats. A broad mutation scan of one loop-forming exon also revealed that exon length systematically affects how readily it circularizes. The mechanism may explain circular RNAs in genes that lack the repeat structures the older model required.
europmc-pmc4522058:
Töres Theorell leads a nine-author team reviewing work settings and depression in BMC Public Health in 2015. Depressive symptoms cause much suffering for staff and heavy costs for employers, and poor work settings are a suspected cause. Earlier reviews had found a few job risk factors but flagged weak methods, and sex differences had barely been checked.

The team kept only forward-looking or strong case-control studies from 1990 to June 2013, each with at least 100 people and measured working conditions. Studies came from Europe and English-speaking countries, with depression tracked by standard forms or clinical interviews. Quality was graded with the GRADE system. The updated review aims to firm up which parts of the psychosocial work setting raise the risk.
europmc-pmc4546158:
Natalie McCormick and four co-authors check whether billing codes can be trusted to find strokes, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Researchers often use administrative databases, built for payment, to study disease. Stroke studies depend on diagnosis codes, and bad codes would skew every count built on them.

The review pooled studies that checked stroke codes against medical records, searching two databases up to February 2015. Seventy-seven studies from 1976 to 2015 qualified. For broad cerebrovascular disease, the standard code sets caught at least 82% of cases in most studies, with specificity and negative predictive value at or above 95%. Positive predictive value mostly ran above 81%, though narrower stroke types scored worse.
europmc-pmc4556158:
Dongwan D. Kang and four co-authors present software that sorts mixed microbe DNA into single genomes, in PeerJ in 2015. Shotgun sequencing of a whole community yields millions of fragments from hundreds of species at once. Binning, grouping fragments by their source organism, lets researchers study species they cannot grow, but older tools miss many species and stall on big datasets.

Their program, MetaBAT, judges fragment kinship by two clues at once: how abundant each fragment is, and its letter-pattern frequency. On synthetic and real datasets it beat rival tools in accuracy and speed, forming hundreds of high-quality genome bins from millions of fragments within hours on one machine. The software is open source.
europmc-pmc4588458:
Simon C. Cork and five co-authors map where a gut hormone's receptor sits in the mouse brain, in Molecular Metabolism in 2015. GLP-1, a hormone best known from the gut, is a key regulator of food intake and energy balance, and its drugs are diabetes mainstays. Yet which brain cells carry its receptor, and which matter, was debated.

Using a mouse engineered so receptor-bearing cells glow, the team found dense populations in the circumventricular organs, amygdala, hypothalamic nuclei, and lower brainstem, with thinner scatter in the hippocampus and cortex. Recordings from glowing neurons in brain slices confirmed the cells respond. Viral targeting let them probe single populations in living animals, giving the field a precise wiring map.
europmc-pmc4588858:
Riccardo E. Marioni leads an eleven-author team testing a DNA-based age clock against fitness, in the International Journal of Epidemiology in 2015. The epigenetic clock estimates age from DNA methylation marks and matches calendar age closely, but why some people's clocks run fast was unclear. The Lothian Birth Cohort 1936, a group followed since childhood, offered a test bed.

Methylation age was measured at ages 70, 73, and 76 in up to 920 members, alongside lung function, walking speed, grip strength, and cognitive ability. The analysis asked whether a faster-running clock went with weaker fitness at the same age, and whether clock speed at 70 forecast later decline. The work probes what the celebrated clock actually measures about aging bodies.
europmc-pmc4632058:
Daniel Money and colleagues presented a 2015 software package called LinkImpute for filling gaps in genetic data from nonmodel organisms. Genotyping always leaves missing entries, and filling them boosts study power. Crops and other nonmodel species lack the reference panels that humans and cattle enjoy. The paper appeared in G3: Genes, Genomes, Genetics.

Their method judges a missing genotype by its nearest neighbours among markers spread across the genome, so it needs no map of marker order. It works on unphased data from species with two different gene copies. Tests on apple, grape, and maize sequencing data showed speed matching the best rival tools, with the least bias in allele frequency estimates. Breeders of under-resourced species gain a practical imputation option.
europmc-pmc4632358:
A 2015 literature review by Tessa Kennedy-Martin and colleagues deals with whether patients in drug trials resemble patients in everyday care. Trials run under tight rules that can exclude many typical patients. The review gathered studies comparing trial samples with real-world populations in cardiology, mental health, and oncology. It appeared in Trials.

From over five thousand abstracts, fifty-two studies qualified. Most found trial samples were highly selected and lower risk than real patients. Older people and those with several conditions were often shut out, and large shares of real patients would have failed trial entry rules. About seventy-one percent of the studies concluded openly that trial samples were not broadly representative, which limits how far trial results can be stretched.
europmc-pmc4700258:
Angela Castoldi, Cristiane Naffah de Souza, Niels Olsen Saraiva Câmara, and Pedro M. Moraes-Vieira reviewed macrophage switching in fat tissue in Frontiers in Immunology in 2015. As obesity develops, immune cells move into white fat, and macrophages become its main white-cell population. These macrophages come in two broad moods. M1 cells drive inflammation and burn sugar fast; M2 cells calm inflammation and help keep lean tissue in balance.

In lean mice and humans, M2 cells dominate. In obesity, M1 numbers climb, and their rise tracks with fat inflammation and insulin resistance, the failure of tissues to answer insulin properly. The review covers the signals that flip macrophages between states and the metabolic programs each state runs. It also notes newer work showing more than two states exist. Understanding the switch matters because calming fat inflammation could ease the path to type 2 diabetes.
europmc-pmc4709858:
Vanina Romanello and Marco Sandri reviewed mitochondrial quality control and muscle mass in Frontiers in Physiology in 2015. Muscle wasting strikes in inactivity, diabetes, cancer, organ failure, and plain aging. In wasting muscle, the mitochondrial network, the cell's power grid, shrinks and malfunctions, and faulty mitochondria send signals that drive further breakdown. Exercise does the opposite, sparking new mitochondria and clearing broken ones. The review connects these threads into one account of how muscle is kept or lost.

Quality control is the hinge: coordinated pathways build fresh mitochondria, repair damage, and digest the hopeless cases, a cleanup called mitophagy. When control holds, muscle holds. When it slips, reactive oxygen species rise and atrophy programs switch on. The authors close with what this means for treatment design: drugs that restore mitochondrial housekeeping might defend muscle across many diseases at once, not just in the gym's absence.
europmc-pmc4742858:
Zhu and eight colleagues rethink how temperature is controlled in photothermal cancer therapy. The standard approach heats whole lesions to 42 to 45 degrees, which kills tumour cells but also cooks nearby healthy tissue. Their system pairs a photothermal material with upconversion nanoparticles that report temperature at the microscopic scale in real time.

The measurements reveal a gap: the temperature right at the light-absorbing particles is high enough to kill cancer cells while the lesion as a whole is still mild. Guided by that feedback, they ablate labelled tumours in living animals with sharp spatial precision and minimal damage to normal tissue.
europmc-pmc4778358:
Marina Saresella leads ten authors in Molecular Neurodegeneration in 2016 testing whether immune alarm complexes switch on in Alzheimer's disease. The complexes, called inflammasomes, release the fever signal IL-1β, long suspected in the brain swelling of Alzheimer's. Hard data in patients, though, had been missing.

The team read blood immune cells from patients at several stages. Gene activity for two alarm types, NLRP1 and NLRP3, and their partner parts ran high in mild and severe disease. Cells carrying the assembled complexes were more common, and they poured out more IL-1β and IL-18. In early memory trouble the parts rose but the complexes did not yet assemble or fire. The authors propose that blocking inflammasome assembly is a treatment route worth testing.
europmc-pmc4808858:
Artemis P. Simopoulos, writing alone in Nutrients in 2016, links a shift in dietary fats to rising obesity. Two fat families, omega-6 and omega-3, compete in the body, and their balance matters. Over three decades Western diets cut total fat yet raised omega-6 and lowered omega-3, moving the ratio from an even balance in ancestral diets to twenty to one or worse.

Animal and cell studies give the two families opposed roles in fat gain, through fat-cell growth, heat-making in fat, gut-brain signaling, and swelling. Studies of people tie a high ratio in blood membranes to higher obesity risk, and a high omega-3 share to lower risk. Raising two omega-3 fats reversed the effect in trials the author cites. The piece urges restoring the balance as obesity policy.
europmc-pmc4889758:
Shannan L. Rossi and co-authors built a fresh mouse model of Zika virus infection in 2016, during the Americas outbreak. Zika had seemed mild, but the outbreak linked it to Guillain-Barré syndrome and small head size in newborns. A Cambodian virus sample, little passaged, caused illness in mice lacking a key interferon receptor, called A129 mice, while normal mice stayed well.

Disease hit younger mice hardest: all infected at three weeks died. Virus peaked in blood by day two, reached the brain by day three, and caused tremors by day six. Strong growth also showed in the testis. A workable model lets labs test vaccines and probe how Zika harms the brain and unborn.
europmc-pmc4928258:
A. Venkataraman and five co-authors test whether resistant starch raises butyrate in the human gut, and why results differ by person. Their study appeared in Microbiome in 2016. Butyrate is a fatty acid made when gut bacteria ferment fiber. It feeds colon cells and helps keep the gut lining sound. The team gave unmodified potato starch to 20 healthy young adults and tracked fecal butyrate and gut microbes.

Butyrate rose on average, from 8 to 12 units per kilogram of feces. Yet people split into three groups: 11 improved clearly, three stayed high, and six stayed low. The clear gain group showed big jumps in starch eating bacteria such as Bifidobacterium adolescentis or Ruminococcus bromii. The authors argue that a prebiotic works only when the right starter microbes are already present in a person's gut.
europmc-pmc4941358:
Wei Chen and four co-authors build iACP, a program that flags anticancer peptides from their letter sequence alone. Their paper appeared in Oncotarget in 2016. Anticancer peptides are short protein chains that can kill cancer cells with fewer side effects than standard drugs. Lab testing of each candidate is slow, so a fast screen helps. The tool studies pairs of amino acids spaced at set gaps in the sequence, a pattern the team tuned for this task.

Strict cross validation tests showed iACP beat the earlier predictors on both accuracy and stability. The team put the tool on a public web server for free use. A user pastes a sequence and gets a verdict on whether it looks like an anticancer peptide. The authors present the server as a first filter for drug hunting. Promising hits still need lab proof before any medical use can be claimed.
europmc-pmc4949558:
H. L. Simpson and B. J. Campbell review how dietary fibre interacts with gut microbes and their chemical output. Their review appeared in Alimentary Pharmacology and Therapeutics in 2015. Fast DNA sequencing had reshaped knowledge of the gut microbiota. Diet, and plant fibre above all, stood out as a lever on which microbes thrive and what they make. The authors searched the medical literature for human and animal work on fibre change.

Habitual diets left clear marks. Agrarian diets rich in fruit and legume fibre went with diverse flora led by Prevotella. Western diets, high in fat and sugar and low in fibre, cut helpful fibre eating bacteria and raised mucosa linked pathogens. Even short diet switches shifted the flora fast. Fermentation products such as short chain fatty acids linked fibre to gut health. The authors say food based trials are the next test of cause and effect.
europmc-pmc4979358:
Hmwe H. Kyu leads a large team measuring how physical activity dose relates to five major diseases. Their dose-response meta-analysis appeared in The BMJ in 2016, as part of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2013. The diseases are breast cancer, colon cancer, diabetes, ischemic heart disease, and ischemic stroke. The team pooled prospective cohort studies and mapped activity reported in varied domains onto one total scale, measured in MET minutes per week.

One hundred and seventy-four articles fed the analysis. Higher total activity linked strongly to lower risk for all five diseases. Most gains arrived by three thousand to four thousand MET minutes per week. That level is several times the recommended minimum of six hundred. Gains beyond it were smaller. The authors argue guidelines built on the minimum understate what activity can do, above all as populations age.
europmc-pmc5030358:
G. Hoarau and a large team of co-authors study gut microbes in families with Crohn's disease, in mBio in 2016. Crohn's is a relapsing gut inflammation shaped by genes and by the gut's own microbes. Most studies track bacteria alone; this team also read the fungi, comparing patients, their healthy relatives in nine family clusters in northern France and Belgium, and unrelated healthy families nearby.

Patients and relatives shared a fungal pattern that set them apart from the unrelated group. In patients, two bacteria, Serratia marcescens and Escherichia coli, ran high while helpful bacteria fell. The fungus Candida tropicalis ran higher than in relatives and tracked with a Crohn's antibody marker. The three rose and fell together, and in dishes built thicker mixed biofilms than any alone, the bacterium gripping the fungus with hair-like fimbriae. Such cross-kingdom teamwork may help drive the disease.
europmc-pmc5069758:
Se Jin Song and seven co-authors test how to preserve stool samples for microbiome studies in mSystems in 2016. Field research often collects feces far from freezers, yet storage changes can alter the microbial community before sequencing. The team compared five preservation methods on human and dog samples, more than 1,200 in all from fifteen donors. Samples were stored for up to eight weeks, with freeze-thaw cycles and heat swings thrown in.

Several cheap methods kept the communities stable for the full eight weeks, while others let the profile drift. The practical payoff is large: reliable room-temperature options open studies of remote human groups and wildlife that freezing logistics would price out. The authors detail which methods held up and which failed. Their benchmark gives microbiome science a firmer base, since conclusions about a gut community are only as good as the sample that reached the lab.
europmc-pmc5150058:
E. Muir reported treating kala-azar with tartar emetic in The Indian Medical Gazette in 1915. Muir, of the Mission Hospital at Kalna, read of Italian success with the antimony drug in infantile kala-azar. The disease is parasitic. It is marked by fever, a swollen spleen, and the dark skin that gives it its name, black fever.

He treated twelve adult cases, nine confirmed by finding the parasite in spleen punctures, and all but one patient who arrived in the last stage recovered or was recovering. A one percent solution went into a vein every second day, the dose rising step by step, with care to keep the fluid out of the tissue. Improvement showed after the first injection, appetite returned after the second, and spleens shrank fast, aided by turpentine injections he used alongside.
europmc-pmc5337858:
Taku Kuwabara, Fumio Ishikawa, Motonari Kondo, and Terutaka Kakiuchi reviewed a swelling signal in autoimmune disease in Mediators of Inflammation in 2017. The signal, IL-17, calls up growth factors and guide chemicals that draw immune cells to a site. In infection, it helps clear bacteria and fungi from body surfaces. In long illness, the same signal feeds harm.

A helper T cell type called Th17 is the chief source, woken by two partner signals from eater cells and tissue. Th17 cells drive joint damage in rheumatoid arthritis and nerve harm in multiple sclerosis, two diseases the review covers in depth. Kin signals that grow and keep these cells are mapped as well. The authors argue that grasping this cell family is key to new drugs, and that blocking IL-17 paths already shows worth in the clinic.
europmc-pmc5342458:
Andrey V. Shubin, Ilya V. Demidyuk, Alexey A. Komissarov, Lola M. Rafieva, and Sergey V. Kostrov reviewed bubble growth inside dying cells in Oncotarget in 2016. When mammal cells meet germs, viruses, or harsh chemicals, large clear bubbles, called vacuoles, can swell in their fluid. The sight has been known for years and often comes with cell death. Its part in death was long unclear, since study stuck at the level of looks.

Fresh work has traced how the bubbles form and what walls they bear. New forms of cell death, not known before, also come with heavy bubble growth. The review sorts those cases and weighs two views. In most, bubble growth seems a side effect of the killing blow, not its cause. In some, the build-up may itself start the death. The pair of outcomes keeps the topic open for more study.
europmc-pmc5381358:
Jason M. Tarkin led a team that tested a new scan for artery swelling in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology in 2017. Swelling inside artery plaques drives their burst, the spark of heart attacks and strokes. The standard glow scan for it is blurry: it lights all hungry cells, and heart muscle glow spills over the heart's own arteries. A sharper tracer could fix both flaws.

Their tracer locks onto a receptor found, in this work, only on the hot form of macrophage, the eater cell that stokes plaque swelling. In cut-out neck plaques, the tracer bound where those cells crowd, and its signal tracked the receptor's gene read closely. In more than forty patients, the scan split culprit arteries from quiet ones in heart and brain cases. The old scan could not match that split for heart arteries.
europmc-pmc5424158:
Chung and co-authors read gene activity cell by cell inside breast tumors. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Bulk tests average a tumor's many cell types together. That hides differences that can change treatment results. Single-cell RNA sequencing separates the mix. The team profiled 515 cells from 11 patients. Copy number patterns split cancer cells from other cells.

Cancer cells shared common signatures within each tumor. They also differed in subtype traits and key pathways. Most non-cancer cells were immune cells. They formed three clusters: T cells, B cells, and macrophages. The T cells looked regulatory or exhausted. The macrophages showed an M2 profile. Both patterns point to immune suppression. The authors say this mix shapes each tumor's behavior. Single-cell views could sharpen how doctors read a patient's cancer.
europmc-pmc5436458:
Etkind and co-authors project how many people will need palliative care by 2040. Their research article appeared in BMC Medicine. About three quarters of people near death could gain from such care. Older populations and chronic illness keep growing. No one had put firm numbers on future need. The team used death records for England and Wales. The records covered 2006 to 2014.

They counted deaths from defined chronic progressive illnesses. They then applied official death forecasts. Annual deaths are set to rise by about 25 percent. If care needs per death stay flat, need grows by the same share. If recent trends continue, need grows by over 42 percent. That means about 160,000 more people per year. Dementia deaths drive much of the rise. Cancer deaths add a large share too. The authors urge health systems to start adapting now.
europmc-pmc5446558:
Reardon and co-authors ask parents what blocks or eases access to mental health care for their children. Their systematic review appeared in European Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. Only a minority of affected children get treatment. Surveys put access at 25 to 56 percent. Parents act as gatekeepers to care. Their views shape whether help is sought. The team synthesized 44 studies, both qualitative and quantitative.

Barriers fell into four groups. System and structure issues came first. Cost, waiting, and rigid services all featured. Views of services and treatment formed a second group. Stigma and distrust held families back. Knowledge gaps formed a third group. Parents may miss signs or not know where to go. Family circumstances formed the last group. The authors suggest fixes on each front. Free, flexible care would help. So would trusting ties with professionals. Better parent education could sharpen problem spotting.
europmc-pmc5463358:
Subramaniam and Federoff review the brain's immune cells as drug targets in Parkinson's disease. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience. Parkinson's kills the nerve cells that make dopamine. Inflammation rises as the damage grows. Cells called microglia drive much of that response. They can play two opposite roles. Some states help repair and protect tissue. Other states poison nerve cells.

In the harmful state, these cells release signals that fuel inflammation. They also emit toxins that harm neurons. In the helpful state, they release calming signals and growth factors. Those support repair and restore balance. Little is known about these states in Parkinson's itself. The authors survey drugs and molecules that might shift the balance. One plan is to curb the harmful state. The paired plan is to boost the helpful one. Doing both at once looks most promising, they argue.
europmc-pmc5466358:
Zeng and co-authors compare the software tools that hunt for circular RNAs in gene data. Their overview and evaluation appeared in PLoS Computational Biology. Circular RNAs form loops instead of straight chains. They can soak up small regulatory RNAs or serve as disease markers. New sequencing data have revealed thousands of them. Many detection tools have appeared in response. Users lacked a fair guide to which tool works best.

The team built an improved simulator for testing. It creates fake reads that mimic real circular RNA signals. They then ran 11 detection tools on both fake and real data sets. Scores covered precision, sensitivity, and overall balance. No single tool won on every measure. Three tools stood out for balance. CIRI, CIRCexplorer, and KNIFE each paired accuracy with good coverage. The authors offer the results as practical guidance for choosing a tool.
europmc-pmc5504258:
Vasile, Dossi, and Rouach present a review in Brain Structure and Function on human astrocytes. Astrocytes are star-shaped brain cells once seen as mere support. Rodent work revealed them as active partners of neurons. Human astrocytes look larger and more varied than rodent ones. Whether rodent findings carry over to people is the core question.

The human cortex holds about 1.4 glial cells per neuron, they note. Gene profiles and shapes differ from those in rodents too. Their roles in synapse care and signal cleanup look stronger in humans. Knowing the gaps matters for translating animal results into medicine.
europmc-pmc5509958:
Genard, Lucas, and Michiels present a review in Frontiers in Immunology on tumor-associated macrophages. These immune cells can fill over half of a tumor's cell mass. Most lean toward a state that feeds tumor growth and spread. Flipping them to a tumor-fighting state could aid treatment. The review asks how standard therapies shift that balance.

Chemotherapy and immune therapies can each push macrophages toward the fighting state. Radiation can too, they report, though dose matters greatly. The pathways behind radiation's effect are traced in detail. Knowing the right dose could sharpen combined treatments. The authors call for trials built around this reprogramming idea.
europmc-pmc5583158:
Mozos and co-authors review inflammation markers for arterial stiffness in Frontiers in Immunology. Stiff arteries predict a higher risk of heart and vessel events. Inflammation helps drive that stiffening. It harms the vessel lining, breaks down elastic fibers, and promotes calcium build-up.

Many studies link stiffness severity to marker levels in blood. White cell counts, fibrinogen, and C-reactive protein all appear. So do adhesion molecules and several cytokines. The links show up across diabetes, kidney disease, and many other conditions. The authors argue the process is at least partly reversible. Joint checks of stiffness and markers could sharpen risk checks. Future drugs may aim at the inflammation itself. Readers get a wide survey of the evidence.
europmc-pmc5612458:
Esteban and co-authors present MRIQC, a tool for automatic quality control of brain MRI scans, in PLOS ONE. Bad scans can bias every later analysis step. Human inspection is slow, tiring, and uneven between raters. Big multi-site studies make it hopeless by hand.

MRIQC extracts quality measures from each scan. A trained classifier then votes accept or exclude. Training used public data from 17 sites, with 1,102 scans. A leave-one-site-out test gave 76 percent accuracy on new sites. A held-out set from two more sites matched that figure. Within one site, accuracy runs high. New sites still trip the tool up, through odd artifacts it never saw. The authors ask for more labeled data and better handling of site shifts. The tool runs locally or free online. Readers get an honest scorecard for automated scan checking.
europmc-pmc5681558:
Ma and co-authors report a mouse study in Nature Communications. It maps how cerebrospinal fluid drains from the brain. Textbooks credit drainage through arachnoid projections into veins. A lymphatic route has long been suspected as well. The team used lymphatic-reporter mice to settle the balance. High-resolution imaging tracked tracers injected into a ventricle.

Tracers spread through paravascular spaces of cortex and pia. They reached lymph nodes fast along nerve routes. Those routes pass through openings in the skull. Noninvasive imaging measured flow to blood and nodes directly. Lymphatic vessels proved the major outflow path. The result held for large and small tracer molecules. Aged mice showed much weaker lymphatic outflow than young ones.
europmc-pmc5686258:
Zhang and co-authors present a meta-analysis in Brain Structure and Function. It maps the brain networks behind response inhibition. Inhibition means stopping actions that no longer fit. An older view tied it to one right frontal region. A newer model sees shared networks serving many tasks. The team pooled 225 fMRI studies with 323 experiments. Tasks split into three kinds of inhibition. They cover resolving interference, withholding actions, and cancelling actions.

Right-side regions lit up across all three kinds. These included the inferior frontal gyrus and insula. Two networks formed the common core of activity. They were the fronto-parietal and ventral attention networks. Differences also emerged between the task kinds. Cancelling leaned more on fronto-striatal circuits.
europmc-pmc5688358:
Rizzatti and co-authors review Proteobacteria as a shared factor in human disease. Their review appeared in BioMed Research International. Proteobacteria form a major gut phylum. The group includes several known pathogens. Many studies report higher levels in sick patients. The authors gather evidence across diseases.

Strongest evidence covers metabolic disorders. Inflammatory bowel disease also shows the pattern. Newer studies point to lung diseases. Asthma and chronic obstructive lung disease appear. The authors call the phylum a possible disease signature. Inflammation runs through all these conditions. That shared thread may explain the link. The review urges more work beyond the gut.
europmc-pmc5800158:
Abbas and co-authors review arsenic harm in plants. Arsenic in soil and water is toxic and can cause cancer. Plants take it up from the ground. Even low levels can change plant growth and chemistry.

The review compares the two main forms, arsenite and arsenate. It traces uptake, movement, and storage inside plants. It explains how arsenic triggers reactive oxygen and cell damage. It also covers plant defenses, from enzymes to glutathione and proline. Readers get a full account of arsenic stress and plant protection. The scale is vast, with arsenic found in more than 200 minerals.
europmc-pmc5827158:
Zhan and co-authors review a bacterial toxin theory of Alzheimer's disease. Lipopolysaccharide, or LPS, coats all Gram-negative bacteria. The authors argue it may help cause the common, sporadic form of the disease. Several odd findings feed that case.

Blood LPS runs threefold higher in Alzheimer patients than controls. LPS shows up in aging and Alzheimer brains, more in the latter. It sits with amyloid plaques, neurons, and myelin-making cells. The proposed chain runs through immune receptors into inflammation and myelin injury. Blocking LPS or its receptors might slow the disease. Readers get a bold, testable account of a familiar disease.
europmc-pmc5845358:
Silvestris and co-authors review how obesity unravels female fertility. Their review appeared in Reproductive Biology and Endocrinology. Excess weight disturbs the brain-ovary hormone axis. Periods falter, ovulation stops, and conception delays.

Fat tissue acts as a hormone organ in its own right. Its signals, the adipokines, stir insulin resistance and inflammation. Eggs mature poorly in that climate. The womb lining also accepts embryos less readily. Miscarriages rise, and assisted conception works less well. Weight loss through lifestyle change can restart cycles and ovulation. The review closes with how infertility in obese women should be managed in practice.
europmc-pmc5863458:
Hoyles and co-authors study how a gut microbe product guards the blood-brain barrier. Their article appeared in Microbiome. Gut bacteria make propionate from food in the colon. The barrier is a tight layer that shields the brain. The team first showed its receptor sits on human brain vessel cells. They then tested propionate on barrier cells in the lab. The dose matched levels found in the body.

The authors report that propionate calmed infection-linked pathways. It also shielded the barrier from oxidative stress. A signalling route called NRF2 drove that protection. The team frames this as a fourth route of gut-brain talk. Known routes run through nerves, immunity, and hormones.
europmc-pmc5872158:
Codjoe and Donkor review carbapenem resistance in Gram-negative bacteria. Their article appeared in Medical Sciences. Carbapenems are among the most reliable antibiotics in use. Resistance to them is now a growing global health problem. It hits pathogens such as Klebsiella pneumoniae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa hardest. Resistance can be built in or carried on transferable genes. Those genes code for enzymes called carbapenemases.

The review gives current detail on how this resistance works. It maps where resistant strains have spread worldwide. Europe, Asia, and South America are well documented. Sub-Saharan Africa remains poorly documented, they note. Such gaps hide the true scale of the threat. The authors supply a full, up-to-date account of the subject.
europmc-pmc5880858:
Haslbeck and Waldorp ask how well network models predict observations. Their article appeared in Behavior Research Methods. Network models map links between many variables as dots and lines. They have grown popular for picturing complex mental phenomena. Most studies inspect the network's structure for insights. How well the model predicts real data got little attention. Yet prediction matters for practice, the authors argue.

A symptom's predictability shows if treating it could help a patient. The authors introduce nodewise predictability to fill the gap. It measures how well each node follows from its neighbours. Code examples cover both one-off and time series data. Readers can compute and plot the measure themselves.
europmc-pmc5909458:
Ruggiero and Richter review G-quadruplexes as targets in antiviral therapy. Their review appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. G-quadruplexes are folded structures in guanine-rich DNA or RNA. They sit in control regions of many genomes. Viruses such as Zika and Ebola carry them too. There they help control key viral steps and latency.

Compounds that bind these folds show antiviral promise, they report. Some act at the genome level, others on transcripts. The review sets out traits that make such binders work best. It also lists what still needs to be done. These tools help probe how viral folds operate. Readers get an updated map of the field.
europmc-pmc5932058:
Shai and co-authors map organelle contact sites in yeast in a systematic way. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. Organelles do not float freely inside cells. Protein tethers hold their membranes close at contact sites. Many contacts, tethers, and functions remain unknown. The team used split glowing proteins to detect closeness.

They found four possible new contact sites, they report. Focus then fell on peroxisome and mitochondria contacts. Two tether proteins, Fzo1 and Pex34, were identified there. Expanding that contact boosted fatty acid burning. The contact thus has a clear body function. Systematic mapping can deepen cell knowledge, they show.
europmc-pmc5964358:
Tong and a large team of co-authors track gut microbiota changes as type 2 diabetes with hyperlipidemia improves under two treatments. Their clinical trial report appeared in mBio. The trial randomised 450 patients to metformin or a Chinese herbal formula called AMC. Treatment lasted 12 weeks. Then 100 patients per group were assessed in depth. Gut microbes were profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing.

Both treatments eased high blood sugar and lipids, the authors report. Both also shifted gut microbiota structure. A Blautia group rose and tracked with better glucose control. AMC beat metformin on insulin resistance and triglycerides. Only AMC raised a Faecalibacterium group tied to diabetes relief.
europmc-pmc6026158:
He and co-authors identify the target of a herbal compound. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. The compound is oridonin, from a Chinese medicinal herb. It was long known to calm inflammation. Its direct target in the body was unknown.

The team show oridonin blocks the NLRP3 inflammasome. That protein complex drives many chronic inflammatory diseases. Oridonin forms a lasting bond with NLRP3. The bond stops a partner protein from joining it. The complex then cannot assemble or switch on. In mouse models, oridonin helped against peritonitis. It also helped in gouty arthritis and type 2 diabetes. Readers get a lead compound for new anti-inflammatory drugs.
europmc-pmc6048158:
Mehra and co-authors report long-term results for pembrolizumab in head and neck cancer. Their pooled analysis appeared in the British Journal of Cancer. The drug blocks the PD-1 immune checkpoint. It was tested in recurrent or metastatic disease. Treatment options after first-line therapy were limited.

The analysis pooled two trial cohorts with 192 patients. Median follow-up reached nine months in the pooled data. The overall response rate was 18 percent. Most responses lasted at least six months. Some continued beyond thirty months of observation. Survival at twelve months was 38 percent. Severe treatment-related side effects affected 13 percent. No deaths were blamed on treatment side effects. The authors support pembrolizumab for this patient group.
europmc-pmc6107958:
Yi and co-authors wrote a review in Molecular Cancer on markers that predict who gains from PD-1 and PD-L1 blocking drugs. These drugs free T cells to attack tumors. They have changed care for some hard-to-treat cancers. Yet many patients do not respond at all.

The review sorts the main candidate markers. They include PD-L1 levels on tumors and immune cells nearby. Tumor mutation load and faulty DNA repair also matter. Gut microbes, blood markers, and past illness may help too. The authors argue that no single test is enough. A combined score could pick the patients most likely to gain.
europmc-pmc6243058:
Duan and co-authors review links between high-fat diets and disease. Eating too much fat is a changeable risk factor. It links to diabetes and some cancers. How it harms health is still poorly understood. The review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology.

The authors focus on inflammation as the bridge. A high-fat diet can trigger lasting inflammation. That inflammation then feeds disease growth. Cancer development is covered as well. The review sets out the main mechanisms involved. Gut changes and immune shifts both feature. The authors argue that grasping these paths matters. The world intake of high-fat food keeps rising. Better knowledge could guide new treatment strategies.
europmc-pmc6271758:
Huang and co-authors review new findings on the chemical makeup of propolis. Their review appeared in Molecules. Propolis is the resinous seal bees make for their hives. It is built from plant resins, wax, oils, and pollen. Bees gather resins from poplars, pines, and many other plants. The mix varies with place, plant source, and bee species.

A database search found 241 compounds reported for the first time between 2000 and 2012. They joined about three hundred compounds known before. Classes span flavonoids, terpenes, and phenolic acids. Folk use covers colds, wounds, and dental care. Lab work supports anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial effects. The authors argue that many compounds act together. That synergy may explain why whole propolis beats single parts. The review maps what is known for future product work.
europmc-pmc6279758:
Bartoschek and co-authors split breast cancer support cells into three distinct subclasses. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The cells are cancer-associated fibroblasts. They fill much of the tumour surroundings. Their origins and jobs were unclear because the group is mixed. The team read single cell gene activity in a mouse breast cancer model.

Seven hundred sixty-eight cell profiles were gathered after a sorting step. Three subclasses stood out with clear gene signatures. Each sat in a distinct place in the tumour. Origins ranged from blood vessel walls to fat tissue and the tumour lining itself. Human tumours showed the same split. Each subclass gene profile also predicted spread risk on its own. Naming the subclasses opens paths to precise drugs against them.
europmc-pmc6375658:
Gentzke and co-authors present a Vital Signs surveillance report in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Using National Youth Tobacco Survey data from 2011 to 2018, they tracked tobacco use among US middle and high school students across seven product types.

In 2018, 27.1 percent of high school students and 7.2 percent of middle school students had used a tobacco product in the past month. E-cigarettes were the most common product at both levels. Between 2017 and 2018, e-cigarette use jumped 78 percent among high school students. That surge erased recent progress in cutting overall youth tobacco use. The authors urge full tobacco control measures plus FDA regulation.
europmc-pmc6417258:
Myint and co-authors present a statistics method in BMC Genomics for reporter assays. Massively parallel reporter assays test thousands of DNA switches at once. Analysis methods for them have been ad hoc, with little head-to-head testing.

Their method, mpralm, uses linear models to test each switch's activity. Across several datasets it proved well calibrated and powerful. It beat existing tools in the first broad comparison of its kind. How barcodes are summed also proved to matter, the authors show. Their tool is offered for labs studying non-coding DNA.
europmc-pmc6440158:
Zheng and co-authors report that a circular RNA in colon cancer, circPPP1R12A, encodes a small protein that pushes tumors to grow and spread. Circular RNAs were mainly known as regulators that sponge up microRNAs; evidence that some also make proteins is newer. Screening tumor tissue found this circle sharply elevated in colon cancer.

Patients with higher levels survived significantly less time. The encoded protein, 73 amino acids long, switched on Hippo-YAP signaling, a growth-control pathway, and boosted proliferation, migration, and invasion in cells and tumors in mice. Knocking the circle down weakened those behaviors. A hidden protein product thus joins the list of colon cancer drivers worth targeting.
europmc-pmc6448958:
Uthman and co-authors test whether three diabetes drugs in the SGLT2 inhibitor class share a direct heart effect beyond lowering blood sugar: blocking the sodium-hydrogen exchanger in heart muscle cells. Mouse heart cells received empagliflozin or dapagliflozin at 1 micromole per liter, or canagliflozin at 3, matching the levels patients carry. All three slowed the exchanger and dropped sodium inside the cells from 12.7 to between 10 and 11.

Computer models placed each drug neatly on the exchanger's sodium-binding site. In whole mouse hearts kept beating outside the body, empagliflozin and canagliflozin also widened heart vessels, while energy stores held steady. Cutting heart sodium as a class effect could matter in heart failure and diabetes, where sodium runs high.
europmc-pmc6464058:
Northstone and co-authors update the roster of the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children, the Bristol birth cohort recruited through pregnancies in 1990 to 1992. The original campaign enrolled 14,541 pregnancies, and the index children have been followed ever since through questionnaires, clinics, samples, and record linkage. Late enrolment matters because cohort studies usually only shrink.

Since age seven, 913 additional index participants joined, 195 of them after turning eighteen, through recruitment drives and opportunistic contact. The baseline now stands at 14,901 index children alive at one year. A three-generation structure, grandparents, parents, and now grandchildren, makes the topped-up sample a continuing resource.
europmc-pmc6477058:
Martin and co-authors review how gut microbes steer the body's chemistry by steering gut hormone release. Hormone-making cells spread through the gut lining secrete CCK, PYY, GLP-1, GIP, and serotonin, which together tune insulin response, blood sugar control, fat storage, and appetite. Bacteria and their products are among the signals those cells listen to.

Bacterial products and cell wall parts reach the sensors in the gut wall and shift hormone output, making the gut flora a chemistry organ by proxy. Diet or drug changes that reshape the flora therefore double as hormone therapy candidates for obesity and metabolic disease. The exact handshakes between certain bacteria and certain cells get the closest reading.
europmc-pmc6513858:
Cravens, Payne and Smolke review ways to make plant natural products in microbes. Their review appeared in Nature Communications. Plant products serve as medicines, flavours and fragrances. Many are hard to make or harvest at scale. Crop supply can fail with pests or bad weather.

Engineers move a plant pathway into a host such as yeast. The work runs in design, build and test cycles. It acts at three levels: host, pathway and enzyme. Hosts must supply enough precursor material. Routes must be planned and missing enzymes found or built. A recent case built a 25-enzyme route to noscapine. The authors also cover making new derivatives and future tools.
europmc-pmc6555258:
Hogan, Chini and Chini review CD38, a surface enzyme that has become a prime drug target, writing in Frontiers in Immunology. CD38 sits on immune cells and breaks down NAD+, a molecule cells need for energy and repair. The authors' own work recast it from a mere cell marker into the body's main NAD+ drain.

Because CD38 faces outward, it also consumes the raw materials cells import to rebuild NAD+. During aging, CD38-carrying immune cells build up in tissues and drag NAD+ levels down, a process tied to the slow burn called inflammaging. In tumors, the same drain can blunt immune attack. The review closes with ways to block CD38 or boost NAD+, from small-molecule blockers to flavonoids, aimed at aging and metabolic disease.
europmc-pmc6602458:
Xu and co-authors present OrthoVenn2, a web server for comparing whole genomes. Their article appears in Nucleic Acids Research. The tool groups orthologous genes across species into clusters. Shared clusters hint at shared function. Diverged clusters hint at distinct roles.

OrthoVenn2 compares up to 12 species at once, up from six. Its species library now spans vertebrates, fungi, plants, and bacteria. An occurrence table shows how clusters overlap between species. An interactive Venn diagram displays the same overlaps. Annotations and summaries attach to each cluster group. A stand-alone version handles larger data sets locally. The server is free to use online.
europmc-pmc6708158:
Zhang and co-authors tested how to make epigenetic clocks more exact. These clocks guess a person's age from chemical marks on DNA. A gap between clock age and real age has been linked to death risk. The team asked whether a sharper clock changes that link.

They trained age predictors on as many as 13,661 DNA samples, mostly from blood. As training data grew, the clock got far more exact. With the best clock, the age gap no longer linked to death in two Scottish birth cohorts. Small training sets, they warn, can be thrown off by the mix of cell types in a sample.
europmc-pmc6800358:
Vázquez-Rodríguez and co-authors mapped how brain structure and function are tethered across the neocortex. White matter wiring promotes synchrony between brain areas, producing patterned activity networks. Whether wiring and activity track each other evenly was unknown. The team tested the relationship region by region across the cortex.

Structure and function aligned closely in primary sensory and motor areas. They diverged in higher-order regions, such as the default mode and salience networks. The decoupling followed the cortex's representational and cellular hierarchies, forming a smooth gradient. A geometry-based model out-predicted a topology-based one in about 70% of nodes. Long connections in higher areas seem less spatially constrained. The gradient reframes how brain organization should be modeled.
europmc-pmc6918658:
Mao and co-authors test a stem-cell signal that may limit heart attack damage. Their study appeared in Stem Cell Research and Therapy. Heart attacks kill heart muscle and carry high rates of death and disability. Tiny vesicles called exosomes, released by stem cells, pass messages between cells after injury.

The team loaded exosomes from human mesenchymal stem cells with a long RNA named KLF3-AS1. In rats and in oxygen-starved heart cells, these exosomes shrank damaged areas. They also cut a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis. The RNA works by soaking up a small RNA, miR-138-5p, which frees a protective protein, Sirt1. Blocking that protein reversed the benefit.
europmc-pmc6990758:
He and co-authors pool trial evidence on acupuncture and acupressure for cancer pain. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in JAMA Oncology. More than 70 percent of cancer patients suffer pain, and nearly half get inadequate control. Standard pain ladders work, but addiction risk and side effects limit them.

Earlier reviews, more than 20 of them, never reached a firm verdict. Newer, stricter randomised trials had also appeared since. The team updated the synthesis across those trials. Acupuncture and acupressure were associated with reduced pain and lower opioid use in the pooled results. Variation between studies was large, which trimmed the certainty grade. The authors call for trials in specific pain types and treatment phases to pin down where these therapies help most.
europmc-pmc7003858:
Fenwick and co-authors review how T cells wear out during HIV infection. Their review appeared in Immunological Reviews. T cells are the adaptive immune system's killers of infected and cancerous cells. When a virus will not go away, constant exposure to its antigens drives T cells into a broken state called exhaustion.

Exhaustion leaves HIV poorly controlled. It persists even in patients whose virus is suppressed by antiretroviral therapy, shaping how fast the disease advances. The markers of exhaustion also help guard the hidden pool of latently infected cells that blocks a cure. Blocking one marker, PD-1, doubled virus-fighting output from patients' CD8 T cells in the authors' own work. After treatment stops, marker levels predict how soon the virus rebounds. The review ends by weighing how these markers might be exploited in cure strategies.
europmc-pmc7006158:
Ono and co-authors review RANKL, a signal that links bone, immunity, and much more. Their review appeared in Inflammation and Regeneration. RANKL tells precursor cells to become osteoclasts, the cells that eat bone. Its partners, the receptor RANK and the decoy osteoprotegerin, form a system without which bone diseases such as osteopetrosis follow.

RANKL was first found as a T cell product that activates dendritic cells. It also builds lymph nodes and shapes immune cell development, a dual role that founded the field of osteoimmunology. The signal reaches further still: mammary glands, hair follicles, body temperature, muscle metabolism, and tumour growth. In skin, sunlight triggers it in surface cells, expanding regulatory T cells that calm inflammation. The review gathers current knowledge of the trio across all these processes. Few single signals, the authors show, touch so many systems.
europmc-pmc7023758:
Lei and co-authors review circular RNAs in human cancer in the journal Molecular Cancer. Circular RNAs are loops of RNA with no free ends. They were long classed as non-coding by-products of splicing. Newer work shows that some of them are in fact translated into small proteins.

The review first sets out what circular RNAs are and what they do. They can soak up microRNAs, tune gene activity, and bind proteins. The authors then explain two routes that may start protein building without a normal cap. They survey the cancer-linked cases found so far. These hidden proteins, they argue, open a neglected part of the human proteome. That could matter for cancer diagnosis and treatment.
europmc-pmc7054558:
Qiu proposes a change of attitude toward missing data in single-cell sequencing in Nature Communications, writing as sole author. Single-cell RNA sequencing reads only a small fraction of each cell's RNA. The missing entries, called dropouts, plague the method. Nearly every analysis algorithm tries to work around them through gene selection, dimension reduction, or filling the gaps with imputed values.

Qiu argues the dropout pattern itself is a useful signal. By converting counts into a simple present-or-absent binary record, a co-occurrence clustering algorithm can group cells using only which genes dropped out together. Across several published datasets, that binary pattern sorted cells into types as accurately as the expression levels of highly variable genes. Recognising dropouts as information rather than damage, Qiu suggests, opens a different direction for building single-cell analysis tools.
europmc-pmc7056458:
Lin and co-authors assess natural compounds as helpers in cancer therapy in the British Journal of Pharmacology. Standard chemotherapy suffers from toxicity throughout the body. Combining several drugs with different targets already improves efficacy and softens side effects. Plant-based products offer a less toxic source of partners, and interest in them as adjuvants keeps growing.

Laboratory evidence suggests herbal extracts such as Solanum nigrum and Claviceps purpurea can help. Pure compounds including curcumin, resveratrol, and matairesinol can weaken cancer's resistance to drugs and protect healthy tissue when paired with antitumour medicines. Traditional Chinese medicine used alongside chemotherapy has improved quality of life and eased bone marrow suppression in lung and gastric cancer studies. The authors add a caution: plant products carry their own adverse effects and can interact with drugs. More work is needed before such supplements earn a routine place.
europmc-pmc7091858:
Zheng and co-authors report that the virus-fighting lymphocytes of COVID-19 patients showed signs of exhaustion, in Cellular and Molecular Immunology. Natural killer cells and CD8 T cells are needed to control viral infections. The team studied 68 patients at two hospitals linked to Anhui Medical University in China, with 55 mild and 13 severe cases.

Total counts of both cell types dropped sharply in infected patients. A surface marker called NKG2A, linked to cell exhaustion, rose on the remaining cells. In patients recovering after treatment, cell counts returned and NKG2A fell. The pattern suggests the virus weakens antiviral defences early, and that blocking NKG2A might restore them.
europmc-pmc7125958:
Kinoshita reviews how mammals build GPI-anchored proteins and what those proteins do, in Open Biology. At least 150 human proteins are held on the cell surface by a GPI anchor instead of crossing the membrane. The anchor attaches to the protein's end and embeds its fat chains in the membrane's outer layer.

Anchored proteins gather in membrane rafts and often sit on one face of polarised cells. Some ferry cargo across cells; others are cut loose and shed. Kinoshita walks through the assembly pathway step by step and gives examples of anchor-dependent jobs, from enzymes to adhesion molecules. Faults in the pathway cause human GPI deficiency diseases.
europmc-pmc7177758:
Yue and López review how MAPK signaling pathways control apoptosis, the orderly death of cells. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. MAPKs are protein kinases that relay signals inside the cell. They guide many processes, from growth to stress response. In cell death, their role is double-sided.

The same pathway can start apoptosis or block it. Which way it acts depends on the cell type and the trigger. The authors lay out the main pro-death and pro-survival routes. They also explain feedback loops that sharpen the response. A simple guide links signal strength and duration to the outcome. Work in frog eggs shows how salt stress uses these pathways. Readers get a framework for predicting cell fate.
europmc-pmc7221158:
Petitprez and co-authors review how the tissue around a tumor shapes response to immune checkpoint therapy. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. A tumor's neighborhood holds immune cells, blood vessel cells, and fibroblasts. Checkpoint drugs work by freeing immune cells already inside the tumor. Who those neighbors are can make or break the treatment.

Evidence points first to the amount and orientation of T cells present. Other components, from vessel growth to scar-like fibroblasts, also sway outcomes. Such features may help select patients for these expensive drugs. They may also suggest drug combinations that warm up cold tumors. The authors gather a fast-growing body of studies. Their message: treating cancer now means reading its whole ecosystem.
europmc-pmc7244758:
Hu and co-authors show how a protein called IGF2BP2 props up a cancer-promoting RNA in pancreatic cancer. Their study appeared in Cell Death and Differentiation. IGF2BP2 normally manages cell metabolism. Its rise in tumors tracks with poor patient outcomes. Cutting it back slowed cancer cell growth in their tests.

The protein works by reading m6A marks on other RNAs. One target is DANCR, a long noncoding RNA that drives cell growth and stem-like traits. IGF2BP2 binds DANCR and raises its levels. Tests in animals confirmed the partnership matters in living tumors. A specific mark site on DANCR was identified and mutated to prove the link. The authors present this reader-and-RNA pair as a therapeutic lead. Pancreatic cancer badly needs such leads.
europmc-pmc7257158:
Hao, Vadgama and Wang review how a small immune signal helps cancers grow and spread. Their review appeared in Cell Communication and Signaling. The signal is CCL2, and its main receptor is CCR2. CCL2 draws immune cells toward tumors. High levels of both have been linked to worse disease in many cancers.

The authors focus most on prostate cancer. They explain how CCL2 and CCR2 support tumor growth, new blood vessels and spread to bone. They also cover links to relapse and to obesity. Work from their group and others is used to judge the pair as a drug target. Readers get a clear map of one pathway in cancer biology.
europmc-pmc7260058:
Warrington and co-authors present XTRACT, a software package that automatically maps white matter tracts in brain scans. Their methods paper appeared in Neuroimage. Tractography traces the brain's wiring from diffusion imaging data. Doing it by hand is slow, and results vary between laboratories.

XTRACT carries a library of standard protocols for pulling out known tracts in both human and macaque brains. The team tested it on Human Connectome Project and UK Biobank scans, plus macaque data, and built atlases of tracts and their endpoints. The protocols held up across data quality, matched known anatomy, and still preserved real differences between people, including twin similarities. The package is released publicly through FSL, so other groups can run the same standard extractions.
europmc-pmc7296058:
Ge and co-authors review the pentose phosphate pathway and its roles in type 2 diabetes and cancer. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Endocrinology. The pathway branches off from glucose processing. It does not make energy currency for the cell; instead it produces NADPH, a molecule cells use for building and antioxidant defense, and ribose 5-phosphate, a building block for nucleic acids.

Those outputs make the pathway a central regulator of the cell's chemical balance and growth. Its enzymes are reported to matter in many human diseases. Growing cells, including cancer cells, depend on its supplies, while disturbed activity features in diabetes. The authors gather what is known about the pathway's enzymes in both diseases and where intervention might help.
europmc-pmc7332158:
Tangcharoensathien and co-authors report a World Health Organization consultation in the Journal of Medical Internet Research on the COVID-19 infodemic. An infodemic is a flood of mixed true and false information during an outbreak. The online consultation crowdsourced ideas from officials, researchers, media, and platforms.

Participants offered 594 ideas for action. The analysis team condensed them into 50 proposed actions for managing infodemics in health emergencies. Core lessons include basing messages on evidence, turning knowledge into clear steps people can act on, and listening to community concerns. Partnerships with social media firms, universities, and civic groups also matter. Readers get a practical framework for fighting rumor alongside disease.
europmc-pmc7337658:
Dweck and co-authors report a global survey study in European Heart Journal Cardiovascular Imaging. It describes heart scan findings in patients with COVID-19. The survey captured echocardiography done in hospitals in April 2020. It also asked which patients gain most from such scans.

The survey covered 1,216 patients from 69 countries across six continents. The authors report that 55 percent had an abnormal scan. Left and right heart problems were both common. Some patients showed new heart attack, heart muscle inflammation, or stress-related heart failure. Severe disease appeared in 15 percent of patients. Blood test markers and symptom severity helped predict who had problems. Scans changed care for one third of patients. Readers get an early global picture of COVID-19 heart harm.
europmc-pmc7408158:
Rébé and Ghiringhelli review interleukin-1 beta in cancer in Cancers. Inside a tumor, this inflammatory signal is made by immune cells, fibroblasts, and cancer cells themselves. Making it takes two steps: priming switches the gene on, then an inflammasome activates the cutting enzyme that matures it.

Once released, IL-1 beta drives gene programs in target cells and acts on immunity, blood vessel growth, cancer cell growth, migration, and spread. Cancer treatments themselves can provoke its release, with opposite effects on progression. That ambiguity frames the review's core question: should doctors block IL-1 beta in cancer treatment, and when? Gene variants and cell context steer the answer, the authors show.
europmc-pmc7424058:
Jurga and co-authors gather what is known about markers that identify microglia, the resident immune cells of the brain. These cells shift shape and role as brain conditions change. Picking the right marker is key to telling one cell state from another.

The review sorts markers by type: general and specific, on the cell surface or inside it, and some that cells release. It shows how to tell true microglia from macrophages that enter from the blood. It also covers active states, from harmful M1-like cells to healing M2-like cells. Human and rodent markers differ, which adds care to study design. The guide helps labs choose markers for work on brain inflammation and disease.
europmc-pmc7453858:
Wolff and co-authors review risk factors for severe and fatal COVID-19. With no vaccine or drug at the time, shielding high-risk people mattered most. Risk clues also hint at where treatments might act.

The review searched PubMed and a preprint set, then sorted risk factors into groups. It drew on 28 records, eleven of them preprints. High age, obesity, diabetes, and hypertension stood out as risks. Poor general health linked with worse courses again and again. Damage to the heart, liver, and kidneys marked severe cases. Clotting problems may drive much of that harm.
