Long records like these show whether safety laws and car design have truly protected the most exposed road users.
plos-pone-0359158:
Madeline Fernandez-Pineda and five colleagues study what miscarriage care felt like during the COVID-19 pandemic, in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. Pandemic rules kept support people out of clinics and disrupted appointments, adding strain to an already painful loss. The authors combined surveys and interviews to capture both the numbers and the women's own accounts of that period.

Seventy-one women in North Carolina who miscarried during stay at home mandates took part, and eighteen gave long interviews. About half rated their care experience as poor. Pandemic hardships such as missing support persons were similar across groups, but women with poor experiences reported clearly higher stress, anxiety, and depression. Among those treated with medicine or surgery, a good care experience went together with lower distress.
plos-pone-0359858:
Álvaro Huerta Ojeda and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on aging and function. It studies community-dwelling older adults, people living in their own homes rather than care facilities. The authors examine the association between the muscle quality index and the time needed to rise from lying face down to standing.

Rising from the floor is a real-world test of strength that matters after a fall. A muscle quality index condenses how much force muscle produces for its size. If the index tracks floor-rise time, clinicians gain a simple screen for older adults losing independence, and exercise programs gain a target.
plos-pone-0360158:
Johannes Aengenheyster, Olav Velthuis, and Alex van Venrooij examined in 2026 what the private museums of wealthy economic elites contribute to the arts. Rich collectors increasingly open museums of their own rather than only donating to public ones. The authors ask whether these institutions are mere bandwagons, fashionable copies of one another, or genuine breeding grounds for artistic innovation.

Their study weighs what private museums add: new exhibition space, support for living artists, and public access to collections that would otherwise stay hidden. It also weighs the concerns, including private taste shaping public culture. The question matters for cultural policy, since cities court such museums while public institutions compete with them for art and attention.
plos-pone-0360658:
Wei Li, Ming Ma, and Jinyue Lu studied in 2026 how the Chinese public judged a cultural heritage scandal across different online platforms. The controversy concerned artifacts donated to the Nanjing Museum and how they were handled. The authors used topic modeling, a computational method that finds themes in large volumes of text, to map what people actually talked about on each platform.

Public judgment in a heritage crisis shapes whether a museum keeps the trust that brings donors and visitors. Comparing platforms shows how the same facts become different stories in different online rooms. Their study offers museums and cultural agencies a method for listening during a crisis, and a record of how this one unfolded.
pmc-10653458:
Qing Xia, Shan Wang, and Jose Weng Chou Wong ask whether online trade shows can nudge firms toward greener habits, in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. Their case is a large trade fair for factory machines in Yiwu, China. They look at how the online format shapes what firms think and do.

One part of the work surveyed 417 firms at the fair held in two thousand twenty-one. A second part drew on talks with 18 people who took part. Traits such as an easy site to move through, vivid images, and ways to join in shaped how firms judged their green results and how pleased they felt. Those views, in turn, went with greener acts on the firms' side. The team says online shows should stay a long-term plan for the trade.
pmc-10691258:
Ishikawa studies how shared views of old age can turn into poor views of one's own aging in twenty twenty-three. The study draws on a survey of adults in Finland about age and aging. It asks which traits link a dim view of old age in society with a dim view of one's own old age.

Women and adults with more schooling were more apt to hold both dim views. So were adults who rated their quality of life as poor. Adults who knew of unfair treatment of older people at work or in care also scored high. The author argues that life context, not age alone, shapes how people judge their own aging.
pmc-10694958:
Zhixiang Mu and co-authors build a wound treatment in 2023 that kills germs without antibiotics. Infected skin wounds are a growing problem, and overuse of antibiotics has bred resistant germs. Their system uses flakes of a mineral called MoS2, coated with a sugar-based carrier that holds nitric oxide gas.

Near-infrared light heats the flakes, and the heat releases a burst of nitric oxide. Together, heat and gas tear germ membranes and drain their energy, wiping them out. After the germs are gone, leftover material releases a trickle of the gas. That trickle draws skin cells in and spurs new blood vessels, which speeds healing. The team calls the flakes a strong candidate for infected wound care.
pmc-10695558:
Di Chen and a large team of co-authors build a tool to predict surgery after acupuncture fails, in a paper dated twenty twenty-three. Their patients had lumbar disc herniation treated at four Chinese hospitals. Of 738 patients, 496 formed the training set and 242 the check set.

Seven factors drove the model, among them smoking, disability score, and disc type. The tool also weighed spinal narrowing and how often needling was done. Its accuracy score hit about 0.90 in both sets. The authors present the chart as a way to flag early who may still need an operation.
pmc-10704758:
Hasan Barati and co-authors report a hard elbow injury case in this 2023 paper. The patient was a 37 year old man with fracture dislocations in both elbows. This pattern is called a terrible triad injury. On the left side the radial head was shattered and the wound was contaminated. His history of substance use also raised care concerns.

Surgeons replaced the left radial head with a cement spacer loaded with antibiotics. The right side fracture was fixed in the normal way. The patient missed all follow up visits after discharge. He returned six months later, which let the team check the outcome then. The case shows a fallback option when standard implants are not advised.
pmc-10709558:
Chunyan Zheng and seven co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-three on why throat cancer of the squamous kind resists radiation care. Radiation is a key weapon against this cancer, yet many tumors shrug it off. The team homes in on a gene switch named YY1. It ran high in resistant tissue and tracked with poor odds for patients.

Cutting YY1 made the cancer cells far more prone to radiation, in dishes and in mice. Deep scans showed YY1 drives a motor gene, KIF3B. That motor talks to a surface protein and holds back the Hippo pathway. With YY1 cut, Hippo wakes and its agent YAP1 is barred from the nucleus. The team flags YY1 as a drug target.
pmc-10710358:
Leah J Martin and three colleagues estimate how many Swedish disease cases routine vaccination has averted since nineteen ten, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Measles, whooping cough, mumps, and polio were the four diseases tracked. National case reports spanned about a century. Pre-vaccination incidence supplied the counterfactual baseline.

Over two million cases were reported across the surveillance periods. The authors estimate more than one and a half million were averted by vaccination. Measles and whooping cough account for most of the total. Mumps and polio contribute smaller shares. Underreporting, especially in early years, makes these figures underestimates. The study quantifies a century of vaccine benefit. It answers hesitancy with the diseases' own arithmetic.
pmc-10712058:
Akram Hoseinzadeh, Seyed-Alireza Esmaeili, and five co-authors train stem cells with helpful bacteria to treat lupus. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, uses mesenchymal stem cells, which can calm the immune system. Lupus is a disease where the body attacks itself. Gut bacteria of certain kinds may tune how the stem cells work.

Mice with a lupus-like illness got cells raised with one of two Lactobacillus strains, or both. Plain cells and no-cell groups served as controls. Tests then counted immune cell types and signal proteins in the blood. The trained cells shifted the immune response in distinct ways by strain. The work points to pairing cells with microbes as a lupus strategy.
pmc-10713258:
Maxime Borgeaud, Alex Friedlaender, and Alfredo Addeo wrote a review in two thousand twenty-three on moving immune drugs earlier in lung cancer care. The cancer is non-small cell lung cancer that can still be removed by surgery. For years the standard was surgery followed by chemotherapy, which added a modest survival gain.

Immune-checkpoint inhibitors free the immune system to attack the tumor. The review weighs giving them before surgery, after surgery, or both. Treatment before surgery can reach more patients, since some never recover enough for later therapy. It can also shrink the tumor and let doctors see the response while the tumor is still in place.
pmc-10713658:
Zhu leads a large team studying mitochondrial cleanup in the heart, in work from twenty twenty-three. Two proteins, PINK1 and Parkin, drive the removal of damaged mitochondria, a process called mitophagy. Faults in it contribute to heart, metabolic, and nerve diseases.

Actin, the cell skeleton, remodels during this cleanup, but the signal link was unknown. The team identifies a protein called GRAF1 as a direct target of PINK1. GRAF1 frees damaged mitochondria from actin anchors and helps Parkin tag them for capture. The finding joins two known pathways into one mechanism for heart cell quality control.
pmc-10714958: Yared Tadesse and co-authors report the case of a 14-year-old girl in Ethiopia with two linked illnesses at once. She had tuberculosis of the lymph nodes. She also had Takayasu arteritis, a rare swelling of the aorta and its main branches. The report appeared in 2023. The pairing is known but hard to treat, above all where tuberculosis is common. The two conditions can blur into each other, and their treatments can clash. The authors trace how the girl was diagnosed and treated, and draw lessons for similar cases.
pmc-10717358:
Su Zhang and six co-authors study drug problems in kidney patients in a 2023 paper. People with chronic kidney disease take many drugs and their bodies handle them differently, so mistakes are common. A clinical pharmacist joined care on a kidney ward of a large Chinese hospital for a year, hunting for drug-related problems and acting on them.

Hundreds of problems were found in nearly half the patients before the pharmacist stepped in. Safety issues were the largest share, and drug choice was the most common cause. Antibiotics and heart drugs were most often involved. Most advice was accepted, most problems were fully resolved, and the share of patients with problems fell sharply afterward.
pmc-10719358:
Shi and a large team of colleagues read long gene spans for high-land fit marks in this twenty twenty-three study. Big span breaks shape more of the code than small point shifts. High folk in thin air bear such breaks tuned to their hard home.

Inside, long reads span three hundred folk from high and low kin groups. Break sorts tied to thin-air acts, fuel use, and lung work fell out. One high-folk break cuts a boost switch and mutes a breath gene. Glass and cell tests proved that break's mute act in full. The team casts break rewires as a core road to high fit.
pmc-10720058:
Chengtian Lv, Yuwen Huang, Ruirong Yan, and Yuanmei Gao examine how a growth factor moves airway muscle cells, in a study published in two thousand twenty-three. In asthma, airway smooth muscle grows and migrates, thickening airway walls and worsening lung function. Vascular endothelial growth factor, VEGF, is already implicated in asthma's progression.

Earlier work emphasized VEGF's effect on muscle cell proliferation. This study isolates migration instead. Wound healing and Transwell assays measured how the cells move under VEGF's influence. The signaling ran through the RhoA and ROCK pathway, a known controller of cell movement. Blocking that pathway offers a candidate strategy against airway remodeling. The authors present their mechanistic evidence as groundwork for such treatments.
pmc-10722558:
James Casey, Jennifer Meijer, Heidi IglayReger, and five colleagues check diet diaries against reality in this two thousand twenty-three pilot study. Self-reported diet is prone to error, biasing nutrition research. Inside a controlled feeding trial, where every menu item was known, participants completed twenty-four-hour recalls that could be verified exactly. Twenty-four adults followed a standard diet, then either a high-fat or high-carbohydrate diet, and their recalls were compared with the provided food.

Total calories were reported accurately. The errors were compositional: the high-fat group underreported fat, the high-carbohydrate group underreported carbohydrate, each presumably nudged by what sounds healthier. Protein was overreported on every diet, specifically beef and poultry. The authors argue that classifying which components get misreported, and in which direction, points to concrete strategies for correcting self-report bias in dietary assessment, rather than treating recall data as uniformly unreliable.
pmc-10729858:
Suginobe leads a large team studying Down syndrome linked lung hypertension in stem cells, in work dated twenty twenty-three. Down syndrome is the most common chromosomal disorder and carries a higher rate of pulmonary arterial hypertension. Vessel lining cell faults drive the lung artery remodeling behind it.

The team made vessel lining cells from induced stem cells, in matched pairs with and without the extra chromosome. That isogenic design isolates the chromosome effect. A pathway joining three regulators, DYRK1A, PPARG, and EGR1, emerged as responsible for the disease traits in the cells. A named pathway gives drug research a concrete target.
pmc-10730658:
Xuwen Peng and four co-authors review intravital imaging, a window into living tumors during immunotherapy. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-three. Cancer immunotherapy works through immune cells moving and acting inside tissue, and flat snapshots miss that motion.

The technique watches cells in real time, in place, with fine detail and multiple colors at once. The authors walk through the full workflow: labeling tricks, optical windows cut into tissue, and ways to analyze the footage. Recent studies show immune cells hunting, pausing, and killing as treatment unfolds. Seeing those dynamics helps explain why therapies succeed or fail. The review argues this living view is now essential for improving immunotherapy design.
pmc-10735658:
Trends in new cases of multiple chronic conditions among older Americans from two thousand to twenty twenty form the subject here. The study was published in twenty twenty-three. Rising multimorbidity strains patients and the care system alike.

Adults aged fifty and over from a long-running national survey were split into nine overlapping cohorts. Four kinds of multimorbidity were defined from seven physical diseases and two mental conditions: general, physical only, including mental disorders, and heart-metabolic. Adjusted rates of new general multimorbidity rose from seventy-six to about one hundred and twelve per thousand person-years across the period. Mental-inclusive multimorbidity rose too. The authors trace how much of the climb reflects who the patients are.
pmc-10735858:
Yu-Chih Chen and Sicong Sun study how money skills and habits link to health in later life. They also ask how the links differ for men and women. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-three. They surveyed more than eleven hundred adults aged forty-five and up online. The survey covered money knowledge, access to financial tools, and day-to-day money behavior.

Access and behavior mattered more for health than money knowledge alone. For men, money knowledge tied more to self-rated health and life satisfaction. For women, day-to-day money behavior mattered more. Access to financial tools also eased worry about retirement for women, but not for men. The authors argue that programs to build money skills should take these gender paths into account. One-size programs may miss what each group needs.
pmc-10737158:
Meki Singleton and Susan Enguidanos study advance care planning among older lesbian and gay adults. Their paper, from twenty twenty-three, asks which traits link to planning for future medical care. Such planning can include a living will. It can also name a person to make health choices if one cannot.

The study uses an online survey of one hundred thirty-nine adults. White, older, and working adults felt more at ease with medical choices. Higher income and a health problem linked to having a living will. The authors say income and work shape planning in this group, not just age or schooling.
pmc-10738558:
Shaelyn Ward and six co-authors checked the author rules of leading journals on aging, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Journals can ask authors to follow reporting guides and to register trials before they start. Such rules cut bias and make research easier to trust and check.

The team read the rules of one hundred top journals in the field. Fewer than half pointed authors to the main guide for trial reports. Many journals said nothing about some common guides at all. Nearly half said nothing about trial registration. The authors urge editors to press for clear rules, so reports in the field become more open and complete.
pmc-10742458:
Charlotte Stubner and co-authors review studies on early-life exposure to PFAS chemicals and children's language development, in work published in 2023. PFAS are long-lasting industrial chemicals found widely in the environment. Language develops from before birth, when the brain is sensitive to hormone disruption from contaminants.

The team searched three databases and found fifteen studies. Most covered general populations with background exposure, and two covered highly exposed groups. Some studies hinted at harm, but the pattern was inconsistent across sex, age at testing, and exposure level. No systematic effect on language and communication was found. The authors note many studies used broad tests with weak validity for language skills. They call for studies over a wider exposure range with sharper language instruments.
pmc-10742558:
Andrey Petrov and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-three study of gel-like blocking materials for treating benign overgrown blood vessel lesions in the head and neck. These gels flow deep into abnormal vessels yet stay controllable, unlike glue or coils. Two lesion types with intense shunting flow were treated.

Records covered patients treated over eight years at one clinic. Outcomes with the gel were compared against coils, glue, and particles used in other cases. Safety, effectiveness, and technical handling were judged. Such malformations and hormone-active tumours share demanding flow, making agent choice decisive for success.
pmc-10742858:
Jing Zhou, Yaan Li, and Mingzhou Wang propose, in twenty twenty-three, a better way to set the threshold in a Duffing chaotic system used to detect weak signals. The system switches from chaos to a periodic state at that threshold, but finding it has been slow and imprecise. Old methods need heavy computation and complex algorithms. Their fix combines two tools: improved permutation entropy, which reads signal order and size and resists noise, and Poincaré mapping, which samples the system's motion at set points.

They call the combined measure PMIPE. Simulations and tests on real underwater sound signals show the method is more accurate, simpler, and more stable than older ways, the authors report.
pmc-10744158:
Taizen Nakase and colleagues examine how two kinds of brain lesion conspire in the symptoms of Alzheimer-type dementia, in this study from twenty twenty-three. Gray matter loss is the famous damage. White matter lesions, scars in the wiring, are the quieter partner. One hundred fifty-six memory clinic patients, with dementia or its amnestic prelude, had both blood-flow scans and MRI.

The pairing mattered, symptom by symptom. Disorientation and poor attention tracked with the precuneus region together with white matter lesions in both hemispheres. Hyperactivity, a behavioral symptom, linked frontal gray matter on both sides with the white matter damage. Patients at the earlier, milder stage actually showed more of these cross-lesion ties than full dementia patients. The authors read dementia's symptoms as duets between tissue loss and wire damage, changing as the disease advances.
pmc-10745758:
Yin and eight colleagues review how sugary carbohydrates affect the brain in twenty twenty-three. Eating the wrong carbohydrates raises risks of obesity and diabetes. Those conditions in turn harm thinking and memory. The gut and blood sugar swings are the two routes examined.

Unhealthy carbohydrate diets disturb the gut environment. Through the gut brain axis, that disturbance impairs cognition. Rapidly digested carbohydrates also cause sharp glucose swings. Swings disrupt brain glucose use, calcium balance, and inflammation control. Unstable glucose harmed the brain more than steady high glucose in cited work. Slow digested and resistant carbohydrates look safer for cognition. The authors discuss better models and selection of healthier carbohydrates.
pmc-10746058:
Diuvenji leads a large team testing a human hormone effect on skin bacteria, in work from twenty twenty-three. The hormone is atrial natriuretic peptide, made by the heart. Prior work showed it can change how an antibiotic acts on bacteria.

The team grew two skin species alone and together, both free floating and in biofilms. Biofilms are sticky groups that resist drugs. The hormone plus azithromycin had mixed effects that hinged on surface type, dose, and species. On water hating surfaces it often opposed the drug. On glass it often helped. Cells also clumped more. The results warn that body signals can shift drug action.
pmc-10749458:
Yanlan Hu and nine co-authors survey what China's medical staff know about treating snakebite. Their cross-sectional study was published in twenty twenty-three. Quick, correct care decides outcomes after a bite, and knowledge gaps among staff are a real risk.

Over twelve thousand staff in twelve provinces answered between mid twenty twenty-two and early twenty twenty-three. The average knowledge score was low, about three points out of twelve. Scores varied with sex, job, region, hospital level, and department. Training, hands-on bite experience, having antivenom on site, and self-rated skill all lifted scores. The authors call the overall level weak and urge targeted training, especially where snakes are common and antivenom is scarce.
pmc-10754558:
Yaqian Xu, Bowei Chen, Jian Yi, and Baiyan Liu pool trials of Chinese medicine for small vessel brain disease. Their meta-analysis from twenty twenty-three covers adjuvant herbal therapy. Small vessel disease grows common as populations age. Chinese medicine is widely used for it in East Asia.

Twenty-seven randomised trials with over twenty-five hundred patients qualified. Thinking scores were a major outcome across trials. Most trials carried unclear bias risk in the assessment. Added herbal treatment improved several outcomes over standard care alone. Safety results were also pooled in the analysis. Evidence quality limits how far conclusions can go. Better-designed trials are needed before strong recommendations.
pmc-10755558:
Matthäus Fellinger and Thomas Waldhör lead a team counting involuntary psychiatric admissions across Austria before and during COVID-19 lockdowns. Their country report was published in two thousand twenty-three. Forced admission is psychiatry's last resort, legally and ethically fraught. Whether lockdowns raised or lowered its use was unknown.

Records covered three years and tens of thousands of admissions nationwide. During lockdown weeks, involuntary admissions fell significantly compared with prior years. Those admitted, though, stayed longer on average. Mechanical restraint accompanied about a third of admissions throughout. The lockdown association held after adjustment, while sex and age showed none. The authors read the dip as access and behavior shifting under restrictions, not need vanishing. Longer stays hint at delayed presentation. The report gives policymakers a rare whole-country baseline.
pmc-10756758:
Chihiro Miura and eleven colleagues wrote a study in twenty twenty-three on how orchid seeds switch on their pact with fungi. Orchid seeds hold almost no food stores, so they must take nutrients from mycorrhizal fungi to sprout. To do so, they borrow the signaling system of a mutual pact that other plants make with such fungi.

The plant hormone gibberellin helps most seeds sprout, yet it blocks fungi from settling in, and orchid seeds barely respond to it. The team found that orchids switch the hormone off as they sprout. That switch turns the pact signaling on by itself, so the fungal partner can move in at once. The work shows how a plant that lives off fungi lines up its sprouting with the arrival of its provider.
pmc-10772358:
Ahmed Elheet and colleagues examined how heart disease and kidney disease travel together in patients at a Saudi Arabian center. The two conditions share risk factors and worsen each other, yet local data were scarce. Writing in twenty twenty-three, the team reviewed patient files from most of that year. Most patients were men, most were in their sixties and seventies, and smoking, diabetes, and high blood pressure were common. The analysis linked artery disease severity, kidney function, and the heart pumping fraction.

As coronary artery disease grew more severe, kidney function fell. A lower pumping fraction also tracked with worse kidney numbers. Age, smoking, and artery disease tracked with kidney dysfunction, while smoking, prior stroke, limb artery disease, body weight, and pumping fraction tracked with artery severity. The authors call for work on treatments that blunt the combined harm.
pmc-10776058:
Khongorzul Erdenebaatar, Joon Moh Park, and Jachoon Koo shared a genome note in twenty twenty-three. They report the full chloroplast genome of Spergularia marina. It is a plant that lives on Korean coasts and bears salt well. No chloroplast genome from its genus had come out before. The team used next-generation sequencing and put the whole molecule together, base by base.

The genome runs about one hundred fifty-two thousand letters. It has the standard four-part form of plant chloroplasts. It holds one hundred thirty-one genes in all. Eighty-six of them code for proteins. The rest are the RNA parts the plant needs for photosynthesis. The team compared seventeen kin in the pink family. This species sat closest to Spergula arvensis. The sequence gives staff a reference to name and sort this coastal genus.
pmc-10831358:
Sukanya Dhar and a large team tie a hold-back immune cell signature to lymphoma care that falls short. Their study from twenty twenty-four tests patients on standard chemotherapy. The R-CHOP drug mix fully cures just about half of patients. Comeback of the cancer and drug resistance drive the shortfalls.

Hold-back cells of the monocyte line were counted in patients. Their signature flagged drug resistance to come on many fronts. It also flagged the cancer coming back after remission. The space around the tumour shelters such hold-back cells. To block them might bring back how well chemotherapy works. A blood signature could flag high-risk patients at the start. Such patients could then get stronger or added care.
pmc-10844658:
Yunhan Zhao and five colleagues connect chronic gut inflammation to a protective peptide's suppression in children, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Children with inflammatory bowel disease often grow poorly and lose bone health. Humanin, a cytoprotective factor found in bone, was their suspect.

Blood from forty patients and forty healthy children was compared. Humanin levels were measured by immunoassay. Growth plate tissue from children's surgeries was cultured with patient serum or with TNF, a key inflammatory signal. Staining tracked humanin and growth-related markers in the tissue. Cell line experiments tested TNF dose effects. The authors report a novel link: inflammation regulates humanin downward. That suppression may help explain stunted growth in pediatric bowel disease.
pmc-10849758:
Schaer and seven colleagues study how bleeding inside tumors helps cancer grow in twenty twenty-four. Small bleeds are common in cancers but are often ignored as a factor. Macrophages clean up red blood cells, so they sit at the centre of this process. The team traced how a red cell product, heme, reshapes these immune cells.

Maps of gene activity showed a cell type clustered near bloody, dead tumor regions. Those cells had a cancer promoting profile driven by a factor called NRF2. Heme switched on NRF2 in macrophages and pushed them toward that profile. The altered cells helped cancer cells invade and spread in lab models. They also resisted reprogramming by immune therapies. Mice with NRF2 locked on in immune cells resisted a key immunotherapy drug.
pmc-11535758:
Sarafian, Robinson, Christov, and Tarchini studied in twenty twenty-four health gaps for Bulgarian Roma folks who moved to the United Kingdom. The Covid wave hit small groups in that land with more force than most. They lived and worked with Roma groups in two cities for the study.

Poor jobs and tight homes, plus hid-ing who they are to dodge bias, cut their reach to care. The wave and the split from Europe made those strains worse in their lives. Kin and group aid nets were a key way to cope, yet those nets are thinning. The team calls for health plans that fit such groups.
pmc-11539258:
Quinn Steiner and colleagues track body makeup and bone strength in college athletes after hip surgery, in this case series from twenty twenty-four. The surgery, hip arthroscopy, fixes a painful clash of bone shapes in the joint, but rest afterward can thin muscle and bone. The team checked whether young athletes bounce back.

Twenty-three Division I athletes had full-body scans before surgery and again over the next two years. Pelvic bone density dipped at three and six months, then returned to its starting level by twelve months. Bone density in the operated leg was higher than at the start by the two-year mark, while leg fat rose over the same span. Total body fat and muscle mass barely moved. The authors advise care teams to watch bone health in the first year after surgery, even in fit young patients.
pmc-11573558:
Heilmeier and eight colleagues link chronic inflammation to cardiovascular risk in systemic sclerosis in twenty twenty-four. Systemic sclerosis damages blood vessels and raises heart disease risk. About a quarter of patients have persistently raised C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation. Whether that predicts atherosclerosis in this disease was unclear.

Sixty-five patients were split into inflamed and non inflamed groups by repeated protein measures. The inflamed group had worse cholesterol and triglyceride profiles. Their estimated ten year cardiovascular risk was significantly higher. Within the inflamed group, protein levels tracked with carotid artery wall thickness. Machine learning models found lipid traits best separated the two groups. The authors identify an inflammatory subtype with higher vascular burden.
pmc-11590858:
Wigham and co-authors set up group consultations in a lower limb musculoskeletal outpatient service. Group consultations have been shown to lift outcomes with greater efficiency. The aim was a faster physiotherapy-led path for common lower limb problems. The new path had to meet rising demand with no loss in patient satisfaction. Three Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles tested the new approach.

Virtual group sessions and face-to-face group sessions were both tried. Four common conditions formed the test set. They were kneecap pain, Achilles tendon pain, sole pain, and knee osteoarthritis. Measures covered patients seen, staff time, patient experience, and outcome scores. One-to-one care took 45 minutes of staff time per patient in the past. Virtual sessions cut that time to 22 minutes per patient. Face-to-face groups cut it further, to 12 minutes per patient.
pmc-11592158:
Yu Chuan Ong and co-authors use computer immune modeling to design vaccine pieces shared across many coronaviruses. Their study appeared in 2024. Three coronavirus outbreaks in twenty years, capped by COVID-19, exposed how unready the world was. A universal vaccine would target the parts of the virus that barely change. The team scanned the spike protein for fragments that T cells and B cells recognize, hunting ones conserved across bat, pangolin, and human coronaviruses, including the MERS virus.

They found 132 candidate fragments, most of them widely conserved. Aligning them revealed overlapping stretches, which were assembled into two lead peptide builds with strong immune-stimulating profiles. The authors present these as starting points for a universal coronavirus vaccine. Lab testing is the next step before any clinical promise can be claimed.
pmc-11593858:
Röhrs, Rohn, and Pfeifer build a scoring matrix to grade food incident reports for use in AI-supported risk spotting. Foodborne illness still strikes one in ten people worldwide each year. Data and smart tools to fight it keep growing. The hard part is using the flood of reports well. Their scheme uses multi-criteria decision analysis to rate each incident. Ratings can feed an AI database that sorts risks on its own.

A set priority level helps surface new or rising threats early. The matrix weighs harm, spread, and other set factors. The authors frame it as groundwork for autonomous risk sorting. Human judgment sets the weights; the machine applies them at scale.
pmc-11600558:
Ozgür Komurcu and a team of co-authors asked if checks before surgery cut early problems. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, watched patients who had planned surgery. It is not clear if routine checks with the sleep doctor change risk. The team tracked blood flow and breathing problems during surgery and in the first day after. They also tracked how long patients stayed in hospital.

The group held more than one thousand one hundred patients with full data. Care ran from late twenty twenty-three to early twenty twenty-four. Readers who run surgical care learn what the pre check buys in safety. The work helps teams judge if the check earns its time and cost for each patient.
pmc-11607058:
Alexander Gabri and ten co-authors tracked long-term results of focused radiation for pituitary tumors, in a study from twenty twenty-four. These growths on the pituitary gland often come back or remain partly after surgery. A tightly aimed radiation treatment, given in one session, is a common next step.

The study followed patients treated over two decades in one population. Most stayed free of tumor growth for many years, with strong control rates at five and ten years. One tumor type, those making growth hormone, proved least likely to regrow. The main side effect was loss of pituitary function, which hit about a third of patients. The authors call the treatment effective but not risk-free.
pmc-11608258:
Gong and five co-authors build prognostic models for young cervical cancer patients, in work from twenty twenty-four. Cervical cancer is a top cause of illness and death among young women. Yet no age specific definition of young cervical cancer, nor tailored prognosis models, existed.

Data on cases from twenty to twenty nineteen came from a United States registry database. Age was split into strata based on its curve shaped relation with cancer specific death, found with spline modeling. Prognostic models were then built and validated for the young group. Age tailored forecasts can guide treatment intensity and follow up for younger patients.
pmc-11608458:
R Haridian Sosa Barrios and five co-authors tell of rare germ gut swell in a patient on belly dialysis. Their case study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Such swell is a known hit of this care and can end the care line. Most hits come from gram-plus skin germs, while gram-less kinds fare worse. The germ here, Acinetobacter ursingii, is rare in this set.

It was the third known case of its kind. Germ drugs put straight in the belly cured the ill with a good end. The germ is hard to name and oft drug-proof, so the team urge two drugs, close watch, and tight care drills.
pmc-11610458:
Jonas Gustafson and co-authors published a study in 2024 reporting high-coverage nanopore sequencing of samples from the 1000 Genomes Project, to build a full catalog of human genetic variation. Nanopore sequencing reads long stretches of DNA at once. Such long reads capture kinds of variation that short-read methods miss.

Fewer than half of people with a suspected inherited genetic condition receive a precise molecular diagnosis after full clinical testing. Long reads may raise that share, but clinicians lack a clean reference set of well-characterized samples for filtering true variants from noise. The project plans to sequence at least eight hundred of the known reference samples. The study presents the first one hundred, drawn from all five continental population groups of the collection. Each was sequenced to a deep level of coverage. The resulting data set will serve as a baseline of ordinary human variation.
pmc-11610558:
Shen and five co-authors show how a gut germ fans bowel swelling in mice in this twenty twenty-four study. The germ grows more common in folks with sore, swollen bowels, yet its role was dim. The team fed it to mice whose bowels were primed to swell by a salt cure.

Inside, dosed mice showed worse gut harm and a weaker gut wall than primed kin. Their gut germ mix also slid out of fair shape as the ill grew. In gut wall flesh, the germ lit a death path in guard cells by a scent route. Dish tests with guard cells showed the same fire-death and scent spill at work. Blocks on that scent route cut the harm the germ caused.
pmc-11614858:
Fábio França Vieira e Silva and nine co-authors test whether a cell-death protein in tumor tissue forecasts how mouth cancer patients will fare. Oral squamous cell carcinoma is rising in incidence and mortality, and better prognostic markers could sharpen treatment choices. The protein Smac/DIABLO promotes apoptosis, the process cancers learn to evade.

Staining tumor samples showed that low Smac/DIABLO levels tracked with worse overall, relapse-free, and disease-specific survival over long follow-up. Low expression also came with more lymph node spread. In adjusted analyses the protein stood as an independent prognostic factor, with hazard ratios well above one for each outcome. The authors propose it as a practical immunohistochemistry marker for risk stratification.
pmc-11622458:
Augustus Osborne and Bright Ahinkorah write on fathers and early childhood in Africa in a 2024 commentary. Research long centered on mothers, but evidence now shows fathers shape thinking, emotion, and social growth in their own ways. Stimulating play and rich talk feed mental growth. Warm engagement builds self-esteem and resilience, and fathers model social skills while encouraging exploration.

Fathers' own mental health, income stability, and co-parenting quality also matter. Yet money pressure, cultural norms, and migration keep many fathers at a distance. The authors outline policy steps to support involved fatherhood and argue that removing those barriers is key to child and teen mental health.
pmc-11624758:
Lee and colleagues reported in twenty twenty-four on muscle loss, air pollution, and thinking skills in older Koreans. Sarcopenia means loss of muscle mass and strength with age. The team drew on a long-running community health study. They studied two thousand two hundred seventy-four adults, with an average age near seventy. Thinking was tested with a standard screening exam.

About nine percent had sarcopenia, and more had possible sarcopenia. Muscle loss was linked to lower test scores and to poor thinking outcomes. In contrast, fine dust exposure over one month to three years showed no link to muscle loss. Dust also did not change the link between muscle loss and thinking. The authors say keeping muscle may help protect the mind.
pmc-11625358:
Evan Smith and four co-authors ask what marks of mind and brain foretell how well older adults learn two kinds of plain video games. Their study is from two thousand twenty-four.

Game-based mind training can lift thought in those past sixty, but how much swings by the way it is done. How one learns the game itself may drive the gain. Thirty-two older adults played an action game and a plan game. The team read their pace of learning in each. A broad mind test and scans of brain bulk were matched to that pace. The aim is to learn which traits count for which kind of game.
pmc-11627158:
Michail Vavourakis and a team of co-authors study whether a twisted thigh bone after hip fracture surgery hurts recovery. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. The twist can occur when a rod is nailed inside the bone to fix a break near the hip.

Seventy-four patients had scans of both hips and knees after surgery. The twist angle was compared with the healthy side. About thirty-one percent had a twist classed as a deformity. The rest had an acceptable angle. Patients were scored on hip function at six months and one year, against their level before the break. Healing, complications, and deaths were also tracked. The study weighs how much the twist matters for daily function after this common operation.
pmc-11628258:
Martínez-López and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a case report of a hidden bowel injury after a car crash. A sixty-five-year-old woman suffered multiple injuries in a traffic collision. Ten days later, swelling appeared on the right side of her abdomen. Scans showed trapped air and a large fluid collection behind the abdominal muscles. Emergency surgery found a perforated jejunum, part of the small intestine. Bile-stained fluid had spread into the tissue planes behind the wall.

Surgeons removed the damaged bowel and rejoined the ends. They washed out the cavities and placed drains for recovery. A dissolvable mesh reinforced the weakened abdominal wall. Negative pressure therapy protected the closed wound during healing. Follow-up scans showed steady recovery with no infection. No hernia appeared over twelve months of follow-up. The authors say such hidden perforations should be suspected after blunt trauma.
pmc-11632658:
Shahadat Hossain and four co-authors create nanomaterials whose assembly can be switched by a lipid tag that hides or shows itself. Their paper came out in 2024. Proteins are attractive building blocks for nanomaterials, but once a protein is made, its structure is normally fixed and cannot adapt.

They fused a calcium-sensitive switch protein to a stretchy, heat-responsive protein chain. When calcium arrives, the switch exposes its fatty tag, which seeks out membranes and changes how the fusion protein clumps. Light scattering and electron microscopy confirmed that assembly depended on both calcium and the lipid tag being present. The authors call this strategy liposwitching. They propose it for synthetic biology and cell engineering, where controllable assembly is valuable.
pmc-11633758:
Zhenfeng Pang and co-authors developed a way in 2024 to hear the nuclear spins that a response strength-boosting method usually hides. Dynamic nuclear polarization borrows the large polarization of unpaired electrons to amplify nuclear magnetic resonance signals. But the nuclei closest to those electrons are shifted so violently by the coupling that their lines vanish from the normal spectrum. The team worked with the polarizing agent TEMPOL in frozen glycerol and water just above one kelvin.

Their method, spin diffusion enhanced saturation transfer, reveals the hidden spins indirectly through their neighbors, and they also logged proton lines spread across a wide rate range. Models and quantum chemical calculations pinned the signals on protons of the TEMPOL molecule itself. 2D tests then showed polarization flowing from hypershifted nuclei to the bulk across the usual spin diffusion barrier, knowledge that can guide better polarizing agents.
pmc-11634158:
Dhrupad Banerjee and co-authors review fresh approaches in stem cell therapy for cancer and brain disease, in an overview from two thousand twenty-four. Mesenchymal stem cells sit at the center, since they can either feed or fight tumors depending on context. Their released packets, called exosomes, carry signals between cells.

Those packets show both pro-tumor and anti-tumor effects across studies. They also sway how tumors answer chemotherapy. Edited stem cells can ferry therapy straight into the tumor's neighborhood. For brain and immune disorders, the cells can rebuild tissue and calm immunity. Personalized, targeted use is the closing theme.
pmc-11634758:
Hifza Javed and co-authors published this study in 2024. It builds a model of how two people feel about each other during a conversation, not just how each feels alone. The goal is social robots that can mediate between people in real settings. Past affect tools read one person at a time, missing the shared mood. The team recorded conversations in uncontrolled settings and pulled features from sound and video.

The model weighs both partners' views to predict the pair's relational affect. Early tests show it can track how the shared mood evolves live. That skill could let a robot step into a souring exchange, lift a flat one, and leave a warm one alone. The authors discuss limits frankly: human ratings are subjective, and real scenes are messy. Still, they frame the model as a step toward robots that truly mediate.
pmc-11635658:
Bruno Vincenzi, Paolo Casali, and eight co-authors report real-world use of a cancer drug in Italy. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, covers pazopanib for soft tissue sarcomas. These are cancers of muscle, fat, and other soft parts. The drug is used after prior chemo in advanced cases that are not mostly fat-based.

A national registry run by the Italian drug agency tracked all users. Data span from twenty thirteen to twenty nineteen. Near two thousand patients took part, a very large group for a rare cancer. The main measure was how long patients stayed on the drug. Dose cuts and their timing were also logged. The registry shows how the drug performs outside strict trials.
pmc-11643658:
Carlos Barba-Ostria and co-authors published a 2024 study of plant pigments packed in tiny capsules, drawn from two old food crops of the high Andes: a purple corn and a purple potato. The pigments, anthocyanins, are known foes of microbes and of rust-like damage. Packed well, they last and work in food and care products. The team studied what the packed pigments can do.

The pigments were packed in a starch-sugar carrier coat. Beam and spectroscopy readings showed the pigments held in the coat in sound shape. The potato pigment led on antioxidant fight, and it hit two cancer cell lines hard. The corn pigment led on antimicrobial fight, even against drug-resistant microbes and film-forming kinds. The conclusion presents the packed pigments as versatile goods for both food and care use.
pmc-11643758:
Wenyuan Zhang and co-authors review plant sugars for use in infant formula in a 2024 article. Human milk is rich in special sugars that feed good gut bacteria and build infant immunity. Formula lacks much of that profile, and formula fed infants often have poorer gut health as a result.

The review covers using dietary polysaccharides as prebiotics, and as partners or products of good bacteria, called synbiotics and postbiotics. Prior studies show effects on gut microbes, gut acid production, and immune development. The combined and product forms looked stronger for shaping microbes and blocking infections. The authors note safety testing in large, long trials is still needed, and they compare milk like options such as pectin and inulin.
pmc-11644258:
Albert Tucci, Miguel Flores-Vergara, Robert Franks, and Stefan de Folter infer gene networks in developing monkeyflower seeds. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses machine learning on time-series gene data. Seeds helped flowering plants spread and diversify widely. Hybrid seed failure also locks species apart permanently.

The team crossed two Mimulus species that produce viable seeds. Gene activity was tracked across seed development stages. Network inference highlighted which genes regulate which others. Active control links in hybrid seeds emerged from the analysis. The results form a reference set for later experiments. Understanding these networks may explain why some hybrid seeds fail. Plant biologists gain targets for testing speciation mechanisms directly.
pmc-11644358:
Kalavathy Rajan, Paula Berton, Robin Rogers, and Julia Shamshina ask if kraft pulping should anchor future plants that turn plants into products, in work from twenty twenty-four. Kraft pulping makes most paper pulp today from wood. It also brings sulfur waste and high water and energy use.

The authors trace the rise of chemical pulping since the factory age began. Gains in yield and cost have not solved waste or full use of wood parts such as lignin. They weigh the bottlenecks that keep plant based goods from being truly green. Other routes to break down wood get a look as well. The piece urges a hard check of old methods before new plants copy them.
pmc-11644858:
Hoejun Jeong and colleagues combine deep learning with dynamic time warping to diagnose a hidden degradation inside nuclear reactors. The core support barrel, an internal structure, is held by clamping force whose degradation can significantly affect plant safety and reliability. Earlier studies could detect that degradation occurred but not pinpoint its size and position.

The method applies time warping to the magnitude of ex-core neutron noise signals in the frequency domain, letting the model learn how sensor values change with damage state. Autoencoder-based representation learning extracts features while preventing overfitting, improving robustness. Experiments show the size and position of clamping force degradation can be accurately predicted. Internal structures cannot be inspected directly while a plant runs. The approach turns vibrations a reactor already emits into a map of its own wear.
pmc-11645958:
Tim Lambert and colleagues studied sugary drink intake in severe mental illness in 2024. People with severe mental illness die early more often. Poor physical health drives much of that gap. The team measured added sugar from sweetened drinks. They used data from routine community mental health care.

Intake of added sugar was four times the general population level. That figure also misses sugar from other snack foods. So true intake was likely higher still. Several poor health factors tracked with higher intake. The authors suggest a simple drink measure. It could flag diet risk when no dietitian is available.
pmc-11647358:
Dafne Capelusnik and co-authors published a 2024 study comparing questionnaires for pain and morning stiffness in a spinal arthritis condition. The condition, axial spondyloarthritis, stiffens the spine and causes chronic back pain. Trials and clinics measure these symptoms with several rival scales, all scored from zero to ten. The team asked which scales measure what they claim, and which best separate patients into known groups.

They used data from a long-running international cohort of patients with the X-ray form of the disease. Eighty-five patients with eight years of records were assessed. Three pain scales and three stiffness scales were tested against set predictions about how they should relate to other measures. All six passed most of the tests. One pain question, covering neck, back, or hip pain, separated groups slightly better than the rest. Night back pain performed worst. Background factors had little effect on the comparisons.
pmc-11647758:
Muscle weakness in many diseases comes with swelling, lost fibers, fat creeping in, and scarring. Kai Yin led a team that reviews the muscle's inner neighborhood and the cells that keep it in balance. At the center sit FAPs, flexible starter cells that never become muscle themselves. Instead they can turn into fat, bone, cartilage, or scar-forming cells, build the tissue scaffold, aid repair, and tend the nerve-muscle link.

When injury or disease upsets the neighborhood, these same cells misbehave and drive the damage patterns doctors see. The review maps the signals that steer the cells, for good or ill. It picks out drug targets on those paths that might restore balance and help muscle heal.
pmc-11647858:
Ryuichi Maekawa and a team of co-authors found a new fluid to peel graphite into thin sheets. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, used a water mix with ammonium hydrogen carbonate as the bath. An electric charge drives the peeling from the top layer down. Such thin carbon sheets draw wide use, and makers want better ways to mass produce them with fresh traits.

The peeled product has a porous two layer shape and stays spread in water for years. Its worn, holed face makes a fine base for metal based catalyst parts. Those parts went on to drive hydrogen making as stand in catalysts. Readers who make carbon sheets get a bath that yields a long lived, catalyst ready product.
pmc-11649058:
Bhavya Balaji and four co-authors describe clearing a blocked windpipe in a child in this two thousand twenty-four case report. Long ventilation and a tracheostomy can leave scar tissue, called granulation, inside the trachea. Large growths are usually cut out by surgery or treated through a scope. Their patient was a six-year-old boy whose windpipe had closed completely. The block followed a tube cuff injury and a long tracheostomy.

The team avoided open surgery. Across several sessions, they widened the passage with a rigid scope and froze the excess tissue with cryotherapy. The airway reopened by this unconventional route. The case offers an option when surgery is risky. Pediatric airway specialists are the readers.
pmc-11653858:
Yaqin Song and co-authors build a chart-based tool to predict severe complications during hospital care for heart attack patients. Such models are lacking for patients admitted through emergency departments. The study covers 1,024 patients treated at one hospital in Changsha between 2020 and 2023. About 717 patients form the group used to build the model, and 307 form the test group.

Analysis of admission data finds seven factors that independently predict severe complications. They are age, heart rate, mean arterial pressure, diabetes, hypertension, triglycerides, and white blood cell count. The team builds a nomogram, a scoring chart, from these seven factors. The chart predicts well in both groups. Calibration checks show predicted and observed rates agree closely, and a curve analysis shows the tool helps decisions across a wide range of risk thresholds. The authors offer it as practical support for emergency clinicians.
pmc-11654058:
Azadeh Dehghani and four co-authors examined how iron deficiency anemia reached Iran's policy agenda, in a study published in 2024. The condition is a moderate-level problem in the country, worst among pregnant women, children, and teenagers. The team used a well-known three-stream framework: the illness as one stream, solutions as a second, and the political mood at home and abroad as a third. Twelve policy documents and 33 in-depth interviews fed the analysis.

The solutions stream stressed staffing in health centers, blocking parasites and chronic illness, and the trio of supplements, education, and food fortification. National and international backing gave the topic favorable conditions. Barriers stood in the way: a treatment-first mindset, tight money, and limited reach of services, hit by sanctions and the pandemic years. The authors urge more spending on prevention before deficiency occurs, not only cures afterward.
pmc-11655458:
Fulvio Riondato, Alberto Alvarez-Barrientos, and Francesco Grandoni introduce a research collection on flow cytometry in animal science in a 2024 editorial. The technique, which reads traits of single cells as they stream past a laser, has drawn veterinary interest since the late nineteen seventies. Yet the field still trails its medical counterpart by a wide margin.

The editors count thousands of veterinary papers using the technique, spread across more than a hundred journals. Growth has been steady and sped up in recent years. They note there is no dedicated journal home for this work. Their collection aims to take the pulse of the field today and showcase recent studies in key areas.
pmc-11655558:
Zhuoshi Li and co-authors show how a gene called MACC1 lets ordinary lung cancer cells turn back into stem-like cells. Tumors hold a mix: stem-like cells that seed growth, and regular cells that can dedifferentiate into them. MACC1 was already tied to lung cancer spread, but its role in this switch was unclear.

Cells rich in stem traits carried extra MACC1, and adding it pushed regular cells toward the stem state, while silencing it blocked the shift. The chain runs through a small RNA: MACC1 suppresses microRNA-25, which normally hastens the decay of a brake gene's message, KLF4. With the brake kept longer, the switch is eased. The authors say the finding may guide precision drugs aimed at cancer stem cells.
pmc-11656058:
Ju-Hee Park and seven co-authors test a cannabis compound in lab dishes in this twenty twenty-four study. The compound, called cannabigerol, was given to two lines of human bowel cancer cells. The team wanted to see if it slowed growth or killed the cells, and by what route.

Growth tests showed the compound held back both cell lines, with the dose that halves growth differing by line. Staining tests showed many more cells dying in a neat, programmed way after treatment. Checks on cell cycle and on death-linked proteins backed that finding. The work is early lab proof only, but it marks the compound as a lead for more study on bowel cancer.
pmc-11657658:
Gautam, Parajuli, and Pandey gauge gut worm load in a native group in Nepal. Years of state deworm work have not cleared worms in all groups. The Badi group has a way of life unlike most of the state. Few past studies probe worm risk in that group.

The team took stool samples from 205 adults aged 18 to 70. Each person also gave facts on home, work, and habits. Three lab methods checked each sample for worm eggs. The team weighed which habits and home traits tracked with infection. Their aim is care that fits the group real risks.
pmc-11658458:
Xiao and three co-authors traced teen sleep problems to exercise and phones in this study from twenty twenty-four. Nearly five hundred adolescents, average age about thirteen, filled out surveys in twenty twenty-four. The team measured activity, sleep trouble, anxiety, and phone dependence. Statistical links were then arranged into a chain model.

More activity went with less anxiety, less phone dependence, and fewer sleep disorders. Anxiety and phone dependence together fully carried the link from activity to sleep. In other words, exercise seems to help sleep by calming worry and loosening the phone's grip. The chain order matters: anxiety first, then phone habits. The authors urge families and schools to push activity for better sleep.
pmc-11659758:
Kei Shing Ng, Jie Lian, Fan Huang, Yan Yu, and Varut Vardhanabhuti wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It uses wrist-worn motion trackers from the UK Biobank to link how much brisk activity adults do with their later risk of chronic disease.

The study followed nearly sixty thousand adults who were free of chronic disease at the start. Their weekly minutes of moderate to strong activity were split into low, middle, and high thirds. People in the lowest third faced clearly higher risks, from about a quarter more to double, across a range of diseases. In men, low activity tracked most strongly with type 2 diabetes and with brain-degenerating disease. The risk rose step by step as activity fell, a dose pattern that strengthens the case for cause and effect.
pmc-11660658:
Dalia Caleffi and four co-authors review what is known about getting patients up and moving after a heart device implant. Their twenty twenty-four scoping review deals with pacemakers and kindred devices, now given to older, sicker patients. Long bed rest after implant is customary, but no consensus backs one schedule.

The team searched six databases and kept eight studies, most of them randomized trials. Three themes emerged: how patients were mobilized, what complications arose, and which device was used. Early movement looked safe and did not raise complications. The chief barrier is the lack of an agreed time and method, though an arm support seems to help. More rigorous work is called for.
pmc-11665458:
Abolfazl Shokri, Mohammad Amin Larki, and Ahad Ghaemi model hydrothermal carbonization of poultry litter. Their twenty twenty-four study aims to recover carbon and inorganic phosphorus. Heat and water turn the litter into higher value materials. Temperature and reaction time are the main settings under study.

One modeling approach mapped how the settings affect recovery. Two neural network models then competed to fit the data better. The multilayer perceptron model won on both accuracy and simplicity. It needed fewer neurons and gave lower error for both products. Its fit scores were near perfect in the tests reported. The results point to better nutrient recycling from farm waste streams.
pmc-11669058:
Amankeldi Salybekov, Aiman Kinzhebay, and Shuzo Kobayashi review cell therapy as a route to kidney repair, in an overview from two thousand twenty-four. Kidney injury and chronic disease are rising with diabetes and high blood pressure, and current care often falls short. Transplanted cells may protect the kidney through signals they release, immune calming, and direct tissue joining.

The review follows the field from animal work to human trials. Gains appear in both sudden injury and chronic disease settings. Open problems include where cells come from, how to deliver them, and how long benefits last. Tuning dose and cell power is the next frontier, they say.
pmc-11671958:
Robert Staruch and four co-authors wrote an article in two thousand twenty-four on tissue loss in combat casualties. Progressive tissue loss has complicated limb wounds in recent conflicts. It can leave a shorter residual limb and can change how rehabilitation goes.

The authors say the burden of wounds in combat is hard to measure. Data sets are of poor quality and lack the detail needed for close analysis. Their article sets out the main hurdles in counting that burden. It also proposes simple steps to improve how data are captured in future. Better records, they argue, would help plan care and support for the war-wounded. The piece is a review and call for better data, not a trial.
pmc-11672458:
Wang and colleagues reported in twenty twenty-four on feeding bile acids to older laying hens. As hens age past their peak, laying can fall and fat can build up in the liver. Bile acids help break down fat during digestion. The team fed one hundred forty-four hens, aged seventy weeks, for five weeks. Birds got a plain diet or diets with a low or high dose added.

The added acids did not clearly change laying output during the trial. Treated hens had more follicles, and their eggs had heavier shells and deeper yolk color. Liver fat fell, and liver cells showed smaller fat spaces. The low dose also shifted gene activity away from making fat and toward breaking it down.
pmc-11673558:
Jiayin Li, Xiaomeng Liu, Deqi Zhu, Haozhe Jiang, and Gengfeng Niu wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It studies how parents' help with homework shapes Chinese students' negative emotions, and what softens or carries that effect.

Homework help is a hot topic in China, praised for lifting learning but blamed for stress at home. The team drew on a national family survey run by Peking University, ending with 494 clean cases. Analysis showed that parent involvement did sway students' bad feelings. A sense of family responsibility carried part of that effect, passing the influence along. Warm, open talk between parent and child changed the strength of the links. The authors read the results through family systems theory and suggest the findings can guide efforts to protect children's mental health.
pmc-11676358:
Decsi and four co-authors test plant conditioners on maize in a paper from twenty twenty-four. They used humic acid alone and humic acid mixed with amino acids. Both are sold to boost plant health, but exact gene effects were not well known.

Field tests measured plant traits and yield after two priming treatments. Yield rose clearly in treated plants. A full gene activity scan then showed which genes switched on. Photosynthesis, cell breathing, and protein making paths were all more active. Those shifts help explain the yield gain, even in a year with extreme rain. The work links a farm input to clear changes inside the plant.
pmc-11677258:
Abdul Ghafar and co-authors present a method from two thousand twenty-four for detecting plant diseases with a real-time vision model. Early spotting of crop disease limits losses, but field checks are slow and expert eyes are scarce. The team trained a custom version of the YOLOv8 object detector to find and classify plant conditions in images.

They evaluated the model first on a held-out test subset from their data. To probe real-world strength, they then ran it on fresh images pulled from web search, which the model had never seen. Results were promising, with high accuracy across plant conditions. The authors stress the model's speed and precision, which suit live monitoring in the field, and its promise for wider farm use.
pmc-11677358:
Jing-Hua Fu and co-authors reinforce concrete beams with basalt fiber bars and steel fibers rescued from old tires. Their study appeared in 2024. Six beams were built, mixing three fiber doses with three bar ratios, then bent to failure while cameras tracked surface strain in three dimensions. The tire fibers slowed cracking, cut bending, and raised both the first-crack load and the final strength. At equal bar ratios, cracking loads rose by up to about forty-three percent and ultimate strength by up to about thirteen.

The team also adjusted the standard strength formula to credit the fibers' pull, and predictions matched the tests well. The authors pitch the pairing as a greener reinforcement: basalt bars do not rust, and the fibers turn waste tires into structure.
pmc-11678458:
Una-Jovana Vajic and co-authors test whether nettle leaf extract can protect the kidneys of rats bred for high blood pressure. Their study appeared in 2024. Earlier work showed the extract lowers blood pressure and fights oxidative stress across the body. Here the team asked whether it guards the kidney itself, and by what route. Rats received water, a standard pressure drug, or one of three extract doses for four weeks.

The standard drug and the middle extract dose both lowered pressure, protein leakage in urine, and signs of stress and scarring in the kidney. The effects matched those of the drug losartan. Notably, the benefit did not run through a master stress switch called NRF-2; some signals tied to that switch even fell. The authors say the extract guards the kidney by a different path.
pmc-11679558:
Vladislav Deigin leads a team on a new peptide that boosts blood cells. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with a ring shaped mimic. Blood cell peptides tend to break down fast in the body.

The lead ring was weighed against a known drug in mice. It raised young blood cell counts in blood and marrow. It worked when given by shot and by mouth alike. That mouth use sets it apart from most such peptides. Tests used both plain and irradiated mice for the checks. Early stage proof is set out in full.
pmc-11684458:
Yuancai Zhang leads a team of seven authors reviewing why teens quit organized sport. They pull the research together through an ecological lens. Youth sport helps body and mind, yet late adolescence loses many players. Their search found five hundred twelve papers. Just eleven of them fit, as peer-reviewed studies of athletes under twenty-five with real data.

Gender gaps got the most study time and did play a real part in dropout rates. By contrast, social, cultural, and ethnic roots got scant note in most studies. Factors in the mind, such as how able a teen feels and how much fun sport brings, also stood out. The team sort the causes by the levels of the Bronfenbrenner model, from the self to the wider culture. They close by naming the blind spots that future dropout research should fill first.
pmc-11685058:
Parent, Stryhn, Hammell, Fast, and Vanderstichel build a forecast model for sea lice on salmon farms in twenty twenty-four. The lice harm farmed Atlantic salmon in the Bay of Fundy in New Brunswick. Farms count lice often, and those counts go into a shared database. The team used counts from twenty sixteen to twenty twenty-one.

Their model tracks adult female lice over time at each farm. It includes treatments, water temperature, and pressure from lice at the same site and nearby sites. Pressure from nearby sites raised lice counts, and the effect fell with distance. Checks within the sample showed good accuracy for short term forecasts. The authors say farm managers can use the model to plan lice control steps.
pmc-11687358:
Nathan Jones and a team of co-authors tested a new way to repair early tooth decay in two thousand twenty-four. Most noninvasive treatments work on the tooth surface, which may limit how well they heal a lesion below it. Their idea uses starch particles loaded with minerals, made to reach the subsurface of early lesions.

The team made particles with calcium, phosphate, and fluoride, plus a fluoride-free version. They treated natural smooth-surface lesions for twenty days, with acid challenge and artificial saliva. Scans showed the particles restored far more mineral than fluoride or water controls. The gain was strongest below the surface, and treated teeth looked less white and chalky. The work is an early lab proof of concept.
pmc-11689158:
Erick Carranza and four co-authors probe how relationships, pain, and resilience intertwine in older adults, in a 2024 study. Feeling well cared for by a partner seems to ease distress in chronic illness. Yet good relationships have also been linked with reporting more pain, a puzzle worth untangling.

The team frames pain as the middle step: relationship quality may shape how much pain a person feels, which in turn sets resilience. Their analysis draws on survey data gathered during the COVID-19 years, when support was strained. A health model that splits inborn capacity from acquired resources guides the test. The work aims to show whether easing pain is the lever through which strong relationships protect well-being in later life.
pmc-11689858:
Lena Rebecca Richardson and five co-authors study older adults who fled abuse and now live in a shelter in western Canada. Their work, from two thousand twenty-four, asks what helps these people feel they belong.

The team re-read talks with ten clients and five staff, through a lens that puts care at the center. Three themes stood out. First, trust grew when staff gave care that bent to each person's needs. Next, clients who cared for each other felt more at home. Last, a sense that care was lacking broke trust and blocked belonging. The authors show how house rules and daily acts shape whether a shelter feels safe.
pmc-11690258:
Dakota Witzel and co-authors link daily good events to thinking skill in over one thousand adults, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Participants kept an eight-day diary and took phone tests of planning and memory. Counts of good days, counts of good events, and mood swings around them were scored per person.

More good days and more good events tied to better planning and better memory. Stronger drops in bad mood after good events also tied to better planning. Stronger lifts in good mood tied to worse memory alone. Stress exposure and schooling were weighed in the math. Readers see good days help thought, but mood response cuts both ways.
pmc-11690458:
Six authors present a study from two thousand twenty-four on partners who care for a spouse or partner living with dementia. Dementia care brings heavy stress, and it can harm the caregiver's own body and mind. The authors focus on the strengths and habits that help caregivers cope, which they call positive adaptive factors.

The study centers on Black and African American caregivers, a group past research has often missed. The authors used personal stories, gathered through narrative inquiry, to explore how culture shapes resilience in this role. A resilience framework, adapted for the study, guided how they read and sorted what caregivers told them.
pmc-11690858:
Ignacia Arteaga and four co-authors study why Latinx people in the United States face more risk of Alzheimer disease and kin forms of dementia. Their work, from two thousand twenty-four, uses close field study of daily life.

The team drew on eighty-four deep talks with older adults and family carers, plus three years of time spent in town centers in two states. They show how strong trust in kin can clash with low pay, poor care access, and ill health in the family. When care work brings in cash the home needs, strain and fights can grow. The paper links these home facts to wider bars to health.
pmc-11691658:
Cathy Maxwell and six co-authors report in twenty twenty-four on how to draw long-term care homes into research. Older adults in care homes can gain from studies on health and daily life, yet homes are hard to sign up. The work grew out of three long studies in two state areas with more than three hundred care homes.

Trust sits at the core of their method. Staff used long ties in the area, reached out to health groups, and made calls more than once. They also gave health checks and fun tasks for the people who live in the homes. Of the homes that first replied, close to half joined. The authors say steady, kind contact works best.
pmc-11691958:
Natalie Turner studies how easily older adults can get self-directed services through Medicaid home and community-based service waivers. Self-direction lets people control their own long-term services and supports. It rests on choice and on power over one's own care. The model lifts health results and care satisfaction. It can also give care in a way that fits a person's culture, yet it stays little used.

Each state picks which services can be self-directed and how many people may do so. So state policy shapes access. Turner used framework analysis and counts on the section 1915(c) waivers that serve older adults. Of 60 such waivers, 35 allowed self-direction. They covered 26 states and the District of Columbia. Most waivers set very low goals for uptake.
pmc-11693158:
Lisa LaRowe and three co-authors ask older adults on opioid painkillers what might push them toward other substances if their opioids are reduced. Their qualitative study came out in 2024. Doctors are urged to taper opioids in this group, but patients may self-medicate the pain that returns.

Three focus groups with ten patients aged sixty-five to ninety-two identified the risks. Intolerable pain, no access to other treatments, distress, and a history of substance use could all drive substitution. Access to alternatives, counseling, social support, and knowing the risks pulled the other way. Participants wanted a clear tapering plan agreed in advance. The authors say deprescribing programs should build those protections in from the start.
pmc-11694658:
Yi-Xiang Chen and five co-authors defend their claim of a rare mineral in Alpine rocks, in a reply published in 2024. The mineral, coesite, forms only under extreme pressure, so finding it in surface-derived rocks proves the continental crust once sank to great depths.

Critics had suggested the signal could come from polishing contamination or from the host garnet crystal itself. The authors answer that no polishing material produces the same spectral fingerprint, and no silicon of the required kind touched their samples. Spectra taken on the garnet alone lack the disputed peak. They maintain their identification stands, with its implication that a slice of the Alps was once buried deep in a collision zone.
pmc-11708958:
Irem Seleoglu and Aynur Demirel sift in a set way lung fix-up care for lung ills that scar the lung and come from ills of the join flesh. Their 2024 review asks if care based on sport helps a group of sick folk. Their ill may stay firm with no stock drug care.

Just four studies met the bar in six stores, which shows how scant such care is here. Mid-grade proof backed gains for lung work and for how gas spreads in the lung. Work skill, grade of life, grade of short breath, and tired state all got more good with mid-grade proof. Proof was thin for gains in strength of breath and limb muscles. The team ends that such care can aid the care-based path back for these sick folk. They call for full trials to make the proof base firm.
pmc-11709558:
Natividad Olivar, Luis Brusco, and Daniel Cardinali review the records of patients with mild cognitive impairment who took melatonin at bedtime. Their retrospective study came out in 2025. Melatonin is the hormone that sets the sleep-wake cycle, which often frays in older adults.

Half of the two hundred fifty patients received a fast-release melatonin dose each night for twelve months, on top of their usual medication. After a year, the melatonin group scored better on standard mental status and cognitive tests. Most other test scores also favored the treated group, except one timed symbol task. Depression scores that started abnormally high improved, and patients reported better sleep and wakefulness. The authors suggest melatonin as a useful add-on treatment in everyday clinic practice.
pmc-11709658:
Qiulan Ma and a large team link an enzyme at nerve synapses to Alzheimer's disease damage and thinking decline. Their study came out in 2025. The enzyme releases a fat that the body converts into inflammatory signals, and animal work had hinted it helps destroy synapses.

The team isolated synapse preparations from donated human brains: healthy, mildly impaired, and Alzheimer's cases. The enzyme's beta form was clearly higher in both impaired groups than in healthy brains. Higher levels went with worse cognition and more of the tangles that mark the disease. The enzyme sat alongside key synapse proteins and tracked with the fat it releases and its inflammatory products.
