The authors ask whether dialing the enzyme down could protect synapses, a question still open.
pmc-11709758:
Aram Aslanyan and a large team give the first detailed chemical portrait of Alzheimer's plaques and tangles in living human brain. Their study came out in 2025. Brain tissue came from patients having shunt surgery for suspected fluid buildup, who had received a labeled amino acid before the operation.

Four of six participants had amyloid plaques. Different amyloid forms sat in different parts of each plaque: some concentrated in the core, others spread evenly. No labeled amyloid had been incorporated into plaques, suggesting they grow very slowly. Labeled tau, by contrast, appeared within hours, and its half-life in brain tissue worked out to about twenty-seven days. Knowing how fast these proteins turn over helps researchers judge how treatments that clear them should behave.
pmc-11710858:
Yuko Denda and co-authors published this study in 2024 on patients in Japan who do not speak Japanese. Language gaps can mar every step of care, from check-ups to treatment. How patients see their own illness shapes how they cope, yet no work had tied that view to speaking skills in this group. The team sent a web survey in early 2024 and kept 354 replies.

Patients who got language help scored lower on speaking skills, yet saw their illness in a more hopeful light. Skill scores split by homeland, stay status, Japanese level, and the tools used to talk. Views of illness split by sex and like traits as well. A stronger sense of control over illness tied to better skill marks. The authors urge clinics to fund language help as part of care, not as an extra.
pmc-11713458:
Yazan Hammad and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on gene scores and amyloid build-up in the brain. APOE is the strongest known gene risk for Alzheimer's disease, but smaller gene effects are often set aside.

The team used a large Alzheimer's data set with gene data and amyloid scans for more than a thousand people. They built scores from many small gene effects, leaving out the APOE region, and a separate score that grades APOE risk by type. The APOE score tracked scan-proven amyloid strongly. A score built from spinal fluid amyloid genes also tracked it, even next to the APOE score. A tau-based score did not reach the same bar. The results say risk grading gains from genes beyond APOE.
pmc-11717158:
Javier Ramos-Maqueda and five colleagues compared two pacemaker lead placement strategies over the medium term. Left bundle branch area pacing tries to activate the heart through its natural conduction system. The comparison treatment was pacing from the right ventricular outflow tract septum. The twenty twenty-four prospective study followed 200 consecutive patients needing pacemakers, split evenly between the two approaches. Success, complications, and procedure times were recorded, along with the newer technique's learning curve.

Success and acute complication rates were similar between groups. The left bundle procedure took longer but needed less X-ray time. Its paced heartbeats were electrically narrower, a sign of more natural activation. Pacing measurements otherwise showed no major differences. The results support the newer approach as feasible for routine implantation.
pmc-11727858:
Anna Deda and a large team compare ways to measure how skin blood vessels react to strong light care. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Lasers and pulsed light are the tools of choice for wide vessel marks on the face. Yet most checks of change rest on rough scales or on the eye alone.

They treat a group of volunteers three times with pulsed light. They then check the skin with three measured tools: a pigment meter, a spectral camera, and a reflectance gauge. The pigment meter shows no clear change. The camera and the gauge each pick up clear shifts at set hues. The camera works best at two key wavelengths, they find.
pmc-11728058:
Sławomir Wojczyk and co-authors survey how 832 Polish doctors in one region cope with work stress, and how resilience shapes their habits. Their study appeared in 2024. Women doctors reached for emotional and practical support more often than men. Surgeons reported more positive reframing, and also more use of psychoactive substances. Doctors under thirty scored lowest on resilience, a worrying gap at career start.

Highly resilient doctors favored active coping: planning, problem solving, and engagement. Low-resilience doctors leaned away from such strategies. The authors call for training that builds resilience early, before poor coping hardens into habit, and for watching the young doctors who start with the thinnest reserves.
pmc-11728758:
Filipe Abadesso Lopes and co-authors report, in twenty twenty-four, a real-life study of a bacterial vaccine that prevents recurrent urinary tract infections in Portugal. These infections are frequent and debilitating, and avoiding antibiotics matters. The vaccine, MV140, is a whole-cell bacterial mix taken under the tongue. Its effectiveness in the Portuguese population was unknown. One hundred twenty-five patients with recurrent infections, complicated and simple, were treated and followed for twelve months. Infection frequency and severity were the main outcomes.

Thirty-eight percent stayed infection-free for the year. Another third had one or two episodes. On average, patients had about three fewer episodes per year than before. Effectiveness held across sex, weight, activity, and several risk conditions, the head text reports.
pmc-11742458:
Shweta Parakh and five co-authors report eye inflammation after injections of a newer drug for wet macular degeneration. Their report appeared in twenty twenty-four. The drug, faricimab, was given to three patients who had stopped responding to older agents.

Two patients developed mild inflammation of the eye's gel within three days. The third showed front-of-eye inflammation the day after injection. No vessel inflammation or blockage appeared. All three settled with steroid eye drops alone. One patient had reacted before to a related drug, hinting at an immune link. The authors urge vigilance, since the same reaction can, in worse forms, threaten sight.
pmc-11742758:
Barrera-Hoffmann and co-authors report a rare labor complication in a case paper from two thousand twenty-four. Air leaked into the space around the heart and lungs during labor, a condition called Hamman's syndrome. It is often triggered by strong straining and is usually mild, but it must be told apart from more dangerous problems.

The patient was a woman aged twenty-one having her first baby. She developed air under the skin and shortness of breath during labor. X-ray and CT scans confirmed the diagnosis. She was treated with oxygen and pain relief alone, and she improved without further problems. The authors stress that fast, accurate recognition guides safe care.
pmc-11752858:
Bislenghi and coauthors trace 30 years of pouch surgery for ulcerative colitis. The surgery removes the colon and builds a pouch from small bowel. It is the top choice when drugs fail or pre-cancer appears. Technique and outcomes may have shifted a lot over time.

The team reviewed all pouch cases in Leuven from 1990 to 2022. The full set held 492 patients across three time spans. Main outcomes were leak at 30 days and pouch failure. New drugs before surgery grew more common in late years. The team weighed how care shifts tracked with patient results.
pmc-11770358:
Paul Erohubie and co-authors measure how often schizophrenia outpatients skip their antipsychotic medicine, and why, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Three hundred ten adults at clinics were interviewed with standard scales for adherence, symptoms, side effects, and insight. Diagnoses were confirmed with a structured interview.

Just over half did not take their medicine as prescribed. Worse illness, substance use, and young age each raised the odds. So did weak social support, single-generation drug regimens, and sharper awareness of symptoms. The authors urge clinics to check adherence often and teach patients steadily. The fixable risks deserve the most focus, they say.
pmc-11784058:
Alberto Elmi and co-authors test in 2024 whether richer cages change stress hormones in lab rats, using hair as the record. Hair stores hormones over months and needs no blood draw. Twenty Wistar rats lived for three months with either a standard tunnel or an extra hanging tunnel as well.

Two hormones, corticosterone and DHEA, could be measured in the hair; cortisol could not. After three months the two housing groups showed no overall difference. Females carried higher levels of all steroids than males, and males in the richer cages had higher corticosterone. The authors say bigger studies are needed to set normal ranges for hair hormones in rats.
pmc-11790658:
Claudia Felicia Pop and a team of co-authors survey self-reported food allergy in Romanian schoolchildren, in two thousand twenty-four. Food allergy rates have risen worldwide in recent decades. Most European countries have such survey data, but Romania did not, so the team sent an online questionnaire to parents in one city.

More than seven hundred families completed the full survey. Just under nine percent reported a food allergy for their child. Cow's milk, strawberry, and egg were the most common triggers named. More than a third of allergic children had needed an emergency visit. The authors found poor sharing of medical details with school staff and call for better education.
pmc-12004358:
David Montefusco and colleagues trace how a fat-making enzyme subunit in the liver licenses the liver to make sugar, in this study from twenty twenty-four. High-fat feeding switches on SPTLC3, part of the machine that builds sphingolipids. Mice engineered to lack it only in the liver answered with lower fasting glucose.

Their liver cells produced less glucose, and isotope tracing showed the sugar-making pathway itself suppressed. The chain ran through signaling: without the subunit, a membrane messenger system dimmed, and the genes of gluconeogenesis lost their drive. Lipid chemistry supplied the link: a specific short-backbone sphingomyelin appears to partner with the messenger enzyme at the cell surface. The work pins a precise lipid-protein handshake behind a whole-body metabolic effect, with diabetes implications.
pmc-12312158:
Wang and a large team boost solar water splitting with magnetic materials in twenty twenty-four. Splitting water with light could supply clean hydrogen fuel for the future. Performance suffers because charges recombine and oxidation is slow. Magnetic fields were an untried lever for improvement, until this work.

A thin magnetic coating was added to a bismuth vanadate photoanode. With an external magnetic field switched on, water oxidation improved clearly. Measurements showed better charge separation at the coating interface. Oxygen release at the surface was also promoted by the field. The trick worked on three other common photoanode materials as well. The authors present this as a general route to better results. It applies even to semiconductors that are not themselves magnetic.
pmc-12699158:
Tao Luo leads a team that tests a targeted nano drug for pancreas cancer. Their work from twenty twenty-five joins imaging and heat therapy in one. The rings carry a dye and aim at a cancer mark called uPAR.

Traits of the rings were checked in lab and in mice. After vein dosing, tumors lit up on both glow and MRI scans. The targeted rings beat plain dye and untargeted rings on contrast. With a magnet field, the rings heated and killed cancer cells. One dose plan was used in a mouse tumor model. Early stage proof is the aim.
pmc-12702158:
Ianei de Oliveira Carneiro and seven co-authors study pet health in poor town zones of Salvador, Brazil, as a One Health case. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Dogs and cats there face poor drains, thin food, and ill care, which keeps germ stores alive. Those stores threat pets, wild beasts, and folks alike.

Surveys plus blood and stool tests covered hundreds of dogs and cats in two zones. A paid clinic group served as the match set. Blood marks split clear twixt town and clinic beasts. Home and street facts tied to blood and germ marks in mixed ways. The team urges spay, food, worm care, and street curb steps.
pmc-12705958:
Thuy-Tien Le and Thi Thuy Hong Nguyen published a 2025 study of workplace safety in industrial zones in Vietnam. Many factories meet safety rules on paper while workers still get hurt. The authors looked for the organizational and behavioral barriers that sit behind that gap.

They surveyed 486 employees in industrial clusters and analyzed the answers with statistical modeling. Two theories guided the work: one about how bureaucracies function, and one about how beliefs shape planned behavior. The results point to structural, cultural, and psychological factors that weaken safety performance, including safety routines treated as mere formality. Naming these barriers helps managers fix safety culture, not just paperwork.
pmc-12717258:
Soon-Chan Kim and co-authors spray chemotherapy as a fine mist inside the belly to beat colon cancer in two thousand twenty-five. The method, PIPAC, pressurizes the drug aerosol so it sinks deeper into tissue than a wash can. Patient response varies, and lab models to sort that out were missing.

Mini-tumors grown from patient tissue, called organoids, were treated with the mist plus one of three classic drugs. Cisplatin gained the most, killing far more cancer cells under pressure. Gene reads showed the mist reshaping cancer pathways tied to cell spread and growth signals, plus cell-cycle gears. The organoid setup offers a test bed for picking who should get the mist treatment.
pmc-12717758:
Susan Waserman and colleagues study how subcutaneous C1 inhibitor therapy changed quality of life for Canadians with hereditary angioedema. The disease brings swelling attacks that can not be predicted and can risk life.

The study joined phone talks over one summer with a checked angioedema quality-of-life questionnaire. Twenty patients took part, half of them women, with a mean age in the early fifties, most with type one or two disease. A concept map from the talks showed what patients valued most, across physical, mental, and emotional parts, function, social life, and medical care. Patients told of better control since the therapy began. Most had fewer attacks, and many had none, or next to none. Gains for feelings stood out, with less stress and anxiety about attacks to come.
pmc-12721758:
Akunchan Shrestha and ten co-authors describe a rare tooth-related tumor in an older woman. Their case report was published in twenty twenty-five. The tumor, a dentinogenic ghost cell tumor, makes up under half of one percent of jaw tumors and mimics other lesions.

The seventy-one-year-old patient had facial swelling and pain at the front of the upper jaw, from below the eye toward the cheek. Scans showed a hollow, expanding lesion with dense contents and a thinned wall. Under the microscope, ghost cells with calcification, island-like growths, and dentin-like material confirmed the diagnosis. Wide surgical removal was the treatment. The report walks through the signs that separate this rarity from its look-alikes.
pmc-12723858:
Ian Moura, Kaitlin Stober, Joseph Caldwell, and Teresa Nguyen measured how many adults with disabilities in the United States identify as LGBTQ+. Both groups face health gaps, yet their overlap has rarely been counted. The team used a large phone health survey from twenty twenty-two, with over two hundred seventy thousand replies across thirty-one states.

Thirteen percent of adults with a disability identified as LGBTQ+, against seven percent of others. Among those needing long-term daily help, the share rose to sixteen percent, the highest of any group. The link between such needs and identity was strong. The authors say better counts can guide fairer health care and support services.
pmc-12729158:
Zengshu Huang and co-authors published this fertility study in 2025. Embryos are often frozen for later transfer, and sometimes thawed ones must be frozen a second time. Clinics worry the extra freeze harms the odds of a baby. The team sifted more than thirteen thousand transfer cycles from one center, spanning 2018 to 2022, and matched like cases against each other.

After matching, 107 cycles used twice-frozen embryos and 214 used once-frozen ones. The twice-frozen group had far lower pregnancy and live birth rates. The harm showed most in women under thirty-five and in single-embryo transfers. Babies who were born looked alike in weight and health. The authors advise clinics to limit second freezes for younger women and to save the best-grade embryos when a refreeze is a must.
pmc-12730058:
Victor Abreu de Lima and eight co-authors redesign the crates that carry chickens to slaughter, using airflow simulation to cool the birds. Transport heat stress threatens poultry welfare and survival, yet crate engineering has seen little research. Four virtual crate designs were compared against the conventional box.

Computational fluid dynamics modeled internal airflow at three transport speeds, and scaled prototypes in a wind tunnel checked the predictions. One alternative design raised average internal air velocity by about a third over the conventional crate at highway speed. It also ran cooler and less humid, with the best thermal comfort indices of the set. Wind tunnel results confirmed real differences among designs. Better crates, the authors argue, are a cheap welfare intervention.
pmc-12730158:
Luo and seven co-authors report a study from twenty twenty-five on a germ behind udder infection in dairy goats. Outbreaks at a farm in Jiangxi Province had cost farmers heavily. The team took tissue and milk samples from sick goats for lab work. Stains, chemical tests, and gene reads name the germ as Staphylococcus caprae. Tests in mice confirm the germ is strongly disease-causing. They then screen thirty antibiotics and many herbal options against it.

Several standard antibiotics work well against the germ in dishes. Penicillin works worst among the drugs they test. Some herbal medicines and plant extracts rival the drugs in effect. The authors list options for treatment and prevention on the farm. They say the work guards goat health and dairy safety.
pmc-12732858:
Jeong Yong Lee and nine co-authors test gene variants in Korean women with repeated pregnancy loss, in a 2025 study. Losing two or more pregnancies in a row affects about five percent of couples, and over half of cases stay unexplained. The gene studied helps control blood clotting and plays a part in pregnancy.

The team compared 388 women with unexplained repeated loss against 377 healthy women. Six variants in the gene were read from blood samples. One variant's double-copy form came with a clearly higher risk of loss. Certain combinations of variants also raised risk, and the pattern held in larger combinations. The results add a clotting gene to the list of factors clinics may one day screen for after repeated losses.
pmc-12734358:
Megumi Matsuyama and seven colleagues published a dental trial report in two thousand twenty-five on mouth splints for teeth grinding in sleep. Grinding, called sleep bruxism, wears teeth and strains jaw muscles. Splints can guide the jaw in different ways, and it is unclear which guidance works best.

Twenty-four adults with sleep grinding each wore two splint types in turn, one favouring balanced contact and one guided by the canine teeth. Each splint was worn at home for over a month. Muscle activity sensors and sleep recorders tracked the nights. Twenty-three people finished, and the two splints showed no clear differences in muscle activity, sleep pattern, or comfort. The authors treat the small trial as groundwork for a larger one.
pmc-12737158:
Four authors report a case in two thousand twenty-five of a vein variant found before birth. The inferior vena cava is the large vein that returns blood from the lower body to the heart. In this variant the vein is interrupted, and blood detours through a smaller vein called the azygos.

The variant was spotted on a routine second-trimester scan and confirmed by a detailed ultrasound of the fetal heart. The baby was born without problems. The authors review how to diagnose the variant and what it can mean over a lifetime. They stress telling isolated cases apart from those paired with other birth defects.
pmc-12737258:
Michael Vernon and four co-authors present a smarter growth cabinet for raising plants in lab studies. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Plant scientists need steady, controlled rooms to test which crops cope best as the climate changes, but standard cabinets are costly and fixed.

The new cabinet runs saved climate recipes that copy real weather shifts. Cabinets can link together for larger trials, and the frame can be rebuilt for different species. It costs under ten thousand Australian dollars. Sensors record climate and plant growth on their own, ready for use with artificial intelligence tools. In tests, the cabinet held its target heat level well while copying weather from Hobart, Australia.
pmc-12738558:
Huimin Wu and three colleagues published a sports science study in two thousand twenty-five on predicting force in incline push-ups. Push-ups build upper body strength anywhere, but how the slope changes the load was poorly quantified. Force plates can measure it, yet a formula would be handier.

Twenty-seven male students did push-ups at three slopes and three metronome tempos with feet raised. Body mass, slope, and tempo fed a regression model for the force through the hands. Predicted and measured forces agreed closely on average, with moderate spread. Tempo linked to peak force differently at each slope. The authors offer the model for setting training intensity without lab equipment.
pmc-12738758:
Laura Amaya-Pascasio and colleagues use score mismatch to predict early recovery after stroke clot removal. Their study from twenty twenty-five builds a formula from admission data. Stroke severity scores sometimes exceed what scans predict. That mismatch may mark salvageable brain tissue.

Patients with large vessel blockages treated mechanically were included. A derivation group produced the expected-score formula. Mismatch percentage compared actual against expected severity. Early improvement meant a large score drop within a day. The mismatch predicted that improvement in the analysis. Such bedside maths could refine patient selection for treatment. It may also set family expectations after the procedure.
pmc-12740758:
Oh and a large team review whether gut microbes can flag breast cancer risk in twenty twenty-five. Gut microbes shape hormone handling and immune response, both tied to the disease. The team pooled thirteen case control studies from several regions. They compared microbe mix in women with and without the cancer.

Over half the studies found lower gut richness in cancer patients. Community mix differed in most studies. One gut genus ran high and one ran low across studies with some stress. Shifts split by region, with distinct genera leading in the United States, Europe, and China. The authors see promise but call for bigger, standard long term studies.
pmc-12745158:
Qiuyue Wu and co-authors published a 2025 study on a blood-and-fluid test for sorting gliomas, a type of brain tumor. Gliomas are classed by their molecular traits, which also hint at how a patient will fare. Spotting those traits without surgery is hard, because very little tumor DNA floats free in body fluids.

The team looked instead at how open the tumor's DNA packaging is at certain spots. Open spots can be read from free DNA in spinal fluid and blood. Using tumor tissue from four donors, they found seventy-two open regions that spinal fluid could reveal. Sixteen regions in blood DNA differed between low-grade and high-grade tumors. A classifier built on those sixteen sorted tumor grade well in training data, and less well in fresh test data. The authors offer the approach as a new kind of marker for glioma class.
pmc-12748058:
Jung Soo Son and co-authors compare traits of three common sexually spread infections in Korea, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Gene-based tests found five hundred cases at one hospital over more than a decade. Most patients were women, with a median age in the late twenties.

The most common germ also had the highest rate of complications. The least common germ was most often felt as symptoms. Among patients retested, about one in seven still carried a germ. One germ type and having symptoms each raised the odds of failed clearing. The authors urge watch on drug resistance and better retreatment plans.
pmc-12751158:
Mohammad Alghosi and co-authors compare warm-up styles for athletes whose shoulders pinch painfully overhead. Their trial appeared in 2025. Twenty-five male athletes with shoulder impingement and twenty-five healthy controls each tried three routines in random order: static stretching, a dynamic warm-up, and both combined. Shoulder rotation range, balance reach, position sense, and strength were measured before, right after, and one hour later.

All three routines improved rotation range, with static stretching giving the largest gains for the injured group. The dynamic warm-up most improved balance reach. The authors conclude the routines are not interchangeable: stretching buys motion, dynamic work buys control. Athletes and therapists can pick by goal, and combining both remains sensible when time allows before training or play.
pmc-12752158:
Ibrahim Maman Laminou and a large team test Niger's front-line malaria drug in kids and hunt gene marks of drug proof. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The drug pair was tried in kids aged five to fifteen with plain malaria at four sites in late twenty twenty-two, with day checks for twenty-eight days. Gene tests told fresh ills from back-sliding ones.

Raw cure rates swung wide by site, from near half to near full. Past gene fix, cure held at or past ninety-three percent at all sites, past the WHO bar. Proof gene flaws ran high in two genes, but none in the kelch gene. South sites showed strain, the team warn.
pmc-12755758:
Felipe Rodriguez and Jeroen Saeij published a 2025 study on how the human body first fights the parasite Toxoplasma gondii. The parasite infects tens of millions of people in the United States alone. Mice rely on defense tools that humans do not have, so the early human response was poorly understood.

Working with human blood cells, the pair found that a special group of T cells senses infected cells through a receptor called BTN3A1. These T cells release signals that switch on natural killer cells, which then make more of the defense protein interferon gamma. Blocking the pathway that makes the sensed molecules weakened the response. The findings name a clear first line of defense in people.
pmc-12756658:
Xiaohong Lin and co-authors pool studies on mobile health tools for people living with transplanted organs, in work from twenty twenty-five. Good follow up after transplant is vital for graft survival. Phone based tools promise support between clinic visits, but firm proof was lacking.

Twenty-three studies with more than two thousand recipients were reviewed, most of them randomized trials. Mobile tools improved self care skill by a clear margin and cut rehospitalization by about half. Death, rejection, and infection rates did not differ firmly between groups. Story based synthesis added gains in drug and care routine adherence. Bias checks used standard tools for both trial types. The authors back mobile support as part of transplant follow up.
pmc-12767458:
Adalberto Campo-Arias and colleagues validated a mental health literacy scale in two thousand twenty-five. The scale measures attitudes and knowledge about mental health. It was first built for adolescents. This study tested the Spanish version in Colombian adults. Participants were adult high school students. Statistical factor analysis checked the scale's structure.

Two broad parts emerged: attitudes and knowledge. Attitudes split further into help-seeking and stigma. Fit statistics supported that structure well. Consistency scores were computed for each part. A valid local tool matters for research and programs. Schools can now measure mental health literacy reliably. Stigma tracking becomes easier across adult learners.
pmc-12771858:
Xiang Cao, Zhencheng Ge, and Yiqing Gong report a frightening but fully reversible complication of a routine eye anesthesia technique. Sub-Tenon's anesthesia is considered the safer alternative to needle blocks for eye surgery. During combined cataract and macular surgery, though, a seventy-one-year-old man woke with vision loss, a drooping lid, a frozen eye, and a dilated pupil in the operated eye.

MRI showed mild fluid around the optic nerve and swelling of the fat behind the eye, with no compression or nerve thickening. Supportive care with oxygen and circulation aids followed. Within twenty-four hours every sign had resolved and vision partly recovered. The case report argues for counseling patients about even rare orbital apex syndrome risk, and for fast recognition when it strikes.
pmc-12780458:
Xiwen Liu and a large team of co-authors review hyperreactivity as a stand-alone clinical idea, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. The term names an oversized body response to a normal trigger, seen after surgery, lung transplant, and COVID-19. No shared frame for it existed before.

The review roots the state in a four-way imbalance across nerve, hormone, immune, and local tissue systems. Traits include early onset, staying power, and wide person-to-person spread. The authors sort its forms by setting and propose marker-based tiers for care. Their goal is sharper spotting and tailored treatment.
pmc-12780658:
Kexing Xi and co-authors find how many lymph nodes doctors should check after pre surgery chemoradiation in rectal cancer, in work from twenty twenty-five. Standard rules push for at least twelve nodes checked. But the pre treatment shrinks node counts, so that rule may misfit treated patients.

Data covered more than sixty-six hundred patients from a Chinese cancer center and a United States registry. In both sets, the twelve node split did not separate survival in a firm way. A data tool set the best cut at seven nodes. Patients below seven nodes fared worse on disease free and cancer specific survival. The node count at that cut stood as an independent outlook factor. The authors back seven as the working floor.
pmc-12784058:
Sung Jin Kim and five co-authors study night-time urination, blood uric acid, and death risk. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Night waking to urinate grows common with age and with body-wide ills. It is tied to a higher risk of death, but the path of that link was not clear.

They use a large population data set that spans a decade. Night urination tracks with higher death from all causes and from heart disease, after other factors are held in check. Uric acid shows a J-shaped link to death: both low and high ends carry risk. A path study finds uric acid carries part of the night-urination effect. Care that targets metabolism may cut the risk.
pmc-12789458:
Cherop and co-authors study how working mothers at a hospital in eastern Uganda manage exclusive breastfeeding. Feeding only breast milk for the first months is key to infant health. Yet jobs often make that hard to sustain. The study ran at Mbale Regional Referral Hospital, where local data had been scarce. A total of 221 working mothers with infants under six months filled in surveys. Ten mothers also gave in-depth interviews.

About 68% of the mothers fed their babies breast milk only. Interviews showed wide gaps in what mothers knew about the practice. Some workplace and family factors helped, while others got in the way. The study gives the hospital a base for better support programs.
pmc-12806658:
Ho-Sook Kim and co-authors compare three stomach acid regimens in healthy adults over fourteen days, in a phase one study from two thousand twenty-five. Thirty-six people took a low dose of tegoprazan twice a day, a higher dose once a day, or famotidine twice a day. Stomach pH was tracked around the clock.

The low twice-daily dose held acid down longest, keeping pH high for about three quarters of the day. The once-daily dose and famotidine trailed well behind by day fourteen. Famotidine also faded over time while both tegoprazan plans held steady. No side effects were reported in the low-dose group. Readers get a dosing case for split low doses.
pmc-12810158:
Bahammam and Rady checked in twenty twenty-five stains and roughness on made white crowns for kids' teeth. They watched twenty young kids with white crowns on top teeth and steel crowns on low teeth. In the lab they ran crowns in a chew sim to read rough change by pair kind.

White crowns that bit on steel crowns had the most stain and rough shift. Metal rub through films on the crowns drove that change, they find. White on white pairs fared far better in the same tests. Pair pick thus shapes how long such crowns last and look, they warn.
pmc-12812658:
Salceda and Vidu study violence in teen romantic and sexual relationships, and how girls can break free of it. They link the problem to social pressure and coercive talk that push girls toward unequal partners. Their study tested a group reading and dialogue program built around the book Radical Love. Fifteen girls aged 15 to 18 took part in the sessions.

The team assessed impact through recorded talks, life stories, and focus groups. The sessions helped the girls push back against coercive talk. Participants reported more freedom to choose safer and more equal partners. The authors present dialogue groups as a practical prevention tool for schools and youth programs.
pmc-12817458:
Julian Ganter and ten co-authors build a machine learning model to place defibrillators where they save the most lives, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. When a heart stops outside hospital, minutes matter, and a nearby defibrillator can double survival odds. Yet clear rules for placing the devices are lacking, and records of past arrests are often patchy.

The team worked in Freiburg, Germany, with over five thousand alerts for suspected cardiac arrest and ninety-five device spots. Their model predicts arrest risk from population and building data alone, with no need for past arrest sites. A greedy search then picked fresh locations step by step. Checks against real arrest records confirmed the picks, and scenarios measured how coverage would grow.
pmc-12817758:
Li and six co-authors trace how a surface protein lifts fat burn in bone cells in this twenty twenty-five study. Fat use gone wrong in bone cells can thin bone and feed weak-bone ills. The protein in scope links to a range of cell talk paths in past work.

Inside, gene tweaks that boost or cut the protein shift fat burn in bone cells. With more of it, a cell power switch flips on and stays on in cell tests. That switch speeds the burn of fats and backs fresh bone growth as a result. The protein holds the switch in its on pose by blocking a self-off fold. Mice with more of it lost less bone, which marks it as a cure lead.
pmc-12823558:
Abadi Atsbaha and six colleagues measure child wasting after war in a town in northern Ethiopia, in a twenty twenty-five survey. Wasting means a child is far too thin for their height, a grave risk in poor regions. Little data existed for Adigrat town after fighting stopped in Tigray. The team surveyed 325 children aged six months to five years in early twenty twenty-five, measuring arm size and asking carers questions.

About seventeen percent of the children were wasted, with five percent in the severe range. Skipping the first milk after birth was among the linked factors the authors report. The rate sits above emergency thresholds. The team calls for food and health support aimed at the youngest children in postwar areas.
pmc-12824358:
Haorui Wang and six colleagues published a mining safety study in two thousand twenty-five on water bursting through a coal mine floor. Mining extra-thick seams shakes the rock below, where pressurised water may wait behind a weak barrier. Tiny rock cracks, called microseismic events, can warn of danger.

The team monitored one working face in a Chinese mine. Most events clustered in one rock layer beneath the seam. Daily energy release, failure depth, and the reach of mining influence all tracked measured water inflow and rock pressure closely. They built a risk scoring model from these live signals rather than fixed geology. Its verdicts matched field readings. The authors offer the approach for mines over strong aquifers.
pmc-12826858:
Poudineh Moghadam, Bazi, Esfahani, and Emadi reviewed virtual clinics for remote care in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Distant and underserved regions suffer more preventable illness and death. Virtual clinics promise to bridge that distance with telehealth tools. The team gathered the published evidence using a formal scoping method.

Thirty-eight distinct benefits emerged from the literature. Better access, lower costs, and less patient travel led the list. Gains also appeared in governance, staff training, and record keeping. Digital prescribing and local technology use showed strong effects in richer countries. The authors conclude that virtual clinics can narrow health gaps. They frame the review as a map for planners.
pmc-12835158:
Gang Li and co-authors published this study in 2025. It tracks how water moves through ion-adsorbed rare earth ore. Mines pump liquid into such ore to free the metals, but heavy injection can destabilize slopes. Sensor points alone cannot watch the whole ore body. The team used a dense electrical resistivity method alongside sensors on a test block. Resistivity readings map where water spreads underground.

Water content and resistivity followed a tight power-law link, which let the team chart the flow. The wet zone grew from a droplet shape to a peach, then a hat shape as injection went on. Lower layers neared saturation while the topsoil stayed dry, forming a possible slip zone. Strength also bottomed out at full saturation. The authors urge close checks in mid and late injection.
pmc-12836958:
Rina Putri Noer Fadilah, Rasmi Rikmasari, Saiful Akbar, and Arlette Suzy Setiawan present a two thousand twenty-five study of an artificial intelligence app spotting tooth decay in schoolchildren's mouth photos. Decay affects most Indonesian schoolchildren, and dentists are scarce. Phone photos plus object-detection models could screen at scale.

Over three thousand labelled intraoral photographs trained and tested a detection model built into an app. Images were graded on a standard decay severity scale. Accuracy was measured with standard detection metrics. The work tests whether automated photo screening can triage children toward the limited dental care available.
pmc-12837058:
Xiaohui Tian, Leibing Ji, and Reyisai Abudulamu report a swollen vortex vein in one eye with no underlying cause, in a case study from twenty twenty-five. Such dilations are rare, often found by chance on imaging, and their look can mimic a tumor or other vascular lesion, inviting needless intervention.

A fifty-one-year-old man showed an abnormal patch in his left eye's lower outer region at a routine exam. Five imaging methods, from color photography and ultrasound to two dye angiographies, ruled out secondary causes. The diagnosis settled as idiopathic cystic vortex vein dilatation. The authors set out the trait's signature across imaging modes so clinicians can recognize it and avoid misdiagnosis.
pmc-12852958:
Dadmehr Yaghoubi and colleagues wrote a 2025 case report about a seventy-nine-year-old man who became seriously ill after a COVID infection. He arrived with lasting fevers, low blood counts, and liver problems. Doctors suspected a rare, life-threatening overreaction of the immune system in which immune cells begin destroying the body's own blood cells.

A scoring tool pointed the team toward an early bone marrow biopsy. The biopsy confirmed the immune disorder and also uncovered a hidden lymphoma linked to the Epstein-Barr virus. Steroid treatment brought rapid improvement. The case shows how several insults stacking together can push the immune system past a tipping point.
pmc-12853858:
Wen-Tao Zhang and seven co-authors trace how gut microbes in cattle shape the fat marbled inside muscle, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. That marbling drives beef quality and price. The team worked with Jiaxian Red Cattle, a Chinese breed prized for its meat, and used several layers of chemical and microbe data.

Fluid from the rumen, the first stomach, pointed to one fatty acid as a key promoter of marbling. Four microbe groups tracked closely with that acid. In high-marbling cattle, a fat-burning path ran slower, so more fat stayed stored. Muscle tissue in those animals held less carnitine and related compounds, which the gut microbes also tracked. The chain links rumen microbes to beef quality.
pmc-13018358:
Subham Pattanaik and five co-authors measure the friction orthodontists fight every time a wire slides through a bracket. That friction slows tooth movement and lengthens treatment. Their bench study crossed three bracket families with multiple wire types and sizes, two hundred forty combinations in all, on a universal testing machine.

Self-ligating brackets produced the least friction. Ceramic brackets produced the most, especially against rectangular nickel-titanium and beta-titanium wires. Conventional metal brackets sat between. The authors conclude that bracket and wire pairing is a real treatment-planning variable, not a matter of taste. Clinicians chasing efficient sliding mechanics, they argue, should reach for self-ligating systems first.
pmc-13132958:
Bruno and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-six on vitamin E levels in multiple sclerosis patients. The disease inflames and degrades the nervous system, often in young adults. Over one hundred eighty Italian patients and near one hundred controls are compared. Patients carry lower blood vitamin E than controls. Within patients, higher levels link to sharper thinking. Higher levels also link to less disability on standard scales. No link appears with depressive symptoms in their models.

All main links survive strict statistical correction. The vitamin separates clinical cutoff groups well. The authors stop short of claiming cause. Trials of supplements are the proposed next step.
pmc-13143158:
Weijing Chen and co-authors mine Chinese social media to map life with a weakened, stretched heart in younger patients, in a qualitative study from two thousand twenty-six. The illness, dilated cardiomyopathy, limits the body and weighs on the mind, yet patient voices from China are rarely heard. Nearly nine hundred posts and answers from a question platform were coded by theme.

Five themes emerged: losing control of the body, emotional turmoil, broken family and work roles, unmet care needs, and rebuilding life. Guilt over burdening family and worry over survival ran through the posts. Peer sharing helped many cope. The authors urge care shaped to life stage and culture.
pmc-13144258:
Thomas Pendergast and six co-authors survey herbicide resistance in a cosmopolitan weed in a 2026 paper. Green foxtail, also a model plant for geneticists, increasingly survives spraying from four herbicide families. The team exposed over two hundred plant lines from North America and Eurasia to herbicides hitting four different target enzymes, and sequenced the target genes in many lines.

Thirty percent of lines set seed after at least one herbicide, and thirteen resisted several classes. Yet gene changes in the targets rarely explained the survival; most differences were silent or outside coding regions. pmc-13147858:
Sebastian Wallon and co-authors lay out a randomized trial asking whether drains are needed after a major pancreas operation, in a 2026 protocol. Surgeons long placed drains after pancreatoduodenectomy, fearing leaks of pancreatic juice. A 2014 trial linked skipping drains to higher deaths, but it lumped all risk levels together. Low-risk patients might safely skip them, early evidence hints.

The DRAIN1 trial enrolls patients at low or intermediate leak risk, scores each one's risk, and randomizes drain or no drain across centers. Morbidity odds will be compared with regression models. The authors aim to settle whether the old gold standard still earns its place for the safer half of patients. The protocol frames the trial before results arrive.
pmc-13155658:
Alohoutade and co-authors model what the RTS,S malaria vaccine could achieve in Benin over ten years. Malaria is the top killer of children under five in the country. World guidance since 2021 backs malaria vaccines for children in endemic areas. West African modeling was scarce outside Ghana. The team built a compartment model of malaria spread. It counted clinical and severe cases the vaccine's first series could avert in young children.

Scenarios varied vaccine coverage side by side with bed net use. Nets remain a core defense in the region. The model weighs how much extra ground the vaccine gains. Results aim to guide Benin's rollout planning.
pmc-13156958:
Mohamoud and five colleagues review the health of mothers and newborns in Somalia in twenty twenty-six. Death rates for mothers and babies there stay among the highest in the world. The review draws on journal studies, national survey data, and reports from aid groups. It asks what drives poor outcomes and what should be done first.

Only about a third of births have a trained worker present. Care before and after birth is also low. The authors blame staff shortages, weak referral links, poor data systems, and low funds. They urge stronger birth care, better transport to clinics, and more work with local communities. Gaps in research on care quality also need filling.
pmc-13159958:
Samita Heslin, a solo author, writes in 2026 about a teaching problem created by clinical AI tools. Medical trainees now learn in settings where AI systems offer recommendations. Sometimes the AI advice clashes with the learner's own clinical judgment, and learners may treat the AI output as objective truth rather than a fallible probability.

Heslin argues that how teachers handle these clashes is an overlooked blind spot in medical education. Worked scenarios show how conflicts arise in training. Without structure, such moments can stunt reasoning skills and professional identity. A four stage framework is proposed to turn conflict into a learning opportunity, with ideas for teaching, assessment, and faculty training.
pmc-13161858:
Jeanne Chartrin and Aymeric Defalque report Dupuytren's disease, a hand disorder of older men, in a twelve-year-old boy. Their case report appeared in twenty twenty-six. Fewer than twenty-five child cases have been published since nineteen fifty-five, so the diagnosis is easily missed.

The boy had a painful, growing lump in his palm. The firm knot clung to the palm's fascia, but his fingers still moved freely. Scans suggested a cyst, yet surgeons considered the disease and removed the fascia. Lab study confirmed it: fiber-forming cells had multiplied and laid down collagen. The authors urge doctors to keep the disease in mind for child palm lumps. Long follow-up is wise, since recurrence risk in children is unknown.
pmc-13163758:
Malgorzata Jacczak-Gozdziak and Marcin Zarowski review what is known about sleep in childhood absence epilepsy, a common childhood epilepsy marked by brief staring spells. Their mini-review came out in 2026. The condition was long viewed as benign, but evidence now links it to wider network problems.

Fine structure within sleep also changes: sleep spindles, brief bursts of brain activity in light sleep, appear less often, particularly in children with thinking difficulties. The authors read this as a sign of disturbed circuits between the thalamus and cortex. They call for more research before these sleep measures guide care.
pmc-13169158:
Hoang and three co-authors price two new Alzheimer drugs by worth in one hundred seventy-four lands in this twenty twenty-six study. The drugs slow the ill yet cost far past what poor lands can pay. A worth price sets what each land should pay for the gain it gets.

Inside, life-grade gains from both drugs were set next to plain care in the model. Rich lands could pay a worth price in the thousands for a course by that math. Mid lands fell to the hundreds, and poor lands to just a few coins. One drug earned a top worth price a fair share past the next. The frame can guide price talks land by land.
pmc-13174858:
Ronnie Napoles and six colleagues describe an unusual case of Heyde syndrome, where a narrowed aortic valve and gut bleeding reinforce each other. The syndrome's classic triad links aortic stenosis, gastrointestinal bleeding, and an acquired clotting factor disorder. Diagnosis is hard when scope examinations find no bleeding source. Their patient was a seventy-three-year-old woman with two weeks of black stools and a week of fatigue. She carried several chronic conditions and significant anemia.

Multiple endoscopies and a capsule study showed blood but no source, and no abnormal vessels were seen. That absence, the authors stress, should not rule the syndrome out. Her bleeding resolved after a catheter-based valve replacement. The twenty twenty-six report walks through the diagnostic reasoning. It reminds clinicians to treat the valve when the pattern fits, even without visible lesions.
pmc-13177458:
Ana-Corina Miller and three colleagues measured what happened when the UK replaced its main disability benefit. The aim was to support extra costs while holding down program growth.

The team linked census records to benefit data for the whole of England and Wales. That let them track who started claiming before and after the change. The chance of moving onto disability benefits fell sharply after the reform. There were early signs of a partial bounce back the next year. The authors caution that slow claim handling may explain part of the drop. More work is needed to split delay effects from true claim success.
pmc-13183858:
Chuyu Lao and four co-authors study blood infections from a hard-to-treat gut germ in a Chinese hospital, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. The germ can resist vancomycin, a key drug used when others fail. The team looked at which patients got the resistant form and how they fared.

They reviewed forty-eight patients in Guangzhou with proven blood infections, from two thousand twenty-two to two thousand twenty-four. About thirty-one percent of cases resisted the drug. Those patients were more often in intensive care, and more of them died. Stay in intensive care and past use of a related drug class were each linked to the resistant form on their own. The results may help local infection control.
pmc-13184558:
Zhen Ma and colleagues wrote a review in 2026 on neutrophils, the most common white blood cells. These cells are first responders against infection. They also help keep the body in balance. The review focuses on the varied states these cells can take. It also covers NETosis, a process where cells cast out web-like traps. Older views treated neutrophils as short-lived and simple. New tools now show far more variety.

The authors trace these cells through infections, autoimmune disease, and cancer. They then survey treatments that target neutrophils or their traps. They also describe new methods that map cell states in fine detail. The review proposes a neutrophil immune clock idea. It frames cell responses as changing over time during illness. That timing view, they argue, could guide when treatments should be given.
pmc-13185858:
Cristine Yde Ohki and co-authors test whether fish-oil fatty acids calm an overactive growth signal in brain stem cells from adults with ADHD. Their study appeared in 2026. The Wnt pathway steers brain development and upkeep, and the group's earlier work found it overactive in cells from children with the disorder. Baseline pathway activity did not differ between adult patient and control cells, unlike the child findings. The team still probed how the fats and the drug moved the signal from that baseline. The authors frame omega-3 as a possible gentle add-on worth further study in adult ADHD.
pmc-13185958:
Wang, Zhang, Cheng, and Deng build a screening model for depression in older hospital patients, in work from twenty twenty-six. Depression is common in older adults and raises illness, death, and care costs. Hospitalized elders are especially vulnerable, yet screening is often skipped.

Clinical data came from more than eleven thousand inpatients aged sixty and up over two years. The team used those records to develop and validate a convenient risk screening tool. A simple score that nurses can apply at admission could flag patients who need full assessment and early support, rather than relying on chance detection.
pmc-13190558:
David Casero-Benavente and colleagues surveyed Spanish nurses in 2026 about how competent they feel when facing intimate partner violence. The researchers surveyed just over two hundred nursing professionals with a validated competence scale built for nurses.

That scale measures four dimensions: intervening and referring, detecting and assessing abuse, documenting cases, and giving psychosocial support. The paper reports where perceived competence ran lowest across the group. Knowing exactly which skills feel weakest tells training programs where to aim. A nurse who doubts her documentation or referral skills may hesitate at the decisive moment. The study turns a vague worry about readiness into a specific training agenda.
pmc-13194558:
Soohyun Chun, Sanghyeon Yu, Hyun Gu Lee, and Man Kim wrote a 2026 review on helping engineered immune cells last longer inside solid tumors. The review gathers new fixes aimed at those power plants. One line targets a misplaced protein that floods the cell with a metabolite locking in exhaustion. Another builds cells that sense low oxygen and import more fuel. Gene editing found switches that stop the cells from killing each other or themselves. A bolder idea transfers whole mitochondria between cells through tiny tubes. The authors also note computer methods to spot when tumors steal mitochondria from the therapy cells.
pmc-13195958:

pmc-13196158:

Before discharge, one hundred twenty-seven children, one hundred thirty-six adolescents, and ninety-three those who care for them completed a satisfaction questionnaire, from which information and participation subscales were built. Gender and diagnosis also shaped some ratings.
pmc-13196958:
Wen Wei Chung and colleagues report a 2026 interview study in Malaysia on a health app for HIV care. HIV is a virus that weakens the immune system. The team asked people living with HIV and clinic staff what would help or hinder use of a phone app for self-care.

They spoke in depth with seventeen patients, nine doctors, and two nurses at one large hospital clinic. People saw gains in knowledge and easier access to visits, refills, and records. They also worried about too much content and about privacy and data safety. Peer or staff endorsement would boost uptake. The findings guide design of an app shaped around patient needs.
pmc-13202658:
Artificial intelligence is arriving in tribal healthcare, and a 2026 symposium report led by Vanessa Hiratsuka records how Alaska Native health leaders want it governed. They also distinguished quality improvement uses from research uses, and called for centralized expertise to guide future implementation across the system.
pmc-13202958: A retraction note issued in 2026 withdraws a 2022 randomized trial by Hytham Atia and co-authors comparing umbilical cord milking with delayed cord clamping in premature newborns. The editor retracted the article after concerns about the randomization process were confirmed by statistical review, which found baseline gaps between groups that proper randomization should not produce. The authors were offered a chance to resubmit a corrected version but did not respond to the publisher. Only the retraction note itself survives here.
pmc-13203358:

The team confirmed the binding with purified proteins using surface plasmon resonance in the laboratory. Short peptides matching the contact points prevented the proteins from joining, which sketches a route to drugs that could strengthen existing cancer treatments.
pmc-13204458:

These cancers shrug off standard chemo but have shown striking responses to immune care in the last decade. The authors walk through test tools, why they fail at times, and hands on ways to dodge those errors. They then trace the shift to single and dual immune care in spread disease, who gains most, and what to do when care fails. Immune care may even allow no surgery paths in early disease.
pmc-13205458:

Later phases prototype and test the chatbot, then examine equity and accessibility for families at risk of digital exclusion.
pmc-13207158:

Grouping users by engagement revealed high, medium, and low tiers with distinct patterns for designers to address.
pmc-13207858:

Knowledge and skill gaps, physical discomfort, the burden of infant care, thin professional and family support, and shaky confidence all appeared in the accounts. Barriers fed each other: weak knowledge dulled urgency, and missing feedback deepened skill doubts, suggesting fixes must work on several fronts at once.
pmc-13208758:

She applied it five times weekly for twelve weeks, tolerating mild to moderate skin inflammation without body-wide effects. Repeat mapping biopsies afterward showed complete clearance of the abnormal pigment cells, supporting cream therapy for carefully chosen patients.
pmc-13215558:

For small collections, a second model adds multi-scale attention, lighter convolutions, and adversarial training. On standard benchmarks the large-data model outperformed a leading compact rival, and the small-data model gained roughly three to four points when training data was cut to a tenth. The author argues that matching architecture to dataset size is the key lesson.
pmc-13216758:

Four prompting strategies were compared, from bare instructions to a multimodule pipeline with post-processing; more structure consistently helped. On held-out notes, the gpt-oss-120B model clearly beat Llama 3.3-70B, reaching F1 scores of 0.88 for symptom extraction and 0.87 for code mapping. The authors argue such pipelines can scale symptom surveillance without exporting patient data.
pmc-13216858:
Seungwoo Kim and co-authors present a 2026 nationwide cohort study from Korea. The question is whether steroid creams, long assumed to stay in the skin, can raise the risk of type 2 diabetes over years of use. Systemic steroids are a known cause; the topical evidence was thin.

They developed diabetes at a modestly higher rate, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.13. Frequent use carried the highest risk at 1.27, and even the moderate-potency group, at 1.15, approached the systemic steroid group's 1.20. The authors advise prescribers to weigh diabetes risk factors when topical steroids are used often or long.
pmc-13217258:
R. K. Rishabh and co-authors present a 2026 case report of a genetic overgrowth syndrome masquerading as acromegaly in a 33-year-old man. He stood nearly two metres tall with coarse facial features, an enlarged tongue, a jutting jaw, and extra nipples, a combination that pointed first to growth hormone excess.

Hormone testing ruled acromegaly out: his IGF-1 was actually low and growth hormone suppressed normally after glucose, while a tiny pituitary spot on MRI looked incidental. He also had mild intellectual disability and a similarly tall younger brother. Gene sequencing found a stop-making variant in GPC3, confirming Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome, with his mother a carrier. The authors urge clinicians to consider overgrowth syndromes behind acromegaloid features.
pmc-13218158:
Helga Birgit Bjørnarå, Gerd Monika Flodgren, and Arnfinn Helleve describe a 2026 protocol for a scoping review of policy monitoring indexes for non-communicable diseases. Proven, affordable policy actions against these diseases exist, such as the World Health Organization's Best Buys, but governments need ways to track whether the policies are being put in place. Several composite indexes have been built for that monitoring job.

Eligible studies must describe a composite index that monitors implementation of government policies aimed at non-communicable diseases or their risk factors, within the World Health Organization's European region. Screening and data extraction will proceed in duplicate, and results will be summarized with descriptive statistics and visuals. The review sits inside the Joint Action PreventNCD project, a European Commission-funded effort across 25 countries.
pmc-13219158:
Kyle Tuohy and colleagues search for pre-treatment clues to who will suffer brain and hormone damage after radiation in a 2026 cohort study. Radiation remains central to treating primary and metastatic brain tumors, but thinking problems and hormone failure can surface afterward, and doctors cannot forecast them. Better prediction would let clinicians warn patients and design preventive studies.

Eighty patients treated at one institution with radiation as part of tumor therapy were assessed across five toxicity measures, with change on a mental status exam as the main outcome. Two findings stood out in adjusted models as the strongest predictors of decline: elevated homocysteine, an amino acid linked to vascular injury, and carrying the ApoE4 variant, tied to Alzheimer's risk. Homocysteine tracked with white matter change on MRI, and ApoE4 with new hormone deficiencies. The team built a nomogram estimating patient risk across all five outcomes and calls for validation.
pmc-13219958:
Jelle P. van der List and colleagues isolate the outcomes of restorative treatment for kneecap lesions in a 2026 review and meta-analysis. Cartilage damage on the patella causes disability, but reviews mixed it with damage to the groove it slides in, blurring the results. It admitted only studies of isolated lesions, with at least ten patients and a year of follow-up.

Thirty-six studies covering 1,058 patients, average age thirty-two and follow-up over five years, met the bar. Implantation was the commonest operation, then osteochondral autograft transfer, then a scaffold, AMIC. Failure risk ran lowest for the autograft at 1.7 percent, with the two near nine percent, though the autograft also treated the smallest lesions. Scores favored the autograft and scaffold on scales. When the analysis was restricted to lesions under three and a half square centimeters, failure rates equalized across three, a nuance they emphasize for planning.
pmc-13220158:
Alison McCallion and seven colleagues investigated a little-studied immune cell, the T-helper 9 cell, in endometriosis. The disease grows endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus, causing pelvic pain and infertility through chronic inflammation. Th9 cells drive several other inflammatory diseases, suggesting a parallel role here. Transferred cells raised a blood inflammatory marker and altered gene activity in mice. The twenty twenty-six study builds the first case that this cell type helps lesions grow, nominating a new drug target for a common, undertreated disease.
pmc-13222558:
Yan Zhao and co-authors survey nanoparticle drug delivery systems for cancer treatment, in a 2026 review. Most cancer drugs poison the whole body while chasing tumors, and metastasis drives most cancer deaths. Carriers covered range from metal particles to liposomes and polymer micelles, including products already approved for patients.

Loading drugs into nanoparticles can dissolve stubborn compounds, keep them circulating longer, and steer them toward tumors. Those traits promise stronger effect with less collateral toxicity. The review explains carrier composition, targeting strategies reaching even subcellular compartments, and approved examples. The authors present the field as the future direction for tumor therapy and a base for faster clinical translation.
pmc-13223658:
Bill Berners-Lee and co-authors explore why eating the DASH way is hard on Montserrat, in a 2026 interview study of sixteen adults with hypertension. The diet, rich in produce, whole grains, and pulses and low in salt and fatty meats, is promoted in local primary care. Interviews held in mid-2025 ran through a behavior lens to sort the obstacles.

Five themes shaped adherence: understanding of hypertension and the diet, access to healthy food, skills and confidence, cultural practices, and readiness to change. Cost, availability, and seasonality of fruit, vegetables, and fish bit hardest. Cooking and growing skills helped, while label reading lagged. Suggested fixes included nutrition education and financial support.
pmc-13224758:
Joud S Makki and colleagues survey a 2026 cross-sectional study of pregnant women in Saudi Arabia about the Tdap vaccine, which guards mothers and newborns against tetanus, diphtheria, and whooping cough. Uptake in pregnancy there remains low, at roughly a quarter to a third of women. Questionnaires from 398 women aged eighteen to forty mapped what they knew and felt.
