Higher education tracked with better knowledge. Most women held positive views of vaccination overall, but about seventy-one percent worried about side effects, pointing to safety-focused education as the lever most likely to raise uptake.
pmc-13225158:
Ziwei Huang and colleagues run a 2026 questionnaire study of orthodontic patients who wear removable braces, asking whether believing masks hide unattractive appliances changes how faithfully patients wear them. The survey covered 214 patients, mostly women aged nineteen to thirty, and recorded recommended versus actual wear time, split between daytime and total hours.

Just over half agreed that masks made unaesthetic appliances easier to accept. Surprisingly, holding that belief came with lower daytime and overall compliance. Patients with neutral feelings about masks wore their appliances more during the day than those with strong views either way. Daytime wear strongly predicted total compliance, and men reported more mask-related acceptance than women.
pmc-13229358:
Winsy Wing Sze Wong and colleagues set out a 2026 trial protocol testing whether immersive virtual reality strengthens a computerised speech therapy for Cantonese speakers living with chronic aphasia after stroke. Script training has patients rehearse personalised everyday dialogues, and about a fifth of stroke survivors face lasting language difficulty. The trial will recruit 120 participants into three groups.

One group will practise scripts inside virtual scenes of daily life, a second will use the same training with still photographs, and a third will receive no training. Assessors who do not know group assignments will score aphasia severity, functional communication, and quality of life before and after. The comparison isolates what immersion itself adds to an established therapy format.
pmc-13229458:
Bianca Thakkar and colleagues describe in 2026 a sixty-one-year-old woman with neurofibromatosis type 1 who had several small bowel tumors at once. Scans showed multiple masses in the jejunum plus a separate lesion near the duodenum. Such stromal tumors in this condition often appear in many places and respond poorly to drug therapy.

Surgeons removed thirty-three centimeters of jejunum that held three masses felt by hand, and testing found four stromal tumors in total. Care continued for the duodenal lesion, which proved to be a neuroendocrine tumor alongside the stromal tumors. The pairing is described as exceptionally uncommon. Careful mapping of each lesion before surgery helped the team choose how much bowel to remove.
pmc-13230158:
Bo Zhu and Hailong Chen compare two scope surgeries for a pinched neck nerve in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Both are keyhole methods done through the back of the neck for a slipped disc. One uses two portals, the other a single channel.

Records covered one hundred twenty-three patients treated from two thousand twenty to two thousand twenty-three. The groups started alike in age, pain, and disability scores. The two-portal group had shorter operating and imaging times. Its neck and arm pain and disability scores improved more at every check. Good outcomes were near ninety-seven percent against ninety-two. Nerve irritation and small tears were rarer in the two-portal group too. The authors favor the two-portal method.
pmc-13231158:
Zeynep Yagmur Yilmaz and Raihan El-Naas report in 2026 a teenager whose overactive thyroid came from eating raw cow thyroid bought online. The nineteen-year-old showed the classic lab pattern of too much thyroid hormone paired with a suppressed control hormone. Antibody tests were negative and the gland looked normal on ultrasound, which pointed away from usual causes.

Supportive care alone settled the illness, and hormone levels fell steadily during the hospital stay. A careful history about diet, supplements, and online health trends proved central to solving the case. Unusual sources like animal organs can hide behind a common hormone picture. Clinicians who ask early about such products may spare patients needless scans and wrong long-term treatment.
pmc-13231558:
Josephine T V Greenbrook and colleagues explore in 2026 how senior doctors keep patients visible as persons while teaching juniors. Hospital work prizes speed and measured output, which can push the human side of care out of view. Seventeen physicians at two Swedish university hospitals gave long interviews about supervising students and trainees.

Supervisors described making personhood a named part of clinical reasoning, not a soft extra. They modeled humility inside steep hierarchies and defended humane values against organizational pressure. Keeping their own ethical focus took steady inner work, fresh reminders, and energy drawn from contact with patients and learners. Teaching renewed their own commitments in return, so formation flowed both ways.
pmc-13232558:
Nicole Novaresi and colleagues target in 2026 a surface protein that helps KRAS-driven lung cancers grow and hide. The protein PCDH7 appears at high levels in lung adenocarcinoma and tracks with poor outcomes for patients. Removing it in mouse models shrank tumors and extended survival, marking it as a drug target.

Antibodies built against the protein blocked a key growth pathway inside tumor cells and slowed tumors across several models. One lead antibody made tumors respond better to two approved pathway drugs given alongside it. A human-ready version also helped immune cells kill tumor cells directly. Treated tumors drew in more active killer immune cells, which strengthened the overall attack.
pmc-13232758:
Mohamed Sarsari and colleagues recount in 2026 a rescue where a heart stent poking far into the aorta was pulled back out with a snare. A sixty-year-old man with diabetes arrived with a heart attack pattern from a tight narrowing at the very start of the left main artery. During the emergency procedure, patient movement pushed the fresh stent too far out, and balloon work bent it.

Leaving the metal jutting out risked clots, loose debris, and valve trouble, so the team chose removal while the stent was still fresh. A loop snare caught and extracted it cleanly, and a new stent was placed in the ideal spot. He recovered without complications, a rare bail-out that worked because it happened early.
pmc-13232858:
Sunny L Jardine and colleagues test in 2026 whether the simple rules managers use to pick fish-passage projects waste restoration money. Agencies often rank barriers by how much upstream habitat they block, sometimes weighting habitat quality by nearby natural land. Western Washington salmon rivers served as the case, with rule-based picks benchmarked against fully optimized portfolios.

Judged on habitat quantity alone, the plain upstream-habitat rule captured nearly all the gain an optimizer could reach. Adding the popular natural-cover quality proxy cut performance almost in half, because it steered picks away from connected habitat. Better rules would score quality in ways tied to actual fish gains. With billions flowing into river repair, rule design is money design.
pmc-13233658:
Lauren Cunniff and Johannes Weickenmeier published a 2026 imaging study on how the brain's fluid-filled ventricles change shape with age. Ventricles enlarge steadily in normal ageing and faster in Alzheimer's disease, yet the mechanical strain this places on surrounding tissue is barely understood. Using Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative scans, the team followed fifty cognitively normal adults aged seventy to seventy-five across four to five years.

Image registration measured how each person's ventricles deformed between scans. Expansion was mostly uniform, averaging just under a millimeter of outward movement, yet strain concentrated sharply along the ventricle edges and the rear chamber called the atrium. About twenty-nine percent of the wall stretched while only a small share shrank, and no sex differences appeared. The maps show where ageing brains bear the greatest mechanical load.
pmc-13233758:
Liisa Hakaste and colleagues published a 2026 pooled analysis tracing metabolic changes in the years before diabetes appears. Adult-onset diabetes splits into subgroups with different causes, from autoimmune and insulin-deficient forms to insulin-resistant, obesity-related, and age-related types. Nine European cohorts contributed 3,309 people who later developed diabetes and 13,963 matched controls, with measurements grouped into three windows before diagnosis.

The subgroups already differed more than a decade ahead. The obesity-related group carried body mass far above controls early and stayed there, while weight climbed progressively in the insulin-resistant group. Insulin responses to glucose also split the groups, running high in insulin-resistant and obesity-related cases but low in insulin-deficient and age-related ones. Even the autoimmune group showed metabolic syndrome features. The findings suggest prevention could start earlier and differ by subgroup.
pmc-13233958:
Chen Wu and colleagues published a 2026 engineering review of silicon carbide pressure sensors built for extreme heat. Jets, geothermal wells, nuclear plants, and even Venus probes need pressure readings where ordinary silicon sensors fail through electrical leakage or warping. Silicon carbide, a wide-bandgap semiconductor, resists heat, radiation, and corrosion, making it the leading replacement material.

The review traces how these heat-proof pressure sensors have evolved. It then walks through the craft of building them from this stubborn stock: chip layout, making the parts, contacts that survive heat, packaging, and strength testing. Laboratory prototypes still fall short on operating temperature range, sensitivity, and long-term stability. The authors close by mapping the technical problems that must be solved before such sensors move from prototypes into routine extreme-environment service.
pmc-13234258:
Haifang Mao and co-authors reported in 2026 on tiny capsules designed to protect citronellal, a fragrant plant compound with antibacterial action. The capsules were built from black bean protein and gum Arabic joined through a process called complex coacervation. Strawberries were the test fruit, because they spoil quickly from microbes, water loss, and softening. The team searched for the best ingredient ratio and acidity for forming the capsules.

A ratio of four to one worked best under mildly acidic conditions, and the capsules trapped the compound efficiently. Encapsulated citronellal stayed more stable during storage and heat, then released slowly over time. Treated strawberries resisted spoilage microbes better and lost less weight and firmness. The findings support plant-based capsules as a preservation aid for delicate fruit.
pmc-13234458:
Haozhou Shen and co-authors reviewed in 2026 tools for measuring frailty before and around surgery. Frailty means reduced physical reserve across body systems, and it raises the risk of complications, slow recovery, and death. Older surgical patients are increasingly likely to be frail, yet standard preoperative checks often miss the condition. The review covered recent advances from 2019 to 2025 plus older foundational studies.

Different tools are compared for how well they predict outcomes and how practical they are in clinics. Strengths, limits, and fit within enhanced recovery pathways receive close attention. The authors note problems with timing, standardization, and adaptation to surgical settings. Their aim is to help clinicians choose a tool and interpret its result for a given patient. Better selection could support safer anaesthesia and recovery planning.
pmc-13235658:
Daina Baublyte and colleagues built in 2026 machine learning models to flag people at risk of gut and digestive organ cancers in South Korea. Cancers were rare in their long-followed cohort, which makes prediction models favour the healthy majority. Their new undersampling method trims the majority class while preserving the population's structure, mimicking matched study designs. Several common resampling tricks served as comparisons across six classifier types.

Only about two percent of more than seven thousand cohort members developed these cancers over fourteen years. Models trained with the new sampling method showed better sensitivity, especially among more complex classifiers. The best model caught roughly three quarters of future cases in the test group. Simpler logistic regression performed in a balanced way even without any resampling in their results. The authors used behavioural and metabolic predictors that patients can plausibly change.
pmc-13236658:
Sayna Norouzi and co-authors interviewed in 2026 doctors, patients, and caregivers across six countries about two rare progressive kidney diseases. Twenty-one clinicians, thirteen patients, and eight caregivers shared experiences of diagnosis, burden, and management between mid-2024 and early 2025. Mild early symptoms often delayed recognition of the diseases in patient accounts. Specialists also cited poor disease awareness and reluctance toward kidney biopsy as barriers.

Exhaustion and deep fatigue ranked as the most burdensome symptoms for patients and caregivers alike. Keeping the disease stable was the treatment goal patients named most often in interviews. Available options at the time were limited, and dialysis weighed mainly heavily on daily life. Caregivers described heavy physical and emotional support roles that strained their own mental wellbeing. Clinicians expressed hope about new drugs then approaching approval for these conditions.
pmc-13236758:
Sergio N. Galarce and colleagues published a modeling study in 2026 on how animals tell familiar objects from new ones. Their work uses Allan Wagner's Standard Operating Procedures model, called SOP, which explains recognition through priming. A primed stimulus draws less exploration because its mental representation is already active.

The authors built a numerical version of SOP and simulated three standard tasks: spontaneous object recognition, relative recency, and object-in-place. The simulations matched the usual preferences for new, earlier-seen, and moved objects. The paper also suggests new experiments that vary spacing, location, and distraction. Such tests could help separate memory effects that come from the object itself from effects carried by context.
pmc-13237258:
Zhaoyi Lu and co-authors applied Mendelian randomization in 2026 to ask whether gut microbes causally change the risk of head and neck cancer. The surviving signals covered two bacterial classes and a list of families and genera, some raising risk and others lowering it. Direction tests supported the assumed causal arrow. pmc-13238258:
Cian P. Most evidence was retrospective, reference standards varied, and several studies carried moderate to high bias risk. pmc-13238358:
Antigona Aliu and colleagues presented a German-language case series in 2026 of ten adults with dermatomyositis, an inflammatory muscle disease, marked by striking violet-red swelling around the eyes. In nine of the ten cases, work-up confirmed an underlying cancer. Drawing on their cases plus published markers and clinical features, the authors propose a simple criteria list to judge whether a patient's dermatomyositis is likely cancer-linked. They argue the eye sign should trigger a careful cancer search. The series is small, so the list is offered as practical guidance rather than proof.
pmc-13238958:

The review synthesizes evidence on molecular markers tied to that resistance. Reliable markers could sort patients before treatment, flag those needing stronger or different therapy, and point to drugs that re-sensitize tumors. The authors frame biomarker-guided personalization as the path to making radiotherapy succeed in more patients.
pmc-13239058:

pmc-13240358:

One marker also ran lower in the deeper belly fat and in patients who had type 2 diabetes. In cultured fat cells, markers shifted with cell maturation, insulin, glucose level, and the diabetes drug metformin, helping explain earlier contradictions.
pmc-13240558:

pmc-13241458:

pmc-13241658:

pmc-13241758:

pmc-13241958:

pmc-13242358:

pmc-13242758:

pmc-13242858:

pmc-13243358:

pmc-13243758:

pmc-13245058:

pmc-13245558:

The authors call wider use of shared questions the next step toward statewide action.
pmc-13247158:

pmc-13248058:

pmc-13248458:

pmc-13250458:

pmc-13251158:

pmc-13251258:

pmc-13251758:

pmc-13251858:

pmc-13252758:

pmc-13253258:

pmc-13253658:

pmc-13254758:

pmc-13254958:

pmc-13257158:

pmc-13257458:

pmc-13257658:

pmc-13258758:

pmc-13260158:

pmc-13263858:

pmc-13264058:

pmc-13264258:

pmc-13264358:

pmc-13264558:

The authors weigh drugs that block DPP4, antibody treatments, and decoy versions of the protein. They frame DPP4 as a broad target for future antiviral work.
pmc-13264858:
Mônica Cristina da Costa Drago Souza and a large team present a 2026 trial protocol on genitourinary syndrome of menopause, a set of vaginal and urinary symptoms from low estrogen after menopause. Vaginal estriol cream helps many women, yet symptoms often persist. The trial tests whether adding a gentle erbium laser treatment beats cream alone.

All women in the trial get the cream daily for two weeks, then twice a week for 16 weeks. Half also get three real laser sessions about a month apart, and half get sham sessions, with neither side told which. The main measure is a vaginal health index four months after the last session. Other checks cover symptom severity, vaginal germ mix, quality of life, and sexual function. Women aged 45 to 70 with clear symptoms can join.
pmc-13264958:
Abdur Rahman and colleagues review evidence linking ultra-processed food with stomach cancer risk, in a 2026 systematic review. Consumption of such foods has risen worldwide. Links with several chronic diseases are known, while evidence for gastric cancer stayed mixed. The review gathered observational studies published over three decades.

Seventeen studies with about 277,000 participants were included. Eight found higher risk with higher ultra-processed food intake, three found none, and six found mixed results. Processed meats, fried foods, and sugary drinks were tied to risk most often. Differences in diet measurement explain part of the variation. The authors see a possible link that needs stronger studies.
pmc-13265158:
Zhongshun He and colleagues investigate baicalin, a plant compound, against melanoma cells, in a 2026 laboratory study. Melanoma is among the most aggressive skin cancers, and treatment options remain limited. Baicalin had shown anti-cancer promise in earlier work. How it acts on melanoma was not fully known.

Melanoma cells treated with baicalin grew, moved, and invaded less, while cell death rose with dose. Computer analyses predicted targets, and docking tests pointed to a growth receptor called EGFR. Further experiments showed baicalin dampened a growth pathway driven by that receptor. Forcing the receptor higher had the opposite effect. The findings suggest a mechanism worth testing further.
pmc-13265258:
Jinjia Zhang and colleagues test a small RNA as a predictor of lymph node spread in stomach cancer, in a 2026 study. Node spread strongly shapes outlook after surgery. Scans detect it with limited accuracy. Data from a public cancer database and a Chinese hospital covered 416 patients.

Four factors independently linked to node spread, including tumour stage and grade. The RNA, miR-1287-5p, added predictive value beyond clinical factors. A chart combining all four estimated spread risk for each patient. Accuracy was strong in the main cohort and moderate in the support cohort. The tool could aid surgical planning.
pmc-13266158:
Ji-Yeong Ku and the team compare gut microbes in Korean Hanwoo calves with viral diarrhoea (2026). Newborn calf gut mixes are still forming, making diarrhoea common and disruptive. Faeces from seven healthy calves and eight with diarrhoea were checked. Two viruses, rotavirus and coronavirus, were found in sick calves.

Overall variety differed little between healthy and infected calves. Cases of the first virus showed lower variety scores than cases of the second. Community make-up split clearly by group. Each virus shifted germ classes in its own way, and a helpful genus fell with both infections. The results support pathogen-by-pathogen gut work in calves.
pmc-13266258:
Qiang Gao and co-authors describe in 2026 DynaTOF, a software system that reads heart ultrasound scans to spot tetralogy of Fallot and judge risk after surgery. This birth defect of the heart is serious, and early, correct detection shapes survival. Data came from four centers and covered 1,986 children: healthy controls, look-alike conditions, and confirmed cases.

Five modules did the work in sequence. They sorted scan views, measured key heart widths, merged video with those measures to make the diagnosis, and predicted later risk scores. A last module split patients into high-risk and low-risk groups. Scores were strong across tasks, so the team sees DynaTOF aiding screening, surgical planning, and follow-up care for babies with this defect.
pmc-13266358:
Youngmin Kim and colleagues rethink the one-hour surgery target for regional trauma centres in South Korea, published in 2026. The metric demands emergency surgery within an hour for bleeding abdominal trauma with low blood pressure. Records covered 425 patients at two centres from 2019 to 2022. Matched comparisons tested the threshold.

Just over half reached surgery within the hour. In-hospital death did not differ between early and delayed groups, even after matching. Age, consciousness, blood pressure, transfusion volume, and injury severity predicted death instead. Complications rose as delay lengthened. The authors propose metrics that capture whole resuscitation quality, not one clock.
pmc-13267158:
Woon Teen Sia and colleagues wrote a 2026 study on how well ultrasound predicts a baby's weight before birth in Malaysia. Guessing fetal weight guides many delivery choices, yet scans are not always on hand in basic care. The team followed women with single babies at a large hospital near the end of pregnancy.

The study covered 153 women scanned at 37 to just under 39 weeks. Estimated weights were within 10 percent of true birth weight for about 69 percent of babies. Accuracy was best when the scan came within a day of delivery. Mother's weight, past births, and diabetes in pregnancy affected accuracy. The authors stress examiner training and wider scan access.
pmc-13267558:
Maureen Walton and a large team test in 2026 a phone app designed to cut cannabis use among young adults who use regularly but rarely seek treatment. Over thirty days, 122 participants answered surveys twice daily and were randomly sent, or not sent, support messages chosen by a learning algorithm. Follow-up checks came one and two months after the trial began.

The app proved workable: most participants downloaded it, completed most surveys, and rated the messages as caring and respectful. Receiving a message lifted short-term engagement with the app, though it did not directly lower next-step cannabis use. People who engaged more tended to report fewer use days later. The authors see promise and call for refining the messages to turn engagement into behavior change.
pmc-13269358:
Yusuke Saito and co-authors identify in 2026 an enzyme from a soil bacterium that breaks down polyamide 4, a bio-based plastic prized for strength and natural degradability. A marine version of the enzyme was known, but the land-based counterpart had never been characterized. The team found the gene in a soil bacterium, then produced the enzyme inside two different host microbes for comparison.

One host, a Brevibacillus strain, secreted enzyme with more than double the plastic-degrading activity of the E. coli version. Computer modeling split the enzyme into three parts: a binding region, a middle region, and the cutting region, with the outer two closely matching the marine enzyme. Similar genes turned up in ocean environmental DNA, hinting at a wide family of plastic degraders in nature.
pmc-13270058:
Jueun Oh, Yoon-Seok Chung, and SangJoon Lee published a review in 2026 on recent advances in mpox, a viral disease whose recent outbreaks spread widely between people. Disease severity, they note, cannot be explained by virus amount alone. The review draws together virus genetics, early immune sensing, inflammation, and immune evasion.

Host factors shape outcomes, including the strength of interferon signaling, control of inflammasomes, which are inflammation switches, and natural killer cell function. People with weakened immunity, including advanced HIV infection, face more severe and prolonged disease. Genetic diversity in the virus and its tricks for dodging immunity are also covered. The authors aim to explain why cases vary so much and to guide care of high-risk groups.
pmc-13271058:
Håkon Reikvam led a 2026 pilot safety study of hypoxic red blood cells, blood stored with oxygen and carbon dioxide removed to keep it in better condition, given by transfusion. Two patient groups were studied: people with blood cancers who need regular transfusions, and people with acute burns having surgery.

Twenty patients aged 27 to 96 received the stored blood, ten in each group. No adverse events linked to the hypoxic blood were reported within 24 hours or up to seven days. Haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein, rose by an average of 1.2 units in the blood cancer group and 0.3 in the burn group soon after transfusion. The authors call the product safe and well tolerated here.
pmc-13271258:
Nada Abu-Shraie is lead author of a 2026 economic analysis of upadacitinib for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, a long-lasting itchy skin disease, in Saudi Arabia. The study used mathematical models to judge whether the drug gives good value to the public payer and what wider use would do to budgets.

Over a lifetime model, upadacitinib at 15 milligrams gave 0.21 extra quality-adjusted life years, years lived in good health, and cost less than the comparison drug dupilumab by an amount given in Saudi riyals. Raising its market share over five years was linked to estimated savings of 1.5 billion riyals. The authors caution that model inputs and local data limits add uncertainty.
pmc-13271558:
Ankush Kawali and colleagues write in 2026 about gene sequencing tests for epidemic retinitis, an eye inflammation that follows a fever. Doctors have long suspected rickettsial infection, partly because patients improve on doxycycline. Standard blood tests, though, rarely prove which germ is responsible.

The team ran a broad sequencing panel on fluid drawn from the front of the eye in cases with inflammation there. None of the samples held the rickettsial or typhoid germs the panel covered. Only three patients tested positive, and those results looked like false alarms from very low read counts. The letter questions how much sequencing adds in this disease.
pmc-13271958:
Zhuqin Xiang and coauthors test in 2026 whether pairing two tissue features predicts survival in mouth cancer better than either alone. Tumor budding, where small cell clusters break away at the tumor edge, signals aggressive spread. Tertiary lymphoid structures, organized immune clusters, signal the opposite.

Records from 510 patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma were scored for both features on stained tissue. Heavy budding matched worse survival, while mature lymphoid structures matched better outcomes. A combined index separated patients more sharply than either feature alone. A prediction chart built on the index plus standard factors performed reliably in validation checks.
pmc-13272158:
Rong Hu and coauthors trace in 2026 a pathway linking iron imbalance to early aging of the placenta in preeclampsia, a dangerous pregnancy condition. The placenta in this disease shows signs of premature senescence, and the protective protein SIRT1 was found reduced in patient tissue. Its partner p53 is a known driver of cell aging.

Lowering SIRT1 in placental cells increased aging markers and harmful secretions while slowing growth and movement. Activating the protein in animals eased both placental aging and disease-like features. Removing excess iron also calmed aging, and clearing aged cells partly restored iron balance, showing the two processes reinforce each other.
pmc-13272358:
Mihajlo Bosnjak and coauthors review in 2026 a paradox at the heart of Parkinson's disease: cells need energy to run their cleanup system, yet energy failure is a hallmark of the disease. The cleanup process, autophagy, normally rises under energy stress, but completing it consumes ATP, the cell's fuel. In Parkinson's, faulty mitochondria drain that fuel supply.

The authors propose a two-phase pattern where mild early energy loss stimulates cleanup while severe loss stalls it midway. Undigested cargo, including worn-out mitochondria, then piles up and deepens the energy crisis. This vicious cycle framing suggests treatment must restore energy, not just prod the cleanup machinery.
pmc-13272858:
Shanshan Xu leads a 2026 study of drug pairs that can cause serotonin syndrome, a dangerous reaction from too much serotonin. Such risks grow as drugs that raise serotonin spread into pain and infection care. The team used a review of past work, United States safety reports, and a check of five drug interaction tools.

High-risk pairs went beyond mood drugs to include the antibiotic linezolid, the pain drug fentanyl, and methylene blue. Strong signals showed for linezolid with sertraline and fentanyl with venlafaxine. The five tools often disagreed, and 10.16 percent of pairs appeared in none of them, so one tool alone can miss real risk.
pmc-13273058:
Pascal Hauff leads a 2026 study using large language models to maintain a database of branded food products. Branded food data help track modern diets, but the data are vast, fast-changing, and uneven in quality. The team built a fully automated pipeline to collect, standardize, and enrich product data down to ingredient level.

A fine-tuned model beat human experts at parsing and mapping product data. Models without fine-tuning performed poorly, while even modest amounts of tuning data improved results a lot. The authors say language models offer a scalable way to keep food databases consistent, and can help estimate ingredient amounts and nutrients not declared on labels.
pmc-13273258:
Thomas Braun and colleagues studied how alpha-synuclein fibrils affect mitochondria in a 2026 cell study. Clumps of alpha-synuclein mark Parkinson's disease and related disorders, and mitochondria, the cell's power units, are also damaged. How the two connect is still not fully clear.

Using electron microscopy, they examined human nerve like cells exposed to alpha-synuclein fibrils. Treated cells showed defects in the folded inner structure of mitochondria. The mitochondria also shed more small bubble like vesicles, a conserved response that echoes how bacteria release membrane vesicles. Protein analysis backed the images, finding shifts in proteins that shape the inner folds and guide vesicle traffic. The authors suggest this shedding may matter for diagnosis and treatment research.
pmc-13273358:
Amy McDermott wrote a 2026 news feature on hydrologic whiplash, sudden swings between very wet and very dry conditions, driven by climate change. She opens with California at Christmas 2022, when severe drought gave way within days to a series of atmospheric rivers. Nine strong storms in three weeks caused flooding, 22 deaths, and billions in losses.

Researchers argue that droughts and floods should no longer be studied only in isolation, since back-to-back extremes can amplify harm. Such swings strain water storage, and forecasting models trained on older data anticipate them poorly, because rapid flips were rarer in the past. The piece urges water managers to plan for whiplash events.
pmc-13273858:
Ventimiglia and colleagues follow men whose PSA stayed stable on prostate drugs after a negative biopsy. Their 2026 journal article is a nationwide Swedish population study. PSA is a blood marker for prostate cancer.

The study used the PCBaSe Xtend database. It included 1,248 men who started 5-alpha reductase inhibitor therapy. These drugs shrink the prostate. Of the men, 901 had stable PSA and 347 had rising PSA. At ten years, cancer incidence was 8.3 percent with stable PSA. It was 18 percent with rising PSA. Most cancers in the stable group were low grade. Prostate cancer death was very low with stable PSA. The standardized mortality ratio there was 0.19. The authors say PSA trends could tailor follow-up intensity.
pmc-13274158:
Xiaoyan Chen and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on how single-color light changes a prized medicinal herb. Salvia miltiorrhiza, known as danshen, is grown for root compounds used in heart remedies. The team exposed plants briefly to ultraviolet, blue, red, or far-red light, with white light as the comparison.

All single colors switched on defense responses, and overall chemical levels mostly fell versus white light. Red light raised the most individual compounds, though. Ultraviolet, red, and far-red light each boosted two key tanshinone compounds while lowering salvianolic acid A. Blue light cut the variety of microbes around the roots. The authors suggest light recipes could raise herb quality.
pmc-13274458:
Mariah K. Hermary and co-authors studied surface layer shedding in a methane eating bacterium in a 2026 paper. Some methanotrophs wear an S-layer, a protein shell over the cell surface. Their species, Methylomicrobium album BG8, turned out to shed this shell in unusual amounts.

Electron microscopy showed constant shedding in this species but not in seven relatives, even one with a similar shell. Shedding continued under every food, metal, and growth condition they tried. Protein analysis of the shed units found shell subunits plus transporters for calcium, vitamins, and iron carriers, which hints the shell helps gather metals. A strain adapted to strong acid lost its shell through gene damage. The authors suggest harnessing the secretion system for industry.
pmc-13274858:
Siqi Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article reviewing adverse events reported after HPV vaccination in the United States reporting system VAERS. Such systems collect voluntary reports and cannot prove a vaccine caused an event, but they can flag patterns. The team mined reports from 2006 to 2024 and required a signal to pass four different statistical tests.

In total, 77,909 reports were analyzed; 68.4 percent involved females and nearly half involved people under eighteen. About ninety percent of events were reported within thirty days of vaccination. Headache and fatigue were the most common complaints. Fainting was the most frequent statistical signal, while a racing-heart condition called POTS showed the strongest signal strength, meriting further study.
pmc-13275558:
Yunzhong Liu and colleagues report a 2026 before-and-after study of a fast-track recovery protocol for elderly hip fracture patients at a traditional Chinese medicine hospital in China. Such fractures bring long stays and many complications. The protocol, called ERAS, bundles early feeding, pain control, and quick mobilization, here with added traditional medicine elements.

Three hundred patients aged sixty-five and over were split by era: 146 treated conventionally from 2022 to 2023 and 154 under the new protocol from 2024 to 2025. The protocol group left hospital about 3.86 days sooner and suffered complications at 7.79 percent versus 15.07 percent. They also stood up far earlier, about twenty-nine versus fifty-three hours, reported less pain, and cost less overall.
pmc-13276458:
Fanny Chereau and a French outbreak team report a 2026 investigation of Cryptosporidium parvum infections. The parasite causes gut illness and spreads through water and food. Cases of one genotype jumped in France during 2025, far above the usual yearly count.

Standard gene typing could not split the outbreak further, so the team added a multi-locus repeat analysis. That method revealed two large, distinct strain profiles. Patient interviews tied one profile mostly to goat milk cheese and the other to packaged lamb's lettuce. Purchase records and traceback work located the product origins, and producers received preventive advice. The authors urge hygiene monitoring for raw milk goods and fresh produce.
pmc-13276558:
Si Wu and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a signaling chain in stem cells that may worsen or heal gum disease. Periodontitis, severe gum inflammation, destroys the tissue and bone holding teeth. Bone marrow stem cells can calm immune responses, and the team probed how an inflammation signal, interleukin-6, steers them.

In mice with induced gum disease, both interleukin-6 and a small RNA it controls were raised. The signal switched the RNA on through a partner protein called STAT3. Blocking the RNA eased an imbalance between two T cell types that drives inflammation. Stem cells pretreated with the RNA blocker were then injected into diseased mice. Treated animals regrew more periodontal tissue, with fewer bone-eating cells and less bone loss. The authors propose this chain as a treatment target.
pmc-13276758:
Barbora Lujka and colleagues study fat-like membrane molecules in colon cancer cells in a 2026 laboratory paper. These molecules, glycosphingolipids, help build cell membranes and steer growth and death signals. Their building block, lactosylceramide, is made by two enzymes that cancer cells may depend on.

The team dialled down each enzyme in a human colon cancer cell line using gene editing. Levels of lactosylceramide and several complex downstream lipids fell as expected. The altered cells then died more readily under oxaliplatin, a standard colorectal chemotherapy drug. Stress responses inside the cells also shifted. The authors frame the enzymes as possible levers for making chemotherapy bite harder.
pmc-13276858:
Di Hu and colleagues look for warning signs of severe Chlamydia pneumoniae pneumonia in children, in a 2026 study. The bacterium causes a share of childhood lung infections, mostly mild, but some cases turn severe. Records came from Hebei Children's Hospital for cases treated between 2023 and 2025.

One hundred thirty-three children were split into non-severe and severe groups under current national guidance. Severe cases ran higher, longer fevers and showed more inflammation in blood tests. Two measures stood out after full statistical adjustment: a lower lymphocyte share and higher IgA antibody levels. The authors suggest these markers could help flag children at risk of worsening, pending wider confirmation.
pmc-13279658:
Nenad Filipović and colleagues published a 2026 editorial opening a journal collection on what is new in bioresorbable materials. These materials do a job inside the body and then dissolve into harmless products. They remove the need for a second operation to take out an implant. They also avoid the long-term risks of permanent foreign material. A device must stay strong for its working life. It must break down at a steady rate and yield only body-friendly products.

The collection spans electronics that degrade, magnesium implants, and polymer systems for heart and vessel use. It mixes perspective pieces with lab reports. One review covers electrodes made from metals such as magnesium, zinc, and molybdenum. Others use polymer-metal mixes, made by casting, printing, or electrospinning to meet soft tissue. The editors present a fast-moving field still short of designs that meet every need at once.
pmc-13280058:
Ewelina Wojciechowska and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a teenager whose high blood pressure traced back to an anatomical band squeezing two arteries. Median arcuate ligament syndrome usually compresses the celiac artery and causes gut symptoms such as pain and weight loss. Their patient, a 15-year-old boy, had none of those complaints. Instead he showed asymmetry between his kidneys and hypertension that stayed uncontrolled even as his amlodipine dose doubled.

Imaging revealed the ligament and the diaphragm's pillars compressing both the celiac trunk and the left renal artery, starving that kidney and driving renovascular hypertension. Surgery released the compression, restored flow in the renal artery, and normalized his blood pressure. The authors stress that this syndrome belongs on the checklist for young patients with hard-to-control hypertension and uneven kidney sizes, even without abdominal symptoms. Early decompression can prevent damage to the kidney's blood supply.
pmc-13280258:
Zhilong Li and colleagues report a 2026 lab study that tunes thulium fiber laser settings for kidney stone work. Lithotripsy uses laser pulses to break urinary stones in dust or fragments. Three parameters were varied: peak power, average power and pulse energy. A decoupling platform and fake BegoStone models let each factor shift alone. Fragmentation, dusting, heat harm and stone kick back, called retropulsion, were all scored.

High peak power with low average power and pulse energy boosted fragmentation and dusting. It also kept heat harm at the low end. Low peak power with high average power and pulse energy cut stone kick back, with no loss in fragmentation or dusting. The multilevel plan can tailor settings to stone site in the urinary tract. Personal settings may raise yield and cut risk in stone surgery.
pmc-13280458:
Carlos Enrique Calvache Benavides and team report a 2026 case of breakthrough fungus infection in a lung transplant patient. Two Aspergillus species, niger and calidoustus, caused the harm. Such fungi are uncommon causes of disease, most in people with weak immune defences. Their patient was a sixty one year old man with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a lung scar illness.

He had a one lung transplant with no early problems. Despite a preventive fungus drug, voriconazole, he developed aspergillosis in his airways. One species is hard to name, as it looks and reads like kin species in standard tests. DNA based tests proved key for exact naming in this case. Exact naming guides the fungus drug choice that can save life in transplant care.
pmc-13280558:
Sameer Lamichhane and team report a 2026 case of a penetrating neck injury, with an arrow impacted at the top of the neck. Penetrating neck injuries are rare in trauma care and need prompt, sound assessment. Selective care has replaced mandatory exploration for such trauma. Their patient was a forty one year old man with an arrow in his neck and no signs of neurological deficit.

The arrow sat in the right posterolateral neck, just behind the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at the C1 C2 vertebra level. It was freed after the entry wound was extended, and removed with a gentle move in the operating room. His post surgery course and follow ups were uneventful. Direct withdrawal in a controlled setting may suit stable patients when the object lies away from neurovascular and aerodigestive tracts, the nerve, vessel and airway paths.
pmc-13280658:
Yuanze Luo and Assam El-Osta wrote a 2026 commentary on a new cancer drug called rezatapopt. The drug targets p53, a protein that guards cells against cancer but is broken in many tumors. One broken form has a small pocket that a drug can fit into. An early trial in patients with that form showed tumors shrinking.

The authors explain why the drug fits only that one form and not others. They note that blood tests for tumor DNA could help track how well the drug works. They also flag side effects such as nausea and a need to take the drug with food. The piece frames the drug as a precise tool, not a broad cure.
pmc-13280858:
Ciera A Price and colleagues tested a battlefield leg brace in a 2026 study. In war zones, care can stretch for long hours before a wounded soldier can be moved. Broken lower leg bones are common and now call for simple splints and a stretcher. The team built a wearable frame that steadies the leg and lets the person walk. They tested two early models with medics and with users acting as the wounded.

Twenty people tried the frame on set tasks in a lab. Twelve more used it in a mock mass-casualty drill in the field. Users rated it well overall, though fit and adjustment need work. Talks with users raised themes of comfort, weight, and strength. The team plans to compare the frame with splints and refine the design.
pmc-13280958:
Candice Y Lumibao published a 2026 perspective proposing resurrection ecology as a tool for understanding how plant-microbe partnerships evolve under global change. Plants interact with microbes around roots, inside tissues, and on leaves, from harmful to helpful partnerships. The interactions feed back between ecology and evolution, but long plant generations make evolution hard to watch. Resurrection ecology revives long-dormant seeds or eggs from deposits, seed banks, or herbarium collections, growing ancestors beside descendants.

The author argues this comparison is powerful for plant-microbe questions, because both partners can be revived across time points. Microbes can alter plant growth and how strongly selection acts on plant traits during drought or warming, while plants reshape their microbes. For perennials whose microbe-mediated evolution may take centuries, dormant propagules are the only window. The piece maps where the approach can reveal these interactions' trajectory and feedback as environments shift.
pmc-13281158:
Xiaoxian Yang and colleagues linked a vitamin in food to low mood in people with fatty liver in a 2026 study. Fatty liver tied to body weight and blood sugar often comes with low mood. The team used a United States health survey from 2017 to 2020. They compared niacin, a B vitamin, in the diet with signs of depression. All who took part had the fatty liver condition. The team checked whether the link was a straight line or curved.

The link curved. Below about ten milligrams of niacin a day, more niacin went with fewer depression signs. Above that point, the link faded away. The pattern held across groups split by age, sex, and other traits. The authors say a modest amount of niacin may be a sweet spot for mood in these patients. They stress that a one-time survey cannot prove the vitamin caused the lift.
pmc-13281258:
Sara-Sophie Poethe and colleagues reprogrammed a harmless soil germ to make a useful drug-like compound in a 2026 study. The compound can kill drug-proof germs, which are a rising health threat. Making it with germs could be cleaner than making it in a chemical plant. The team started with a germ strain that already made a related compound in surplus. They added genes from other germs and from a silkworm moth, hunting for the best mix.

The moth gene won, giving a clear yield of the target compound. Tuning the food broth, with urea and an amino acid as key parts, lifted yield further. Balancing the two added genes more than doubled the final amount. The tuned broth also raised yields of two sister compounds. With an extra feed, the germ made a new variant never made this way before.
pmc-13281358:
Leo Goldstein and colleagues compared wrist bones in cats and small dogs in a 2026 study. The wrist, or carpus, is a small joint with seven bones and many ligaments. Cat wrist injuries are hard to treat, and proof to guide care is scarce. The team scanned eighty wrist joints from twenty cats and twenty toy breed dogs. Fine scans measured the spongy bone inside, its struts, spacing, and outer shell.

All the bones held spongy bone at their core. Cats had fewer but thicker struts than the small dogs. Their struts sat farther apart as well. Cats also packed more bone into each joint and wore a thicker outer shell. The authors say these built-in gaps matter when vets judge a cat's wrist injury. Care plans borrowed from dogs may not fit cats.
pmc-13281758:
Youyun Shi and colleagues tested a blood ratio as a survival clue in stomach cancer in a 2026 study. The ratio pairs an enzyme that rises with cell damage against albumin, a blood protein that falls with poor nutrition. The team looked back at five hundred sixty-eight patients whose stomach cancers were cut out at one hospital. Patients were split into low- and high-ratio groups. The team compared survival and hunted for factors that stood on their own.

On its own, the ratio did not predict survival across the whole group. Body weight index did, with higher values guarding survival. Cancer stage and drug care before surgery each worsened the outlook. In a simpler look, the high-ratio group lived shorter lives overall. That gap showed most clearly in stage two cancer. The authors call the stage hint a lead for larger, forward-looking studies.
pmc-13281858:
Ori Daniel Belson and colleagues tracked referral shifts to a brain and eye clinic in a 2026 study. The clinic, at a large Israeli hospital, treats nerve and vision problems that overlap. The team read first-visit records from two three-year spans a decade apart. The early span ran from 2007 to 2009, with about fourteen hundred patients. The later span, 2017 to 2019, held more than two thousand. Sources, ages, complaints, and final diagnoses were compared.

Later patients were older on average. Eye doctors and child doctors sent far more patients in the later span. Nerve doctors and rehab specialists sent fewer. Vision change complaints and double vision diagnoses both rose. Two diagnoses grew in weight after age and sex checks: pressure buildup in the skull, and tumors pressing on vision paths. The authors say demand for this niche care is growing and aging.
pmc-13282058:
Arman Bahmani and co-authors describe three 2026 cases of lichen planus affecting the oesophagus, the tube that carries food to the stomach. Lichen planus is an inflammatory condition, meaning body tissues become swollen and sore, better known on skin and in the mouth. In the food tube it is rare and often missed, since its signs overlap with other causes. All three patients had trouble swallowing and pain on swallowing.

Camera exams showed peeling lining, sores, and narrowings of the tube. Tissue tests were not conclusive, though they fit a lichen-like pattern of injury. Usual acid-blocking drugs helped little. All three tried swallowed steroid creams meant to coat the tube. Two gained little relief, and one needed repeated stretching of the tube plus feeding support. The authors call for wider awareness and for standard treatment plans, which do not yet exist for this condition.
pmc-13282258:
Risa Fukuda and co-authors wrote a 2026 cohort study comparing a moisturiser cream and petroleum jelly on the skin barrier in adults with and without eczema. Eczema, here atopic dermatitis, weakens the outer skin layer and lowers natural moisture factors. Twelve adults without eczema and twelve with it applied each product to a different forearm daily for twenty-eight days. A light-based method measured water, fats, and acids in the outer skin layer.

Twenty-three people finished the study. The cream raised a key skin fat, ceramide, in both groups, mainly in upper layers. It also raised lactic acid and skin hydration in the eczema group. Petroleum jelly raised ceramide across layers only in the non-eczema group and did not lift hydration in eczema skin. The authors judge moisturisers better suited than plain jelly for repairing this barrier problem.
pmc-13282358: Zheng Fang wrote a 2026 mathematics paper on the Elephant Random Walk, a model of movement with memory. Conditioning on the first steps acts as training. When the walker is set to stand at a matching position after those steps, Fang measures the first return time to the origin. In the diffusive regime that time follows a power law set by the memory parameter. In the critical regime it grows exponentially. Fang reads it as how fast the walker forgets its training.
pmc-13282458:
Jie Li and co-authors present a 2026 study building an immune-inflammation score to predict outcomes in head and neck cancer. This cancer group varies hugely in outlook and in its tumour microenvironment, the mix of cells around the tumour. The team combined gene network analysis with immune and inflammation gene sets across three patient cohorts. They compared machine learning methods to build the most robust score.

A random survival forest model won, and its score predicted survival in all cohorts. High scores meant worse survival and held up as an independent warning sign. Scores tracked with immune cell patterns, checkpoint molecules that tumours use to evade attack, and mutation profiles. pmc-13283258:

pmc-13283858:

pmc-13283958:

pmc-13284058:

pmc-13284458:

pmc-13284558:

pmc-13284758:
Debashish Nayak and Samarjit Bisoyi reported in 2026 a rare trauma case combining a torn ascending aorta with a broken breastbone. pmc-13285358:

pmc-13285458:

pmc-13285558:

pmc-13285658:

Some microbe waste goods, above all pyocyanin, dim the glow that oxygen sensors read, skewing results in biofilm work. pmc-13286158:

pmc-13286758:

pmc-13286958:

pmc-13287058:

pmc-13287158:

pmc-13287458:

pmc-13288858:

pmc-13292658:

pmc-13292858:

pmc-13293258:
