Cuts in the strand the guide reads suppressed activity to degrees set by position, while cuts in the opposite strand boosted it. Applying those rules produced an activator pair that detected a microRNA at attomolar levels, roughly four hundred eighty times more sensitive than an intact activator. The boost enabled profiling of five microRNAs inside living cells for machine learning classification of cancer cells, and the trick extended to an enzyme and a chemical target as well.
pmc-13394458:
Lanhao Qin heads a 2026 team that built an eye-inspired chip for spotting motion, modelled on birds of prey. Drops of oil in a raptor retina focus light, and the chip copies that trick with gold cores wrapped in a mineral shell. The shell turns light into hot charge carriers with great speed. A full wafer held a grid of 32 by 32 sensing points.

Every point in the grid worked, with small spread between them. The array answered in just over two milliseconds and stored light levels in five-bit steps. After brief training it named motion direction with near-perfect scores. The authors pitch the chip for cars, traffic watch, and guard systems.
pmc-13394558:
Anastasios Makris leads a 2026 twin study of breath holding, asking how much genes shape the skill. People vary widely in how long they can hold breath with the face in cold water. Twelve identical and ten non-identical twin pairs each did five longest-possible holds. The team compared pairs to split gene effects from shared home effects.

Genes explained most of the spread in hold time and in blood pressure rises. They also explained much of the spread in lung size. For heart rate and some flow measures, the maths needed for a firm split did not hold. The authors stress that heritability is about spread, not fate.
pmc-13394858:
Yaxiang Jia and colleagues review, in 2026, virtual reality exercise for children and teens with autism. Beyond social traits, many young people with autism struggle with planning skills and movement. The team gathered fifteen studies with 439 youths who did active games, motion-sensing training, or augmented reality exercise. Nine studies fed into pooled maths.

Pooled results point to gains in planning and self-control skills. Proof grade was moderate, though the range of true effects crossed zero. Effects on social behaviour and repeated behaviours were mixed across the few studies that checked. Movement gains are covered in the full review. The authors call for larger, more alike trials.
pmc-13394958:
Anpei Li and others test a SETD2 block to boost a menin drug in MLL-fusion blood cancer in a 2026 study. SETD2, a gene-marking enzyme, has played a two-faced role in this blood cancer, curbing tumors when lost yet marking grim odds when raised high.

Gene typing of lost SETD2 marked it as a half-dose tumor curb, while SETD2 and menin blocks joined forces to kill cells, halt growth, ripen cells, and drive cell death. SETD2 block made cells keen for menin block by cutting H3K36me3 marks. The paper backs a drug pair for a blood cancer that spurns most cures.
pmc-13395258:
Tianya Liu, Ji Wu, and Ivan Steenstra test, in 2026, how sharing blame with AI shapes doctors' judgement. Ninety-six doctors worked ten case puzzles in a mock clinic. Each group got a different rule for who answers for errors: the doctor fully, both equally, a shifting split, or no AI at all. Only the rule changed between groups.

The shifting split won clearly, lifting accuracy and trimming overconfidence. Full blame on the doctor added nothing over the control group. Equal sharing hinted at worse accuracy and clearly worse confidence balance. The authors say who carries the risk changes how closely doctors check AI advice. Design of blame rules is part of safe AI use.
pmc-13395358:
Rebecca Pabst and co-authors build, in 2026, a trait-based forecast of which mosquitoes may invade new lands. Only a few species have spread so far, but invasions have sped up with world trade. The team logged 26 traits for 184 species of medical concern. Forest models linked traits to the odds of travel and of settling after arrival.

Species from Asia and Australia scored as most likely movers. Love of human-made breeding sites, heavy rain zones, and harsh heat also raised the odds. The models flagged 24 fresh species as likely travellers, and 17 of those as likely settlers too. The authors urge guards to watch the flagged list first.
pmc-13395458:
Elena Spinetti and co-authors model, in 2026, how a cell stress sensor grabs unfolded proteins. The sensor, IRE1, sits in the cell's folding workshop and fires a rescue program under strain. No clear picture showed it touching unfolded chains directly. The team ran long atom-level simulations of the sensor's sensing part.

The sensor's head did grip unfolded protein bits in two pockets at its centre. Those grips could steady larger sensor clusters that switch the program on. A helper named BiP was also shown blocking the cluster face, which keeps the sensor quiet in calm times. The model settles clashing past claims, the authors say. It maps the first step of the stress alarm.
pmc-13396058:
Hanie Raufi and others review CDK9 as a drug target in blood cancers in a 2026 paper. CDK9 drives gene copying stretch-out, feeding short-lived cancer genes and anti-death proteins, and its wild activity shows up in blood cancer, marrow cancer, and big B-cell lymphoma.

Inside the P-TEFb crew, CDK9 tags RNA polymerase II and histones, keeping cancer programs on and breeding drug spurn. Blocking CDK9 hits cancer cells' need for fast gene copying. The review tours first drug blocks and the snag of hitting a cell engine used all over the body with care.
pmc-13396558:
Sercan Özkaçmaz and co-authors asked whether a liver cyst's density, read from a CT scan, can separate two look-alikes. One is a harmless simple cyst; the other is a hydatid cyst, a parasitic sac that needs different care. Their 2026 study tackles a real diagnostic knot, since the two look nearly identical on scans.

Cysts were included only when the diagnosis was settled by tissue tests, blood tests, or the look of the removed sac. Density was measured in Hounsfield units on contrast-enhanced scans for 51 hydatid cysts and 36 simple ones, and the averages compared. A clean density cutoff would spare patients extra tests and steer surgeons correctly before anyone operates.
pmc-13396658:
Xing and co-authors explain, in 2026, why formamidinium perovskite solar cells decay, tracing the damage to the interface where the working alpha phase meets the inert delta phase. Their microscopy and diffraction work shows the boundary between the alpha phase's 011 plane and the delta phase's 110 plane carries tensile strain. That makes it the active site where the alpha-to-delta transformation ignites and spreads.

Acting on that mechanism, they seeded the perovskite with two-dimensional perovskitoid material that bonds preferentially to the delta phase's 110 plane, forming a strained 2D-delta interface with 4.24 percent lattice mismatch in the reported analysis. The large strain scrambles delta-phase orientation and blocks formation of the dangerous alpha-delta boundaries. Cells built this way reached 25.61 percent efficiency, and unencapsulated devices kept 90 percent of their initial efficiency after 1,000 hours at 70 percent relative humidity. The authors offer the interface rule as a universal stabilization strategy.
pmc-13396858:
Enrico Prajiante Bertolino and co-authors report a ruptured, infected aortic aneurysm caused by a bacterium better known in horses, in a 2026 case report with a literature review. Streptococcus equi rarely infects people, and an infected aneurysm seeded by it is rarer still, as well as often fatal.

A 72-year-old man had emergency open surgery: the diseased aorta was rebuilt in place with a polyester tube graft soaked in the antibiotic rifampin, with a ready-made branch for the kidney artery. A false aneurysm later bulged at the upper join, and cultures from surgery grew the horse bacterium. He left hospital on long-term antibiotics meant to suppress any remnant.
pmc-13397658:
Brian Otaalo and others gauge antibiotic prescribing rightness among people with HIV in a Ugandan outpatient clinic in a 2026 study. Sub-Saharan Africa bears high antimicrobial resistance driven by wrong antibiotic use, yet outpatient prescribing data for HIV patients were thin.

Reviewing prescriptions from 2016 to 2022 across general, urgent care, and tuberculosis clinics, the team judged rightness by noted indication, drug, dose, frequency, and duration against national guidance. The audit counts where prescribing strays and why. Stewardship programs gain a baseline for guarding antibiotics in HIV care across Ugandan outpatient clinics.
pmc-13398158:
Qorinah Estiningtyas Sakilah Adnani and co-authors examine why involving local stakeholders in global health research so often falls flat. Their 2026 viewpoint draws on published work and experience inside a multinational respiratory research programme. Funders increasingly demand engagement, especially in low- and middle-income countries, yet what it looks like on the ground is rarely inspected.

Structural limits, fuzzy ethics, power gaps and cultural mismatches can hollow out the exercise until it becomes theatre. The authors argue engagement only turns real when it is reflective, properly funded and backed by institutions over the long term. Flexible models fitted to each setting, they say, serve communities better than a tick-box shaped far away.
pmc-13398758:
Yu Zhang and colleagues let an AI evolve dye molecules that glow in the second near-infrared window. Their 2026 study builds the AI4NIR-II pipeline, joining quantum chemistry calculations, transformer prediction models and generative design. Such dyes (glowing between 1,000 and 1,700 nm) pierce tissue deeply with little background haze, prized for imaging and light therapy, but finding them by hand is slow trial and error.

Starting from two fragment families, the model trained on about 16,000 molecules with computed absorption and emission values. It then proposed, scored and refined new candidates in rounds, a self-driven loop needing far less bench work. The authors present the loop as a template for smart molecule hunting generally.
pmc-13399158:
Amy M Kemp reports the first year of BRAIN-FIT in 2026, a community program offering brain-health screening outside clinics in mid-sized cities and nearby rural areas. Rural adults often face long distances and few specialists when they want checks that might catch dementia risk early. The program brings a single-day, many-domain screening to trusted local sites, staffed largely by supervised students from several health professions.

Across 7 sites in 3 cities, 18 events enrolled 163 adults. Of these, 119 joined the longer study with a full screening day, and 95 percent finished every station. Screening commonly turned up raised cardiometabolic measures, weaker physical endurance, poor sleep, and hearing or vision problems. Thinking and language scores mostly stayed in the functional range. Sixty-three participants answered a follow-up survey four weeks later about behavior changes. Kemp presents the model as a workable way to flag changeable risk before serious decline sets in.
pmc-13399358:
Nanako Tomioka and co-authors used a large Japanese longitudinal study to test whether social capital protects older adults against oral frailty, in a 2026 analysis. Oral frailty, a decline in chewing, swallowing, and remaining teeth, threatens nutrition and independence. The data came from the Japan Gerontological Evaluation Study, with 31,378 community-dwelling older adults assessed in 2019 and again in 2022.

Over the three years, 21.6 percent of participants developed oral frailty risk by the study's predictive model. The share was higher among lower-income participants, 24.6 percent, than among the better-off, at 19.9 percent. Higher individual social capital, social cohesion, and civic participation each came with lower odds of oral frailty across income groups. Community-level civic participation also helped, and its protective association ran stronger for lower-income participants, a statistically significant interaction. The authors suggest that encouraging social participation could narrow the income gap in oral health among older adults.
pmc-13399558:
Gu and Xu present a study from twenty twenty-six on white noise plus coaching for new mothers with late milk onset. The study reviews one hundred twenty first-time mothers at one hospital. Half got standard breastfeeding guidance alone over four weeks. The other half got the same guidance plus white noise sessions. The team compare feeding rates, latch scores, anxiety, and milk measures. Baby stress and growth are tracked as well. After care, the combined group shows a higher exclusive breastfeeding rate.

The combined group also scores better on latch and milk onset speed. Anxiety in mothers and stress in babies run lower in that group. Babies gain more in weight, length, and head size by four weeks. The authors back the low-cost add-on for wards.
pmc-13399858:
Siddharth Padmanabhan and co-authors present a repair for radial tears of the meniscus that adds the patient's own fibrin clot as biological mortar, in a 2026 technique paper. A fibrin clot, made from the patient's blood on the back table, carries platelets and growth signals into exactly that dead zone at almost no cost.

Thirty milliliters of blood are drawn and left to clot undisturbed for seven minutes, then stirred with a textured glass rod until a firm clot forms. It is trimmed, lassoed with braided suture, and delivered into the tear through a cut-down pediatric endotracheal tube used as a cannula. The tear is then closed with polydioxanone sutures in horizontal and vertical mattress passes arranged as a hashtag, or ripstop, grid that resists pulling through. The authors pitch the method as low-complexity biological insurance for any high-risk meniscus repair.
pmc-13400158: The notice is a correction only. It amends a 2023 Cell Reports Medicine article by Ori Fridlich and colleagues on where cell-free DNA in blood after exercise comes from. In Figure 1C, the pie chart for Runner 1 at rest was accidentally duplicated from Runner 2. The corrected figure carries the right chart, and the legend to Figure 1D is also corrected. The authors state the data were always correct and no conclusion changes.
pmc-13400458:
Falastine Das, Susmita Parashar and Aparna Kulkarni review, in 2026, how high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy affect heart health in mothers and their children for years afterward. These disorders affect about one in ten pregnancies worldwide and remain a leading cause of harm around birth.

Mothers face a much higher chance of lasting high blood pressure within two years, plus later heart failure, coronary disease and stroke. Children exposed in the womb also carry higher adult risks. Shared genes, womb programming and lasting immune changes may explain the pattern. The authors call for checks starting right after birth, lifelong follow-up and care plans that treat mother and child together.
pmc-13400658:
A Prkić and colleagues report, in 2026, Dutch registry data on radiocapitellar arthroplasty, a partial elbow replacement for damage on the radial side of the joint. The option suits cases too severe for keyhole surgery but not needing a total elbow replacement. Published evidence on it is thin.

The national register held just 33 such operations performed between 2014 and 2024, followed for a median of over six years. Nine needed revision surgery, most often because the radial part loosened within three years. Wear after injury was the top reason for the first operation, and half the patients had prior elbow surgery. Estimated ten-year survival was sixty percent. The authors urge careful counseling and trial-based use.
pmc-13401158:
Santosh Jayant and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on how biotechnology has been folded into modern medicine and pathology. It spans gene-based testing and multi-omics, digital pathology, and computing tools for health data. The technologies support disease detection, drug development, and day-to-day care decisions.

Across the review, the authors trace how molecular biology, nanotechnology, and computing changed the study of gene variation, marker proteins, and tumor diversity. It also changed the study of immune pathways in cancer, inherited disorders, infections, heart disease, and autoimmune illness. They also cover gene editing, nano-scale drug carriers, immune-based therapy, biologics, and targeted drug delivery. These tools can hit tissues more precisely and cause less off-target harm. The piece gives readers a broad map of where these tools now sit in routine care.
pmc-13401458:
Li, Dohan, and Abramson argue, in 2026, that time deepens inequality for terminal cancer patients. They draw on 196 in-depth interviews with 96 patients, plus five years of fieldwork across nine cancer clinics, with patients approaching the end of life. Their concept is time misalignment: the clash between when patients can act and when systems, employers, families, and bureaucracies allow action to happen, which sorts agency among the well-off.

Patients had to triage colliding demands of treatment, work, family, and paperwork schedules. They reconcile disease trajectories with official timetables that assume different speeds, and anchor today's decisions in a future they could plan for, one that cancer keeps dissolving. The authors name three forms: schedule conflict, trajectory mismatch, and anticipation uncertainty. Advantaged patients found this labor resource-draining and goal-displacing as disease advanced. The analysis, combining fieldwork with correspondence analysis, reframes time as a ruptured relation between agency and context.
pmc-13402258:
Glória M C Lacerda and co-authors give the first genetic portrait of Micropleura vazi, a worm parasite of caimans in Brazil, alongside fresh detail on the female body. Earlier accounts of the species left gaps and disagreements, and no gene data existed at all, partly because the worms are hard to collect. Their hosts here were Caiman yacare, a South American crocodilian.

Under light and scanning electron microscopes the team found features never reported in this species, including phasmids and esophageal gland nuclei, and fixed the true position of the vulva. Gene reads from the 18S and 28S regions supported Micropleura as one natural group and placed its family as sister to the guinea worm family. Their trees also argue that another family, Philonematidae, stands valid and apart. No males turned up, which the authors link to seasonal timing seen in related worms.
pmc-13403358:
Ziqian Wu and colleagues pair an early ultrasound warning sign with a learning-based forecasting model to predict liver graft fate after transplant. Early allograft dysfunction is hard to spot, and long-term event-free survival is harder. Their first analysis tested hepatic artery ultrasound measures taken within four days of surgery. The second built prediction models from ultrasound image features gathered at six time points, using a Vision Transformer against a classic radiomics rival.

An artery resistive index below 0.55 soon after surgery linked to early dysfunction. Its negative predictive value of 92.2 percent made it a strong rule-out. The transformer nomogram predicted three-year event-free survival with accuracy scores of 0.951 in training and 0.831 in outside validation, edging the best clinical model. The authors require prospective testing before clinical use.
pmc-13403458:
Emma Torbica headed a 2026 lab study on why semen may help the mpox virus spread during sex. Fluid from several donors made the virus far better at entering skin and fiber cells. The boost also held for other pox viruses and for virus taken from patients.

The cause traced to tiny fiber clumps built from semen protein pieces. Those fibers helped virus stick to cells and get inside. A small tool molecule that breaks the fibers removed the boost. Two current mpox drugs still worked under the boosted conditions. The findings name a fresh target for blocking spread.
pmc-13403758:
Vindhya Prakash, Nishanth S, and Kashish Goyal told in 2026 of a man whose pierced eye hid its own wound. A stone strike left the 58-year-old with pain, redness, watering, and sudden sight loss in one eye. A leak test came back negative, and no torn tissue showed at first look.

One clue stood out: a lone air bubble sat inside the front of the eye. That bubble hinted the surface wound had opened, then sealed itself shut. Quick surgery restored the globe's shape and steadied the eye. Clinicians should treat such a bubble as a warning, even when leak tests pass.
pmc-13403858:
Yiming Su and eight co-authors report a way to grow a rare class of immune cells in bulk for cancer care, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. The cells, called V-delta-1 T cells, can kill tumor cells but are scarce in blood and hard to expand. The team used a custom antibody plus a mix of growth signals to multiply them.

From a small blood sample they grew about ten billion pure cells, far past what store-bought methods yield. The cells kept a youthful form and killed tumor cells better than a sister cell type. They also shrugged off the lactic acid that builds up in tumors. A guard protein called PARP1 helped them do so. Versions fitted with lab-built receptors also shrank tumors in mice. The authors pitch them as an off-the-shelf cancer therapy.
pmc-13404858:
J Jane Pillow and colleagues present CIRCA DIEM, a 2026 protocol testing day-night light and sound cycles for very early babies. Infants born before 32 weeks lose the mother's body-clock signals at birth. Intensive care units usually keep light and noise steady around the clock, which may disturb brain development.

Across Australasian centres, 868 infants will be assigned to cycled conditions or routine unit care until discharge home. Babies in the cycle group wear eye masks and ear plugs from 8 in the evening to 6 in the morning. The main question is whether thinking skills at age two improve under the cycle. Assessors who score the children will not know each child's group.
pmc-13407758:
Kathryn C. Collins and co-authors test, in 2026, whether brain-stimulation measurements give the same answer twice in healthy adults. Magnetic brain stimulation gauges how excitable the brain-to-muscle pathway is. Clinicians lean on its readings. The study enrolled 51 neurologically intact adults. Each repeated an identical session five to seven days later. Arm and hand muscles on both sides were tested.

Judged strictly, nothing measured was reliable enough: every index, from motor threshold to response size, latency, silent period, and recruitment curves, had a confidence range dipping below the acceptable line. One measure, active threshold in the non-dominant biceps, came closest. Average differences between sessions were small, but the spread around them was wide, and the change needed to count as real varied by muscle. The authors counsel caution in interpreting single readings.
pmc-13407858:
Rebecca Blue and co-authors review the infection record of NASA's health program for astronauts in a 2026 study. Before flight, crew members enter quarantine, show proof of vaccination and immunity, use protective gear, and train with their support staff. The goal is to stop illness before launch and in orbit, where care is limited.

The team gathered records from US missions from the Apollo era through 2024. They counted cases where a breach, a slip in protocol, or an exposure during the health period led to crew illness. In the large set of missions they reviewed, they judged how often such events occurred and what raised the risk. The findings test whether decades of strict routine have worked, and where the routine still leaks.
pmc-13408058:
Chumin Ni and co-authors build, in 2026, a smarter funnel for finding hidden diabetes in heart patients. People with coronary heart disease carry high rates of undiagnosed diabetes. Standard fasting glucose and HbA1c miss cases that only a glucose tolerance test catches. The team therefore analysed national survey data on 287 heart patients and 8,904 controls without known diabetes.

Newly found diabetes was 3.4 times more prevalent in heart patients, 22.1 against 6.5 percent. Standard screening missed exactly half of the heart patients' diabetes, all recoverable by tolerance testing. Adding serum albumin to the two standard markers produced a model with strong discrimination, and it reclassified risk meaningfully better than the standard pair. The authors propose albumin-enhanced triage to aim the burdensome tolerance test where it pays.
pmc-13408158:
Matevž Rumpret and a large team describe in 2026 how a common streptococcal bacterium disarms antibody-driven defence. Their focus is LILRB3, a restraining receptor found in large amounts on neutrophils, the white blood cells that swallow and kill bacteria. The bacterium involved is Streptococcus agalactiae, a cause of serious infection in newborns and older adults.

Laboratory work showed that a surface protein of the bacterium binds LILRB3 and clusters it, which then dampens the signals that normally trigger a respiratory burst and bacterial killing. Strains carrying this trait belong to lineages linked with invasive disease in older adults. For readers, the study names a concrete evasion trick and suggests why infections can take hold when antibody responses weaken with age or illness.
pmc-13408358:
Zheng-Yuan Zhang, Han-Chao Chen, and a large team demonstrate in 2026 the quantum Zeno effect acting on a single atom's movement through space. The effect says frequent measurement can freeze a quantum system's evolution, though it had rarely been watched in an atom's actual position. The group used an optical trap as a repeated measurement pulse and tracked atom loss.

Measurements held back the spreading of the atom's quantum state, and the team mapped how pulse frequency, strength, and position change the outcome. Varying the protocol prepared distinct motion states on demand. Moving the trap during measurement even carried the atom in a chosen direction faster than gentle adiabatic dragging allows. Cold-atom researchers gain a measurement-based toolkit for engineering atomic motion.
pmc-13409558:
Cristina Benites and co-authors gather in 2026 every reported case of an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour inside the jawbone, thirteen in all, and add a fourteenth of their own. These tumours mix spindle cells with inflammatory infiltrate, grow slowly, and mimic cancer on scans despite being benign, with a habit of returning locally. Their new patient is a fifteen-year-old girl.

Her tumour was removed and the jaw rebuilt in the same operation using the approach nicknamed jaw in a day, restoring normal mouth function with no recurrence at one year. Across the reviewed cases, complete surgical removal likewise produced favourable outcomes. The authors detail the imaging features. They name the look-alike diagnoses pathologists must exclude, and the molecular markers that secure the identification. Oral surgeons gain a compact reference for a tumour most will never see.
pmc-13411158:
Yiming Liu and co-authors survey in 2026 how nanotechnology might calm the misdirected immune attack behind Sjögren's syndrome. The disease dries eyes and mouth as immune cells invade tear and saliva glands. Today's care mostly eases symptoms or damps the whole immune system, without repairing glands.

The battleground is the local immune neighborhood: gland cells, immune cells, signal proteins, and stray lymph tissue. Tiny carriers can aim drugs squarely at that neighborhood. Platforms covered include polymer and fat particles, mineral particles, body-mimicking shells, and gels. Goals stretch beyond quieting inflammation toward restoring immune tolerance and regrowing working glands, with smart, computer-designed carriers flagged as the next wave.
pmc-13411358:
Peng-Yu Chen and co-workers test in 2026 a sponge-derived compound against aggressive mouth cancer cells. Oral squamous cell carcinoma spreads readily and ends poorly for many patients. The compound, stellettin B, comes from the marine sponge Jaspis stellifera.

In two cancer cell lines the compound halted growth while sparing normal mouth lining cells. Death came mainly through a backup route: two DNA-cutting proteins moved from the cell's power stations into the nucleus after damage, bypassing the usual executioner enzymes. Spread slowed as cell identity markers flipped back toward a settled, less mobile state. Gene scans also showed quieter growth signaling. Early dish results mark the compound as a candidate worth animal testing.
pmc-13415558:
Uri Bright and colleagues run the largest genetic study yet of fibromyalgia, in 2026. Their genome wide search combined cohorts holding 85,139 cases and over 1.6 million controls across European, African, and Latin American ancestry groups. Extra power came from borrowing related pain study data in a multi-trait analysis.

Ten loci linked to fibromyalgia in European ancestry participants, one in African ancestry, and twelve across ancestries. Most loci were already tied to pain, thinking, autoimmunity, or general health. Genetic overlap ran strong with chronic pain, post-traumatic stress, and depression, each at correlation levels near or above 0.69. Modeling placed fibromyalgia mainly among pain and autoimmune traits, with nerve mechanisms underneath.
pmc-13415658:
Michelle Juknaviciute Laursen and colleagues dissect how the human lipid flippase ATP8B1 switches itself off, in 2026. Flippases move fats between membrane layers to keep cell surfaces asymmetric. Many carry tail extensions that brake their own activity, and this team tested tail pieces as synthetic peptides against a shortened enzyme.

The far end of the tail proved key, likely touching the enzyme's inner domains in passing. One contact pair stood out: an arginine in the tail binding a glutamate in the moving A domain. A short peptide spanning just thirteen tail residues was enough to inhibit the enzyme. Faults in this flippase cause a liver disease, so activation strategies matter.
pmc-13415758:
Mathou and colleagues compare the brains of four shrimp species at hydrothermal vents, asking how nervous systems adapt to darkness, pressure, and plumes. Vent shrimps occupy niches around the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, from dense swarms to loners farther out. Their 2026 study uses tissue staining, antibody markers, micro CT scans, and 3D rebuilds. It maps the brain and its blood supply in the four vent species, plus a coastal relative.

All vent species shared a brain with mushroom bodies, hubs where senses merge and memories form, outsized for their build. Their visual centers shrank against the coastal shrimp's, fitting the near dark, while the retina stretched along the back, longest in swarm formers. A visual satellite center was missing in vent species, hinting they barely track motion. Smell lobes kept one layout but varied in size and count by species, matching each niche's chemistry and diet.
pmc-13417858:
Sanchit Mehta and co-authors trace a fatal course of methotrexate poisoning in a 64 year old with lymphoma, in a 2026 case report. The chemotherapy drug had been tolerated before, yet prior heart damage from anthracycline treatment changed its handling. After infusion for brain directed therapy, the patient developed kidney shutdown, low blood pressure, and shock.

Drug levels stayed extremely high despite an antidote enzyme and dialysis. Fluid around the lung held a large drug store, a third space trap that kept leaking drug back into the blood. Clearance took 35 days of continuous dialysis, and the patient moved to comfort care. Heart failure is flagged as a key risk.
pmc-13418458:
Chail Shah and colleagues reviewed in 2026 a lethal overlap syndrome that strikes intensive-care patients on cancer immunotherapy. Checkpoint drugs can unleash a triple attack resembling myasthenia gravis plus muscle inflammation plus heart muscle inflammation, mimicking sepsis, pneumonia, clots, and heart failure at first glance.

Early antibody tests and heart imaging often look normal, so the review urges fast multi-system checks with muscle enzymes, serial troponins, heart tracings, and imaging, alongside infection screening and prompt drug withdrawal. Critical-care teams gain a structured rescue path for a syndrome where hours and missed heart inflammation decide survival.
pmc-13418558:
Preeti Sinha and a large team run a pilot trial of probiotics added to standard care for depression in older adults, published in 2026. Fifty eight patients aged 60 or more with moderate unipolar depression were randomised at two centres to daily probiotics or placebo for 12 weeks, with 12 more weeks of follow up. The strains were Lactobacillus helveticus and Bifidobacterium longum.

Depression and anxiety scores improved over time in both groups, with modestly lower overall scores in the probiotic group, though change patterns did not differ significantly. Quality of life rose in both groups equally. A brain growth factor rose higher with probiotics. Over half the participants dropped out, limiting conclusions.
pmc-13418758:
Felix Seelemeyer and colleagues weigh reusable against single-use flexible scopes for bladder checks in outpatient urology. Their 2026 study comes from a German center that performs 337 of these checks each year, many for bladder cancer follow-up. The team counted the full cost of each route, from purchase and repairs to cleaning and staff time.

Cost models covered both a basic setup and full gear replacement, with break-even points worked out for each. A survey added the views of 13 physicians and 25 nursing staff across five practices, scored on set scales. Staff rated both scope types on image quality, handling, and daily workflow fit. The paired cost and user data give clinics a grounded way to choose between the two systems for routine work.
pmc-13419958:
Fang-Hui Zhu and colleagues pool studies comparing catheter valve replacement in patients born with a two-leaflet aortic valve against the usual three-leaflet form. The two-leaflet form is a major cause of valve narrowing, yet trial proof for the catheter route in these patients stayed thin. Their search covered four major databases for studies with one-year outcomes.

The pool held 31 studies and 192,691 patients in total, a very large base for this question. Death from any cause at one year ran lower in the two-leaflet group, with pooled odds of 0.84 in the reported model, while heart-related death showed no firm gap between groups. Safety and benefit profiles otherwise looked alike. The results ease fears that the catheter method suits only standard valve anatomy.
pmc-13420258:
Mu Qin and colleagues build a tiny drug carrier that releases its cargo in acid, aimed at retinoblastoma, the main eye cancer of childhood. Care for this cancer is hampered by the blood-retina barrier, drug resistance, and harsh side effects on the whole body. Their carrier wraps the repurposed drug nitazoxanide inside a metal-framework shell that breaks down where tissue turns acidic.

The particles loaded drug to roughly 58.6 percent of their mass in the reported figure and measured near 231 nanometers across, a size suited to reaching tumor tissue. pmc-13421358:

pmc-13421458:

pmc-13421758:

pmc-13422358:

pmc-13422858:

pmc-13423158:

pmc-13423958:

pmc-13425458:

pmc-13425958:

pmc-13426058:

pmc-13426358:

Interest has surged in compounds that can tune this node for disease prevention and treatment.

pmc-13427458:

pmc-13427658:

pmc-13427858:

pmc-13428158:

pmc-13428258:

pmc-13430858:

pmc-13431858:

pmc-13432858:

pmc-13432958:

pmc-13434558:

pmc-13434658:

pmc-13434758:

pmc-13435258:

pmc-13435758:

pmc-13436558:

pmc-13437658:

pmc-13437958:

pmc-13439058:

pmc-13439358:

pmc-13439558:

pmc-13439758:

pmc-13440458:

pmc-13440758:

pmc-13441158:

pmc-13444258:

pmc-13445958:

pmc-13446358:

pmc-13447058:

pmc-13447158:

pmc-13447358:

pmc-13447558:

pmc-13447858:

pmc-13448658:

pmc-13448858:

pmc-13454258:

pmc-13457958:

Detection strength also swung by bacterial species, warning labs that method choice alone can redraw a microbiome portrait.
pmc-13487958:
Binsong Liu and colleagues chart polycystic ovary syndrome across low- and middle-income countries in a 2026 analysis of Global Burden of Disease estimates from 1990 to 2023. The hormone condition affects fertility, weight, and long-term health. Figures covered prevalence, new cases, and years of healthy life lost among people aged ten to fifty-four in 131 countries, grouped by national income.

Those countries held more than seventy percent of global cases. Burden rose over the period and tracked partly with income per person, while many differences stayed unexplained. Onset peaked in the teenage years everywhere. Projections to 2050 suggest a falling overall burden, with lower-middle-income countries moving the other way, a split planners should note.
pmc-13488058:
Hang Liu and colleagues combine hormone and gene data to explain egg laying in a local chicken breed in a 2026 multi-omics study. Birds from a self-bred white-feathered, green-shelled line were split into high and low layers by egg count at forty-three weeks. Brain, pituitary gland, and ovary tissue, the three levels of the hormone axis that controls reproduction, were sampled for gene activity and steroid hormone measures.

Three steroid hormones differed between the groups, including progesterone and estradiol. Gene changes numbered in the hundreds in the brain and far fewer in the ovary, clustering in signaling, hormone making, and nerve communication. Network analysis nominated twenty-five candidate genes. The authors offer the map for breeding more productive local hens.
pmc-13488158:
Xinguang Jin and colleagues ask whether fully exposing the parathyroid glands during thyroid surgery protects their long-term function in a 2026 prospective study. The tiny glands control blood calcium and are easily damaged when the thyroid and nearby lymph nodes are removed for cancer. One surgeon treated 133 patients, grouped by whether all four glands were found and exposed during the operation.

No patient in the fully exposed group developed permanent gland failure, while two patients in the other group showed lasting low function on blood tests. Average hormone levels ran higher in the exposed group over six months of follow-up. Glands were also reimplanted more often when fully exposed, a step that can rescue a gland at risk.
pmc-13488458:
Melanie Orlando and co-authors reveal the structure of a bacterial protein that both moves nutrients and sends signals, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. The protein governs carbon use, slime growth, and harm traits in a Pseudomonas germ. How it senses one key nutrient and passes the signal on was unclear.

A frozen microscopy structure shows how the nutrient binds in the transport part. A small partner peptide sat in a stable grip on that part, though it was not needed for growth on the nutrient. Computer motion studies showed how a proton gradient drives the shape shifts that move the nutrient.
pmc-13490358:
Yavuz Ekincioglu and co-authors design a new compound aimed at the BRAF protein in lung cancer in a 2026 chemistry and modeling study. The molecule joins pyrimidine and imidazole rings to a thiosemicarbazone unit, a sulfur-bearing group known for anticancer activity. Computer docking placed the compound snugly in the BRAF enzyme pocket, touching eight key amino acid sites in the reported model. In dish tests it slowed a lung cancer cell line meaningfully at the highest dose tried. Drug-likeness screening passed standard oral drug rules. The authors present it as a lead scaffold needing much further work.
pmc-13490458:
Tangelapalli and team used deep learning to estimate wireless channels in massive MIMO networks, the many-antenna systems behind modern mobile coverage. Every antenna pair's channel must be measured with pilot signals, but pilots eat airtime, and nearby cells foul each other's pilots. Their 2026 study trained fully linked and convolutional networks to infer channel values from a minimal set of pilot symbols, testing against two standard methods.

The learning method produced lower gauging error than both least-squares and minimum mean-square standard methods across the cases modeled. Its advantage persisted when pilot cross-talk and cross-cell cross-talk were dialed up, the exact situations that break standard math. Fully linked networks carried the strongest results in the multi-cell scenarios reported. Tangelapalli concludes learned methods can trim pilot overhead while honing the channel knowledge that beam shaping depends on.
pmc-13490858:
Svoboda and a large plant science team in Austria studied in 2026 how the fungus Fusarium graminearum attacks wheat. The fungus causes head blight, a ear rot disease, and it makes both toxins and auxin, a plant growth hormone. In sick plants of a weak wheat type, auxin levels rose far above normal. The fungus, they found, can split plant defence compounds built from tryptamine, a step that frees the tryptamine for reuse. Seven fungal genes for copper amine oxidase enzymes, which drive the next step, were knocked out one by one. The strain that lacked all seven made much less auxin in lab tests and spread far less well in wheat. Its output of the toxin deoxynivalenol, though, stayed the same as the normal strain.
pmc-13491758:
Gilbert Ti-enkawol Nachinab, John Ndebugri Alem, and George Bernard Coffie survey in 2026 how nurses at Bolgatanga Regional Hospital in Ghana understand and follow workplace safety rules. Nurses in low-resource hospitals face sharper exposure to infection and injury, so the team questioned 136 nurses drawn at random from five hospital units. Scores measured knowledge, attitudes, and everyday practice on a four-point scale.

Nearly all nurses scored high on knowledge, and four in five held positive attitudes toward safety measures. Practice told a different story, with fewer than one in three showing good safety habits. Education level separated scores in all three domains, and the three scores rose and fell together. The authors recommend refresher training, written protocols, and monitoring systems from hospital management and regulators.
pmc-13491958:
Jiaquan Mao and eight co-authors review in 2026 how nanoparticles could force cancer cells into three newly recognized forms of regulated death. Tumors survive by dodging cell death, which also breeds drug resistance and spread. Disulfidptosis collapses cells under sugar starvation, anoikis kills cells that lose their anchoring, and PANoptosis blends three death programs into an inflammatory cascade that can rally immunity.

Small-molecule triggers for these pathways suffer from off-target harm and poor delivery, so engineered nanoparticles aim the dose at tumors and release it on cue. The review pairs each death pathway with matching nano strategies and with combinations alongside chemotherapy, radiation, immune therapy, light, and sound treatments. Remaining hurdles include targeting precision, managing the inflammation these deaths provoke, and personalizing the approach.
pmc-13492858:
Kartikawati and colleagues present a 2026 case study of how accreditation improved child nutrition services at an Indonesian residential care home in Karawang, West Java. Before accreditation, meals were irregular and unmonitored, and several children risked malnutrition. The accreditation process forced concrete reforms at this home for children who live away from family care.

The home wrote standard procedures for nutrition, planned meals against national guidelines, began routine body measurements of the children, and required caregiver training. Afterward, services ran consistently, monitoring was in place, and fewer children were at risk of malnutrition. Training also raised caregiver accountability, the authors note. One home's story cannot prove a national policy, but it shows the mechanism by which paperwork standards become fuller plates: procedures, planning, measurement, and trained staff.
pmc-13493858:
Pandey, Kumar, and Bisht study perfect optical vortices, ring-shaped laser beams whose radius is supposed to stay fixed no matter how much twist the beam carries. That twist is called topological charge. The stability makes the rings attractive for microscopy and for trapping tiny objects, but real generators distort them. The 2026 team used a programmable phase device to create the beams, then added angular unevenness around the ring and watched the shapes change across many charges.

Without distortion, tidy single rings survived only at moderate charges; stronger twists broke into multiple Bessel-like rings and the radius crept upward. Moderate unevenness ironically cleaned the beams up, merging the extra rings into one open ring with adjustable lopsidedness. Under extreme unevenness every charge produced look-alike rings, and intensity-only measurements could no longer tell the charges apart.
pmc-13494158:
Sturgeon and a large team investigate why severely malnourished children keep dying even after hospital care. They focus on a damaged gut lining that lets bacterial products leak into the blood. Their 2026 substudy enrolled 264 children with complicated severe malnutrition at hospitals in Zimbabwe and Zambia. It measured gut leakiness with a two-sugar urine test, plus bacterial toxin and inflammation markers, from admission through a year after discharge, against 173 well-nourished neighbourhood children.

On admission, the malnourished children's guts were about two and a half times leakier than the controls' on the sugar test. Leakiness stayed abnormal long after discharge. Higher leakiness travelled with stronger inflammation and, crucially, with greater risk of death and hospital readmission during follow-up. The authors argue the leaky gut is not a side detail but a driver of the well-known post-discharge death toll.
pmc-13495158:
Yun-Sheng Chen and co-authors profile, in a 2026 study, the mental and mood symptoms of Parkinson's disease in a Taiwanese group, with a focus on sex differences and test quality. Symptoms are common in the disease yet often missed or unevenly measured. The team enrolled 92 patients and 57 healthy peers and ran a battery of movement, thinking, and mood checks.

About a third of patients had dementia and a quarter had depression. Women scored lower on thinking tests and higher on depression and behavior scales than men, marking a heavier burden. Doctor-run thinking tests caught ninety percent of dementia cases, while a caregiver-rated scale caught only a quarter. A doctor-rated mood scale likewise beat a self-report one for depression. Most scores tracked with age, disease length, and movement severity. The authors urge routine, sex-aware mental checks in Parkinson's care.
pmc-13498458:
Riya Mercy Jacob and Jaico K Paulose examine in 2026 how common social anxiety and low self-esteem are among medical students in Kerala, India, and whether the two travel together. Medical training brings heavy study pressure and frequent public judgement, which can feed fear of social situations. The authors surveyed students at one medical college hospital over a period spanning 2019 to 2021.

Of 600 eligible students, 507 replied, and standard scales measured social anxiety and self-esteem with set cut-off scores. About two in five students met the threshold for social anxiety, and about one in four had low self-esteem, which was strongly linked to anxiety even after accounting for gender. Women were more likely to report low self-esteem, and most students traced symptom onset to their late teens.
pmc-13499158:
Gijs Aertssen and co-authors report in 2026 how long replacement hip and knee joints last in people with inherited bleeding disorders. Joint replacement relieves pain from joint damage caused by repeated bleeding, yet surgery in this group has long carried extra risk. Using routine care data from one centre spanning 1989 to 2025, the team measured survival of the implant until a first revision operation.

The series covered 128 knee replacements and 64 hip replacements. Knee implants survived at rates close to general population figures even 25 years on. Hip implants held up well at 15 years and dipped lower by 25 years in a small remaining group. Joint infection predicted knee implant failure and occurred more often in patients with treatment inhibitors, while one hip stem fixing method predicted hip failure in older patients.
pmc-13499758:
Jorge F Máspero leads a 2026 registry report describing patients who start dupilumab for asthma in everyday practice. The antibody drug blocks signals driving type 2 inflammation, and enrolment spans Latin America, the Middle East, Russia, and Singapore. Trials had already shown benefit in moderate to severe asthma, yet real-world starters needed characterising. Of 376 enrolled patients, most were women and most had never smoked, with an average age near the late forties in the reported figures. Most sat at the highest treatment steps for asthma severity and averaged two severe flare-ups in the prior year. Allergic rhinitis and chronic sinus disease with nasal polyps were each reported by well over half, and blood markers of type 2 inflammation ran high, painting a heavily burdened group.
pmc-13500458:
Ondrej Klicnik and co-authors present in 2026 a compact method for steadying photon polarisation in satellite quantum key distribution, a technology that uses quantum signals to share encryption keys. Air turbulence and satellite motion constantly twist polarisation, which corrupts the entanglement the keys rely on, so twisting must be measured and corrected before detection. Their system uses liquid-crystal plates that adjust polarisation electrically, guided by a bright classical beacon beam travelling the same path as the quantum signal.

A liquid-crystal polarimeter estimated polarisation well from few measurements, balancing speed against precision, and crystal switching speed proved a key design constraint for real-time use. Simulations of an entanglement-based protocol showed only a moderate rise in error rate from measurement slips, staying within secure key limits. The authors pitch the approach as a practical fit for satellite hardware.
pmc-13501658:
Yasushi Umezaki leads a seven-author team reporting a 2026 study of a paper-based game tool in an obstetrics and gynaecology clerkship at Saga University in Japan. Learning on clinical rotations varies with whichever cases happen to appear, and digital gamification can be hard to run on busy wards. The quasi-experimental study covered 102 fifth-year students between October 2023 and September 2024. Fifty-two students used a stamp rally card listing 20 observable clinical tasks mapped to clerkship competencies, each stamped after an instructor verified it; fifty followed the conventional rotation.

The stamp group reported higher satisfaction, sense of achievement, self-efficacy, and self-directed learning on the study's rating scales. Their documented task completion reached 92.3 percent against 75.9 percent for the comparison group in the reported averages. Short-term written examination scores were also higher, at 85.0 against 78.2 on the test's scale. Students said the card clarified expectations and made progress visible.
pmc-13501858:
Shashikant leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 hospital study of a blood marker in cervical cancer at a centre in Indore, India. Vascular endothelial growth factor, VEGF, drives the new blood vessels tumours need, so its blood level might betray tumour burden. Over twelve months the pathology department enrolled fifty diagnosed, untreated patients whose cancer was confirmed by tissue examination. Serum VEGF was measured by ELISA, and levels were set against tumour grade, type, and clinical and tissue features.

Levels ran above normal across the group, averaging 670.89 picograms per millilitre. The marker climbed as tumour grade rose, tying it to how aggressive the cancer looked under the microscope. No clear link appeared with the histological type of tumour. The authors propose serum VEGF as a non-invasive prognostic aid for sorting patients by severity and watching treatment response, while calling for larger studies to confirm the role.
pmc-13502358:
Karen R Morin reports a 2026 case examining why some aid in dying deaths take far longer than expected. The patient, a 66-year-old woman left with one-sided weakness by a stroke, had refused medical care for years. She had untreated skin cancers, minimal fluid intake, severe malnutrition, and one bowel movement a month. Every offered bowel aid, from softeners to enemas, was declined. She qualified for aid in dying on terminal illness and capacity, and entered hospice.

Aid-in-dying drugs must be swallowed and absorbed through the gut, so a sluggish bowel and an empty, wasted body threaten the five-drug oral protocol. Her death after ingestion was prolonged. Morin argues assessment protocols catalogue risks such as poor gut function well but describe behavioural patterns, like chronic refusal that builds constipation and immobility, far less thoroughly. Screening, the report urges, should weigh the patient's habits alongside the chart.
pmc-13503458:
Naomi Feldheim and three co-authors study the zeros of a class of random functions on the complex plane in this 2026 paper. The functions keep the same law under twisted shifts linked to the Weyl-Heisenberg group. The class covers Gaussian entire functions and many cases that are not analytic, where winding numbers can be plus or minus.

The team proves that the charged zero count, which weights each zero by its winding number, always spreads in a hyperuniform way. Its variance grows only with the radius of the disk, not with the area. They also give a case where the plain zero count fails that test. For signal work, counts of spectrogram zeros stay close to their mean over large windows, while counts of maxima do not.
pmc-13503658:
Unnati Vaghela and four co-authors report a 2026 breeding study in brinjal, the eggplant grown across South Asia. Yield varies a great deal from cross to cross and from place to place. The team set out to find parent plants that pass on high yield and to map how alike the parents are in their genes.

Pairings of twelve female lines with four male lines yielded 48 hybrids, grown at three sites. Four parents stood out for passing on high fruit yield per plant. Three crosses paired well for yield in their own right. Gene markers grouped the sixteen parents into three clusters. The most unlike pair sat far apart, which hints at strong hybrid vigor if they are crossed.
pmc-13503958:

Thirteen patients with new gut cancers had both the new scan and standard contrast CT. Both scans found every main tumor. At the level of single spread sites, the new scan was more sensitive overall, catching ten sites the CT missed, most in the belly lining and its folds. CT caught two sites the new scan missed. In one patient the new scan found hidden belly spread, which raised the stage and changed care.
pmc-13504058:
Yujie Li, Yunwei Wei, and Yangjun Li build machine learning models to predict when colorectal cancer spreads to the liver, in a 2026 study. The liver is the top site for such spread, and early warning lets doctors stage and treat patients with more care.

Records for more than 41,000 patients came from a U.S. cancer registry, split into training and test sets. Eight models learned from eleven clinical facts; about seven in a hundred patients had liver spread. A gradient boosting model scored best in testing. On outside hospital data its score fell but stayed useful. Weight analysis named a blood marker and the two spread stages of the tumor as the top inputs. The team built an online calculator for clinic use.
pmc-13504758:
Jehad F. AlSamhori leads a team surveying how shift patterns affect health workers in Jordan, in a 2026 study. Round-the-clock care leans on night shifts, which strain sleep, thinking, and mood. Workers may lean on stimulants to stay alert, which adds its own risks.

The survey drew 445 staff from four hospitals, with most on night shifts. Night workers reported far more fatigue, headaches, and tremors than day workers. Memory and learning problems were also more common in that group. Caffeine and stimulant use ran higher at night. Depression scores sat in the mild range and anxiety in the moderate range overall. Links between mood symptoms and body or thinking complaints were stronger among night staff. The authors urge targeted support for night teams.
pmc-13505058:
Berrin Bilgiç and three colleagues grade how three chatbots answer common questions about ADHD, in a 2026 study. Twenty-two questions drawn from public sources went to ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek in fresh sessions. Two child psychiatry specialists scored each answer, and repeat rounds on other days tested steadiness. All three scored high on accuracy, led by ChatGPT at about 91 percent. Gemini and DeepSeek did better on basics and diagnosis, while ChatGPT led on treatment and outlook. The authors back the tools as support, never as a stand-in for a clinician.
pmc-13505158:

All care sat inside a fast-recovery pathway, and the judges of tube placement quality were kept unaware of group assignment.

After exclusions, 130 patients were analysed, and every breathing tube was placed successfully. Acceptable placement conditions were near universal in all three groups, with no clear differences between them. Surgical working space, recovery times, and hospital stay also matched across groups. Early pain scores and one inflammation marker ran higher in the continuous-relaxant group in exploratory checks. The authors say lower exposure looks workable under careful, standardised conditions, while calling for trials that add precise muscle monitoring.
pmc-13507158:

The spacer also pins each bit through interface coupling, which aids heat stability. Signals were read from a bit about four nanometers wide, and field flips wrote binary values on demand. pmc-13507358:

Liver, lung, brain, and heart samples all resolved cellular and subcellular detail. AI segmentation handled the huge image volumes. Biobank archives become a resource for nanoscale anatomy.
pmc-13507758:
Taeyeong Kim and five co-authors trace how a drug-resistant germ recycles pieces of its own cell wall, in work published in 2026. Lab tests confirmed that the enzyme binds directly to that outer section of AmpG1. Cells missing AmpG1 built up wall fragments, ran short on a key building block, and grew in odd shapes. They also became more sensitive to a major class of antibiotics. The work shows that coupling wall cutting to import keeps the recycling line fed.
pmc-13508258:
Eva Kajti and four co-authors test whether structured teaching at discharge speeds recovery after heart surgery, in 2026 work. Recovery and quality of life were scored with standard questionnaires before and after, with phone follow-up over twelve weeks.

Patients who received the teaching scored higher on recovery quality than the control group. Their quality of life scores were also higher after surgery. For busy wards, the study gives trial evidence that time spent teaching patients pays back in smoother recovery.
pmc-13508358:
Wanhua Zhang, Xinyi Zi, Manjun Zhang, and Weina Zhang report a 7-year-old girl whose belly pain turned out to be a calcium crisis from a parathyroid tumor, in a 2026 case report. Such tumors are exceptionally rare in young children and usually cause thirst or tiredness instead. The girl arrived with colicky pain and repeated vomiting that mimicked appendicitis. Doctors first tamed the calcium with fluids, a water pill, and two targeted drugs. Surgery then removed the overactive gland. The team notes that this surgery can normalize blood chemistry and protect bones from lasting harm. pmc-13508458:

Those pathways push the guide cells to stir up helper T cells in a harmful pattern. A licorice-derived compound blocked both pathways and nudged the guide cells toward a calming form. pmc-13510258:
Łukasz Bojkowski, Vivian de Oliveira, and António Fernando Boleto Rosado examine problematic internet use, self-esteem, and well-being among athletes, in 2026 work. The authors urge coaches to treat self-esteem as one modest factor among many, not a master key.
pmc-13510458:

Music's mood shaped brain responses to both word kinds in the data. Concrete words felt music's pull across several stages of processing. Abstract words showed the music effect mainly at a late stage. The pattern fits the idea that ideas lean on context for feeling. Music may thus prime language in stage-by-stage different ways. Brain waves were sorted into early, middle, and late processing stages.
pmc-13510758:

The study followed 200 women aged twenty to forty, split by cycle day at placement, all treated by one doctor with one technique.

Pain scores ran far lower in the mid-cycle group than in the early group. Bleeding during placement was also lower mid-cycle, with most women showing little or none, against a far smaller share in the early group. Later outcomes, including painkiller use and bleeding pattern, were tracked as well. The authors say mid-cycle timing may ease the visit and lift acceptance of the method.
pmc-13512758:
Massey and co-authors published a 2026 cross-sectional study called Find Your Float, on drowning risk in people of African, Caribbean, and Asian heritage. Massey reports eighty-nine of them floated successfully for the full two minutes. Body fat percentage correlated strongly with buoyancy in the group's measurements. The authors back community based, jointly designed practice sessions alongside existing safety campaigns to close the equity gap.
pmc-13515958:

Each circuit showed its own exponent, yet the values held steady. Spread across a wider heat range, the supposed scatter formed a clear pattern. Feeding the measured exponent into the standard heat analysis produced a strikingly steady lifetime relation and a much smaller true activation energy. Part of the accepted energy value, he suggests, was an artefact of ignoring how the exponent drifts with heat. pmc-13516758:
Dula and colleagues assessed how well maternal health nurses in southern Mozambique handle two obstetric emergencies, severe pre-eclampsia and bleeding before birth, in 2026 health workforce research. Of 191 participants, most were mid-level nurses, averaging 33 years of age across the sample. On the survey day, 82.7 percent had provided prenatal consultations, yet only about half knew the national standards for those visits. Just 44.5 percent scored above 50 percentage points on the competency measure used in the study. Dula argues the gap between daily practice and tested emergency skill is wide. Training and supervision, the authors suggest, need to target the emergencies most likely to kill mothers.
pmc-13517258:

Arsenic and cadmium answered fast and shared a core stress-and-detox programme by one day. Their flavours differed: arsenic leaned toward membrane transport and immune signalling, cadmium toward protein quality control. Vanadium and uranium kept quiet early, then developed their own signatures by twenty-four hours, vanadium touching transport and cell division, uranium touching RNA splicing and cell-death signals. Schilz's team concludes that shared pathways explain common kidney harm, while each metal's private signature shapes its particular risk profile.
pmc-13518458:

pmc-13518858:

In 68 patients, the team captured nerve-derived vesicles from serum and measured their protein cargo. Higher levels of clumped alpha-synuclein, the protein that aggregates in Parkinson's, tracked with worse total non-motor scores, hallucinations, and attention or memory problems. Other vesicle proteins linked to mood-related severity. Meloni and colleagues present clumped alpha-synuclein as a candidate marker needing follow-up over time.
pmc-13519258:
Lorena Diniz Macedo Silva Maia and colleagues compared teaching methods in 2026 at an elementary school. Lessons covered diseases that pass from animals to people. pmc-13554158:

pmc-13554858:

pmc-13555058:

pmc-13555158:

pmc-13556058:

pmc-13556158:

pmc-13557858:

pmc-13559558:

pmc-13559958:

pmc-13560358:

pmc-13562358:

pmc-13562558:

pmc-13563358:

pmc-13567458:

pmc-13568458:

pmc-13570658:

pmc-13570858:

pmc-13572558:

pmc-13579858:

pmc-13580258:

pmc-13581758:

pmc-13583358:

pmc-13584058:

pmc-13584158:

pmc-13585158:

pmc-13585458:

pmc-13586358:
